title: The US is winning the AI race. Jensen Huang could have blown it
abstract: AI Tech Nvidia The US is winning the AI race. Jensen Huang could have blown it Nvidia’s chips are powering America’s AI boom. Of course Chinese spies are interested. Nvidia’s chips are powering America’s AI boom. Of course Chinese spies are interested. by Robert Hart Nov 10, 2026, 7:04 PM UTC Image: Bloomberg via Getty Images Part Of Everything we know so far about the Nvidia spy scandal targeting CEO Jensen Huang see all updates Robert Hart is a London-based reporter at The Verge covering all things AI and a Senior Tarbell Fellow. Previously, he wrote about health, science and tech for Forbes . As espionage targets go, Jensen Huang is perhaps one of the least surprising on Earth. The Nvidia CEO runs one of the world’s most valuable companies, controls the in-demand technology fueling the AI boom, and is cozy with presidents, CEOs, and all manner of important people. He also wears a cool leather jacket. Which makes Huang’s admission that he had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy — reportedly while her spying was known to US intelligence and even President Donald Trump — all the more shocking. The fallout goes well beyond his marriage, his reputation, or Nvidia itself. Experts tell The Verge the incident threatens to disrupt the entire US AI industry, potentially jeopardize national security, and could undermine America’s efforts to maintain its fragile technological lead over China in AI. “With those chips, the US lead could vanish in a matter of weeks or months.” Nvidia is the undisputed leader in advanced computer chips, among the AI industry’s scarcest resources. While many ingredients go into building AI models — including talent, energy, capital, and data — top-tier chips are one of the most important, and Nvidia is one of a handful of companies with the expertise to design or manufacture them at the cutting edge. That makes it a gatekeeper to hardware that has become a key bottleneck in global AI development. US companies — including Meta, Anthropic, and OpenAI — are racing to develop chips of their own, in part to reduce their dependence on Nvidia, even as they spend billions securing ever more compute. For China, the US’s main rival at the frontier of AI, that bottleneck is even tighter. To maintain its technological lead, the US has restricted the sale of the most advanced AI chips to the country in the hopes of slowing its progress in the sector, which has been impressive and is thought to trail the US by a matter of months. In response, China has made developing domestic alternatives a strategic national priority, though its leaders still lag Nvidia at the bleeding edge. At the same time, a thriving black market for restricted Nvidia chips has emerged. Experts tell The Verge that China could exploit access to Nvidia to accelerate its own development, or to impede the US development of AI. Getting its hands on more Nvidia chips is the most obvious win for Beijing, says Emily Kilcrease, a senior fellow and director of the energy, economics, and security program at the Center for a New American Security (CNAS) think tank. China has advantages in other parts of the AI race — including abundant energy and a solid ecosystem of open weight models — but without the latest Nvidia chips, it “cannot close the gap with US frontier capabilities,” Kilcrease tells The Verge . “With those chips, the US lead could vanish in a matter of weeks or months.” It is not clear how successful the alleged spying operation has been on that front. There is no public evidence indicating that Huang himself has helped direct restricted Nvidia chips toward China or that sensitive information about them was obtained from him. But companies linked to the alleged spy, Alice Huang — no relation to Jensen — have reportedly enabled at least $7 billion of Nvidia chip sales to China. Brookings fellow Kyle Chan tells The Verge that a concern for US industry could be that companies with alleged ties to China may have had priority access to Nvidia’s latest GPUs. “In a time of chip scarcity,” that would make it much harder for American companies to access them, Chan says. Huang is also a prominent critic of American restrictions on chip sales, and Nvidia spends a formidable amount lobbying in Washington. Last year, he successfully secured White House approval to start exporting Nvidia’s H200 AI GPU chips to “approved customers” in China and other countries. Crucially, Huang also has the ear of President Trump as well as other world leaders, giving him great influence over policy decisions. Hardware is not the only thing of value China could get from close access to Huang, Sunny Cheung, a fellow for China studies at the Jamestown Foundation think tank, tells The Verge . “I actually think too many people are focused on whether somebody managed to steal Nvidia’s trade secrets,” Cheung says, calling it a “very narrow way” of looking at espionage. “I would hope Jensen Huang isn’t foolish enough to hand over the blueprints for Nvidia’s next-generation chips to a suspected Chinese intelligence operative.” The Nvidia CEO’s relationships with other tech executives, senior policymakers, and Trump himself give him an unusually intimate view into how some of the most powerful people in the US are thinking and planning. Beijing could use information on how American companies are planning major infrastructure expansions, their compute requirements, or broad industry trends to inform its own investments and industrial strategy, Cheung says. Huang’s intelligence value could extend well beyond AI, too. “That information alone could be extremely valuable,” says Cheung, pointing to insights Beijing could glean into White House thinking about export controls or the private views of Silicon Valley executives on China and Taiwan. “When so much of America’s AI infrastructure depends on one company, any significant security or governance problem at Nvidia can create uncertainty across the industry.” But helping China advance is only one side of this equation. Disrupting Nvidia — as this scandal clearly has — could destabilize America’s entire AI industry. More than most companies, Nvidia is remarkably closely tied to the identity and reputation of its rockstar CEO. Huang cofounded the company more than three decades ago, and ever since then he has served as its president, chief executive, and a member of the board of directors. Despite holding a relatively small stake in the company, in many ways Nvidia is Jensen Huang. Nvidia shares have slumped since news of the affair broke. “When so much of America’s AI infrastructure depends on one company, any significant security or governance problem at Nvidia can create uncertainty across the industry,” Cheung says. Kilcrease echoes those concerns, warning that the scandal could “destabilize” the company. At the very least, she says the various investigations already underway “will consume an immense amount of bandwidth within the company,” creating a very real risk of weighing down Nvidia’s day-to-day operations. If those distractions begin to affect Nvidia’s ability to execute — slowing decisions, product rollouts, or the allocation of already scarce chips — the consequences could quickly reach customers. The AI labs and hyperscalers such as OpenAI and Anthropic “could have a real issue accessing the vast amounts of compute they need,” Kilcrease says, adding that switching to other hardware “takes time.” In a race to build increasingly powerful AI, time is a precious resource. Experts say China trails the US closely, meaning that even modest delays for American companies can help Chinese rivals catch up. Nvidia is almost certain to face further disruption as investigations continue, though the extent to which the turmoil will roil the rest of the industry may be difficult to measure. For China, however, the scandal could be about to backfire spectacularly now everything is out in the open.

title: ChatGPT is getting verified AI ‘Business Agents’
abstract: AI News OpenAI ChatGPT is getting verified AI ‘Business Agents’ ChatGPT’s new AI agents represent companies and can help with things like comparison shopping. ChatGPT’s new AI agents represent companies and can help with things like comparison shopping. by Jay Peters Nov 10, 2026, 6:00 PM UTC Image: OpenAI Jay Peters is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme. ChatGPT is going to let you chat with verified “Business Agents” that represent a brand to help you with things like comparison shopping. The feature, available first to “eligible” e-commerce and online service businesses in the US, is launching as part of a suite of business-focused features in ChatGPT being announced today in beta . You can start talking with a Business Agent if a business that has created one appears in a response from ChatGPT. While chatting with a custom agent, you can ask about a business’s offerings and ask follow-up questions, like asking about differences between two different products. Businesses can specify a Business Agent’s instructions and provide business context so that the agent knows how to respond. Image: OpenAI Chats with Business Agents will be clearly labeled and separate from your main ChatGPT conversation, OpenAI says. To help people know that they’re talking with an agent that actually represents the business, companies will be able to claim their organization and get verified through a feature called Business Hub. (OpenAI isn’t sharing specifics about its verification methods because there are different methods for different businesses, VP of monetization Benji Shomair said in a press briefing.) Business Hub will also let companies see insights such as mentions in ChatGPT responses and top “discovery topics” where their business pops up. “Today’s announcement is an early step in bringing businesses more deeply into ChatGPT,” OpenAI says in a blog post. “We’re starting with the foundations: accurate business information, useful insights and conversations that help people make informed decisions.” As things evolve, “we’ll explore more ways for businesses to connect with customers — directly or through agents and in ChatGPT and beyond. Our goal is to make ChatGPT more useful for people making decisions, and give businesses new ways to participate and grow.” Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates. title: The indie game community is in disarray over AI and Big Walk
abstract: Gaming AI Entertainment The indie game community is in disarray over AI and Big Walk Big Walk’s developers said that they used AI ‘sparingly’ to help work through ‘difficult technical challenges.’ Big Walk’s developers said that they used AI ‘sparingly’ to help work through ‘difficult technical challenges.’ by Jay Peters Nov 10, 2026, 5:32 PM UTC If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement. Image: Panic Jay Peters is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme. Some Independent Games Festival (IGF) jurors published a statement yesterday saying they would not vote for games that use generative AI in “any capacity.” Soon after, the developer of indie hit Big Walk has published a statement saying it “sparingly” used AI in the “final stretch” of the game’s development to “help work through difficult technical challenges and bugs.” According to the jurors’ statement , a copy of which was posted by Austin Walker, while this year’s IGF entries have been “incredible,” there has been “a significant increase” in the number of games “developed with generative AI tools,” leading to “fairly intense discussion and disagreement” with no “universal consensus.” The statement includes a list of beliefs, including that generative AI has “negative effects,” that AI-generated code is “not an exception to these harms,” and that use of AI tools is “not a forgone conclusion in our industry.” IGF jurors that signed include Telling Lies and Immortality creator Sam Barlow and Celeste composer Lena Raine . The jurors say that the statement doesn’t speak for IGF as an organization or for all IGF jury members, noting that some voiced concern about being able to safely sign “without professional blowback.” One contentious title was apparently Big Walk , the co-op adventure game from Untitled Goose Game developer House House. In a statement to Aftermath and posted on its website , House House said that “In some cases, snippets from LLM responses were copied as a starting point to be modified into game code—we’d estimate that well under 0.1% of Big Walk’s code had anything to do with this usage, and generative AI was not used in any other context when making the game.” House House said its “primary use case” of LLMs was “to research, via chatbots, issues we encountered with third-party code,” including fixing an issue with shadows by modifying LLM-suggested code. House House noted it turned to the “LLM chatbot” after researching the problem “extensively” and even speaking to an engineer at Unity. The studio said it disclosed its AI usage as part of its IGF submission, though it has not disclosed AI usage on Big Walk ’s Steam page because “the platform does not request disclosure of code or chatbot usage.” “This is not an endorsement of, or argument for, the use of AI tools, however minimal,” House House said. “We have some concern that voluntary disclosures like this might contribute to the normalisation of this technology, or its treatment as ‘inevitable’. We support the work of those who are trying to limit the harm generative AI is doing to videogames and our world, and apologise that Big Walk’s LLM usage may not meet their standards.” House House didn’t have an AI policy in place when it developed Big Walk, which it described as a “failure,” and said it will “work to have a more comprehensive policy going forwards.” Barlow said after we published this post that Big Walk was not the “impetus” for the IGF’s discussion, but it became the “tricky edge case — well what about this minimal use of AI, what about when your favorite game, or team uses it?” Barlow added that “This is not a call to boycott a certain game, or to economically hurt a team — this was about a single award’s show of many and what that award should mean to reflect our ‘indie’ alternative to mainstream and larger scale game development.” Walker also shared a long blog post that’s worth reading about his position on AI and the IGF awards. Update, November 10th : Added posts from Barlow and Walker. Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates. title: Anthropic has its own AI-powered office suite now
abstract: AI Report Anthropic Anthropic has its own AI-powered office suite now The company is courting white-collar workers ahead of its IPO. The company is courting white-collar workers ahead of its IPO. by Hayden Field Nov 10, 2026, 5:30 PM UTC Image: The Verge Hayden Field is The Verge’s senior AI reporter. An AI beat reporter for more than five years, her work has also appeared in CNBC, MIT Technology Review, Wired UK, and other outlets. For years, Anthropic has been known for its focus on enterprise and coding tools that attract high-flying corporate clients, inspiring competing frontier labs — like OpenAI, SpaceXSI, and Meta — to copy its strategies . Earlier this year, Claude Code went through its own particular hype cycle . And now, Anthropic is trying to expand its footprint to other knowledge workers with an AI-powered suite of office tools. At an event in San Francisco on Tuesday, Anthropic unveiled new tools for non-technical workers who spend a lot of time attending meetings, brainstorming new ideas, and analyzing metrics: Claude Meetings, Claude Sheets, and Claude Whiteboards. The tools allow for Claude to join a meeting, take notes, lay out ideas on a shared whiteboard, edit spreadsheets alongside employees, or turn a presentation into a one-minute explainer video. The new “Artifacts,” or Anthropic’s version of graphical UI, come two and a half years after Artifacts first debuted, and join existing tools like Claude Docs, Slides, Design and Motion. Claude Whiteboards, Sheets, and Meetings are all now available in beta, with the first two available to all paid plans and Meetings available for Teams and Enterprise subscriptions. The company also announced that Claude Data (formerly known as Claude Dashboards when it was introduced in beta in October) is now generally available to all paid plans. Image: Anthropic Nicholas Lin, who works on product at Anthropic, told The Verge in a pre-briefing that Claude Code “changed how engineers work a year ago” — and now, the company is looking to knowledge workers as “the gap we’re hoping to close.” “I think there’s still a lot of friction when it comes to adopting AI for non-developers,” he said. The company also unveiled new interactive connectors that allow for users to open apps from partnered companies, such as HubSpot, Adobe, and Atlassian, inside Claude. The company launched Model Context Protocol about two years ago, and its marketplace of tools has grown to more than 9,000 plugin options; now, Lin says, the company is looking to make those connections a lot deeper, so that users don’t have to switch tabs to access the services they use every day and instead just embed them into Claude. For example, with the new tools, people can access a native Adobe PDF editor or a HubSpot marketing campaign tracker inside Claude itself. Image: Anthropic The tools follow other AI companies’ offerings in recent years: Google’s Gemini can join meetings and take live notes, and so can OpenAI’s ChatGPT, in some cases, via its “record” feature. Gemini is also well-versed in creating spreadsheets (thanks to Google Sheets), and Google has a lot of different “interactive connectors” for its suite of office tools. At OpenAI’s DevDay last month, OpenAI leaned even further into integrated apps and connectors in order to make its new Dots agents more useful. Anthropic is following in some of their footsteps, plus trying to gain new ground in the AI agent race. The company is under a lot of pressure to generate more revenue and drive more product engagement ahead of its IPO, as it’s slated to potentially make the most valuable public debut of all time. And although that will turn heads, it also translates to a lot of pressure from investors, who want to see a viable path to profit at Anthropic. The tools Anthropic debuted on Tuesday are some of the company’s first native products for non-technical knowledge workers. Lin said that although Claude Cowork, one of the company’s other tools for non-engineers, is essentially a wrapper for Claude Code, that tool was aimed at the “technical parts of [Anthropic’s] non-technical audience,” Lin said. “Now we want to expand that reach toward everybody else.” Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates. title: eBay appears to have shut the door on third-party AI agents
abstract: Tech AI Meta eBay appears to have shut the door on third-party AI agents Silicon Valley is promising an AI agent revolution, but retailers and service providers keep blocking them.﻿ Silicon Valley is promising an AI agent revolution, but retailers and service providers keep blocking them.﻿ by Mia Sato Nov 10, 2026, 4:20 PM UTC Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge, Getty Images Mia Sato is features writer with five years of experience covering the companies that shape technology and the people who use their tools. eBay appears to have blocked AI agents, including Meta’s Muse, from browsing on the platform — the latest speed bump in the AI agent race. A reader tells The Verge that for several weeks he’s had his Muse agent browse and curate a daily digest of watches for sale on platforms like eBay, including a link to listings, price, shipping details, and relevant notes about condition or style. This weekend, though, Muse was unable to pull any links or details from eBay, with Muse saying it was blocked from the site. The Verge was able to re-create the experience using other search requests, and in some cases we found that Muse instead directed users to outside sites that mirrored eBay listings. Shopping is frequently invoked as one area where AI agents can augment or improve the human-driven experience. Technology companies tout the use of agents to book travel, find deals, and even purchase goods and services on behalf of humans. But AI agents are regularly getting blocked from accessing retailers’ sites , calling into question how useful they can really be. eBay previously updated its user agreement to ban the use of tools like “buy-for-me agents” and “LLM-driven bots” that place orders without human review. Until recently, though, agents like Muse were able to browse the site and pull listings for users. AI is becoming embedded throughout the platform for the discovery, personalization, and selling process, eBay spokesperson Sybille St. Arromand told The Verge in an email. St. Arromand declined to directly answer whether eBay recently imposed new limits on AI agents. “As it pertains to third-parties, we take a selective approach to how they access and interact with our marketplace. We have restricted agent access in certain cases, including unauthorized scraping and training on our data,” St. Arromand said. “We have ongoing discussions with potential partners and are evaluating ways third-party agents could help new customers discover eBay’s unmatched inventory, and our focus is on preserving the trusted end-to-end experience that buyers and sellers expect from eBay.” Meta declined to comment. Retailers and service providers who’ve enthusiastically added AI features to their platforms have shown varying levels of comfort with third-party agents accessing their sites. On one end of the spectrum is Amazon, which is blocking external agents entirely from browsing or shopping. Some retailers like Target have restrictions in place that allow agents to successfully browse in some instances but get blocked in others. Shopify, meanwhile, has opened its catalog of a billion listings so that shoppers can set up their agents to purchase items on their behalf . Throwing agents into the e-commerce mix has the potential to upend how people shop online, partly because retail sites are largely assuming they’re selling to humans, with human limitations, and not swarms of bots. For example, The Verge discovered in October that someone could use Muse to effectively hold product listings hostage on The RealReal, a secondhand designer consignment site, by having an agent continually add the product to the user’s cart. The RealReal updated its bot system after The Verge ’s reporting. But as retailers tweak their sites in real time to handle bots, it remains unclear how widespread agentic commerce is. In fact, there are signs that most people are not using AI this way. Uber said it fulfilled only four rides via third-party agents in Q3 and only around 500 Uber Eats orders during the week of Halloween. DoorDash similarly said it fulfilled only “several hundred” orders placed via third-party agents. It reported 993 million total orders last quarter. title: Gemini Decisions API: Fast, calibrated multimodal decisions
abstract: Gemini Decisions API: Fast, calibrated multimodal decisions Nov 11, 2026 | Introducing the Gemini Decisions API, powered by our new Gemini Decision 1 model. Evaluate up to 1,000 yes/no, choice, and rubric-scoring questions in a fast, single pass across text, images, audio, video, and PDFs. Min Choi Product Manager, Google DeepMind Felix Yu Principal Scientist, Google DeepMind Your browser does not support the audio element. Listen to article [[duration]] minutes This content is generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental Voice Speed Voice Speed 0.75X 1X 1.5X 2X Read AI-generated summary We are introducing the Gemini Decisions API to help you make fast, probabilistic choices across text, images, audio, video, and PDFs. This tool computes confidence scores for multiple questions in a single pass, providing a cost-effective way to route queries, grade content, or check policy rules. You can start building today by accessing your API key in Google AI Studio and reviewing our documentation for Python, JavaScript, and REST guides. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. Today, we’re introducing the Gemini Decisions API, a new endpoint for fast, closed-set decisions powered by our new Gemini Decision 1 model (gemini-decision-1), available through the Gemini API in Google AI Studio . The Decisions API gives you purpose-built primitives for bounded choices like tool selection, policy checks, model routing, and context grading. You can pass one multimodal input across text, images, audio, video, and PDFs (up to 256K tokens) along with up to 1,000 independent questions. Rather than generating answer text token by token, Gemini Decision 1 scores your candidate options in a single forward pass, returning probabilities and confidence scores in 150-250 ms end-to-end latency at $0.10 per 1M input tokens with zero output tokens billed. Strong performance and calibration On benchmarks spanning agent routing, reasoning, ranking, and multimodal understanding, Gemini Decision 1 leads across the suite, with the lowest calibration error. Gemini Decision 1 scores options without token-by-token decoding, keeping median latency 50-100 ms of model compute (150-250 ms end-to-end), across multimodal inputs and contexts up to 16K tokens, remaining nearly flat from 1 to 100 questions per request. With zero output tokens billed, Gemini Decision 1 with the Decisions API is nearly 5x cheaper across the shared benchmark suite than Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite with the Interactions API. Native multimodal evaluation across three decision types in one pass Built on Gemini’s native multimodal architecture, Gemini Decision 1 can process text, images, audio, video, and PDFs directly in a single forward pass. You can combine modalities in one shared input, such as pairing a call recording with account metadata or a scanned PDF claim with damage photos, and tune resolution on image and video inputs to control visual detail and token cost. You can evaluate multiple questions against that shared input in a single request, mixing yes/no checks, multiple choice, and rubric scores. Every answer includes a confidence score (from 0 to 1) so your code can route ambiguous cases to a fallback or human reviewer: noul (Yes/No): Estimates the probability that a yes/no condition holds, with optional true and false description criteria. choice (Multiple Choice): Selects from 2 to 255 choices, returning the winner and normalized probabilities for every candidate. score (Ordered Rubric): Grades inputs across an ordered rubric (starting at 0), returning a continuous weighted score and per-level probabilities. The input field uses the same Content block format as the Interactions API . Here is how to check a photo of a breakroom counter, together with a text note, against all three question types in one request: from google import genai client = genai.Client(http_options={"api_version": "v1beta"}) result = client.decisions.create( model="gemini-decision-1", input=[{ "type": "image", "uri": "https://storage.googleapis.com/generativeai-downloads/images/spill.jpg", "mime_type": "image/jpeg", }, { "type": "text", "text": "Breakroom counter check before the 9 AM client meeting.", }, ], questions={ "has_spill": { "type": "noul", "instructions": "Is there an uncleaned liquid spill on the counter?", }, "next_action": { "type": "choice", "instructions": "Which cleanup action fits the scene?", "criteria": { "wipe_with_cloth": "Small counter spill with a cloth or towel already nearby.", "dispatch_janitorial": "Large floor hazard, broken glass, or active leak.", "ready_for_meeting": "Counter is clean and ready.", }, }, "severity": { "type": "score", "instructions": "Rate the severity of the counter mess.", "criteria": [ "Clean and ready.", "Minor localized spill.", "Major spill or safety hazard.", ], }, }, ) How teams are building with the Decisions API Teams across Google are already using the Decisions API as a low-latency control plane, shipping features simply by defining options rather than training custom classifiers or waiting on generative calls: Dynamic model routing in Gemini Notebook: Gemini Notebook uses the Decisions API as a real-time router to instantly direct incoming queries to the optimal model tier and thinking level for each request. The Decisions API classifies intent in milliseconds to serve everyday queries with up to 40% lower latency while reserving deep reasoning models for complex tasks. Rapid design iteration in Stitch: The new rapid canvas experiment in Stitch uses the Decisions API to generate playable wireframes of a product flow in seconds and to apply edits made by voice or tap almost instantly. When the flow feels right, one click hands the screens off to the full Stitch experience for deeper design polish. Emoji selection in CC: CC from Google Labs uses the Decisions API to pick the right emoji reaction from a palette of more than 200 options in a fraction of a second, so reactions appear instantly without adding latency. Safety layer for MCP tools in Search : Google Search uses the Decision API to detect adversarial behavior and content against adversarial evals with high efficacy within the latency envelope. Stitch Rapid uses the Decisions API to design an entire product flow in seconds (1x speed). Start building today Gemini Decision 1 is priced at $0.10 per 1M input tokens and $0 for output tokens, with an API no-cost tier you can use in Google AI Studio for prototyping. Your shared input is billed once per request no matter how many questions you evaluate (each question adds only its own instruction and criteria tokens). There are no output-token charges, variable thinking-token bills, or separate audio transcription and OCR costs. You can start building today by grabbing an API key in Google AI Studio , trying our Doorstep Parcels , Speed Sketch , and Find the Zoo Keeper demo apps, and following the Python, JavaScript, and REST guides in the Decisions API documentation . Ecosystem integrations are rolling out across OpenRouter , LangChain , Vercel , LiteLLM , Pydantic AI , Pipecat , LiveKit , and OpenCode alongside the google-genai SDKs, with support coming soon to Gemini in Google Cloud. title: Try Tabletop: Customizable, collaborative spaces for groups to plan, play and do more together.
abstract: Try Tabletop: Customizable, collaborative spaces for groups to plan, play and do more together. Roman Nurik Design & Engineering Lead, Google Labs Nov 11, 2026 Whether you’re planning a family trip, running a rec league or hosting a potluck, coordinating as a group is easier when everyone can pitch in, build and decide together in one place. Today, we’re introducing Tabletop , a new Google Labs experiment built for real-time collaboration. Just add in your links, files, and ideas, then prompt @tabletop — or pick a starter template — to generate custom interactive trip itineraries, dinner polls, expense splitters, and tournament brackets. Once your space is ready, drop the invite link in your group chat to let everyone jump in and use it at the same time, like in a Google Doc. Tabletop is rolling out in the U.S. (18+) via waitlist. Pull up a chair and sign up at labs.google/tabletop .

title: Experience the art and legacy of Dr. Esther Mahlangu
abstract: Experience the art and legacy of Dr. Esther Mahlangu Nov 11, 2026 | Discover Google Arts & Culture's online retrospective of the South African artist, which features more than 45 curated stories, virtual tours, and her early memories brought to life with AI. Dr Nontobeko Ntombela Senior Lecturer, Department of Curatorial, Public and Visual Cultures, Wits School of Arts, University of the Witwatersrand Your browser does not support the audio element. Listen to article [[duration]] minutes This content is generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental Voice Speed Voice Speed 0.75X 1X 1.5X 2X Read AI-generated summary Dr. Nontobeko Ntombela presents the first online retrospective of artist Dr. Esther Mahlangu on Google Arts & Culture to honor her 91st birthday. This collection features over 45 stories, archival materials, and AI-generated recreations of her early life to preserve Ndebele heritage for a global audience. You can explore the full exhibition and learn more about her artistic legacy by visiting the Google Arts & Culture website. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. Dr. Nontobeko Ntombela presents the first online retrospective of artist Dr. Esther Mahlangu on Google Arts & Culture. You can explore over 45 stories, rare archival materials, and murals documenting her life and artistic legacy. We used artificial intelligence to recreate undocumented memories from her early years before her first recorded works. This project preserves Ndebele culture by combining historical research with new video technology for a global audience. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. We are celebrating artist Dr. Esther Mahlangu with a new online retrospective on Google Arts & Culture. Because some of her early history was missing, we used artificial intelligence to recreate her childhood memories based on her own stories. You can now explore over 45 exhibitions, view her murals, and learn about Ndebele culture from anywhere in the world. This project preserves her artistic legacy for you and future generations to enjoy. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. Explore other styles: General summary Bullet points Basic explainer Today we’re sharing the first online retrospective of artist Dr. Esther Mahlangu on Google Arts & Culture, honoring her pioneering spirit on her 91st birthday. More than 45 stories and a rich archive covering her art , life , and legacy are now accessible to a global audience. For many years, I have worked closely with Esther and her family. It’s a relationship built on years of research and a deep admiration for her as both an artist and a person. It was out of this long-standing connection that the vision for “‘ Then I Knew I Was Good at Painting’: Esther Mahlangu, a Retrospective ,” was born. My goal has always been to present a comprehensive exploration of her life and work, contributing to my long-standing research on South African women artists who have made an impact on the arts since the early 20th century. Through my research, I gathered a rich collection of her work, including large-scale murals , intimate pieces , and rare archival materials . But the archives didn’t include anything from her life before 1980, so crucial pieces of her history were missing. This void challenged us to find new ways to tell her full story. A collaboration session with Esther Mahlangu, Nontobeko Ntombela, and the Google team. In collaboration with Google Arts & Culture, we used AI to visually recreate Esther’s undocumented memories . The process brought us closer to her work and prompted further recollections from Esther herself. This project brought our curatorial and archival work together with the technical expertise of Google DeepMind and Google Arts & Culture Lab, alongside research and design studio Domestic Data Streamers’ synthetic memories initiative. Through a series of workshops and interviews , we were able to document a missing period of Mam' Esther's history, from when she started painting at age 10 until her first documented works in 1980. These stories — such as the moment she discovered her talent for painting as a 10-year-old using feathers instead of a brush — became the source material for our work. Following the methodology from the synthetic memories initiative and using archival material, the team generated still images based on Esther’s memories. They then used Veo to turn the images into videos that brought Esther's early days to life. The stories also contribute to the online archive of Esther’s life on Google Arts & Culture. More than 45 exhibitions , curated in collaboration with Art of Contemporary Africa, Iziko Museums of South Africa, the British Museum, the Jean Pigozzi Collection, the National Museum of Women in the Arts, and Serpentine, tell the story of how she came to be known in the world, through her artwork , archives, Street View , and more. Portrait of Esther Mahlangu taken at Botshabelo, c. 1980-1991; Art of Contemporary Africa | Source Esther Mahlangu: Untitled, 2014; Art of Contemporary Africa | Source The Esther Mahlangu Art Studio at the Esther Mahlangu Homestead, 2025; Art of Contemporary Africa | Source Installation of the Esther Mahlangu retrospective at Iziko South African National Gallery, 2024; Art of Contemporary Africa | Source Esther Mahlangu: Ndebele Abstract, 2019; Art of Contemporary Africa, courtesy of the Larry Warsh Collection | Source This project demonstrates a new way to approach the preservation of cultural heritage, with technology that’s guided at every step by a respect for personal memory and historical accuracy. It is my hope that this retrospective cements Esther’s place as a pivotal voice in global contemporary art, invites audiences to reimagine the possibilities of her archive, and ensures her story and her artistic vision can inspire generations to come. Explore the exhibition at goo.gle/esther-mahlangu . Posted in:

title: Gemini Intelligence: New features, on more devices
abstract: Gemini Intelligence: New features, on more devices Nov 10, 2026 | Gemini Intelligence is now available on more devices, including motorola signature 27 and Pixel 10. See how expanded capabilities across these devices help you do more. Karthik Thirumalai Product Director, Android AI Your browser does not support the audio element. Listen to article [[duration]] minutes This content is generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental Voice Speed Voice Speed 0.75X 1X 1.5X 2X Gemini Intelligence 1 brings the best of Gemini to Android devices, helping your devices work harder for you. Earlier this year, we announced Gemini Intelligence , and this summer devices started rolling out — from the Pixel 11 to the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra, Z Fold8, Z Flip8 and S26 series. 2 Today, we’re introducing new features built for Gemini Intelligence, and expanding capabilities to more of Android’s most advanced devices . 3 Here’s a look at what’s new. Gemini Intelligence on more devices, including motorola signature 27 and Pixel 10 Gemini Intelligence is coming to even more devices. Motorola is introducing its first Gemini Intelligence device, motorola signature 27 , which is available for pre-order in the U.S. on November 19. And with today’s Pixel Drop , Pixel 10, Pixel 10 Pro XL, and Pixel 10 Pro Fold get the latest features for Gemini Intelligence. Alongside this expansion, we’re bringing some of our favorite capabilities to more devices and regions, helping handle the busywork so you can focus on what matters. Rambler 4 — which turns spoken thoughts into clean, organized text in real-time — is now available on Pixel 10, Pixel 10 Pro, Pixel 10, Pro XL and Pixel 10 Pro Fold, as well as the new motorola signature 27. And task automation 5 — which lets you ask Gemini to handle logistics like ordering food, hailing rides, or booking reservations across your favorite apps — is expanding to the UK, India, and Japan. Build custom widgets with a prompt Create My Widget 6 , which is rolling out over the next few weeks, lets you design a personalized widget with a simple description in your own words — no coding required. Whether you want a dashboard for your upcoming trip, a monthly spending tracker, or a race day countdown, Create My Widget can pull in information from Gmail, Calendar, and Search to create a custom widget just for you, giving you the information you want at a glance on your homescreen. Get personalized tech support with Device Assistance Device Assistance 7 helps you control, change, or fix your device by just asking your phone for help. Ask Gemini to clear up space on your device, check which apps can access your location, or mute distractions while making sure important calls still come through. Gemini deeply understands your device so it can act as your personal device expert. Experience proactive help across a range of screens Gemini Intelligence is designed to support you across whatever screen you’re using. Last month we launched Googlebook , the first laptop designed for Gemini Intelligence. And if you have a Pixel phone with Gemini Intelligence, it will soon bring proactive suggestions to Android Auto — connecting the dots across your apps to surface helpful, personalized suggestions 8 when you need them. For example, if your friend texts you to ask where you are meeting for a pilates class, Gemini Intelligence on Android Auto can find your confirmation email and instantly suggest sending the address with a single tap. Plus, in the next few weeks, Create My Widget is coming to Pixel Watch. You’ll be able to design widgets that keep the details that matter to you right on your wrist. Posted in:

title: We’re bringing Adobe’s creative and productivity tools closer to your everyday Google apps.
abstract: We’re bringing Adobe’s creative and productivity tools closer to your everyday Google apps. Nov 10, 2026 Today at Adobe MAX, we announced we’re expanding our partnership with Adobe. Switching between apps to edit a PDF or fine-tune an image can quickly break your focus. Our partnership will bring Adobe’s creative and productivity tools directly into the Google products you use every day. It will also bring Google’s frontier AI models into Adobe’s apps. Here’s what’s coming: Work faster with PDFs: You’ll soon have a direct pathway from Google Drive and Gmail into Adobe Acrobat, surfaced as a suggested app across both services, including an “Edit with” entry point in file previews. Create right where you search and chat: Adobe is expanding its connectors in Gemini and Gemini Enterprise with Acrobat and additional creative tools. Adobe will also bring its creative tools to AI Mode in Google Search. Powering creatives and enterprises: Businesses will be able to use Adobe’s CX Enterprise Coworker agent in Gemini Enterprise — an AI assistant that helps teams design graphics, work with PDFs, and launch marketing campaigns without switching apps. Exploring editing experiences with DeepMind: Adobe and Google DeepMind will explore new editing capabilities for creative professionals, starting with an image model for Photoshop that could enable near-real-time edits.

title: Google Cloud launches Gemini for healthcare.
abstract: Google Cloud launches Gemini for healthcare. Nov 10, 2026 Google Cloud has announced Gemini for healthcare , an AI solution engineered to unify fragmented clinical, operational, and administrative systems. Moving beyond simple information retrieval, it enables healthcare teams to turn siloed data into coordinated action. Clinicians lose nearly 28 hours each week to paperwork and administrative tasks, fueling burnout and straining budgets. By integrating specialized skills and data connectors with existing third-party systems, the platform brings together critical information from electronic health records, billing platforms, clinical guidelines, and Medicare datasets. Gemini for healthcare reasons across this context to orchestrate and execute complex, multi-step workflows — such as medical records synthesis and prior authorization review — within defined guardrails and with appropriate human oversight. Initially available in preview alongside launch partners including HCA Healthcare, Highmark Health, and Northwell Health, it resolves bottlenecks and reclaims valuable staff time for patient care. Learn more on the Cloud blog .

title: BotPsy: On-Device Personal Assistant with a Sub-Billion-Parameter Agentic Language Model
abstract: Back to Articles BotPsy: On-Device Personal Assistant with a Sub-Billion-Parameter Agentic Language Model Team Article Published November 11, 2026 Upvote 16 +10 Milan Gritta milangritta Follow qvac Jihye Back happy-jihye Follow qvac JinUk, Cho jucho2725 Follow qvac ohjoon kwon joooon Follow qvac Patrik Lambert patrik-lambert Follow qvac Mathias Buus mafintosh Follow qvac Amril Nurman Nurman Follow qvac Frontier cloud LLMs carry high operational costs that can fluctuate unexpectedly, and relying on such third-party models introduces vulnerabilities, as providers can modify, deny, or deprecate access at any time. Furthermore, proprietary models offer limited customization for specific workflows, while posing risks to privacy, data control, and transparency. Besides, not every task demands frontier-level intelligence: small, specialized agents can be equally capable on specific tasks and significantly cheaper to run, since many routine or smaller workloads can be processed efficiently on-device. As intelligence per parameter continues to improve rapidly, we aim to stand at the forefront of this shift toward performant, privacy-focused, self-hosted models. Tether AI Research introduces BotPsy , a 0.8B-parameter model introduce BotPsy , a 0.8B-parameter model designed for function calling and agentic workflows, built on top of Qwen3.5-0.8B and suitable for on-device deployment. BotPsy is a "personal assistant" that uses tools to perform a variety of simple tasks for the user, in domains such as web search & research, travel & lifestyle, commerce & finance, business & customer operations, device & vehicle control, files & documents, calendar, and email & messaging. Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty. BotPsy achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) tool-use and agentic performance for its size, outperforming every model of up to 1.2B parameters that we tested (Figures 1 and 2). Designed for secure on-device workflows, it provides exceptional instruction-following reliability and efficiency while keeping user data private. As a small model, BotPsy still makes mistakes and is not intended for high-stakes use; please read the Intended Use and Limitations for more information. 🤗 Model (safetensors) | 📦 GGUFs (bf16, Q8, Q4) Figure 1: BotPsy-0.8B significantly outperforms its base model and leads five of the six tool-use and agentic benchmarks, including against Qwen3.5-2B-Think (2.5× its size); only on Claw-Eval does Qwen3.5-2B-Think edge ahead. Figure 2: Knowledge: tool-use training preserved and improved BotPsy's general knowledge compared to similarly sized models, though overall knowledge still scales primarily with parameter count. Instruction following: BotPsy excels at following explicit instructions and multi-turn tasks, though its performance drops as instructions accumulate and lags in lower-resource languages. Copyright Complaints We will take appropriate actions in response to notice of copyright infringement. If you believe your work has been used or copied in a manner that infringes upon your intellectual property rights, please email data-apps@tether.io identifying and describing both the copyrighted work and alleged infringing content to file a notice of infringement. Key Highlights Benchmark results Twice the performance of its base model: BotPsy roughly doubles the agentic capability of Qwen3.5-0.8B-Think on key benchmarks: BFCL v4 rises from 23.4 to 44.0, ACEBench from 30.1 to 58.7, and τ-bench from 23.2 to 51.5 (mean of the retail, telecom and banking subsets). Best agent in its category: BotPsy outperforms leading models in the ≤1.2B-parameter weight class (Qwen3.5-0.8B-Think, LFM2.5-1.2B-Think, MiniCPM5-1B-Think) on all six tool-use and agentic benchmarks: BFCL v4, ACEBench, τ-bench, ToolSandbox, Claw-Eval and BrowseComp-Plus. Outperforms its larger sibling: BotPsy has the highest score of all models tested on five of the six benchmarks, beating Qwen3.5-2B-Think, a model 2.5× its size, on BFCL v4 (44.0 vs 37.7), ACEBench (58.7 vs 55.4), τ-bench (51.5 vs 46.5), ToolSandbox (64.6 vs 41.2) and BrowseComp-Plus (4.5 vs 2.8). Only on Claw-Eval does Qwen3.5-2B-Think lead (48.9 vs 46.5). Model capabilities More reliable in multi-turn workflows: On τ²-bench, where the agent must hold a long customer conversation, follow a strict policy, and act on the customer's behalf, it scores 82.5 in telecom, ahead of Qwen3.5-2B-Think (69.3). On BFCL v4's multi-turn tasks, it rises from 7.5 to 46.1 over its base, nearly double Qwen3.5-2B-Think (23.8). Grouped by application, its multi-step scores lead all models tested in commerce and services (58.3 vs 47.4 for the next best, Qwen3.5-2B-Think) and in device and system management (46.1 vs 31.9). Knows when (not) to call tools: An agent that acts must also know when not to act. On BFCL v4's hallucination tests, which check that the model declines when no appropriate tool exists, BotPsy scores 86.1, the highest of all models tested. On ACEBench's special cases, where the request is incomplete, contains wrong parameters, or cannot be served by the given tools, it scores 51.3, up from 13.7 for its base model. Follows instructions while preserving knowledge: BotPsy specializes in tool use while preserving general skills. Instruction following improves sharply, with IFEval rising from 59.7 to 90.8 and IFBench from 22.0 to 55.9, the highest IFBench score of all models tested. General knowledge also improves, with GPQA Diamond rising from 33.2 to 38.1 and MMLU-Pro from 41.6 to 48.9. On all four benchmarks, BotPsy outperforms every other model of 1.2B parameters or fewer that we tested. Safety, efficiency and deployment Safer than leading models in its category: In automated red-teaming across six harm categories, BotPsy produces unsafe responses 21% of the time, compared with 36% for its base model. This is the lowest rate of all models of up to 1.2B parameters (LFM2.5-1.2B-Think: 35%; MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 47%). Under prompt-injection attacks, which matter most for agents that read untrusted tool outputs, the unsafe rate drops from 46% for its base model to 31%. More efficient reasoning and less looping: On questions that all five models answer correctly, BotPsy reaches the answer with about 3× fewer reasoning tokens than its base model on GPQA Diamond (3,690 vs 11,563) and 2.7× fewer on MMLU-Pro (1,912 vs 5,105). Across all IFBench attempts, its rate of getting stuck in repetitive reasoning loops falls from 22.9% to 1.4%, and runs that hit the 32k-token limit fall from 28.3% to 0.2%. Shorter, more decisive reasoning should reduce latency on-device. Open-source and ready to use: BotPsy will be released with open weights under the Apache 2.0 license for research and educational use. It will be available in three precisions (bf16, Q8, Q4), as Hugging Face safetensors and as GGUF files for the QVAC SDK and llama.cpp. Broader Vision Building upon the foundation of BotPsy, future development by Tether Data, S.A. de C.V. (“Tether AI Research”, “we”, “our”) will focus on expanding on-device agentic capabilities to seamlessly integrate with an even broader array of hardware and local services. Tether's Hypersearch will evolve to support more robust decentralized peer-to-peer (P2P) queries, further ensuring private, encrypted web searches that bypass corporate trackers. QVAC Fabric local fine-tuning mechanisms will be optimized to adapt more deeply to individual user preferences, workflows, and specialized tool environments. Future iterations will allow the smartphone interface to smoothly delegate heavy computational tasks to home PCs or trusted secure P2P nodes during offline-online transitions. Privacy protocols will be continuously strengthened to guarantee that all personal data, credentials, and decisions remain strictly on local hardware.

title: Token Pooling-Aware Training for Multi-Vector Embedding Models
abstract:
Back to Articles Token Pooling-Aware Training for Multi-Vector Embedding Models Published November 11, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 20 +14 Tom Aarsen tomaarsen Follow Multi-vector embedding models give each query token its own opportunity to find a match in a document. This makes them wonderfully expressive for search, but those document vectors add up quickly. A corpus with millions of documents can contain hundreds of millions of vectors! Token pooling makes these representations smaller by merging similar token vectors. The more aggressively I compress them, however, the easier it becomes to lose something useful. Pooling-aware training teaches the encoder to preserve the information that matters when its vectors are merged, helping you retrieve better from the same storage budget. In this post, I'll explain how pooling works, train a model for compressed retrieval with Sentence Transformers, and explore the resulting quality and storage tradeoff. With pool_factor=4 , my normally trained model retains 94.6% of its unpooled NanoBEIR nDCG@10, with a 4x reduction in document vectors. Token pooling-aware training raises that retention to 97.8% at the same storage budget! Let's see how. This post builds on pooling-aware training studied in Stefan Josef's Learn to Pool and LightOn's pooling regularization study , which also explores targeted training and adaptive budgets. Here, I'll focus on understanding the method and putting it to work with a short, reproducible Sentence Transformers example. Pooling-aware training improves retrieval quality at the same vector budget. Details below. Table of Contents Why Multi-Vector Retrieval Needs So Many Vectors Token Pooling Choosing a Pooling Budget Calibrating Adaptive Pooling Token Pooling-Aware Training A Loss Wrapper in Sentence Transformers Optional Kernel Acceleration Using the Trained Model Evaluation Results Combining Compression Techniques References Code and Models Why Multi-Vector Retrieval Needs So Many Vectors A single-vector embedding model compresses an entire document into one vector. Multi-vector models such as ColBERT instead keep a collection of contextual token vectors, allowing different parts of a query to match different parts of a document. For example, a query about a laptop with a long battery life can find evidence about the laptop in one part of a document and battery endurance in another. With MaxSim scoring, each query vector selects its best matching document vector, and those scores are added together: MaxSim ⁡ ( Q , D ) = ∑ q ∈ Q max ⁡ d ∈ D q ⊤ d \operatorname{MaxSim}(Q, D) = \sum_{q \in Q} \max_{d \in D} q^\top d MaxSim ( Q , D ) = q ∈ Q ∑ ​ d ∈ D max ​ q ⊤ d Even with the 2-bit or 4-bit residual quantization supported by Fast-PLAID , storing hundreds of vectors per document adds up. At 4 bits per residual coordinate, 200 vectors of 128 dimensions require 12.8 KB of quantized residuals per document, or 12.8 GB across a million documents. Pooling each document to 50 vectors reduces that to 3.2 GB, at the same dimensionality and precision. The useful observation is that many document vectors can be similar. Several tokens might describe closely related concepts, creating an opportunity to represent them together. Token Pooling HierarchicalTokenPooling groups similar token embeddings using Ward hierarchical clustering . Starting with one group per token vector, it repeatedly merges the two groups that cause the smallest increase in how spread out the vectors are within their groups. This spread is measured by the sum of squared distances from each vector to its group's mean, so Ward's method favors compact groups of similar vectors. These merges build a hierarchy of progressively larger groups, letting us choose a level of compression that fits our budget. We then represent each group by its mean and normalize the resulting vectors again, ready for MaxSim scoring. You can make compression proportional to document length: from sentence_transformers.multi_vector_encoder.modules import HierarchicalTokenPooling pooling = HierarchicalTokenPooling(pool_factor= 4 ) With pool_factor=4 , documents retain approximately one quarter of their original vectors, so longer documents can keep proportionally more capacity. By default, the first token is protected from merging and pooling applies only to document embeddings, leaving query embeddings unchanged. Choosing a Pooling Budget HierarchicalTokenPooling offers three alternative controls: Setting What it expresses max_tokens=16 A maximum of 16 vectors per document, including protected tokens. pool_factor=4 Approximately one quarter of each document's original vectors. distance_threshold=... A shared Ward merge-distance threshold, allowing vector counts to vary with embedding geometry. This distinction matters when document lengths vary. With pool_factor=4 , a longer document can retain approximately one quarter of its vectors, allowing its representation to grow with its content. With distance_threshold , the vector count can grow when more distinct embeddings need to be preserved. Calibrating Adaptive Pooling Adaptive pooling uses a shared distance threshold to merge similar embeddings more aggressively while preserving more vectors for documents with distinct content. It can be used with any multi-vector model, including one trained without a pooling-aware objective . Rather than choosing a threshold manually, you can calibrate it for a target average vector count. Given a representative sample of your corpus in calibration_documents : from sentence_transformers import MultiVectorEncoder from sentence_transformers.multi_vector_encoder.modules import HierarchicalTokenPooling model = MultiVectorEncoder( "lightonai/LateOn" )
calibration_embeddings = model.encode_document(calibration_documents)
threshold = HierarchicalTokenPooling.calibrate_distance_threshold(calibration_embeddings, target_tokens= 16 )
pooling = HierarchicalTokenPooling(distance_threshold=threshold) # Apply pooling, targeting an average of 16 vectors per document document_embeddings = model.encode_document(documents_to_index, token_pooling=pooling) Calibration only needs document embeddings and returns a threshold you can reuse when indexing. The target is an average, so individual documents can receive more or fewer than 16 vectors. The achieved average can also change on another corpus. Token Pooling-Aware Training Pooling can already be useful on an ordinary multi-vector model. The difficulty appears when a document contains a distinction that matters for retrieval, but merging its vectors makes that distinction harder to recover. The original training objective never required the model to work with these compressed representations. But, you can teach it to do exactly that. If you've used Matryoshka embeddings , the training principle will feel familiar. Matryoshka applies a retrieval objective at several embedding widths, teaching smaller prefixes to remain useful. Pooling-aware training applies the objective to representations with fewer token vectors. For my example, each training batch contributes two losses: Retrieval using the original document embeddings. Retrieval after compressing documents to approximately one quarter of their original vectors. I average them: L = 1 2 L u n p o o l e d + 1 2 L p o o l e d \mathcal{L} = \tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{unpooled}} + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pooled}} L = 2 1 ​ L unpooled ​ + 2 1 ​ L pooled ​ The first term teaches the model to retrieve with its full representations. The second teaches it to arrange its token embeddings so that useful matches survive pooling. Both objectives update the same encoder, giving it feedback about retrieval before and after compression. Ward clustering makes discrete decisions about which tokens belong together.

title: Pay for Hugging Face Hub with your Google Cloud Account
abstract: Back to Articles Pay for Hugging Face Hub with your Google Cloud Account Published November 10, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 12 +6 Zaïd Alhadad zaid-alhadad Follow Pierric Cistac pierric Follow Simon Pagezy pagezyhf Follow Michelle Habonneau michellehbn Follow You can now link your Hugging Face organization to your Google Cloud account, so that your Hugging Face usage shows up on your Google Cloud bill instead of being charged to a credit card. Get started on the Google Cloud Marketplace . Why pay through Google Cloud? Hugging Face is where teams find, build and run open models: from hosting private models and datasets, to running GPU workloads with Jobs , deploying models with Inference Endpoints , calling thousands of models through Inference Providers , or hosting demos on GPU Spaces . If your company already runs on Google Cloud, adding a new vendor and a corporate credit card just to use these services can slow things down. By linking your organization through the Google Cloud Marketplace: One bill : your Hugging Face usage appears on your existing Google Cloud invoice, next to the rest of your cloud spend. No new vendor to onboard : purchases go through your existing Google Cloud billing account and procurement process. Everything is covered : upgrading your org to a Team or Enterprise subscription, pay-as-you-go compute (Jobs, Inference Endpoints, Inference Providers, GPU Spaces, ZeroGPU quota extension), and additional storage at public Hugging Face pricing . If you're an admin of your Hugging Face organization, here's how to set it up, step by step. 1. Subscribe to Hugging Face on the Google Cloud Marketplace Go to the Hugging Face Hub listing on the Google Cloud Marketplace, select the Google Cloud project you want to use, and click on "Subscribe". You are now on the subscription page. Select the billing account to be charged, review and accept the terms, then click "Subscribe". Once the order is placed, Google Cloud asks you to finish setting up your account with Hugging Face. Click on "Sign up with Hugging Face" to be redirected to Hugging Face. 2. Link your Hugging Face organization You are now on Hugging Face, where you can select the organization you want to link to your Google Cloud account. Only organizations where you are an admin are listed. Select it and confirm. You are then redirected to the billing settings of your organization. The payment method section now shows the linked Google Cloud account, with a pending status. Every cloud marketplace subscription is reviewed by the Hugging Face team before paid usage starts being billed through it. While the subscription is pending, usage keeps being billed to the organization's existing payment method, if any. 3. Subscription approved Once your subscription is approved, you will receive an email confirming that your Google Cloud account and Hugging Face organization are linked. Organizations that already have a credit card on file switch to cloud marketplace billing at the start of their next billing period. Organizations on the free tier with no credit card on file usually switch immediately, so their paid usage is billed through the cloud marketplace right away. To confirm it, open the billing settings of your organization : the Google Cloud account is now shown as the organization's active payment method. Congratulations! Your organization is now billed through your Google Cloud account. All members of your organization can use Hugging Face compute services, and the usage will show up on your Google Cloud bill. A few things worth knowing: Google Cloud replaces the credit card as the organization's payment method. Usage is metered and reported to Google Cloud, so adding credits is not available while the organization is billed through the marketplace. Included credits still apply : if your organization has a Team or Enterprise subscription, the monthly included credits are applied before any pay-as-you-go usage is reported to Google Cloud. Monitor your usage at any time from the billing section of your organization settings , and find the charges in the Billing reports of the Google Cloud console. Linking and unlinking are audited : both actions are recorded in your organization's audit logs . Thanks for reading! You can find more details in the billing documentation . If you have any questions, please contact us at billing@huggingface.co .

title: Decision Models in Hugging Face
Google Launches Gemini Decisions API With Gemini Decision 1 at $0.10/M Tokens
abstract: Google has launched the Gemini Decisions API , powered by a new model, Gemini Decision 1 ( gemini-decision-1 ). The Gemini Decisions API does not generate text. It scores up to 1,000 typed questions against one shared input and returns calibrated probabilities. For developers, this targets the small branching calls inside agents: routing, policy checks, tool selection and grading. Google prices it at $0.10 per 1M input tokens, with zero output tokens billed. Gemini Decision 1 is a specialized multimodal model from Google built for closed-set decisions. It reads text, images, video, audio and PDFs in one prefill pass. Output token usage is always 0. Your code branches directly on the returned numbers. Each request has 3 parts: a model ID, a shared input , and a map of questions. The docs define 3 question types: Every answer carries a confidence value from 0 to 1. Google suggests routing low-confidence cases to a fallback or a human reviewer. Questions are scored in parallel and cannot see each other. Standard models decode an answer token by token, then your code parses it. Gemini Decision 1 instead scores your candidate options in one forward pass. Google reports median model compute of 50-100 ms and 150-250 ms end to end. That holds for inputs up to 16K tokens and stays nearly flat from 1 to 100 questions. Billing follows the same design. The shared input is billed once per request, however many questions you ask. Each question adds only its own instruction and criteria tokens. There are no thinking-token, transcription or OCR charges. Google tested Gemini Decision 1 against 3 rivals. They are TypeSafe Jev 1.14 , GPT-6 Luna on OpenAI Decisions and Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite. All figures below are self-reported by Google. Refusals and safety blocks count as incorrect. Source: Google blog benchmark table . The calibration result is the clearest gap. Gemini Decision 1’s error of 0.0250 is about half of Jev 1.14’s 0.0494. That matters when you set confidence thresholds for automation. On cost, Google says it is nearly 5x cheaper than Flash-Lite across the shared suite ($0.88 vs $4.14). The endpoint is live on the Gemini Developer API (v1beta) and needs google-genai SDK 3.2 or later. A no-cost tier is available for prototyping in Google AI Studio . Python, JavaScript and REST guides are in the documentation . Ecosystem support is rolling out across OpenRouter , LangChain , Vercel AI SDK , LiteLLM , Pydantic AI , Pipecat , LiveKit and OpenCode . Support in Gemini on Google Cloud is listed as coming soon. Google already uses it internally. Gemini Notebook routes queries to model tiers with it, serving everyday queries with up to 40% lower latency. Google Labs’ CC picks emoji reactions from more than 200 options. Stitch’s rapid canvas uses it to build playable wireframes in seconds. Check out the technical details , docs and model page . title: Google DeepMind Releases AlphaGenome 2 for Cell-Type-Specific Variant Effects
abstract: Google DeepMind has released AlphaGenome 2 , a DNA model that predicts variant effects in specific cell types. AlphaGenome 2 is a conditional sequence-to-function model. It reads 1 Mb of DNA plus a target cell state. Its predecessor averaged across bulk tissues. The new model resolves closely related cell types and adapts to unseen single-cell datasets without fine-tuning. It is available through the AlphaGenome API for non-commercial research. AlphaGenome 2 is a U-Net style model with a convolutional encoder, an 11-block transformer and a decoder. AlphaGenome 1 predicted a fixed catalog of thousands of tracks in parallel. AlphaGenome 2 instead predicts outputs for 1 condition per call. The condition is a 256-dimensional embedding. It modulates activations through FiLM layers in the encoder, transformer and decoder. Conditioning only the decoder or output layers gave minimal gains. Conditioning the encoder and transformer drove most of the improvement. Outputs cover RNA coverage, CAGE, splicing, chromatin accessibility, histone marks, TF binding and contact maps. CpG methylation is new. That encoder was trained on over 100 million human scRNA-seq profiles, largely from CELLxGENE. Researchers can pass raw counts and get a condition embedding. The docs allow up to 256 cells per call. On GTEx tissues, median Pearson r for cross-tissue expression changes rose from 0.61 to 0.71. Within tissues, explained cell-type variance rose from 23% to 34% for scRNA-seq. The main result is on TenK10K single-cell eQTLs across 28 immune cell types. At 90% precision, AlphaGenome 2 recovered 30% of causal variants. AlphaGenome 1 fine-tuned on single-cell data recovered 16%. Direction-of-effect recall rose from 23% to 43%. On held-out ENCODE-rE2G CRISPRi data, enhancer-gene AUPRC reached 0.78. AlphaGenome 1 scored 0.73, a Borzoi ensemble 0.61. The gap was widest for enhancers 100 to 2,500 kb away: 0.62 versus 0.48. For assay imputation, AlphaGenome 2 beat the Avocado baseline on 166 of 181 held-out tracks. On an unseen Parkinson’s cohort, it reached 41% recall versus 17% for cohort-tuned Scooby . *Benchmark rows come from the AlphaGenome 2 paper and are DeepMind’s own evaluation. AlphaGenome 2 and Colab tutorials are live through the API. An API key is free for non-commercial use . Commercial research is in private preview. The alphagenome Python package exposes the model under alphagenome.models.v2 . DeepMind also released precomputed atlases. One covers enhancer-gene links across 640 primary cell conditions. Another scores about 7 million common and GWAS variants across 510 conditions. Both are on the downloads page . Check out the paper , the DeepMind blog , the API docs and the GitHub repo . title: Marktechpost AI Launches GPU Leaderboard and the Deploy It Chrome Extension
abstract: Marktechpost has launched GPU Leaderboard , a free cloud GPU price comparison for AI inference. It also shipped GPU Leaderboard: Deploy It , a Chrome extension for the same data. The site reads on-demand and spot prices from each provider’s own pricing page. The goal is simple: answer “what GPU do I need, and where is it cheapest?” in one place. GPU Leaderboard is a pricing dashboard that ranks rentable cloud GPUs by price per GPU-hour. It is built for teams running inference. The v1 application has 4 views: You pick an accelerator, GPU count, duration and utilization. The calculator then prices that exact run at every provider. An optional model field narrows the list. The default example is 8×H100 for 72 hours at 90% utilization. That bills 576 GPU-hours. The cheapest result is $967.68 at Latitude, at $1.68 per GPU-hour. The median across 15 providers is $1,716.48. The most expensive is $3,545.28 at CoreWeave. The calculator also shows a “real” cost per used GPU-hour. Idle time is still billed, so $1.68 at 90% utilization becomes $1.87. This is the number most budget sheets miss. GPU Leaderboard: Deploy It brings the price data to where developers pick models. Per its store listing, it works in 3 places: Try it at gpuleaderboard.com and install the Deploy It extension from the Chrome Web Store. title: MBZUAI’s IFM Releases PAN 2, an Open 29B World Model for Physical AI
abstract: The Institute of Foundation Models (IFM) at MBZUAI released PAN 2 , an open world model for physical intelligence. The PAN 2 world model takes a scene and a text action and simulates the outcome as video. IFM announced it on X on November 10, 2026. Weights, training code and inference code ship under Apache 2.0 . For robotics and agent developers, the pitch is simple: test a plan in simulation before acting on it. PAN 2 is a general-purpose world model from IFM that simulates how a scene changes after an action. It follows the Generative Latent Prediction (GLP) architecture from IFM’s Critique of World Models paper. It succeeds PAN , released in November 2025. The goal is simulative reasoning . An agent proposes plans, PAN 2 simulates each one, and the agent acts on the best. PAN 2 splits simulation into 2 kinds of reasoning : IFM’s ablation shows the LLM matters. With no conceptual reasoning, full-plan completion drops from 34.0% to 0.0%. Step completion falls from 75.1% to 8.7%. A format-only rewrite recovers part of the gap, reaching 27.8% full-plan completion. IFM also dropped gameplay, animation and simulation footage after early training. A 9B test model trained without it won 58% of blinded votes. All numbers below are self-reported by IFM. Its own test suite covers 6 capabilities across 300 single-action cases, plus 100 multi-step tasks. *Scores from IFM’s PAN 2 model card , run by IFM. The blog reports different Cosmos 3 Super and LTX-2.5 plan scores. PAN 2 supports text-to-video and image-to-video. You can run it through Hugging Face Diffusers , vLLM , FastVideo or the repo’s generate.py . The default sampler uses 50 steps, flow shift 9 and guidance 2.5. A clip defaults to 241 frames, about 10 seconds. Each GPU worker loads the full 29B model in BF16. IFM publishes no VRAM figure or generation time. Prompts work best as structured captions. IFM ships a Conceptual Reasoner skill for Claude Code and Codex that rewrites free text. Captions have a hard budget of 1,536 tokens. IFM strongly recommends the separate pan2-guardrail . In IFM tests, it cut unsafe outputs from harmful T2V requests from 33.9% to 1.5%. It also blocked 11.5% of benign T2V requests. title: Fish Audio Releases Live 3, a Full-Duplex Voice Model That Reacts in 186 ms
abstract: Fish Audio has released Live 3 , a full-duplex voice model built for real-time voice agents. The Fish Audio Live 3 full-duplex voice model keeps listening while it speaks. That lets a caller pause, say “mm-hmm,” or change their mind without breaking the call. For developers, the pitch is simple. Turn-taking moves out of hand-tuned pipeline rules and into the speech model. Live 3 is a full-duplex voice model from Fish Audio that listens and speaks at the same time. The core argument is that speed and timing are different problems. An agent can reply fast and still speak at the wrong moment. A pause after “What time do you open?” usually ends a turn. A pause in the middle of a phone number does not. Most voice agents split recognition, reasoning, speech generation and turn-taking across separate pipeline stages. Fish Audio team states that Live 3 moves conversational timing into the speech model. It was trained on real human conversations to learn when to acknowledge, wait, respond or stop. They framed the old approach as piling on “more rules and more thresholds.” Fish Audio instead wants the model to learn timing from data. A separate reasoning layer still holds the agent’s instructions and tools. The Fish Audio team walks through 3 behaviors: Fish Audio states Live 3 can decide to respond in as little as 186 ms . That figure covers short reactions such as “mm-hmm,” “okay” and quick confirmations. The full answer is prepared in parallel. This is a floor for small reactions, not time-to-first-audio for a complete reply. Fish Audio has not published a latency distribution. Third-party tracker OrcaRouter also reports no Artificial Analysis score for Live 3 as of November 11. Live 3 is available on the Fish Agent Platform , through the Fish Audio API, and on-premises for enterprises. The Agents platform is in public beta. Agents expose a REST surface under /v1/agent/* . Browser sessions run through @fishaudio/agent-client or @fishaudio/agent-react . Agents can answer phone numbers, connect over WebRTC, or sit in a website widget. The Live 3 page lists 2,000,000+ library voices, including cloned voices. A pending docs pull request shows Live 3 enabled with voice.engine: "live3" . With it on, speech recognition is fixed to fish_audio:transcribe-stream-1 . Fish Audio’s current docs say that model also classifies overlaps as interruptions or acknowledgements. The Live 3 page lists $0.035 per minute , down 50% from $0.07 , until December 31, 2026. It says the plan includes Live 3. The pricing docs say the $0.07 list rate covers STT, TTS, basic LLMs, knowledge retrieval and tool calls. Phone calls add $0.01 per minute . A number costs $1.20 per month . New accounts get a $5 trial balance. ElevenLabs scores come from Artificial Analysis, as reported by ElevenLabs. OpenAI and Google figures are self-reported. Check out the launch post , try it at fish.audio/live3 , and see the Agents docs . title: Meta FAIR Releases e-means: An Algorithm Beating k-means in 10x Fewer Epochs
abstract: Meta FAIR researchers have released e-means , a drop-in replacement for Lloyd’s k-means algorithm. The e-means clustering algorithm reaches the loss Lloyd’s k-means gets in 25 epochs in 1.4 to 2.6 epochs . It ships in FAISS 1.16.0 under faiss.contrib.e_means . For anyone building vector indexes, quantizers or data-curation pipelines, clustering is often the slowest offline step. e-means targets exactly that step. e-means is a mini-batch k-means algorithm from Meta FAIR that updates centroids with exponential moving averages. Every k-means variant keeps a sum S and a count N per cluster. The centroid is S divided by N. Methods differ only in how S and N change. Older assignments fade, so centroids track recent data. The research team expa Lloyd is a corner case: full batch with α = 1. On DEEP, that corner sits 1.8% above the best loss. The team tested plain gradient descent as an alternative. At its best setting, it ended 1.6% (DEEP) and 0.4% (SIFT) above EMA. The authors suspect EMA wins because centroids always stay inside the hull of their assigned points. Two fitted scaling laws set batch size B and initial step α0 from dataset size n, cluster count k and epochs T. On held-out datasets, median regret was 0.07% for the step law. The step then follows a cosine schedule from α0 to 0.1α0. [EMBED: e-means interactive explainer] All numbers below are self-reported by the authors. The release thread shows a 1-CPU-thread demo. Lloyd took 4.39 s for 25 epochs. e-means took 0.43 s for 2.2 epochs. One Lloyd step touched 100,000 points (0.176 s). One e-means step touched 512 points (0.001 s). Mini-batch noise also helps escape bad local minima. On a 5-blob toy, Lloyd stayed stuck on 46% of 200 starts. e-means stayed stuck on 0%. Revival matters at large k. On DEEP with 16,384 clusters, proportional splitting left 47 dead clusters (0.3%). With revival off, 4,313 clusters (26.3%) died. Check out the paper , the blog post and the FAISS code .
