title: Zyphra Releases ZONOS3-Mini: Open-Source TTS With 100M Active Parameters
abstract: Zyphra has released ZONOS3-Mini , an open-source text-to-speech model built for real-time use on local devices. The ZONOS3-Mini text-to-speech model is a sparse Mixture of Experts (MoE) with 800M total and 100M active parameters. It supports zero-shot voice cloning and word-level delivery control. Weights ship under Apache 2.0. For AI devs, size is the key point. It runs in a browser tab, on a laptop or on a server GPU. ZONOS3-Mini is a compact zero-shot voice-cloning TTS model from Zyphra that runs in real time on-device. Zyphra trained it on 112 NVIDIA H100s in 2.5 days. It follows ZONOS2 , which used 8B parameters and an 86 Hz codec. That size limited where ZONOS2 could be deployed. Zyphra changed 3 layers of the stack : Identity controls cover age, gender, accent and voice texture through speaker embedding vectors and accent task vectors. Delivery controls cover pace, emotion, projection and liveliness through activation steering. Learned alignment heads let steering apply to specific words during streaming. A separate edit model, based on a VoiceCraft recipe, can modify sentences after generation. Zyphra evaluated the model on its new ZTTS2-Eval benchmark. It covers 35 languages of clean read speech and 20 languages of in-the-wild recordings. A Capability Index uses item response theory over 420 items. ZONOS3-Mini in speaker-embedding mode scores 66.2 on that index. Fish Audio S2 Pro scores 61.7 and MOSS-TTS v1.5 scores 60.2. On the clean set, ZONOS3-Mini posts 7.79 WER and 83.4 speaker similarity. There are caveats. Zyphra built and ran the benchmark. Reference-clip mode scores only 44.7 on the index. Its clean-set MSR-UTMOS quality score of 3.07 trails Fish S2 Pro (3.16) and Qwen3-TTS 1.7B (3.54). *From Zyphra’s ZTTS2-Eval explorer , all-language set. ZONOS3-Mini in speaker-embedding mode. Run by Zyphra, not independently verified. Latency figures use different GPUs and are not directly comparable. title: Anthropic Launches Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2: Same Model, Different Safeguards
abstract: Anthropic just released Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 . Claude Fable 5.2 is a frontier model from Anthropic for long-horizon coding, research and agentic work. Mythos 5.2 is the same underlying model with fewer cyber and biology safeguards. It beats Opus 5.5 on most evaluations and costs less than the 5.1 models. They are one model. Fable 5.2 adds classifiers that block high-risk cybersecurity tasks and most research biology. That lets Anthropic offer it to all users. Mythos 5.2 drops those blocks. Access runs through the Cyber Verification Program and the Life Sciences Verification Program . When Fable blocks a query, users get an answer from Opus 4.8 (cyber) or Opus 5 (biology). Anthropic reports about 55% fewer blocks than Fable 5.1. That splits into roughly 60% fewer in cybersecurity and 40% fewer in biology. Anthropic published one table comparing Fable 5.2 with Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra and Gemini 4 Carbon. All scores are self-reported. Key results: Fable 5.2 does not lead everywhere. Gemini 4 Carbon wins AutomationBench (53.9% vs 51.4%). Opus 5.5 holds a higher AA-Briefcase Elo (1800 vs 1785). Effort levels matter here. On FrontierCode 2.0, Fable 5.2 at High effort scored 45.3%. That matches Opus 5.5 at its best (45.5%) for roughly half the cost per task. On Humanity’s Last Exam, Fable 5.2 at Low effort matches Opus 5.5’s top score. Anthropic puts that at less than one-tenth of the cost. On Chartography, Medium effort reaches 66.4%, above Opus 5.5 at Max (64.4%). Outputs are up to 30% faster than the 5.1 models. An optional fast mode speeds generation up to 2.5x. Anthropic lists several long-running agent experiments: Anthropic tested Mythos 5.2, the version without cyber and biology safeguards. On an automated behavioral audit, it scored 2.67 (lower is better). Opus 5.5 scored 2.79. In a sandbox-escape evaluation with 1,800+ scenarios, Mythos 5.2 used out-of-sandbox credentials in 3.1% of cases. Opus 5.5 did so in 3.3%; Mythos 5.1 in 21%. Anthropic also states that it limited specific AI R&D skills during training. Kernel optimization and LLM architecture work sit at about Opus 5.5 level. Full details are in the system card . Fable 5.2 costs $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. Fast mode costs $16 and $80. The API ID is claude-fable-5-2 . It is live on the Claude Platform , AWS, Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure. Fast mode covers Claude Code, the Claude Platform, Google Cloud and Microsoft Foundry. Mythos fast mode is limited to Verification Program members. Anthropic still recommends Opus 5.5 as the daily driver. Fable is positioned for the hardest open-ended technical work. *Benchmark rows come from Anthropic’s launch table . Anthropic ran or reported these scores; they are not independently verified. title: Meta Releases Muse Ember, a 1M-Context Model for High-Volume Agent Work
abstract: Meta Superintelligence Labs has released Muse Ember , its smallest and most efficient model. Meta Muse Ember is a hosted multimodal reasoning model built for the repetitive steps inside agents. Meta lists tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction and long document parsing as targets. It scores 36 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, level with Claude Haiku 5.5 at max effort. Meta puts its cost at about $0.14 per index task. Muse Ember is a small reasoning model from Meta for high-volume agent subtasks. It is the fourth model under the Muse brand , after Spark, Glimmer and Wonder. Meta positions it below its larger models. Muse Wonder handles the hardest problems and Muse Spark covers coding and agentic workflows. Ember takes repeatable coding and agent tasks at scale. Meta’s own framing: Muse Wonder plans, Muse Ember handles the volume. Muse Ember is the first model Meta trained using Muse Wonder Full, its largest model. The model natively accepts text, images, audio and video. That lets an agent read screenshots, charts, scanned pages, voice memos and meeting recordings without a separate model. It also operates desktop apps from screenshots. The 1M-token context window fits a full codebase or document set in one call. Output runs up to 512K tokens, 4x the 128K cap on both rivals. All results below are at max reasoning effort, as reported by Meta. Some come from Artificial Analysis (AA), others from Meta’s internal suite. Muse Ember costs $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens . Cached input costs $0.004 per million. Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna list the same base rates. With identical list prices, the cost gap must come from tokens used per task. On Meta’s chart, Ember at max scores 35.8 for $0.136 per task. Haiku 5.5 at max scores 36.2 for $0.411. Luna’s best setting scores 27.8 for $0.152. Artificial Analysis summarised this as matching Haiku at a third of the cost per task. Long prompts widen the gap on paper. Haiku 5.5 charges $0.50 and $2.50 above 100K prompt tokens. GPT-6 Luna doubles input rates above 272K input tokens. Meta lists no long-context tier for Ember. *Benchmark rows as published by Meta in its launch post and evaluation report , sourced from Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 and Meta internal runs. Ember is available on the Meta Model API and in Muse Code , Meta’s coding agent. It supports the Responses API. Partners in early testing included Box, Cline, Oracle, Cloudflare and You.com. title: Where Does Abacus.AI’s Smaug Model Improve Performance the Most?
abstract: Where Does Abacus.AI’s Smaug Model Improve Performance the Most? Abacus.AI applied the same fine-tuning recipe to three very different open-weight models. The gains landed in completely different places & that tells you more than any single benchmark score. By KDnuggets on November 11, 2026 in Partners Sponsored Content TL;DR: Smaug Flash posts the line's largest jumps: +14.3 pts in agentic coding, +13.7 on AutomationBench, +19 on NL2Repo-Bench - directly targeting DeepSeek V4 Flash's failure mode in long tool-use loops. Smaug Mini (28B) beats Claude Sonnet 5, Claude Opus 4.6, and GPT-5.6 Luna on IFBench, AutomationBench, and JobBench - despite a slight dip in LiveBench agentic coding. Smaug Agentic shows the smallest score deltas (+0.3 overall) but ran 113 tasks over 7+ hours with a median of 78 agent steps and zero infrastructure errors - behavioral stability is the story, not the numbers. In all three cases, the gains concentrate where the base model's gaps were widest. Same recipe, different floors. Significance of AI Agents' Performance An AI agent could provide an output without completing the task. In real-world scenarios, there is a need for the agent to comprehend the user query, identify an appropriate tool, analyze output, and take subsequent actions. After some number of cycles, the model would veer away from the initial goal, thus compromising on the credibility of the result. It presents a problem for teams developing reliable agents. While a chatbot provides a response to a single request, an agent has to retain its context and make decisions based on related actions. With the extension of workflow, there would be additional cost implications as well as chances of mistakes. Abacus.AI experienced similar shortcomings in its own operations, with agentic tasks taking several hours to complete, maintaining a large amount of context from stage to stage, and frequently invoking tools from other documents, APIs, and databases. These operations could run out of steam or not be completed successfully at all. Abacus.AI describes its findings on its research page in the following way: “Making a state-of-the-art model work like a good agent is a training challenge, not a prompting challenge.” General language models, despite their abilities, were not always ready for extended usage. Prompt caching eventually became less effective, and context grew bigger. The basic approach was to improve the models unaided instead of trying to compensate for their shortcomings by using prompting or weight adjustments that would fix the identified problems. This way of working has resulted in creating the family of Smaug models . It is essential not only to ask how effective these models are but also where the fine-tuning works the best. The performance of the models depends greatly on the model and task type. What Is the Smaug Line? Smaug is a family of three open-weight models fine-tuned by Abacus.AI for agentic workloads. Each model is built on a different open-weight base, chosen for a distinct point on the capability–efficiency curve. All three are publicly available on Hugging Face. A common methodology involving human-curated, actual agentic trails and artificial data based on hard cases was used for all the three bases, which is why the gain patterns are comparable and the differences are meaningful. Model Base Model Optimized For Size Smaug Flash DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 Always-on enterprise agents, speed + cost 304B Smaug Mini Qwen3.8-27B Multimodal, compact, one-off tasks 28B Smaug Agentic Kimi K3 Frontier-scale, long-horizon coding 2.8T (MoE) Applying the same recipe to three very different bases is itself a research claim: that the methodology is general enough to produce consistent, measurable improvements regardless of architecture or scale. What follows examines each model's results to determine where that claim holds strongest — and where trade-offs emerge. Smaug Flash: The Biggest Gains in the Line Smaug Flash is where the Smaug methodology delivers its largest benchmark jumps. It is an agentic fine-tune of DeepSeek V4 Flash, often known as the workhorse of the line, built for enterprise self-improving agents that run continuously. Its base, DeepSeek V4 Flash, is fast and cost-effective but susceptible to spins and confusion in long-context tool use. The fine-tuning targeted that specific failure mode. The results on LiveBench reflect this precision. The +14.3 point gain in agentic coding ranging from 46.8 to 61.1 is the largest single-category delta in the entire Smaug line. On AutomationBench, the score improved by 13.7 points (25.1 to 38.83), and on NL2Repo-Bench the gain was 19 points (54.2 to 73.3). These are not marginal improvements; they represent the model closing a genuine capability gap in exactly the workflows it was designed for. Smaug Flash vs DeepSeek V4 Flash vs Claude Sonnet 5: Source: abacus.ai/smaug ¹ = vendor-reported score, not run under Abacus.AI's harness. LiveBench Category-by-Category Breakdown: Source: abacus.ai/smaug These modest reductions in Data Analysis (-0.2) and Reasoning (-0.4) could be seen as a trade-off since it is more important to hone these skills to be useful for production agents, for example, the ability to use tools correctly and process longer contexts, than to retain full performance in reasoning. In terms of the benchmarks evaluating these skills, Smaug Flash outperforms Claude Sonnet 5. Smaug Mini: The Surprising Story Smaug Mini is an advanced iteration of the Qwen3.8-27B model and the small-scale version of the Smaug series with 27 billion parameters. The model is intended for multimodal tasks such as image/video interpretation, instruction following, and tool use. With its comparatively smaller size, deployment could potentially become easier under certain conditions of hardware and inference configuration. It is important to note that Smaug Mini has achieved higher performance than several advanced closed models in certain benchmarks where the latter usually excel. Smaug Mini vs Base and Frontier Closed Models: Source: abacus.ai/smaug ¹ = vendor-reported score, not run under Abacus.AI's harness. LiveBench Category Profile for Smaug Mini: Source: abacus.ai/smaug Basically, Smaug Flash has the biggest LiveBench gain in agentic coding, but because Qwen3.8-27B, the base of Smaug Mini is already strong at coding-style tasks, it’s largest gains are in Mathematics (+3.5) and Reasoning (+2.8) which leaves no room for improvement. The fine-tuning found the gaps that were actually open. On NL2Repo-Bench, Mini also gained 13.5 points over its base (42.3 to 55.8), a gain worth noting for code-related workflows. The twist is important: Smaug Mini's agentic coding score (-0.6) is actually slightly lower than its base, yet it leads Claude Sonnet 5, Claude Opus 4.6, and GPT-5.6 Luna on IFBench (instruction following), AutomationBench, and JobBench. JobBench in particular shows a 17.1 point gain over the base (33.4 to 50.5). Herein lies the distinction between what a benchmark category is able to measure and what the model is capable of achieving in reality — since different benchmarks measure different abilities, and a drop in one area does not mean a lack in others. Smaug Agentic: When Behavior Matters More Than Numbers Smaug Agentic is the largest one in this line-up. It's a fine-tuning of Kimi K3, which is the state-of-the-art Mixture of Experts model from Moonshot AI, with 2.8 trillion parameters. Its benchmark deltas over the base are the smallest of the three Smaug models. The research page states this directly: "the behavioral change is bigger than the deltas." Smaug Agentic vs Kimi K3 Base: Source: abacus.ai/research LiveBench Category Profile for Smaug Agentic: Source: abacus.ai/smaug Two benchmarks where the base model wins should be stated clearly: Terminal-Bench 2.1 (86.5 vs 88.3) and MMMU-Pro (81.0 vs 81.6).

title: What Senior Data Science Job Postings Actually Ask for in 2026
abstract: What Senior Data Science Job Postings Actually Ask for in 2026 A data-backed breakdown of the skills, credentials, and capabilities that hiring managers are screening for in senior roles right now. By Vinod Chugani on November 11, 2026 in Career Advice There's a persistent gap between what data scientists think employers want and what hiring managers actually write into job descriptions. That gap is widest at the senior level, where requirements have shifted more in the past two years than in the previous five combined. In 2026, senior data scientist postings reflect a field that has moved decisively beyond the "build a model in a notebook" era. Employers are screening for production-grade technical depth, comfort with AI tooling that didn't exist two years ago, and a set of business and communication skills that many technically strong candidates still underestimate. This article draws on analyses of thousands of active U.S. job postings, including a detailed review of 500 postings from LinkedIn , Indeed , and Glassdoor ; an analysis of 7,000+ postings for AI skill frequency; and job market data from 12,148 postings tracked by Axial Search . The goal is to show exactly what senior data science roles ask for in 2026. The findings are specific, and some of them will surprise you. The Baseline Has Risen: What "Table Stakes" Looks Like Now The first thing the posting data makes clear is that skills once considered advanced have become entry requirements at the senior level. Three things appear in the majority of all data science postings, senior or otherwise, and none of them are optional. Python (74% of Postings) Python continues to dominate as the most frequently required language across all data science roles. The postings have become more specific about which Python skills they want, though. The 2026 market is not looking for pandas fluency alone. Senior role descriptions routinely call out scikit-learn for machine learning pipelines, PyTorch or TensorFlow for deep learning, FastAPI or Flask for model deployment, and increasingly, LangChain or LlamaIndex for large language model (LLM) integrations. If your Python skills stop at data manipulation and basic visualization, you sit in the bottom half of the candidate pool for most senior positions. SQL (64% of Postings) SQL continues to appear in nearly two-thirds of all data science postings, and that number climbs when you look specifically at senior roles. What has changed is the depth expected. Senior postings increasingly specify advanced SQL capabilities: window functions such as ROW_NUMBER , RANK , and LAG/LEAD ; complex common table expressions and nested subqueries; query optimization and execution plan analysis; and familiarity with cloud-native SQL variants like BigQuery SQL, Snowflake SQL, and Redshift SQL. For senior roles, vanilla SQL is not enough. Machine Learning (69% of Postings) Machine learning appears in 69% of data scientist job postings. At the senior level, the emphasis has shifted from building models to owning them across their full lifecycle. Postings now call out MLOps far more consistently than classical algorithm knowledge. Feature engineering and model interpretability ( SHAP , LIME ) appear regularly in regulated industries such as finance and healthcare. The clearest signal in the 2026 data: employers want people who can deploy and maintain models, not just train them in a Jupyter notebook. What Sets Senior Roles Apart: The Skills That Separate Levels Beyond the baseline, several skill categories differentiate senior postings from mid-level ones. These are the requirements that most frequently appear specifically at the senior and staff levels. Cloud Platform Fluency (62% of Postings, Higher at Senior Level) Cloud expertise has become structural rather than supplementary. In an analysis of 500 postings, 62% mentioned at least one cloud platform. The breakdown by platform: Microsoft Azure at 28.5%, AWS at 19.7%, Google Cloud Platform at 14.2%, Snowflake at 11.8%, and Databricks at 9.3%. Senior postings go further than mid-level ones in what they expect. Rather than general cloud familiarity, they specify services: AWS SageMaker for machine learning workflows, AWS S3 and EC2 for storage and compute, Google Vertex AI , Azure ML , and BigQuery for data processing. The underlying message is that a senior data scientist should be able to deploy and scale production systems on their preferred cloud, not just run notebooks on it. One notable finding: approximately 20% of data science job postings explicitly request a cloud certification. The AWS Certified Machine Learning Specialty (9.3% of postings), Azure Data Scientist Associate DP-100 (8.4%), and Google Professional Data Engineer (7.1%) lead the list. Postings that specify a cloud certification tend to carry noticeably higher salary bands. MLOps and Production Skills (Increasingly Required at Senior Level) The shift from modeling to production systems is the defining technical change in senior data science requirements over the past two years. Senior postings now routinely include tools such as MLflow for model tracking and versioning, Apache Airflow for workflow orchestration (mentioned in nearly 9% of all data science postings, skewing toward senior roles), dbt for analytics engineering, Docker and Kubernetes for containerization and deployment, and CI/CD pipelines through GitHub Actions or Jenkins . An analysis of 12,148 U.S. data science postings found that hands-on technical execution ranks higher than boardroom influence as the defining leadership characteristic employers screen for. The practical implication: senior data scientists are expected to build and ship, not just direct others who do. Generative AI and Large Language Model Skills (31% of Postings, Climbing Fast) This is the fastest-growing requirement category in the 2026 posting data. Across 500 postings analyzed between April and May 2026, 31% explicitly mentioned generative AI (GenAI), LLMs, or prompt engineering skills. That figure was effectively zero in 2023. A separate analysis of more than 7,000 postings found that AI skills appear in roughly two out of three postings overall, with about half expecting candidates to have specific AI skills or work on AI projects. Among AI skills, LLMs lead, with approximately one in four postings naming them specifically. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), AI agents, and natural language processing follow. AI requirements concentrate at the mid and senior levels. Research from the FutureProof Data Science newsletter found that 73% of postings mentioning AI skills target mid-level (43%) and senior-level (30%) roles, while entry-level postings account for less than 6%. This confirms that AI fluency is now an expectation for experienced practitioners, not a specialist add-on. The specific skills appearing in senior postings include: Experience with LLM APIs ( OpenAI , Claude , Gemini ) RAG implementation and vector database management ( Pinecone , Weaviate , Chroma ) Agentic AI workflow design, including multi-agent orchestration using LangChain, CrewAI , or AutoGen Prompt engineering, listed by name in 14% of postings LLM fine-tuning and evaluation methods Real senior job postings from 2026 illustrate the pattern directly. Wells Fargo listed "strong full-stack agentic AI skills" as a requirement for its Agentic AI Senior Lead Data Scientist role. The American Chemical Society posted a senior role requiring hands-on production experience with LLM applications, RAG, multi-agent systems, and model fine-tuning. Deloitte's senior consulting role asked for experience architecting end-to-end agentic systems that combine LLMs with enterprise data pipelines. These are not edge cases. They reflect a broad shift in how senior data science work is defined. Statistics and Mathematics (58% of Postings) Statistical depth remains a consistent requirement at the senior level.

title: 9 Key LLM Inference Metrics Explained in 5 Minutes
abstract: 9 Key LLM Inference Metrics Explained in 5 Minutes Learn how to measure LLM inference performance using key metrics and formulas for latency, token generation speed, and system load. By Bala Priya C , KDnuggets Contributing Editor & Technical Content Specialist on November 11, 2026 in Language Models Introduction A high token throughput doesn't necessarily translate to a fast user experience in a large language model (LLM) application. The first token may take too long to arrive, or subsequent tokens may stream too slowly, especially under concurrent load. Throughput alone doesn't capture these differences. LLM inference metrics help break performance down into measurable components, from the initial response delay to token generation speed and overall system load. This article covers nine key metrics, their formulas, and how to use them to evaluate latency, identify bottlenecks, and track performance over time: Per-request latency: time to first token (TTFT), end-to-end latency (E2E), token generation time, time per output token (TPOT), and inter-token latency (ITL) Latency across many requests: mean, median, and tail percentiles Server load: requests per second (RPS) and tokens per second (TPS) Service quality: goodput We start with the timeline of a single request. Reading a Request Timeline Four values define most of the latency metrics below. The value \( t_{\text{send}} \) is the moment the request leaves the client, \( t_{\text{first}} \) is the arrival time of the first output token, \( t_{\text{last}} \) is the arrival time of the last output token, and \( N_{\text{out}} \) is the number of output tokens. ITL also needs the arrival time \( t_j \) of each individual output token, where \( t_1 = t_{\text{first}} \) and \( t_{N_{\text{out}}} = t_{\text{last}} \). Laid on a timeline, the three timestamps cut a request into two segments: Request timeline: wait for first token, token streaming, and whole request Before \( t_{\text{first}} \), the request may wait in a queue, and then the server runs prefill, which processes the prompt and produces the first token. After \( t_{\text{first}} \), the server runs decode and emits tokens one step at a time, usually one token per step. Each latency metric below measures one of these segments or the whole span. Measuring Latency The first six metrics describe how long a user waits, for one request and then across many. 1. Time to First Token TTFT is the delay between sending a request and receiving the first output token. It includes network travel, any wait in the server queue, and the prompt-processing step, so it grows with server load and with prompt length. \[ \text{TTFT} = t_{\text{first}} - t_{\text{send}} \] Interactive chat applications watch this number most closely, because it sets how long the user stares at a blank screen. 2. End-to-End Latency E2E latency is the total wait, from sending the request to receiving the last token. \[ \text{E2E} = t_{\text{last}} - t_{\text{send}} \] It is the sum of the first-token wait and the streaming time that the next metric measures. 3. Token Generation Time Token generation time is the duration of the streaming segment: how long the server takes to deliver every token after the first. \[ \text{TokenGen} = t_{\text{last}} - t_{\text{first}} = \text{E2E} - \text{TTFT} \] Token generation time grows with the number of output tokens, so judge the speed of the stream with TPOT (discussed next), which divides that length out. 4. Time per Output Token TPOT is the average time between output tokens after the first one. It spreads the token generation time evenly over the tokens that follow the first. \[ \text{TPOT} = \frac{\text{E2E} - \text{TTFT}}{N_{\text{out}} - 1} = \frac{\text{TokenGen}}{N_{\text{out}} - 1} \] The first token belongs to TTFT, which is why the denominator is \( N_{\text{out}} - 1 \), and why TPOT is undefined for a reply with a single token. Benchmarking tools disagree on details here: some include TTFT in the average, and some use ITL as another name for TPOT. Confirm the definition before comparing results across tools. 5. Inter-Token Latency ITL is the gap between two consecutive output tokens. A request with \( N_{\text{out}} \) tokens has \( N_{\text{out}} - 1 \) gaps, and each gap is its own measurement. \[ \text{ITL}_j = t_{j+1} - t_j, \quad j = 1, \dots, N_{\text{out}} - 1 \] For one request, the mean of its ITL values equals its TPOT. Across \( R \) requests, the two averages weight the data differently. Writing \( N_i \) for the output tokens of request \( i \), the mean ITL counts every gap once, and the mean TPOT counts every request once: \[ \overline{\text{ITL}} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{R} \sum_{j=1}^{N_i - 1} \text{ITL}_{i,j}}{\sum_{i=1}^{R} (N_i - 1)} \qquad \overline{\text{TPOT}} = \frac{1}{R} \sum_{i=1}^{R} \text{TPOT}_i \] A few long requests dominate the first average, and the second gives short and long requests equal say. ITL also keeps every individual gap, which is where a stall in the stream shows up. 6. Mean, Median, and Tail Percentiles Latency varies from request to request, so one number per request becomes a distribution across many requests. The mean is the average of all values and follows outliers The median, also called P50, is the value that half of the requests fall at or below and reflects the typical user P99 is the value that 99% of requests fall at or below and shows the tail, with P90 and P95 as softer versions Apply all three to TTFT, TPOT, and E2E separately. With the \( N \) measured values sorted in ascending order as \( x_{(1)} \le x_{(2)} \le \dots \le x_{(N)} \), the nearest-rank method gives: \[ \bar{x} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i \qquad P_k = x_{\left(\left\lceil \frac{k}{100} N \right\rceil\right)} \] Compute each percentile from the raw samples of all servers combined, because an average of per-server P99 values is not the P99 of the combined traffic. Measuring Throughput and Goodput The last three metrics describe the server as a whole, over a measurement window from \( t_{\text{start}} \) to \( t_{\text{end}} \). 7. Requests per Second RPS counts the requests the server completes per second of wall-clock time. \[ \text{RPS} = \frac{N_{\text{completed}}}{t_{\text{end}} - t_{\text{start}}} \] RPS ignores how much work each request carries, so compare it only across runs with the same mix of prompt and output lengths. 8. Tokens per Second TPS counts the tokens the server processes per second across all active requests. It has an output form and an input form. Writing \( N_{\text{prompt},i} \) for the prompt tokens of request \( i \): \[ \text{TPS}_{\text{out}} = \frac{\sum_{i} N_{\text{out},i}}{t_{\text{end}} - t_{\text{start}}} \qquad \text{TPS}_{\text{in}} = \frac{\sum_{i} N_{\text{prompt},i}}{t_{\text{end}} - t_{\text{start}}} \] State which form a quoted number uses, since a workload with long prompts and short replies can post a high input TPS while producing few output tokens. 9. Goodput Goodput is the rate of successfully completed requests that meet your service-level objectives (SLOs), which is how serving benchmarks such as vLLM compute it. An SLO is a latency limit, such as a ceiling on TTFT or TPOT, and a request counts only when it satisfies every limit. The DistServe paper uses the term for a capacity instead: the maximum request rate a GPU sustains within its latency constraints. Writing \( s_{\text{ttft}} \), \( s_{\text{tpot}} \), and \( s_{\text{e2e}} \) for those limits, request \( i \) is good when: \[ \text{TTFT}_i \le s_{\text{ttft}} \;\land\; \text{TPOT}_i \le s_{\text{tpot}} \;\land\; \text{E2E}_i \le s_{\text{e2e}} \] Counting the good requests and dividing by the window gives goodput: \[ \text{Goodput} = \frac{N_{\text{good}}}{t_{\text{end}} - t_{\text{start}}} \] Goodput never exceeds RPS, and the gap between them is the rate of requests that missed at least one target.

title: How to Use AI for Enterprise BI
abstract: How to Use AI for Enterprise BI Learn how AI can make enterprise business intelligence more accessible, automate reporting, uncover insights faster, and improve decision-making with the right governance. By KDnuggets on November 10, 2026 in Partners Sponsored Content Businesses continue to face challenges with fragmented data, time-consuming reporting, and poor visibility into critical insights. Some still rely on spreadsheets and disconnected systems, while others have invested in business intelligence (BI) platforms but struggle to make analytics accessible and useful to more employees. This article explores practical applications of AI in enterprise analytics and key considerations for successful adoption. Learn how America’s leading stamp dealer is replacing manual reporting with real-time insights to improve operations while reducing IT reliance. Check out this webinar with Mystic Stamp’s IT Director for practical tips on modernizing BI and aligning implementation with enterprise needs and user expectations. How AI Can Improve Business Intelligence The value of business data lies in how effectively organizations can use it to understand performance and respond to changing needs. AI creates new opportunities to improve how employees work with information and get meaningful results. Simplifying Access to Business Information Business users often depend on IT teams or analysts to answer questions that existing reports do not cover. Even self-service tools may require familiarity with data structures, report builders, or query languages. A straightforward operational question can therefore become a time-consuming reporting request. AI-powered conversational analytics offers a more direct way to retrieve information. For example, an operations manager could ask, “How many orders are awaiting fulfillment today?” and follow up with, “Can you break that down by warehouse?” The system interprets these questions and presents the figures without requiring the manager to write SQL or build another report. Modern BI platforms offer this capability through natural language interfaces connected to business datasets, allowing employees to get answers to everyday questions independently. Improving Business Analysis Accessing business data is one thing; deriving insights that inform timely decisions is another. Teams may have comprehensive dashboards yet struggle to connect findings across functions and understand their business implications. AI-assisted insights can examine multiple business metrics together, propose explanations, and help users evaluate potential actions. For example, if a retailer faces recurring stockouts despite adequate overall inventory, AI in modern BI platforms could analyze demand patterns, warehouse stock distribution, and supplier lead times to suggest likely bottlenecks and replenishment priorities. Accelerating Business Response Time-sensitive findings can go unaddressed when teams struggle to communicate their significance or notify the people who need to respond. AI helps turn analytical findings into narratives that teams can share, discuss, and use to coordinate next steps. It can also flag emerging issues and notify the people who need to respond. Nowadays, these data stories and alerts can be embedded in BI dashboards to focus users on immediate priorities. Tune in to this fireside chat for proven advice on planning, building, and managing AI-powered business intelligence. Get tips on how to select the right solution, prepare your data, and choose test cases to deliver quicker value and encourage broader adoption. Guardrails for Adopting AI in Enterprise BI AI can make business analytics more accessible, but its value depends on the information and business context behind the answers. Incomplete data, inconsistent definitions, or weak governance can make otherwise useful AI features harder to trust. Modern BI platforms offer an advantage here: their managed data connections, analytical models, security, and reporting practices can provide a stronger foundation for AI-enabled analytics. The following considerations show how businesses can use that foundation to avoid common pitfalls. 1. Ground AI in Trusted, Current Business Data A precise-looking answer is not much help if it relies on incomplete or outdated information. For example, an AI comparison of today's orders with last month's sales could be misleading if the underlying extract has not been refreshed. BI platforms help by connecting operational systems, preparing datasets, and managing refresh schedules so AI can work from a more dependable picture of the business. 2. Standardize Business Metrics and Definitions Consistent information also requires consistent business definitions. If one team means gross sales by “revenue” and another means net sales, AI could return conflicting answers to similar questions. Governed metrics and semantic models in BI platforms help anchor AI responses to the same calculations and terminology used in official reports. 3. Enforce Security and Access Controls Natural-language access should make information easier to find, not easier to expose. A sales representative, for instance, should not gain access to restricted financial or employee records simply by phrasing a question differently. BI platforms already support roles and data-level permissions that AI interfaces can be designed to respect. Organizations also need to review what data is passed to any external AI service. 4. Make AI-Generated Results Verifiable An AI-generated explanation is most useful when its supporting evidence can be checked. If AI suggests a decline is related to a particular customer segment, for instance, users should be able to examine the relevant figures and assumptions. BI reports, governed calculations, and drill-down views provide reference points for validating the finding before acting on it. 5. Maintain Human Oversight and Accountability There is also context that no report captures completely. AI might suggest lowering inventory just before a major promotion, for example. With shared BI reports as a common reference, business teams can weigh the evidence alongside operational plans and decide which recommendations make sense. The platform supports the discussion; people remain accountable for the decision. 6. Monitor Accuracy, Adoption, and Business Value The strongest evidence of AI's value comes from daily use. Are employees finding answers faster? Are fewer routine requests reaching IT? Are teams responding sooner to important findings? BI usage and performance measures can help establish a baseline and track these outcomes, while AI-specific monitoring identifies accuracy issues, integration problems, and costs. Bringing AI and Enterprise BI Together AI opens up exciting possibilities for businesses to get more value from their data, but realizing its full potential requires the right business intelligence foundation. Modern BI platforms like LANSA BI bring together and standardize data from across the enterprise, allowing AI to deliver more consistent and relevant results. LANSA BI integrates with leading AI model providers to enhance natural-language querying, analysis, and data storytelling for business users. It also enables developers to embed AI-powered BI directly into business applications to streamline workflows. This helps employees get the information and insights they need to align on decisions and act faster, with less reliance on IT. Enterprise-grade security and governance controls help protect sensitive information and maintain oversight as usage expands. title: Integrating LLM Translation into Your Scikit-Learn Pipelines with Scikit-LLM
5 Techniques for Fine-Tuning LLMs Without Breaking the Bank
abstract: 5 Techniques for Fine-Tuning LLMs Without Breaking the Bank Learn five practical ways to fine-tune LLMs on a budget, from LoRA and QLoRA to Unsloth, DPO, and right-sizing your GPU, with working code for each technique. By Shittu Olumide , Technical Content Specialist on November 10, 2026 in Language Models A team gets a quote from a vendor: fifty thousand dollars to build them a " custom AI model " trained on their support tickets. Someone on the team, skeptical, spends a weekend testing the actual technique that quote was based on. The real GPU bill comes out under ten dollars. That gap isn't a rounding error, and it isn't unusual. Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) has a reputation as a research-lab-only activity, and for full fine-tuning of a frontier model from scratch, that reputation is earned: training runs at that scale really do cost tens or hundreds of millions of dollars. But adapting an existing open-weight model to a specific task is a completely different cost category now, and most of the guides explaining that gap either stop at one technique or never show real, runnable code. This article does both. It covers five distinct techniques for fine-tuning LLMs cheaply — from parameter-efficient methods like low-rank adaptation (LoRA) and quantized low-rank adaptation (QLoRA) to faster training tooling, cheaper alignment objectives, and the infrastructure decisions that quietly double most people's bills — each with a real use case and working code. What Fine-Tuning a Large Language Model Actually Means Fine-tuning takes a model that's already been pretrained on a broad, general corpus and trains it further on a narrower, task-specific dataset, so its behavior shifts measurably toward what you actually need — a particular format, a specific domain, a consistent tone — without starting from nothing. It's worth placing that next to the other ways to shape a model's behavior, since fine-tuning is a genuine choice among several, not the default. Prompt engineering, few-shot examples, and retrieval-augmented generation all shape what a model produces without touching a single weight, which is exactly why they're faster to try and easier to update, per the framing in Let's Data Science's 2026 guide to the space. Fine-tuning is the option that actually changes the model itself. That's a meaningfully bigger commitment than editing a prompt, which is why it's worth being deliberate about when it's genuinely the right call. Why Teams Actually Fine-Tune It's worth being specific here rather than hand-wavy, since "fine-tuning makes the model better" doesn't hold up under scrutiny: a frontier model prompted well is often already excellent. Three real situations tip the scales toward fine-tuning specifically. The first is behavioral consistency at scale: needing a model to reliably behave a certain way across thousands of calls rather than hoping a system prompt holds under pressure every single time The second is an exact output schema or format that a general-purpose model won't commit to reliably, no matter how the prompt is worded The third is narrow domain vocabulary or a specific brand voice that would otherwise need re-explaining in every single prompt, quietly inflating token cost on every call forever It's just as important to be honest about when it isn't the right call. According to hjLabs' 2026 best-practices guide , roughly 80% of requests that arrive framed as "we need to fine-tune a model" turn out to be solvable with better retrieval instead. Fine-tuning is a real, durable capability upgrade when one of the three situations above genuinely applies. It's an expensive way to patch a prompting or retrieval problem when it doesn't. Which Large Language Models Can Actually Be Fine-Tuned Before touching any technique, it helps to know what's actually on the table. Several open-weight model families support fine-tuning directly, with mature tooling and active communities behind them: Llama 3.x , Qwen 2.5 and 3 , Mistral , Gemma 2 through 4 , and Phi . All five techniques in this article apply cleanly to any of these. For teams that don't want to touch training infrastructure at all, managed fine-tuning APIs are a real, current option. OpenAI and Google both offer fine-tuning on select models through their own platforms, and pay-per-token LoRA fine-tuning is available directly through providers like Together AI and Fireworks , trading a slightly higher per-token training cost for zero infrastructure to manage. One honest scaling caveat is worth flagging early, since it changes the math significantly: everything in this article assumes a dense model in the roughly 2B to 13B range, where these techniques run comfortably on a single GPU. Past around 70B parameters, and especially once a model is a sparse mixture-of-experts rather than a dense architecture, even QLoRA needs a genuine multi-GPU node just to hold the quantized weights in memory. The Real Cost of Fine-Tuning a Large Language Model Here's where the numbers actually land as of mid-2026, and it's worth seeing the full range before assuming any one figure is representative. Parameter-efficient methods on a small 2 to 8B model routinely run under \$10 in raw GPU time, while full fine-tuning of a larger model on premium infrastructure can exceed \$10,000. Getting more specific, Stratagem Systems' rates verified in July 2026 put a LoRA or QLoRA fine-tune of a 7 to 8B model at \$3 to \$10 in GPU time (two to four hours on a rented A100), or under \$3 on a rented RTX 4090, with a 70B QLoRA run landing around \$15 to \$30. Here's the detail that actually matters most for planning a real project, though: GPU hours are now the smallest line item in the whole process. The real spend is dataset creation, multiple iteration runs, and evaluation — work that recurs every time the base model updates. That's precisely why complete, real-world projects still land in the \$5,000 to \$15,000 range even when the compute itself costs single-digit dollars. The Five Techniques at a Glance Before going deep on each one, here's the map. Two are algorithmic, one is a tooling optimization, one changes the training objective, and one is an infrastructure decision. They're designed to stack rather than compete. Technique What it optimizes Typical cost impact Hardware needed LoRA Trainable parameter count Cuts compute and storage sharply vs. full fine-tuning A GPU with enough VRAM to hold the full model at 16-bit QLoRA Memory footprint Removes GPU budget as the limiting factor entirely A single consumer GPU, often 8 to 24GB Unsloth Training speed and memory Cuts wall-clock rental time on top of LoRA/QLoRA savings Same as LoRA/QLoRA, often less Direct preference optimization (DPO) Alignment training pipeline Skips the reward-model and reinforcement learning infrastructure that reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) needs Same as whichever adapter method it's paired with Right-sized GPU Hardware rental cost Often the single biggest line-item saving of the five None specifically; it's a procurement decision Technique 1: Low-Rank Adaptation LoRA is the foundational technique the rest of this article builds on, so it's worth understanding the actual mechanism rather than treating it as a black box. Instead of updating every weight in a model during training, LoRA freezes the entire base model and injects small, trainable low-rank matrices alongside the existing weight matrices. The idea, from Hu and colleagues' original 2021 paper , rests on the hypothesis that the weight changes needed to adapt a model to a new task have a low intrinsic rank, meaning a much smaller set of parameters can capture nearly all of the useful adaptation. In practice, that means training a tiny fraction of the model's total parameters, often under 1%, while leaving the original weights completely untouched. Here's a real, working example: fine-tuning Llama 3.

title: Anthropic launches roadshow for proposed initial public offering
abstract: Today Anthropic, PBC launched the roadshow for its proposed initial public offering of its Class A common stock. The proposed offering consists of 825,000,000 shares of Class A common stock. Of these, 801,351,354 shares are being offered by Anthropic and 23,648,646 shares are being offered by certain existing stockholders. Anthropic will not receive any proceeds from the sale of shares by the selling stockholders. Anthropic also expects to grant the underwriters a 30-day option to purchase up to an additional 123,750,000 shares of its Class A common stock. The initial public offering price is expected to be between $70.00 and $78.00 per share. Anthropic has applied to list its Class A common stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol “ANT.” The proposed offering will be made only by means of a prospectus. title: Introducing Claude Whiteboards, Claude Sheets, and Claude Data
abstract: Today we’re launching Claude Whiteboards and Claude Sheets in beta, and Claude Dashboards (opens in new tab) becomes generally available as Claude Data. Whiteboards is a shared board where your team brainstorms with Claude, Sheets is a spreadsheet Claude builds and edits with you, and Claude Data adds data stories, certified queries, and live sharing. These are available on all paid plans. Working with Claude on a project often meant moving the output over to another tool or program, where Claude didn’t have live access to follow progress and changes. Now, your documents, boards, sheets, and dashboards can stay in Claude, with access for your team to continue editing together. When ready, you can bring the outputs directly into tools from our partners and continue working there. Claude Whiteboards Many people use Claude as a thought partner, but brainstorming with it has typically meant copy-pasting the results elsewhere so you can then start brainstorming or collaborating with your coworkers. Now, you can talk through a messy plan out loud with Claude, and Claude can turn it into a board with a timeline with owners and dates, so you and your team can collaborate in real time. In a retro meeting, for example, everyone can add their notes, and Claude can group them by theme and draft the action items for each person. You can focus on any part of the board by dragging a box around it and asking Claude questions. When you’re done brainstorming, Claude can turn the board into a doc or deck, or bring it into tools like Lucid, Miro, or Vani by Zoho, where you can continue working on it with your team. Claude Sheets Claude can now generate spreadsheets with tabs, formulas, formatting, and drop-downs, often from just a prompt like asking for a campaign tracker or a hiring budget. It can edit in the cells, outlining each new edit so you can track changes. You can share sheets with your team, so you and Claude can work on them together. For now, sheets have simple spreadsheet functionality, but we are working on adding more. When you need the full functionality of Excel, you can export your file to .xlsx or CSV, or use Claude for Excel (opens in new tab) . You can also continue working in partner tools including Airtable, Asana, monday.com, and Smartsheet. Claude Data Claude Dashboards (opens in new tab) launched in beta in October, enabling teams to ask quick questions of their company’s data in tools like Amazon Redshift, BigQuery, and ClickHouse. Starting today, it’s generally available as Claude Data. We changed the name because the way companies use their data is broader than dashboards, and the product now covers how they work more broadly. Certified queries and live sharing are in beta. Here are some ways teams can use Claude Data: Create certified definitions of metrics. Your data team can certify the queries everyone should use, so you don’t end up building or working on dashboards with conflicting data. Charts built on these metrics carry a "certified" badge showing they’re certified. Craft stories from data. You can work with Claude in Claude Data to draft data stories or narrated videos from your metrics, for you to review before sharing. Share current numbers with everyone. With live sharing, your colleagues can see up-to-date numbers when they open a shared dashboard, even if they don’t have access to the connectors that keep that data current. Viewers see the results of the queries you’ve approved, and can’t run others with your access. Match your look-and-feel. Design systems are now supported in Claude Data. Get faster loading with caching. Previously, every dashboard would reload on every load. Now, dashboards support caching, and refresh cadences can be set on a per-dashboard basis. Track changes over time. Claude Data now has tracked changes, so you can see who has made edits and roll back to a specific version if needed. Our partners for Claude Data include Amplitude, Mixpanel, Omni, PostHog, and Sigma. Work in your other tools, too Starting today, interactive connectors (opens in new tab) can open as full apps beside your conversation or in full screen, so you can work in tools like Adobe, Atlassian, Box, and Notion yourself, or ask Claude to make changes with you. Getting started Claude Whiteboards, Sheets, and Data work on web, desktop, and mobile. Claude Data needs a data connector, such as a warehouse or CRM. For admins: On Team plans, all three are on by default. On Enterprise plans, Claude Whiteboards and Sheets are off by default, and Claude Data turns on by default on November 19, 2026. You can change these anytime in Organization settings > Artifacts.

title: More ways to work with Claude: Sheets, Whiteboards, and Interactive Connectors
abstract: We've seen Claude Code change how developers work. Engineers went from manually coding line by line, to describing ideas and reviewing what Claude built. It reconnected them with the joy of building. Our goal is to bring that magic to every team, and today we're expanding what Claude makes possible. We're introducing new artifact types with Claude Sheets, Claude Whiteboards , and Claude Data . We're also making it easier to work in your most-used apps with an upgrade to interactive connectors . Claude Meetings is coming soon. All your connectors and context In Claude Code, the context Claude needs is already in the codebase. For other teams, context sprawls across emails, apps, and drives. Claude reaches it through connectors built on the Model Context Protocol (opens in new tab) (MCP), the open standard we introduced for connecting AI to the tools you use. Claude Marketplace lists more than 9,000 connectors and plugins, including community-built ones. Interactive connectors (opens in new tab) take this further. Starting today, partners can embed their apps directly in Claude, so you can work in Adobe, Atlassian, and others without switching tabs. Plugins from Salesforce (beta), NetSuite, and Workday (beta) come with built-in skills, so sellers can prep for a call, accountants can analyze financial data, and HR teams can handle time off and expenses. Bring ideas to life faster, together Starting today, Claude can build spreadsheets, whiteboards, and dashboards with your team. These work with its existing abilities to create documents, slide decks, and designs (opens in new tab) , and with Claude Motion (opens in new tab) (beta), which helps you turn content into short animations. In each one, Claude quickly picks up what you need, so your thinking sets the pace of work: New artifact types (opens in new tab) : In Claude Sheets, your team and Claude build spreadsheets together, collaboratively organize data, create and edit formulas, and work across multiple tabs. Claude Whiteboards is a digital whiteboard that your team can use to lay out and organize ideas together in a meeting, then ask Claude to summarize the findings. Claude Data (formerly Dashboards) connects to tools like Snowflake and Salesforce and can use definitions your data team certifies (beta) to create dashboards, visual data stories, or narrated short videos. You can also ask Claude to build custom artifacts for the way your team works, like an account tracker, a daily briefing, a project status board, or a contract review table. Since Claude carries the same context through every step, an idea can carry over from a whiteboard to a spreadsheet to a dashboard, without the need to reiterate the details. Coming soon, Claude Meetings will let you add Claude to a call to take notes and update the documents your team is working on during the conversation. Teams already working this way Inside Anthropic, non-technical teams are starting to get as much out of Claude as our engineers. Our legal team worked with Claude to build a Slack-based legal review tool that automatically draws redlines from the team’s own playbook. This brought marketing reviews from three days down to 24 hours, and easy fixes are made before a lawyer reviews the draft. Our finance team turned a long business update document for executives into an interactive page, and now the whole team updates it together with Claude. Neither of these teams writes code, but they're experts in their fields. They used Claude to turn that knowledge into tools that saved them time, and that others can use. Our customers are working this way too: “At Datadog, Claude has extended from coding to knowledge work. Our product managers are using Claude to move from an idea to a feature brief, PRD, and testable prototype much faster, giving them more time to focus on customer needs, product judgment, and the right problems to solve. When someone builds something good with Claude at Datadog, it spreads fast.” Yanbing Li, Chief Product Officer, Datadog At Gusto, one member of the commercial legal team built a tool in a few hours that turns negotiated terms into signature-ready contracts. Turnaround went from over a week to hours, with that person still reviewing anything negotiated. Gusto “Claude and HubSpot work seamlessly together, so our CSMs have all the context they need to walk in prepared for every call. Live dashboards in Claude pull from HubSpot to show what matters for each call and which customers to reach out to next, and follow-up emails are drafted within 30 minutes of a call ending. Work that used to take hours every week now runs in the background, so our team can focus on helping customers build better solutions, prove value, and grow better.” Jon Dick, Chief Customer Officer, Hubspot “At Accenture, Claude is helping us transform the way our legal teams work. We're excited about the opportunity to reimagine legal workflows and unlock new ways for our legal professionals to support our business.” Mindy Lok, Legal Chief Technology Officer, Chief Intellectual Property Officer, Accenture “Our FP&A team used to spend about 10 hours every forecast cycle on slides, commentary, and validation. title: Your apps can now open in Claude, and Claude can work in them
abstract: Earlier this year, we launched interactive connectors (opens in new tab) to bring a small live view of tools into Claude. Starting today, where a connector supports it, you can open a tool beside your conversation or expand it to full screen, and ask Claude to work alongside you and make changes directly. This is rolling out on the web and in the Claude desktop app on all plans, as part of the new Claude experience (opens in new tab) that brings chat and Cowork together. You’ll see these features once your account is updated with the new Claude or your organization turns it on. What’s new: Claude can work in your open tools. You can ask Claude to make changes to a page, row, or file that you have open and approve its actions the same way you approve a connector’s actions. Changes appear in the tool as Claude makes them, so you can keep working right alongside it. The whole tool opens next to your conversation. You can work in the tool and hide the chat or go full screen when you need room. For tools like Confluence or Notion, that means you get the full editor, signed into your own account, rather than a limited preview. Open a connected tool directly, without having to write a Claude prompt. When you want Claude’s help, you can ask from the same screen. Pin the tools you use most. You can arrange them alongside your artifacts and access them with one click in your sidebar and the + menu. Work with Claude in the tools you use We’re starting with a small group of tools from our directory, including Asana, Canva, Carta, Dropbox, monday.com, Smartsheet, Vercel, and Webflow. Here’s what you can do with some of the tools available in Claude today: Adobe. Ask Claude to retouch, edit and add effects to photos; highlight, edit and redact PDFs. Atlassian. Open a Confluence page beside your chat, ask Claude to write and edit, and review its changes live on the page. Box. Open a Box file beside your chat, ask Claude to revise it, and compare the versions side by side before you keep the changes. HubSpot. Prioritize pipeline tasks and follow-ups, then act on them in Claude. Notion. Ask Claude to create a Notion doc or database. Build as you chat, or edit it yourself, without leaving Claude. Figma, Harvey, and Shopify are also building integrations, and we encourage other developers to do the same. For developers: built on MCP Apps Interactive connectors run on MCP Apps, the open extension to the Model Context Protocol (opens in new tab) that lets an MCP server bring its own interface into AI applications. An MCP App you build isn’t limited to Claude and can run in any AI application that supports the extension (opens in new tab) . Until now, MCP Apps in Claude have mainly appeared as interactive views in the conversation. Claude now supports more of the extension, such as app tools, along with embedded sites, so a developer’s full app can run inside Claude. Support for these capabilities is in public preview for developers. Developers can start building with them today. Read our docs (opens in new tab) to start building. Getting started You can connect the tools we mention above from the directory (opens in new tab) , then open any tool from your chat or pin it to your sidebar. For admins: If your organization already allows all of a connector’s tools, its new features appear as they roll out. Admins can restrict a connector’s tools the same way they do today.

title: How Curative is building a national provider network with agents on Claude
abstract: In our series, How startups build with Claude , we highlight how startups are transforming their industries with AI. In this article, we share how Curative built a hierarchy of agents on Claude to sign provider contracts about 50 times faster than its team did in 2025. The quick pitch Name Curative Founded 2020; launched its health plan in 2022 Founders Fred Turner (CEO), Isaac Turner (CTO), Tami Wilson-Ciranna (President) Stack Claude Platform, Claude Code, bespoke claims system Growth $150M Series B at a $1.275B valuation. 165,000+ members and 1,200+ employers (Dec 2025). 23,000 provider contracts signed with Gwen. 2,000 to 2,400 new contracts a week, up from 2,100 in all of 2025. Curative sells health insurance to employers, with $0 copays and $0 deductibles for in-network care once members complete a Baseline Visit. Curative didn’t start out in insurance. It started as a lab startup and ended up processing 10% of all US COVID-19 tests according to their internal estimates. As a result, they started working with nearly every insurer in the country. Its British founders, used to a system where patients don’t pay for care, saw inefficiencies and set out to build a payer focused on prevention. They realized they had significantly underestimated how hard building a national network would be. “Sometimes naivety is good in startups, because you don’t know that it’s impossible. And then along the way you figure out a way to make it not impossible,” said Curative CEO Fred Turner. “Last year we signed 2,100 contracts, twice as many as we did the year before, but at 2,000 a year, we realized it would still be a 30-year build. There is a reason there are only a handful of national networks and they were all built about 30 years ago.” Curative needed to accelerate contract signings, but hiring alone couldn’t close a gap that size. Their solution: Gwen, an agent that works one provider deal from initial outreach to signature, surrounded by smaller agents that review its rates, check its messages, answer its questions, and escalate to humans for non-standard pricing. Here is how they built it and what broke along the way. Gwen: the provider contracts agent Gwen works both inbound and outbound leads. Each run of Gwen handles a single provider, mostly on Claude Opus, so nothing from other deals influences it. For example, if a practice fills in the form on Curative’s website, Gwen will research the practice and reply with proposed rates based on a purchased claims data set and price-transparency files payers are now required to publish. Gwen will show providers these market rate data to help with negotiations. The rate reviewer runs on Sonnet. When Gwen wants to exceed its standard rate template, it writes out why, and the reviewer decides whether the rate makes sense. “For a long time there was a big approval queue where Gwen had to get rates approved if she wanted to go a certain amount above the template, but we relaxed over time. Having a second agent review rates worked better than just giving Gwen more authority,” said Fred. The Sonnet rate reviewer clears about two-thirds of Gwen’s requests and then anything non-standard goes to Fred for approval. “The requests I see are from a big medical group or someone with a weird request that would come to me even if this wasn’t an agent-led motion,” said Fred. Outbound deals take more persistence, because practices are busy. Some providers’ replies come after the fourteenth email and the ninth fax. Image used with permission from Curative. A judge, which runs on Haiku, reads every communication before it’s sent. Curative added it after Gwen copied providers on internal notes about how high it could go. A blocked message comes back with the reason, so Gwen can rewrite it and try again. Each contract takes about 20 million tokens to complete, roughly a tenth of the original cost. These efficiencies enable one of Curative’s core strategies: signing smaller providers that have often been overlooked by larger networks. “The agent will happily give you the same level of attention whether you are a large hospital system or if you’re a solo provider,” Fred explained. “From that agent’s perspective, this provider is its only focus.” During negotiations, Gwen checks practice redlines against Curative’s policy document, then writes Python to merge both sides’ changes into a final document. From form to signature, the process can be as quick as an hour. Once the contract is signed, a separate credentialing agent checks the provider’s licenses, and agents load the provider’s data and contract so claims can price against it. Curative’s contracting team has grown from 45 to about 55 people since Gwen launched, each about 2.5 times as productive. They hand Gwen cold outreach and paperwork and take over warm leads by phone. Curative pays its contracting team on Gwen’s deals too, so people and agents share one target. “People’s work becomes more about the relationship and less about paperwork,” said Fred. Fred also believes faster contracting helps small practices stay independent. “If you start a medical practice and it takes three months to get in network and credentialed, you’re just not getting paid for three months,” he said. Gwen is not Curative’s only agent. Brad, another Opus-based agent, helps sell Curative’s plan to employers, mainly through brokers. Brad follows up with brokers on each quote and helps underwriters move faster by pulling employee data out of the spreadsheets underwriters used to scrub by hand. Using human-agent teams, Curative can now answer emailed or faxed claims disputes in under 30 minutes, with a letter specific to that claim. “Claims dispute responses used to take about 90 days and now take under 30 minutes by email or fax,” said Fred. “Most payers use a set of templates that are mail-merged together. That leaves a provider deeply unsatisfied, because usually the template doesn’t actually explain what’s going on. Now providers get a customized letter that explains the specifics of the individual claim, what’s happening, and why.” All of their agents sit on bespoke claims, prior authorization, and finance systems that 13 engineers rebuilt this year with Claude Code. The team had once sized building a claims system alone at 100 engineer-years. “We’re not trying to plug [these agents] into a claim system,” Fred said. “The claim system is Python running in AWS, and it has an MCP and it has an API, and Claude wrote it, so it understands it.” What Curative learned from building agents that negotiate with people Here’s what the Curative team learned about how to build agents that negotiate with people. Start with one general tool. “We started off with, ‘Oh, we’ll have tools,’ and that doesn’t work that well, because redlining is quite complex,” Fred said. “What we found works best is that the model just has one tool, which is run Python, and it does all the redlining with a docx library. It works beautifully.” Meet people on their channel. A fax tool more than doubled Gwen’s win rate. Many providers now handwrite on a printed fax and fax it back. “It’s meeting people where they are,” said Curative CTO Isaac Turner. “Yes, they have email, but really they’re comfortable in fax.” Keep each run isolated. One Gwen run sees one provider and keeps no memory across deals. Brad, Curative’s sales agent, does keep memories, which works but needs care. “You can end up making notes that are wrong and then get into these doom loops, where it has a bad memory that can never be cleared,” Fred noted. Improve the system from outside the run. Every few days, Fred gives Claude Code the same prompt: sample the last 10,000 runs, flag anything weird, and open a PR to fix it. “The improvement loops come from running Claude Code over lots of historic conversations and asking how could this have gotten better,” he said. Experiment away from PHI first.

title: Evaluating the Evaluators: Investigating LLM Judges for Personalized Writing Style Assessment
abstract: research area Human-Computer Interaction , research area Methods and Algorithms Workshop at NeurIPS content type paper published November 2026 Evaluating the Evaluators: Investigating LLM Judges for Personalized Writing Style Assessment Authors Natalie Mackraz‡, Andrew Silva, Aini Putkonen, Brihi Joshi†**, Joelle Alcaidinho, Arnav Arora§**, Barry-John Theobald, Katherine Metcalf‡ View publication Copy Bibtex This paper was accepted at the Can We Trust AI Evaluation? Workshop at NeurIPS 2026. We evaluate how good large language model (LLM) judges are for personalized writing tasks. This is important when a user’s preferred writing style is known (e.g., “upbeat”) and an LLM judge is used to evaluate whether generated text adheres to this preference. We examine how the writing task, the combination of generator and judge LLM, the evaluation objective, and general commonsense and reasoning ability impact LLM judge performance. To this end, we generate text with four LLMs for three long-form writing tasks, collect human labels evaluating which of two responses is better, collect judge-LLM, pairwise-ranking annotations, and then compare the human and judge LLM annotations. We find that judge quality correlates weakly with general LLM ability measured using MMLU (Pearson’s ρ ≤ 0.2) and varies by both writing task and evaluation criteria (i.e., general helpfulness versus style personalization). We also find that LLM evaluators are more consistent and performant using paired comparisons rather than scoring responses independently. Finally, we find that the “strongest” LLMs do not most reliably reproduce the human evaluations, which we hypothesize relates to exaggerated sensitivity to subtle details that human annotators and weaker LLMs ignore. ‡ Equal contribution † University of Southern California § University of Copenhagen ** Work done while at Apple Related readings and updates. title: On the Importance of Gating: Memorization vs. In-Context Learning in State Space Models
abstract: research area Methods and Algorithms , research area Speech and Natural Language Processing conference NeurIPS content type paper published November 2026 On the Importance of Gating: Memorization vs. In-Context Learning in State Space Models Authors William L. Tong†**, Aryo Lotfi, Emmanuel Abbe, Kostas Vaggelakos, Vishnu Banna, Etai Littwin, Josh Susskind, Cengiz Pehlevan†, Eran Malach View publication Copy Bibtex State Space Models (SSMs) have emerged as a compelling alternative to Transformers, enabling sequence modeling with constant memory and linear compute. Although SSMs exhibit reasonable performance and favorable computational characteristics, they continue to lag behind Transformers on tasks that require in-context learning and precise retrieval, slowing their adoption for large-scale language modeling. In this work, we demonstrate that both the success and failure of SSMs in these domains can be explained by studying the role of the gating mechanism, a prevalent component in modern recurrent networks. Specifically, we show through theory and experiments that this gating mechanism causes SSMs to first learn an in-weights “memorization” solution, while delaying, or even preventing, convergence to a correct in-context learning solution. Importantly, this happens even in cases where there are no fundamental limitations due to the architecture or its memory capacity. On the other hand, we find that gating is often beneficial for improving generalization to long sequence lengths. Our results illuminate the crucial role of the gating mechanism in shaping both the training dynamics and generalization of SSMs, and provide a basis for understanding and improving linear-time models. † Harvard University ** Work done while at Apple Related readings and updates. title: Weighted State Souping for Efficient Long-Context Retrieval
abstract: research area Methods and Algorithms , research area Speech and Natural Language Processing Workshop at NeurIPS content type paper published November 2026 Weighted State Souping for Efficient Long-Context Retrieval Authors William L. Tong†**, Aryo Lotfi, Emmanuel Abbe, Josh Susskind, Cengiz Pehlevan†, Eran Malach View publication Copy Bibtex This paper was accepted at the Workshop on Personalized, Aligned, Long-term Memory for AI Systems (PALM) at NeurIPS 2026. State space models (SSMs) combine fast inference and fixed state size with competitive language-modeling performance. Recently, state souping has been proposed as a procedure whereby an SSM independently encodes chunks of tokens like documents, tool definitions, or memory records. The resulting state encodings may be cached and recombined to cheaply construct a context for downstream queries. However, both state souping and vanilla SSMs deteriorate on long, crowded contexts, limiting their utility for long-horizon domains. To address this issue, we propose weighted state souping, a simple method that learns query-dependent weights for composing cached states. The resulting models improve long-context performance substantially across both single- and multi-hop document question answering, needle-in-a-haystack retrieval, variable tracking, and tool use. Our method can be further adapted into an efficient sparse variant, yielding near-constant encoding cost with respect to context length while preserving (and sometimes improving) performance. We also present simple theoretical arguments that illustrate why souping works and when it may fail, and discuss informally the advantages of weighted souping. Weighted state souping thus combines reusable context representations with selective retrieval, offering an efficient approach to language modeling over large collections of documents, tools, and other forms of structured context that increasingly dominate modern agentic workloads. † Harvard University ** Work done while at Apple Related readings and updates. title: Validating GPU Platforms with Runtime AI Inventory via the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory
abstract:
As teams deploy and scale AI workloads using NVIDIA Dynamo , Kubeflow, or Slurm , tracking what actually runs requires visibility beyond the platform configuration captured in a recipe. Application teams define and update these workloads independently of the platform recipe, so a reproducible deployment bundle alone cannot establish which workload artifacts are running on each node. Mutable image tags like :latest add another layer of complexity. Two nodes can end up running different code under identical tags, and a node that pulls next week may retrieve an image that was not covered by an earlier security review. NVIDIA AI Cluster Runtime (AICR) , an open source modular component of the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform , now includes a qualified AI bill of materials (AIBOM) component to close that gap. An open source project created by Google, k8s-aibom tracks AI workloads running on Kubernetes. Two stock recipes select k8s-aibom by default: h100-gke-cos-inference and h100-gke-cos-inference-dynamo . Other GKE recipes can opt in during generation with --runtime-inventory enabled. Recipes selecting it can opt out with --runtime-inventory disabled. AICR turns known-good GPU platform configurations into version-locked recipes and reproducible deployment bundles. Each recipe records the desired configuration for one hardware, cloud, OS, and intent combination: its components, version pins, values, constraints, deployment ordering, and validation expectations. AICR generates reproducible deployment artifacts from fixed recipe, catalog, and bundle inputs. Bundles include checksums; signing is optional through aicr bundle --attest . Qualification with k8s-aibom is a specific claim, not a rubber stamp. AICR binds the exact upstream source, chart, CRDs, and digest-pinned controller image as one tested set, verifies provenance against Google’s expected build identity, reviews rendered RBAC and security defaults, and exercises installation, upgrade, health, and uninstall on the deployment paths it tested. This blog will enable you to configure your Kubernetes runtime using AICR to provide a validated, performant configuration for your cluster. Figure 1. NVIDIA DSX brings together the technologies needed to design, build and operate AI factories Two ends of the same problem AICR and k8s-aibom look at different parts of the AI infrastructure lifecycle. AICR helps platform teams generate and validate known-good configurations for GPU-accelerated Kubernetes. It works at the runtime deployment layer: drivers, operators, kernels, Kubernetes components, deployment configuration. k8s-aibom looks higher up the stack and later in the lifecycle of the cluster. It watches Kubernetes workload and pod APIs and emits a CycloneDX 1.6 AIBOM for each recognized AI workload. Coverage is bounded: Only supported workload kinds carrying a recognized AI signal are inventoried. Coverage includes native Dynamo graphs, NIMService, LeaderWorkerSet, DisaggregatedSet, and CronJob resources. Tracked child workloads are combined into their owner’s AIBOM. AICR answers k8s-aibom answers Is the GPU infrastructure built from a known and validated configuration? What AI assets are actually running on that infrastructure? Table 1. The value at each level of the stack. One provides control and reproducibility of the configuration for GPU-accelerated Kubernetes, while the other adds workload discovery and traceability in that cluster. Concretely, AIBOM helps you: Find unregistered or shadow AI workloads in namespaces selected for reporting Identify models, inference runtimes, agents, and RAG components Track external AI APIs and vector databases Detect changes or drift in AI dependencies Support security reviews, incident response, and compliance audits Both projects arrived at this from opposite sides of the same problem, and recognized it as such . AICR records qualified deployment intent and evaluates it against a cluster at a point in time. k8s-aibom observes supported AI workloads and records what it found, including how confidently each attribute was determined.
