Neither view is sufficient for AI governance on its own, and the boundary between them is exactly where accountability is missing today. Using AICR with k8s-aibom These examples reflect AICR v1.2.0 and its catalog, which pins k8s-aibom 1.6.2. Use a CLI build matching this catalog to reproduce the examples. Start with a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster running Kubernetes 1.32 or later, with NVIDIA H100 GPU nodes using Container-Optimized OS and GKE-managed drivers and device plugins. The following workflow generates a recipe, renders it into a bundle, deploys it, and validates the result. Nothing is hand-assembled and nothing is tuned by hand. With the same AICR version, catalog, and generation inputs, recipe resolution produces the same configuration. The last step checks the cluster against it. That is the half AICR brings to this pairing: a validated GPU platform quickly and repeatably. k8s-aibom then keeps inventorying supported AI workloads. Generate the recipe aicr recipe \ --service gke \ --accelerator h100 \ --os cos \ --intent inference \ --output recipe.yaml The new k8s-aibom component is selected as part of the recipe, not bolted on afterward. You can query any resolved value without generating a file: aicr query \ --service gke --accelerator h100 --os cos --intent inference \ --selector components.k8s-aibom.version
# 1.6.2 Bundle and deploy Create a deployment bundle with the default Helm deployer. Replace the example node selectors with labels present on your system and GPU node pools: aicr bundle \ --recipe recipe.yaml \ --system-node-selector nodeGroup=system-pool \ --accelerated-node-selector nodeGroup=gpu-worker \ --output ./bundles The bundle is one directory per component, ordered by the dependency graph, each carrying its values, checksums, and install script. AICR supports a number of deployers via --deployer flag, including helmfile , flux , and argocd . Verify the generated bundle, then install it: (cd ./bundles && aicr verify . && chmod +x deploy.sh && ./deploy.sh) Once deployed, the k8s-aibom controller runs in the k8s-aibom-system namespace. AICR uses the main chart’s CRDs rather than the companion k8s-aibom-crds chart. Helm bundles include a CRD apply step; Flux and Argo CD handle updates through their controllers. Helmfile, Terraform, and Fleet require the documented manual CRD update when the transition calls for it. Check the installed storage version: kubectl get crd aiboms.aibom.k8saibom.dev \ -o jsonpath='{.spec.versions[?(@.storage==true)].name}'
# v1beta1 Validate aicr snapshot --output snapshot.yaml
aicr validate --recipe recipe.yaml --snapshot snapshot.yaml \ --phase deployment --phase conformance The k8s-aibo m health check runs as part of the deployment phase. It requires the controller deployment to be available, the cluster-scoped AIBOMControllerConfig to report a current Ready=True , and both CRDs to report the storage version the pinned chart expects. A matching storage version does not prove the full CRD schema is current. During upgrades, also verify the target schema and check for Degraded=True with reason SchemaPredatesController ; see health and readiness . Opt a namespace in Inventory is opt-in per namespace. The label controls which namespaces emit AIBOM records; it does not narrow what the controller reads. Informers still cache workload and pod specs cluster-wide, including container arguments and inline environment values. No sink and no secret access are configured by default, so nothing leaves the cluster without an explicit decision. kubectl create namespace prod-jobs
kubectl label namespace prod-jobs aibom.k8saibom.dev/enabled=true Run an inference workload Supported workloads carrying a recognized AI signal are inventoried automatically when their namespace opts in. For a simple demonstration, here is a vLLM deployment serving Qwen.

title: Running AV Reasoning Models Within Onboard Compute and Latency Limits
abstract:
Autonomous vehicle (AV) developers need reasoning models that can operate within the compute and latency constraints of an onboard system. Larger models provide a foundation for developing these capabilities, but moving them into a vehicle requires additional work to reduce model size, preserve useful reasoning, and validate performance on the target hardware. NVIDIA Alpamayo 2 Edge addresses this need with an adaptive reasoning vision-language-action (VLA) model designed for real-time operation on NVIDIA DRIVE AGX Thor . Built on the 2B Nemotron-based reasoning backbone of NVIDIA Cosmos 3 Edge and paired with a diffusion action expert, it leverages surround-camera observations, temporal context, and navigation inputs to generate Chain-of-Causation (CoC) reasoning and future driving trajectories. It reasons adaptively , generating reasoning only when needed, reducing unnecessary token generation and conserving inference compute during routine driving. Alpamayo 2 Edge is post-trained with closed-loop reinforcement learning (RL) in NVIDIA AlpaGym , improving closed-loop driving performance by 48.9% on top of the best-performing checkpoint without closed-loop RL. Together, these capabilities give developers a strong, edge-ready foundation for bringing reasoning-based driving into an onboard stack. Making a reasoning model compact enough for onboard deployment introduces a key challenge: preserving the quality of its reasoning and driving behavior as model size is reduced. This requires a way to measure reasoning quality and use that feedback to improve the model. NVIDIA AlpaJudge is the human-calibrated evaluation and reward model used in Alpamayo 2 Edge development to evaluate reasoning traces, select higher-value training data, and provide RL rewards. This post introduces Alpamayo 2 Edge, explains its inference optimization on DRIVE AGX Thor, and explores three ways to use AlpaJudge in AV development workflows: Run AlpaJudge-RB and AlpaJudge-RF on a PhysicalAI-AV sample, inspect their scores, and adapt the evaluation to policy-generated reasoning Select training examples that expose useful learning opportunities Use human-aligned reasoning scores as rewards for post-training Together, these workflows connect an edge-oriented driving model with a repeatable process for measuring and improving it. Bring reasoning-based driving to the edge An onboard driving model must interpret a changing scene and produce a useful trajectory within the system’s inference budget. The key question is how much driving and reasoning capability a model retains under that constraint. Figure 1. Alpamayo 2 Edge processes multi-camera video, ego-motion history, and navigation instructions to generate adaptive causal reasoning and driving trajectories, with support for optional visual question answering To balance model capacity and efficiency, Alpamayo 2 Edge leverages multiple new features: A 2B-parameter Nemotron-based reasoning backbone, sized for onboard inference Adaptive reasoning, reducing unnecessary token generation and conserving inference compute during routine driving Offline distillation, training with CoC reasoning autolabels generated by Alpamayo 2 Super Closed-loop reinforcement learning post-training in AlpaGym , in which the model learns from the consequences of its actions end-to-end in simulation Multi-resolution inputs to efficiently encode surround-view observations online Speculative decoding with DFlash2 to accelerate online reasoning without sacrificing quality Recipes for quantization and inference acceleration with NVIDIA TensorRT and NVIDIA TensorRT-Edge-LLM Figure 2, below, shows how these choices translate into capability, comparing Alpamayo 2 Edge with Qwen-Drive-1.0 across closed-loop driving, open-loop trajectory prediction, and scene understanding and reasoning. Figure 2. Alpamayo 2 Edge (2B) compared with Qwen-Drive-1.0 (4B) across closed-loop driving, open-loop driving, and scene understanding and reasoning benchmarks. Of note, Alpamayo 2 Edge achieves approximately 60× the distance between at-fault incidents in AlpaSim Early partner feedback also highlights Alpamayo 2 Edge’s driving performance and inference speed: “Within days of getting early access to Alpamayo 2 Edge, we had it running closed-loop in NuRec reconstructions of our own London street recordings. In our early simulation tests, Edge kept its lane in more than twice as many runs as Alpamayo 1.5, recovered from lane offsets about 40% more often, and out of the box planned roughly twice as fast as our hand-tuned Alpamayo 1.5 server on the same GPU.” — Matas Simonavicius, CTO, PORT “Alpamayo 2 Edge demonstrated impressive generalization capabilities, reducing displacement error (minADE) by 13.6% and lateral prediction error (RMSE) at 3 seconds by 46.1% compared to Alpamayo 2 Super in our zero-shot evaluation, despite substantial differences in sensor configurations. Fine-tuning on our own driving data delivered a further 44.2% reduction in displacement error compared to the Alpamayo 2 Edge baseline. Within just a few days, we went from receiving the model to running our first tests on a real vehicle.” — Luca Crotti, co-founder and motion planning lead, Niulinx Video 1. Niulinx’s driving demonstration shows the vehicle stopping for a traffic officer’s signal and yielding to pedestrians at a crosswalk “In less than 48 hours, we made NVIDIA’s Alpamayo 2 Edge run at 10 Hz on AGX Thor for real-time planning.”— Hans Salomonsson, CEO and co-founder, Embedl Video 2. Side-by-side comparison of Alpamayo 2 Edge running in PyTorch and with Embedl optimization, showing differences in planning speed, latency, and reasoning output The Alpamayo 2 Edge repository’s inference script shows how the model operates: It takes in surround-view camera observations over time, navigation text, and historical ego-motion to produce CoC reasoning traces and future trajectories. import torch
import transformers from alpamayo2_edge.checkpoint import load_model
from alpamayo2_edge.load_physical_aiavdataset import load_physical_aiavdataset
from alpamayo2_edge.helper import prepare_model_inputs, to_device
from alpamayo2_edge.models.utils import fuse_traj_tokens data = load_physical_aiavdataset(**clip)
model, loading_info = load_model("nvidia/Alpamayo2-Edge") settings = dict( seed=43, top_p=0.98, top_k=None, temperature=0.6, num_traj_sets=1, num_traj_samples=1, max_generation_length=256, diffusion_kwargs={"inference_step": 10},
) prepared = prepare_model_inputs(data, model.config, model.tokenizer)
prepared = to_device(prepared, device="cuda") """Seed text and diffusion sampling, then run the model on prepared inputs."""
torch.manual_seed(settings["seed"])
generator = torch.Generator(device="cuda").manual_seed(settings["seed"])
with ( torch.inference_mode(), torch.autocast( device_type=torch.device("cuda").type, dtype=model.dtype, enabled=model.dtype != torch.float32, ),
): xyz, rot, _, extra = model.sample_trajectories_from_data( prepared, num_traj_sets=settings["num_traj_sets"], num_traj_samples=settings["num_traj_samples"], top_p=settings["top_p"], top_k=settings["top_k"], temperature=settings["temperature"], max_generation_length=settings["max_generation_length"], diffusion_kwargs={**settings["diffusion_kwargs"], "generator": generator}, return_extra=True, ) In particular, note that the model will now produce special <NOMINAL> tokens instead of reasoning traces sometimes, indicating routine driving and conserving inference compute. Retaining quality during deployment When downloading the model from Hugging Face, by default, Alpamayo 2 Edge’s weights are represented in BF16 and it is directly runnable as a PyTorch model on any supported NVIDIA GPU. To run at real-time on DRIVE AGX Thor, however, Alpamayo 2 Edge must be further inference-optimized.

title: Agent Substrate: Advancing Kubernetes for Agents at Scale
abstract: AI agents spend most of their time idle, waiting on a human prompt, a tool result or a model response. Kubernetes wasn’t built for that. Running one Pod per session holds memory for sessions that aren’t doing anything, and deleting Pods between turns pays a multi-second cold start every time and loses the agent’s state. RL post-training hits the same wall. Agent Substrate, now donated to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) Sandbox, is an open-source, security-hardened, zero-trust runtime for sandboxed agents, engineered to safely run millions of agents and tools with 10x higher density than standard containers. It multiplexes many sessions over a small pool of worker Pods. Idle sessions are checkpointed, memory and filesystem included, and restored onto whichever worker is free when the next request arrives. As agentic infrastructure fragments into proprietary runtimes that bypass Kubernetes, NVIDIA is contributing upstream to keep this work open. This post covers which workloads suit Agent Substrate, what is being built upstream, and how the project works with KAI Scheduler and NVIDIA Dynamo components in the DSX AI Factory Platform . The shape of an agent workload Traditional web services run as a relatively small number of long-lived instances. Agents follow a different pattern: they wake up and take one step, running a shell command, editing a file, calling a test suite or calling an LLM. Then they wait, sometimes for milliseconds and sometimes for minutes, before the next step. The agent’s state (its filesystem, its processes, its working directory) has to continue between steps. Kubernetes struggles because spinning up a compute Pod for an agent means a trip through the API server, admission, etcd, the scheduler, the kubelet, image pulls and network setup. That takes seconds, which is fine for a service that runs for weeks. It’s far too slow for a sandbox that must appear, run a 10 ms bash command and get out of the way, hundreds of times per second. This leaves platform teams with two suboptimal choices: either keep one Pod warm per agent and pay for compute that is idle almost all the time, or create Pods on demand and pay a cold start penalty on every step. How Agent Substrate works Agent Substrate uses Kubernetes for running a pool of ready pods. It creates a separate control plane that maps a large set of actors (agents and their environments) onto that smaller pool of workers. When an actor goes idle, it is snapshotted out of its sandbox (gVisor or a microVM) and its worker is freed. When the actor is called again, it is restored into whichever worker is free, with its memory and filesystem state intact. Waking an actor doesn’t require a new trip through the API server, scheduler or kubelet. Agent Substrate restores the actor onto an existing worker instead. The worker pods are still ordinary Kubernetes Pods, so cluster scheduling, quotas and placement policies still apply as we describe later. The use cases driving demand We see three kinds of workload driving demand for Agent Substrate: Coding assistants and agent serving: A coding agent alternates between LLM calls and work in its own environment: cloning a repository, editing files, running builds and tests. Users expect the environment to persist between turns and to respond immediately. A platform serving thousands of these sessions can’t afford a dedicated warm sandbox for each one. Reinforcement Learning (RL) post-training with agentic environments: RL with verifiable rewards runs GPU trainers and generation servers alongside a fleet of CPU-heavy environments (code sandboxes, compilers, browsers, simulators) that execute actions and check results. Sandbox demand arrives in bursts as rollout batches dispatch actions. A training run can grow from a few hundred sandboxes in early experiments to many hundreds of thousands in production. The slowest environment determines when the trainer gets its next batch, so cold starts on that path leave GPUs idle. GPU sandboxes for research: A researcher’s coding agent needs a GPU, not to serve a model but to compile CUDA code, benchmark a kernel or run a numerical calculation. It launches a GPU sandbox on a shared cluster, runs the job and deletes the sandbox. Supporting this across an organization requires many short-lived, isolated GPU sandboxes that start quickly and share a limited pool of GPUs fairly. Upstream work: What’s landed and what’s next Each contribution below started from one of those use cases. All of this work is public in the Agent Substrate repository : When every worker is busy, the next request waits instead of failing: In an oversubscribed system, such as a coding-assistant platform at peak or an RL rollout burst, a user’s next turn can arrive while every worker is busy. Agent Substrate used to return an error immediately, even though another actor would usually free a worker a moment later. Request parking in the Agent Substrate router ( #221 ) holds the request and retries the resume until a worker frees up, with a bounded wait and a cap on how many requests can wait at once. A follow-up ( #1229 ) makes sure requests to already-running actors never get stuck in that line. Giving agents a GPU inside their sandbox: The research GPU sandbox described above, along with GPU-backed RL environments such as simulators. We are working on device-pluggability that adds device support on Kubernetes Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA). Device vendors plug in their devices through a profile, each container in a sandbox requests only the devices it needs ( #752 ), and the same model works for both gVisor and microVM sandboxes. NVIDIA GPUs will be the first supported device. One container can’t starve or kill its neighbors: An agent sandbox often runs the agent’s workload next to helper containers for logging, proxying or metrics. Some of those may be untrusted. A runaway container shouldn’t consume the whole sandbox’s memory and take the agent down with it. Per-container CPU and memory limits for microVM sandboxes ( #859 ) addresses that issue. A container that exceeds its memory limit is stopped on its own, and the rest of the sandbox keeps running. Preserving GPU sandboxes across suspend and resume When an agent pauses to wait for human review, its sandbox should release the GPU and resume later with its compiled artifacts and loaded data still in place. Supporting that requires saving and restoring both the agent’s state and the GPU state. Restoring GPU state introduces hardware compatibility constraints. A GPU checkpoint can usually be restored only onto the same GPU model, and sometimes only with the same driver version. Agent Substrate proposes a design to address this. Device vendors describe how to pause their devices safely and which device properties a snapshot depends on. Agent Substrate records those properties with each snapshot and restores the sandbox on a matching device, or falls back to a clean cold start if none is available. The design is vendor-neutral and builds on DRA. NVIDIA GPUs are the first target; the design can be extended to other hardware types. NVIDIA Dynamo: Connecting the agent loop to the inference loop Agent Substrate manages where agents act; inference runtimes manage where they think. Both face a similar efficiency challenge: keeping idle sandboxes warm wastes CPU and memory, while rebuilding model context on repeated model calls wastes GPU cycles. Scaling each layer independently improves utilization. Coordinating them can also reduce latency and preserve reusable context as agents move between tool execution and model calls. NVIDIA Dynamo , the open-source distributed inference framework, provides that coordination. Agent Substrate activates, suspends and restores stateful agent environments across a pool of warm sandbox workers. Dynamo orchestrates inference across GPU workers. The Dynamo router sits between them and connects what the agent is doing with what is happening on the GPUs.

title: Start and Restore GPU Workloads in Seconds with NVIDIA Snapshot
abstract: NVIDIA Snapshot , a new open-source component of the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform , makes initialized GPU workloads reusable across inference replicas—speeding startup and recovery. When inference demand spikes or a replica fails, available GPUs don’t translate immediately into serving capacity. Initializing an LLM workload—a process known as a cold start—can take minutes, delaying scaling and recovery. Snapshot is a checkpoint and restore system for GPU workloads on Kubernetes. It captures a fully initialized workload—including CPU and GPU memory—and restores that state on compatible infrastructure, bringing inference capacity online in seconds instead of minutes. Figure 1 shows the startup sequence. Snapshot skips repeated workload initialization; infrastructure provisioning and container image loading remain outside the measured restore path. Figure 1. Cold-start sequence: provision the machine, load the container image, start the inference engine, load model weights into GPU memory, compile with torch.compile, and capture NVIDIA CUDA graphs This post explains how Snapshot checkpoints and restores GPU workloads, how platform teams can integrate it, and how restore times compare with cold starts across three inference engines. Snapshot for AI factory operations Originally developed for NVIDIA Dynamo inference workers, Snapshot provides checkpoint and restore capabilities that other inference engines, schedulers, controllers, and platforms can integrate. Snapshot provides two operations for GPU Pods: Checkpoint : Once a workload is fully initialized, capture its CPU and GPU memory as a portable artifact. Restore : Start a new Pod from that artifact on any node with the same GPU model and driver. The process continues from where it was checkpointed, so weight loading, compilation, and graph capture are skipped. Both operations use Kubernetes custom resources. To checkpoint a Pod that is already running, create a PodSnapshot that names it. To start a Pod from a template and checkpoint it as soon as it is ready, create a SnapshotJob instead. To restore, add the annotation nvidia.com/restore-from to a new Pod, naming the PodSnapshot to restore from. The workload only needs a small handshake to pause before the checkpoint and resume after the restore. The repository has ready-made examples for vLLM, SGLang, and NVIDIA TensorRT LLM . Snapshot can checkpoint and restore compatible workloads that span multiple GPUs on a single node as a single checkpoint artifact across ranks. This supports fast startup for large mixture-of-experts (MoE) models using parallelism strategies such as tensor parallelism (TP), data and expert parallelism (DEP), and decode context parallelism (DCP). Workloads must meet Snapshot’s checkpoint/restore and runtime compatibility requirements . See the example configurations . Benchmarks Design partners have also evaluated Snapshot on their own workloads: Crusoe , an upstream contributor to Snapshot, reduced GLM-5.3 Pod readiness time from roughly 8 minutes to 31 seconds on NVIDIA HGX B300. Saturn Cloud , a token factory platform, benchmarked NVIDIA Snapshot for scale-from-zero inference, cutting vLLM startup from 2–8.5 minutes to 6–34 seconds on NVIDIA HGX B300 . The following benchmarks show how Snapshot accelerates inference startup across vLLM, SGLang, and NVIDIA TensorRT LLM (TRT-LLM)—with models from 600 million parameters to mixture-of-experts (MoE) models with 1 TB checkpoints on 8 GPUs. Across all tested configurations, Snapshot brings a replica back in under 45 seconds, 8x to 36x faster than a cold start. Methodology Each configuration was tested using two strategies on the same hardware and software stack: Cold start: The workload starts from scratch. The clock runs from process launch until engine initialization returns, before inference. The measurement is divided into four phases (Table 2): Startup: Starting the engine and worker processes, importing Python libraries, and setting up communication between GPUs. Some just-in-time (JIT) kernel compilation also happens here. Model load: Reading the model weights and constructing the model’s tensors, including any engine-specific conversion or repacking done while loading. Initialization: Preparing the loaded model to serve: memory profiling, allocating the key-value (KV) cache and runtime buffers, and other kernel and runtime preparation. Compilation, autotuning, and graph capture: Compiling kernels (for example, with torch.compile ), autotuning them for the GPU, and capturing CUDA graphs. Snapshot: The workload is restored from its checkpoint. The clock runs from the moment Snapshot is asked to restore until the workload is serving again. The measurement is divided into four stages (Table 3): Agent setup: The Snapshot agent on the node locates the checkpoint artifact and prepares the target Pod and GPUs. Checkpoint/Restore in Userspace (CRIU) restore: CRIU, the standard Linux tool for checkpointing processes, reads the process image from storage into host memory. Speed is set mostly by the storage backend. CUDA restore: Copying GPU state back into GPU memory. Wake/remap: Adapting the process to the new node and waking the engine. Both measurements exclude pulling the container image and setting up the container runtime. The KV cache release is triggered before every checkpoint, so it is not part of the artifact. Table 1 also reports checkpoint time and size: how long it takes to capture a fully initialized replica and how much storage the stored artifact requires. This is a one-time cost per model and configuration. Setup GPU: NVIDIA B200 NVIDIA driver: 615.71.09 Storage backend: VAST (NFS) Inference engines: vLLM 0.31.0 SGLang 0.5.21 TensorRT LLM 1.3.0 Results The benchmarks show four main findings. Restore times stayed under 43 seconds: Across all tested configurations, Snapshot restored replicas in 3.6 to 42.7 seconds—8x to 36x faster than cold start. The largest MoE models, with checkpoints of about 600 GB to 1 TB across eight GPUs, restored in under 43 seconds compared with cold-start times of 6 to 19 minutes. Restoring skips more than weight loading: Cold-start time includes loading weights, compiling and autotuning kernels, and capturing CUDA graphs. Snapshot restores the initialized workload, skipping these repeated steps. Checkpointing pays off with the first restored replica: In every tested configuration, checkpoint time plus restore time was shorter than a single cold start. Checkpoint creation took 15 seconds to 5.5 minutes, depending on the model and configuration. Moving GPU state dominates large restores: For the eight-GPU MoE configurations, restoring GPU state took 18 to 29 seconds. Restoring CPU process state with CRIU took 4.2 to 10.8 seconds. Figures 2 to 4 compare cold-start and Snapshot restore times for vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT LLM across the tested models and parallelism configurations. Table 1 provides the data for every configuration, including checkpoint time and size. All times are in seconds. In the figures and tables, TEP8 denotes tensor and expert parallelism across eight GPUs . Figure 2. vLLM: Cold start compared with Snapshot for every model and parallelism tested. Snapshot brings each replica up in 4.7 to 39.6 seconds Figure 3. SGLang: Cold start compared with Snapshot for every model and parallelism tested. Snapshot brings each replica up in 3.6 to 42.7 seconds Figure 4. TensorRT LLM (TRT-LLM): Cold start compared with Snapshot for every model and parallelism tested. Snapshot brings each replica up in 7.79 to 33.55 seconds Model Engine Parallelism Weight size (GB) Checkpoint size (GB) Checkpoint time (s) Cold start (s) Snapshot agent restore (s) Speedup Qwen3-0.6B vLLM TP1 1.50 8.13 15.30 104.43 4.66 22.40x Qwen3-0.6B SGLang TP1 1.50 9.42 20.71 87.08 3.59 24.26x Qwen3-0.6B TRT-LLM TP1 1.50 8.04 20.07 121.26 8.15 14.88x Qwen3-14B vLLM TP1 29.54 37.71 19.98 122.76 5.72 21.45x Qwen3-14B vLLM TP2 29.54 48.29 38.37 139.63 6.19 22.

title: Manage Kubernetes Clusters for GPU Infrastructure with NVIDIA Kubernetes Engine
abstract:
NVIDIA is announcing two open source projects for building and operating managed Kubernetes services on GPU infrastructure—NVIDIA Kubernetes Engine (NVKE) and NVIDIA Kubernetes Recipes (NVKR). Both are new projects available in public preview. AI Factory customers often want to consume GPU capacity through the Kubernetes APIs, tools, and ecosystem they already use, with the factory operating their clusters. Delivering this service requires API-driven provisioning, tenant isolation, upgrades, and recovery, backed by service commitments. It also requires qualifying GPU hardware, networking, drivers, and runtime software across GPU generations and Kubernetes versions. NVKE and NVKR divide this work between cluster management and reproducible software builds. NVKE provides the software to run a managed Kubernetes service, installed on the factory’s infrastructure, with APIs to provision and manage clusters. NVKR builds the operating system images, container images, and packages those clusters need, using recipes that define validated combinations of software versions and GPU generations. AI Factories retain control of their software, operations, service, and customer experience. Teams can adopt NVKE and NVKR projects together or independently. Figure 1. The NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform Both NVKE and NVKR are components of the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform , which helps AI factories design, build, and operate GPU infrastructure. Both projects are available on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 license, so teams can inspect the code, develop in parallel, and contribute improvements. During the public preview, APIs, configuration, and behavior may change between releases. NVKE and NVKR are not yet recommended for production workloads. See preview status and known limitations . This walkthrough covers building a node image with NVKR, deploying the NVKE management plane, and provisioning a customer Kubernetes cluster. How NVKE and NVKR work together NVKR builds the software: It produces node images, binaries, container images, and Helm charts from specific source versions and records the build inputs. NVKE manages the clusters: It uses those artifacts to provision and operate Kubernetes clusters. Teams can use the projects together or separately. NVKE has no runtime dependency on NVKR, and NVKR can build artifacts for other Kubernetes management systems. nvkectl starts a temporary seed cluster on a bootstrap host and uses it to form a management cluster. The NVKE management plane, including the REST API and controllers, runs on the management cluster. The management plane creates workload clusters for AI factory customers, each with its own Kubernetes control plane, etcd, and node pools. Machines come from NVIDIA Infra Controller (NICo) , which manages bare-metal lifecycle, through CAPNICo , the Cluster API infrastructure provider for NICo. A node must present an attested SPIFFE identity before it receives join credentials. The NVKE telemetry pipeline, an OpenTelemetry-based Helm chart, collects logs, metrics, and traces and exports them over OTLP to a monitoring backend. Figure 2. How NVKR, the NVKE management cluster, NICo, and workload clusters fit together Inside each workload cluster, teams add the GPU-accelerated runtime with AI Cluster Runtime (AICR) , node packages with NodeWright , and break-fix automation with NVSentinel . NVKE is a Certified Kubernetes AI Platform and Certified Kubernetes Installer , conformance tested on Kubernetes 1.36. From bare metal to a customer cluster This walkthrough describes how to provision a customer Kubernetes cluster starting from servers installed in a rack by building a node image with NVKR, deploying the NVKE management plane with nvkectl , and creating a customer cluster through the NVKE API. The NVKE documentation lists every flag and option, along with the most up-to-date steps. Walkthrough prerequisites: Three CPU servers for the management cluster, plus a separate Linux bootstrap host on the site network with containerd, nerdctl, kind, Helm, and kubectl Three CPU servers for the workload cluster control plane A pool of GPU servers for worker nodes A NICo installation with enrolled capacity A Linux build host with Docker and KVM support An HTTP server for the node image, a container registry for the controller image, and internet access to download the open source images and Helm charts used during installation Build the node image NVKR defines the Kubernetes software configuration that NVIDIA validates for NVKE and provides the reproducible pipeline that turns that definition into deployable artifacts. NVKR builds node images from version-pinned sources and records every input, so teams can identify the software included in each image and can rebuild it later. The management cluster and each node pool can run different images, such as one per CPU architecture or GPU generation. Teams clone the NVKR repository on the build host. They then run the quickstart script to build nvkectl , the NVKE controller image, and its Helm chart, and a second script to build the node image, named node-image-01 in this walkthrough. $ git clone https://github.com/dsx-ai-factory/nvkr.git && cd nvkr
$ bash scripts/nvkr-quickstart.sh
$ NVKE_OS_ARCH=amd64 scripts/nvke-os-local.sh node-image-01 The node image build compiles the NVKE node agent and OVN-Kubernetes from source and adds checksum-pinned upstream releases of the Kubernetes 1.36 packages and the SPIRE agent. It then boots a virtual machine from the Ubuntu installer, installs the agents, and stages the Kubernetes and networking packages on the disk. The result is a QCOW2 disk image. Teams push the controller image to a registry, copy nvkectl to the bootstrap host, and put the QCOW2 on an HTTP server. Deploy the NVKE management plane The NVKE management plane runs on a Kubernetes cluster called the management cluster. Teams run the following command on the bootstrap host to begin creating the management cluster: $ nvkectl bootstrap site -f site-a.yaml \ --nvke-controller-image registry.example.com/nvke/nvke-controller:<tag> The site specification file, site-a.yaml, includes the inputs that NICo needs to provision the three servers for the management cluster. The bootstrap command starts a temporary Kubernetes cluster on the bootstrap host. This temporary cluster uses kind to run a single Kubernetes node and hosts the NVKE software needed for the setup. The NVKE controller asks NICo for three servers, which NICo boots from the previously built node image. When all three nodes have joined, the bootstrap process deletes the temporary cluster, leaving the management cluster. Teams then install the NVKE management plane on the management cluster and run nvkectl config set-site to connect the command-line tool to the NVKE API. Publish a release set that customers will run Customers choose a release by name from those that the AI factory publishes. They do not work directly with operating system images or cloud-init configuration. A release set has three components: A machine image holds the iPXE script NICo runs to boot a server. A cluster release pairs a machine image with the cloud-init configuration that prepares a control plane node and records the Kubernetes version that cloud-init installs. A node pool release provides the corresponding image and configuration for worker nodes. $ nvkectl create machineimage -f machineimage.yaml
$ nvkectl create clusterrelease -f clusterrelease.yaml
$ nvkectl create nodepoolrelease -f nodepoolrelease.yaml Create a customer cluster A customer cluster request includes the same NICo inputs as the site specification, plus a Kubernetes version. The control plane and each node pool have their own instance types, VPC prefix, and release. In this example, the control plane and GPU node pool reference releases named k8s-1.36.3-amd64 . name: customer-a
controlPlaneKubernetesVersion: 1.36.3
etcdEncrypted: true
controlPlaneVIP: 10.0.20.

title: Introducing the Web Search API on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: AI agents and applications that answer questions about recent events, product releases, prices, or regulations need information newer than their model’s training data. Until now, Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore delivered that information to agents through AgentCore Gateway , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. That means creating a gateway and a web search target and calling the tool from an MCP client. The setup fits platform teams that share one search policy across many agents, but it’s more than you need when your own code only requires search results. Today, we’re announcing the Web Search API on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. With it, your own code can search the web with a single API call. It returns ranked results from a web index that Amazon operates, each with a text extract and, when available, the page title, URL, and publication time. You call it from the AWS SDKs or the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), signed with the same AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) credentials you use for your other AWS services. There are no resources to create first. Authenticate, call, and get results. Use it in an application, an agent loop you write yourself, or a data pipeline. The AgentCore Gateway is the recommended path for most agentic workloads. It gives agents one secure Model Context Protocol (MCP) endpoint that combines web search with your other tools. It also handles inbound and outbound authentication, semantic tool selection, and optional MCP sessions . But developers told us they also need a lower-level integration point for scenarios where the gateway is not the right fit: The Web Search API complements the gateway. It runs on the same search infrastructure that powers Alexa+, Kiro, Quick, and other Amazon products, with the same quality and compliance posture, exposed as a direct API operation. The Web Search API is the InvokeWebSearch operation on the bedrock-agentcore data plane, the same endpoint that other AgentCore tools such as AgentCore Browser , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, use. Requests are signed with AWS Signature Version 4 (SigV4) from your standard AWS credentials, so there’s no API key or secret to manage. Figure 1: How a Web Search API request flows The calling identity needs one IAM permission on an AWS managed resource. It’s the same action and resource that a gateway’s service role uses for web search, so one policy covers both routes. For details, see Grant permission to call the API . The following example searches two trusted domains for pages published in 2026, in the US West (Oregon) Region (us-west-2), with the AWS SDK for Python (Boto3) : Every result has a text extract. The title, URL, and publication date come back when the index has them, so read them with get . One result from a live call, shortened: That’s the full integration. If your code runs on AWS Lambda , Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) , Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) , or Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) , the execution role provides credentials automatically. Add the permission to that role, and the same code runs unchanged. Here are two ways to get a first result: There’s no resource to create and no API key to manage. Authenticate, call, and get results. The Web Search API fits naturally into popular agent frameworks. LangChain agents get it through the AgentCore web search tool in langchain-aws 1.9.3 and later: The tool can also hold rules that the model can’t change, such as domains to exclude, a date floor, and a search budget. It returns its results as data that your code can check. For a complete example, see the daily dependency watch sample . It researches three package ecosystems in parallel with LangGraph , and checks every finding against its sources before it reports anything. If you prefer to wrap the call yourself, a plain LangChain tool works too: Without a framework, the WebSearchClient in the AgentCore Python SDK wraps the same call and returns results with parsed dates. langchain-aws 1.9.3 and the AgentCore Python SDK 1.26.0 add Web Search API support, so install those versions or later. Because the Web Search API uses standard IAM authentication, you get enterprise controls from the first call: Quotas apply per account. For the defaults and how to request an increase, see Quotas for Amazon Bedrock AgentCore . By default, each account can send up to 10 requests per second in each Region, and you can request an increase. For details, see AgentCore Web Search Service Quotas . Agents and pipelines that handle sensitive data often run in private subnets with no route to the internet. With AWS PrivateLink , that code can call the Web Search API through an interface VPC endpoint in your VPC. Traffic between your VPC and the API stays on the AWS network, and you don’t need an internet gateway, a NAT gateway, or a proxy to reach it. Figure 2: Calling the Web Search API through AWS PrivateLink To set it up, create an interface endpoint for the AgentCore data plane service, com.amazonaws.<Region>.bedrock-agentcore , in each VPC and Region that calls the API, and turn on private DNS: With private DNS turned on, the API’s standard Regional name, bedrock-agentcore.us-west-2.amazonaws.com , resolves to the endpoint’s private IP addresses inside your VPC. The Boto3 and AWS CLI examples in this post run unchanged, with no endpoint URL to set. The endpoint’s security group must allow inbound HTTPS (port 443) from the resources that call the API. PrivateLink also gives you controls on top of IAM: PrivateLink works the same way in every Region where the Web Search API is available. Interface endpoints are billed at standard AWS PrivateLink pricing . For details, see Call AgentCore Web Search through AWS PrivateLink . You can try the Web Search API in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore console before you write any code. In the navigation pane, under Connections , choose Web Search . Figure 3: Web Search in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore console Figure 4: A test search with included domains The console signs each call with your own IAM identity, so your role needs the bedrock-agentcore:InvokeWebSearch permission. Both paths search the same index. They differ in a few ways. A gateway can also authorize callers with a JSON Web Token (JWT), while the API authorizes with IAM only. On a gateway, an administrator can set domain lists on the target that apply to every request without the calling agent seeing them. With the API, each request carries its own filters. The field names differ too: the API takes searchQuery , publishedAfter , and publishedBefore , and the gateway’s MCP tool takes query , from , and to . For more guidance, see Choose between the API and the Gateway connector . The Web Search API meters to the same usage type as the gateway connector, so it’s billed at the Web Search rate of $7 per 1,000 queries. Because no gateway is involved, there are no gateway charges. For details, see Amazon Bedrock AgentCore pricing . The Web Search API is available in the US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Europe (Ireland), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Asia Pacific (Sydney) Regions. For the current list, see Supported AWS Regions . Use the following resources to help you get started.

title: ICYMI: What landed for AI builders in October 2026
abstract: At AWS, we believe AI builders should be able to choose the right model for every task, trust their agents in production, and see clearly what their AI workloads cost. That belief guides how we invest across our portfolio. Amazon Bedrock gives you access to leading models and the tools to build and scale AI applications securely. We extend this foundation with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , which provides the platform to build, connect, and optimize agents using any model and any framework. That includes Strands , our open source agent development toolkit. Together, they take you from first prototype to production. As agents move into core business workflows, the bar rises. You need the flexibility to use different models as tasks, budgets, and latency targets change. When a primary model is throttled or unreachable, your agents must keep working. They also must act within limits you set and return output other software can use as is. Their answers must stay grounded in sources you allow, and their cost must hold up at high volume. What we shipped in October addresses each of these needs. New models help you match each task to the right price and speed, from high-volume subagents to real-time voice. Amazon Bedrock and AgentCore updates keep agents available, hold them to the processes you define, and help you trust what they return. New pricing and cost reporting make spend more predictable. Strands adds new ways to build, contain, and test agents. Run fast, low-cost subagents. Claude Haiku 5.5 is built for subagents and high-volume, cost-sensitive work. According to Anthropic, it is the most capable Haiku yet and costs around 75 percent less than Claude Haiku 4.5 for most tasks. It is also the first Haiku with effort controls, so you can tune cost against intelligence for each task. In a multi-agent setup, a model such as Claude Opus 5.5 can plan the work and hand well-defined coding, tool use, and browser automation tasks to Haiku. This keeps running many agents in parallel affordable. Get near-flagship results at a lower price. OpenAI GPT-6.1 Terra is now generally available on Amazon Bedrock. On OpenAI’s Agents’ Last Exam evaluation, it performed on par with GPT-6 Astra and completed tasks more than three times faster than GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol. Its input and output token prices are at least 50 percent lower than those of GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-5.6 Terra. It accepts text and images with up to 1 million input tokens, which suits drafting proposals, interpreting technical drawings, and building agents that work across business systems. For latency-sensitive work such as real-time coding assistants, GPT-6.1 Sol now also offers Ultrafast mode . Build voice agents that reason in real time. Amazon Nova 2.5 Sonic , our latest speech-to-speech model, improves reasoning, instruction following, and tool-calling accuracy, with lower latency at the same price as Amazon Nova 2 Sonic. A customer service agent can now look up an order, check return eligibility, and start a return in a single conversation. Pick specialized models for coding and video. GLM 5.3 by Z.ai is an open-weight model for agentic coding and long-horizon software engineering, with a 1-million-token context window and prompt caching, available to eligible enterprise customers. TwelveLabs Pegasus 1.5 turns entire videos into structured, time-coded metadata. It reads visuals, audio, and on-screen text in a single pass, with no separate ingestion pipeline. Use more models in AWS GovCloud (US). Claude Haiku 5.5 and OpenAI GPT-5.6 models with cross-Region inference are now available in AWS GovCloud (US). Daybreak Red from OpenAI , a model for authorized security work, is available to eligible customers in AWS GovCloud (US-East). Regulated teams get more models while maintaining US data sovereignty. Build and operate agents from your terminal. AgentCore CLI, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, is now generally available in version 1.0 . We rebuilt it with faster startup, a consistent command structure, and support for more AgentCore resources. You can work with harnesses, runtimes, memory, identity, gateways, and payments directly or through a project. Existing projects move to version 1 with one command. The result is one tool from local development to day-to-day operations. Keep agents available when a model is throttled. AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, now supports the Amazon Bedrock InvokeModel APIs and model fallback . Your existing Amazon Bedrock SDK code can point at the gateway without per-provider code changes. When the primary model is throttled or unreachable, the gateway routes the request to the next model or provider in a chain you define. A circuit breaker skips destinations that are failing. The gateway can also reach private targets in your virtual private cloud (VPC) using certificates from your own private certificate authority . Your agents stay available without retry logic in every client. Turn your business workflows into agent tools. You can now use AWS Step Functions workflows , including your existing Standard and Express workflows, as tools through AgentCore Gateway. Your business logic stays in a workflow you already run and trust, so you don’t rebuild it inside the agent or rely on a prompt to follow it. The agent decides when to run a workflow, and Step Functions runs each step exactly as you defined it. For example, a support agent can start your refund workflow, and every refund still goes through the same eligibility check, approval, and credit steps. Get JSON your systems can use as is. Structured outputs are now available for all Claude models on Amazon Bedrock. You receive schema-compliant JSON without custom parsing or retries. You can extract every required field from an earnings report, or route support tickets with entities that always match your data model. Keep answers grounded in sources you trust. Web Search on Amazon Bedrock now supports domain filtering and user location for requests made with the OpenAI Responses API. You can allow up to 100 domains, block up to 100 domains, and return results relevant to a geography. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails then checks that answers stay true to their sources. Its new Standard tier for contextual grounding checks costs the same as the Classic tier, covers conversational and reasoning responses, and supports more languages. With both, you can control where answers come from and catch hallucinations in more of your applications. Pay for agent memory based on what you use. AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, now prices short-term memory by the data your agents ingest, retrieve, and store , instead of a flat rate per event. Most workloads see lower costs, and small-payload use cases see the largest reductions. You can also set a time-to-live on long-term memory records to meet retention requirements and control storage costs. See what drives your Amazon Bedrock spend. AWS Cost Explorer, AWS Budgets, and AWS Cost Management Dashboards now break down Amazon Bedrock cost by model, model provider, inference type, and feature, at no additional charge. Finance and platform teams can find their most expensive models or set a budget alert for a single model, in the billing tools they already use. To lower input costs, Advanced Prompt Optimization can now also shorten your prompts, returning a shorter version only when it scores at least as high on your evaluation. Ship voice agents in a few lines of code. Strands Bidi Agents , for building two-way, speech-to-speech voice agents, are now generally available, with direct support for Amazon Nova Sonic, OpenAI, and Gemini models. Bidi Agents reconnect to the model in the background, so long calls keep going past a provider’s session limit. A voice agent can also hand longer work, such as research, to another agent and explain the results aloud. Let local agents work within your limits.

title: The attendee’s guide to the AWS re:Invent 2026 AI/ML track
abstract: From November 30th to December 4th, Amazon Web Services (AWS) will hold its annual premier learning event: re:Invent . At this event, attendees will become stronger and more proficient in various areas of AWS technology through a variety of experiences: keynotes given by AWS leaders, interactive working sessions led by AWS experts, and fun, immersive activities such as live entertainment and games at re:Play . There are over 2,000 learning sessions that focus on specific topics at various skill levels, and the AI/ML (AIM) track has more than 140 unique sessions for you to choose from. We’re here to help you identify the sessions that best fit your needs. Even if you can’t join in person, you can catch up with many of the sessions on demand and even watch the keynotes live. If you can join us, then remember that we offer several types of sessions that can help maximize your learning in a variety of AWS topics. re:Invent attendees can choose to attend breakouts, chalk talks, builder sessions, workshops, and code talks. The breakout sessions are recorded and uploaded a few days after to the AWS Events YouTube channel , while the rest are live non-recorded interactive sessions. Here are the details for each session type: With so many sessions to pick from, it helps to know how the pieces fit together. Here is how AWS thinks about its AI offerings, so you can decide where to begin and where to focus. AWS offers a comprehensive AI portfolio in the cloud. It covers everything from the physical infrastructure and AI chips that power AI workloads up through ready-to-use agentic solutions that teams can adopt today. Understanding how these services work together helps you navigate re:Invent and focus on the sessions most relevant to what you’re building. Global Infrastructure – It all starts with data centers designed and optimized for AI workloads. These facilities are built to handle the power, cooling, and networking demands that large AI training and inference jobs require. AI Chips – Running inside those data centers are two compute options: AWS Trainium , purpose-built for high-performance AI training and inference, and NVIDIA GPUs for teams that need GPU-based acceleration. Customers choose based on their workload, performance requirements, and cost targets. Data Foundation – AI is only as good as the data behind it. AWS Context connects your data across storage, databases, analytics, and search services, giving models and agents access to the right information at the right time. Models, Training, and Inferencing – This is where models get built, trained, fine-tuned, and served. Amazon Bedrock gives you managed access to hundreds of leading models from multiple providers through a unified API. Amazon SageMaker AI gives you full control to train, fine-tune, and deploy custom models on dedicated infrastructure. Many customers use both depending on the workload. Agent Development and Management – Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is where you build, deploy, and manage AI agents. It supports any model or provider mix, including models from both Amazon Bedrock and SageMaker AI, so teams can design agents that pick the right model for each task without being locked into a single provider. Agentic Solutions – At the top of the stack sit purpose-built agents that are ready to use. Kiro helps developers ship correctly the first time with spec-driven development. AWS Quick connects your applications, tools, and data into a personal knowledge graph that learns how you work. Amazon Connect delivers agents for customer experience, hiring, supply chain, and healthcare. AWS Marketplace gives you access to partner-built AI solutions. Security, Governance, and Cost Optimization run across every layer of the AI stack. They are built into the foundation, with hardware-level isolation at the chip layer and controls that enforce what agents can access and do. The AI-focused sessions at re:Invent span the full stack. Whether you’re evaluating AI chips, serving models in production, building custom models, deploying agents, or adopting ready-to-use solutions, this guide helps you find the sessions that matter most. Use it to build a smarter re:Invent schedule. The artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) track primarily focuses on three core layers of this stack: AI chips , models, training, and inference , and agent development and management , with security, governance, and cost optimization woven throughout. The following sections start at the chip layer and move up through models and agents. Then come sessions that tie the stack together. The guide ends with other relevant topics, such as sustainability and infrastructure where you run your AI workloads. Within each section, sessions for newcomers come first and technical deep dives come last. Want to skip ahead? Jump straight to the topic you care about: These sessions cover the core AWS AI services together: Amazon Bedrock, Amazon SageMaker AI, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and the AI chips that they run on. They help you make architecture choices that still work as your usage grows. New to AI on AWS? Start with AIM204 . It walks through the whole stack. You will see Trainium and Graviton chips, model inference on Amazon Bedrock and SageMaker AI, and production agents on AgentCore. If you’re already building, try AIM364 . It helps you choose between Amazon Bedrock and SageMaker AI, and shows when to use both. The example is a real agentic coding app that runs on AgentCore. Other sessions dig into specific production problems. If you own data strategy, attend AIM363 . This chalk talk shows how governed data products feed customization, inference, and agents. It also explains why cost levers like prompt caching, distillation, and batch inference work better on clean data. Need to prove the value of AI? AIM319 looks past cost to business impact. A live demo across the AI stack shows how to measure return on investment (ROI) and compare cost per outcome. Experienced builders should look at AIM443 . In this 400-level chalk talk, you build a training pipeline on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod. You bring in company data and keep governance in place. Then you deploy the same model to Amazon Bedrock for inference or to AgentCore for agents. AWS gives you two main choices of AI chips for training and inference: NVIDIA GPUs and AWS Trainium. Start with the one you use today, then explore the other. AWS offers a wide range of Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instances with NVIDIA GPUs. These sessions show how to run AI training and inference on them securely and reliably. Start with AIM2210 for the latest on GPU instances. In AIM3301 , a customer shares how it gets the most from its GPU capacity by optimizing GPU scheduling. AIM392 explains when EC2 G7e and G7 instances are a good fit in place of P-series instances. Want to tune AI infrastructure with self-managed agents? Join AIM346 . If you prefer hands-on learning, try AIM345 on disaggregated inference serving. In AIM344 , you find the cause of real GPU cluster failures and how to recover from them. In the AIM347 workshop, you can practice GPU performance engineering. For data processing, see AIM3312 . It shows how Amazon EMR with the NVIDIA cuDF plugin for Apache Spark runs jobs up to 3.7x faster on EC2 G7 instances than on comparable CPU instances without code change. The session also covers DuckDB on GPUs. AWS Trainium is a family of AI chips purpose-built for next-generation deep learning training and inference. It delivers high performance at lower cost. Trainium runs on AWS Neuron, the software stack that connects Trainium to familiar frameworks like PyTorch, so teams build without rewrites. Customers who adopt Trainium-based Amazon EC2 instances may see better price performance than comparable instances. If you’re new to Trainium, AIM211 is the place to start. It traces the full stack, beginning with the silicon and working up to the application.

title: Automating AWS Agent Registry updates with push-based architecture
abstract: Every time a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server published in the AWS Agent Registry, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, gains a new tool or updates its schema, the registry record must be updated too. Without automated push-based sync, consumers discover stale metadata. For organizations managing multiple MCP servers across accounts, such a sync keeps catalog records current within an existing governance workflow. In most enterprise deployments, a catalog’s value depends on its freshness. If a developer deploys a new tool on Monday, but the registry record still reflects last week’s schema, consumers lose trust in the catalog. Stale metadata directly reduces registry reliability, leading teams to inadvertently build dependencies on inaccurate information. When an engineer adds a tool to an MCP server but forgets to update the catalog: Multiplied across teams, this lack of automation erodes trust in the registry. Organizations ultimately fall back on ad hoc discovery mechanisms like hardcoded endpoints, informal knowledge sharing, and stale documentation. In this post, we outline an event-driven architecture that automates these updates using AWS CloudTrail, Amazon EventBridge, and AWS Lambda. The following solution brings these services together into an event-driven pipeline that detects runtime changes and synchronizes them to the registry automatically. The architecture supports both multi-account and single-account environments: The sample uses two accounts, but you can scale the architecture for multiple accounts, with Account A as the registry account and multiple AWS accounts similar to Account B for different MCP servers. The following diagram shows the end-to-end event flow for an update to an MCP server in Account B. The captured event is forwarded to Account A, where a Lambda function queries the MCP server for its tools and updates the matching registry record. Figure 1: End-to-end event flow for a cross-account MCP server update, from the CloudTrail event in Account B to the registry record update in Account A. The architecture uses five AWS services: After it’s deployed, the pipeline runs the following end-to-end workflow: This flow assumes that the Agent Registry in Account A already contains a pre-registered record for the MCP server (created during initial onboarding). The Lambda function in this sample updates existing records only. It doesn’t generate new ones. This same flow works in a single-account setup where all resources (registry, Lambda, Amazon EventBridge rule, and MCP server) reside in one account. In that case, skip the cross-account forwarding step. Events flow directly within the same account’s Amazon EventBridge bus. This section walks through the workflow for a single MCP server update with two accounts as depicted in the architecture diagram. The same flow executes independently for each server that emits an UpdateAgentRuntime event. The Lambda handles one event at a time, scaling naturally with the Amazon EventBridge invocation model. When a developer deploys or updates an MCP server, the UpdateAgentRuntime API is called, either by the AgentCore CLI ( agentcore deploy ) or directly. AWS CloudTrail records this as a management event in Account B, with a delivery delay of approximately 5–15 minutes. The event is then delivered to Account A’s default Amazon EventBridge bus. For a cross-account setup, Account B’s Amazon EventBridge forwards matching events to Account A’s event bus through a cross-account rule. The Amazon EventBridge rule target in Account A invokes the sync Lambda, passing the full CloudTrail event JSON as the input payload. The Amazon EventBridge rule pattern: The Lambda parses the runtime ARN from the event. It extracts the hosting Account ID and AWS Region to dynamically construct the target MCP server’s URL-encoded invocation endpoint. The Lambda authenticates using a two-step identity flow. It exchanges its execution identity for a temporary workload token. The Lambda then trades this token for a scoped OAuth bearer token through the target account’s credential provider. Credential providers are per-account ( CREDENTIAL_PROVIDER_{ACCT_ID} ), so one Lambda authenticates MCP servers across multiple accounts. Using standard MCP streamable-HTTP mechanics, the Lambda establishes an active session through an initialize request. After the session is active, it calls tools/list to fetch the complete array of currently exposed tools and schemas. The Lambda queries the central Agent Registry to locate the corresponding record. It searches APPROVED records for one whose mcpServer.data contains the runtime ARN embedded during record creation (see the Deployment section). To minimize unnecessary writes, tool lists are normalized (sorted by name, compared using name + description + inputSchema). The registry update only fires when a change is detected. If the schemas differ, the Lambda logs the exact additions or removals and pushes the fresh definitions to the registry record. AWS Agent Registry enforces a governance lifecycle on each record: Draft -> Pending Approval -> Approved (or Rejected/Deprecated). Administrators configure approval settings at the registry level. These settings control what gets published, who reviews it, and whether records require manual approval before becoming discoverable. Only records in Approved status are visible to consumers through search, catalog browsing, or the registry’s MCP endpoint. When the Lambda updates a record with new tool definitions, the record automatically reverts to Draft status. Consumers continue to see the previously approved version. A curator or administrator must then approve the update before the new metadata becomes discoverable. This way the automated updates cannot bypass organizational review, and administrators retain full control over what is exposed to consumers. The following table outlines steps in the automation pipeline: Before deploying this solution, verify that the following are in place: Organizations often use multiple accounts, where the registry is in one account but the MCP servers are in others. This sample outlines the multi-account scenario, which you can convert to a single-account scenario by following the instructions. In this sample, before the sync pipeline can work, a registry record must exist with the runtime ARN explicitly embedded in its server schema. You can use the following code to create the registry record and include the runtime ARN in the record’s mcpServer.data field. This is what the Lambda matches against to correlate AWS CloudTrail events to records: The Lambda only syncs to APPROVED records. After making the update, the registry record is in the DRAFT stage. It must move through the governance workflow for the change to be discoverable. To maintain a strong security posture, zero client secrets are stored in the Lambda environment variables. The function relies entirely on mapping environment variables to reference runtime workload identities, provider names, and permission scopes. This rule acts as the pipeline trigger, listening for UpdateAgentRuntime management events within the local account or arriving from cross-account Amazon EventBridge bus forwarders: To avoid ongoing charges, delete the following resources when you are done: You can find the cleanup code in the sample repository . The sample code outlined here (and in the full sample) can be extended in several ways: The AWS Agent Registry gives organizations a governed, discoverable catalog for their AI agents and MCP servers. The push-sync Lambda pattern closes the freshness gap: when a server change is detected, the registry record is updated automatically and securely, within the constraints described in the Known limitations section. Updates revert the record to DRAFT status and must pass through the approval workflow before becoming discoverable again.

title: How DXC Technology built a multi-model AI substrate on Amazon Bedrock
abstract: This post is co-written with Nick Tamburro of DXC Technology. When an AI agent can act on a production server at a bank or a hospital, access to a capable foundation model is only the starting point. Recent public incidents, in which autonomous agents took destructive actions their operators never intended, show that the real risk is rarely the model alone. It’s an agent holding more authority than its task requires, with nothing in the architecture to stop it. Avoiding that starts with a substrate that governs model access at the infrastructure level. Amazon Bedrock provides that substrate. Through a single managed interface, it gives DXC OASIS access to multiple foundation models: Anthropic Claude, Amazon Nova , Meta Llama, and open-weight families. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails enforce content filtering, personally identifiable information (PII) redaction, and denied-topic policies uniformly across every model. AWS PrivateLink keeps inference traffic within the customer’s virtual private cloud (VPC), and serverless scaling avoids self-managed GPU infrastructure as a failure point. Because these are system-level controls rather than bolt-ons, they gave DXC Technology a governed foundation for what no model layer can deliver on its own: a trusted harness that orchestrates, governs, and audits AI agents across enterprise IT operations at scale. Model availability varies by AWS Region. See Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock . DXC Technology runs managed IT services for some of the world’s most regulated organizations: banks, hospitals, and government agencies. With more than 115,000 employees across 70 countries, DXC operates mission-critical systems where resilience and governance are non-negotiable. When DXC set out to build DXC OASIS, the harness for mission-critical IT operations, the team separated the problem into two layers. The first is a governed model substrate built on Amazon Bedrock. The second is the trusted harness built on top: DXC’s own orchestration, governance, and assurance layer. In this post, we explore how DXC built the resilient, flexible model substrate beneath DXC OASIS on Amazon Bedrock. We also show where DXC drew the line between what the substrate provides and what the harness must provide. Since general availability in March 2026, DXC OASIS has reduced resolution time by 95% on average across 56 measured use cases. Across every model, customer data stays within the AWS data boundary: prompts and completions are not shared with third-party model providers and are not used to train the underlying foundation models. “Our customers operate complex, business-critical environments and need both choice and resilience in how they adopt AI. Amazon Bedrock provides access to a broad ecosystem of models with the governance, security, and operational controls required at enterprise scale. That flexibility allows us to use the right model for the right task, adapt as technology evolves, and stay focused on delivering measurable business outcomes for our customers.” — Dan Gray, President, GIS, DXC Technology DXC OASIS separates the question of which model from the question of how work gets done. Amazon Bedrock is the substrate: a governed gateway to foundation models (FMs), reachable through one consistent API, with security and networking controls that keep traffic inside the AWS perimeter. The harness is everything DXC builds on top: orchestration across tools and systems, operational context drawn from 60 years of runbooks and escalation logic, policy enforcement, human-oversight gates, and full auditability of every agent action. The main risk DXC designed against was coupling the system to any single provider, framework, or deployment target. The following diagram shows the key AWS services in the DXC DXC OASIS architecture. Engineers and operators reach the system through Amazon Route 53 and an Application Load Balancer inside the customer’s Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) . The DXC OASIS agent runtime runs on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) in a private subnet. There, a supervisor agent delegates to capability agents that draw on a knowledge base, AWS Secrets Manager, Amazon EventBridge, and Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) . Every model call leaves the subnet through a VPC interface endpoint and AWS PrivateLink to reach Amazon Bedrock, so inference traffic doesn’t traverse the public internet. AWS Identity and Access Management (AWS IAM) , AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) , TLS 1.2, Amazon CloudWatch, VPC Flow Logs, AWS CloudTrail, and OpenTelemetry provide security and observability across every layer. Figure 1: The DXC OASIS architecture on AWS DXC began building DXC OASIS as a prototype in early 2025. A cross-functional team reached general availability in March 2026, scaling toward 130 customer environments on Amazon EKS with per-tenant namespaces and GitOps rollout. Building the substrate involved the following tasks: Every model DXC OASIS uses (Anthropic Claude, Amazon Nova, Meta Llama, and open-weight families) is reached through Amazon Bedrock model inference. A provider outage or deprecation therefore becomes a routing decision, not a system rebuild. Uniform access isn’t the same as uniform behavior, however: models differ in capability, response style, and failure modes. Substituting one model for another is an assurance activity as much as a routing change. Before a model enters production routing, the harness (not the API) evaluates it against DXC OASIS task suites. For more information, see Getting started with Amazon Bedrock . Resilience in DXC OASIS isn’t one control but the compounding of several. The following table summarizes the resilience controls and what each does for DXC OASIS. Beyond resilience, DXC OASIS also addresses data residency and sovereignty. Regional inference controls and AWS PrivateLink keep inference within approved AWS Regions and off the public internet, meeting the data-handling expectations of regulated tenants. The strategic reason DXC built on Amazon Bedrock is optionality. Because every model sits behind the same API, the team routes each task to the most appropriate model on cost, latency, and capability, and adopts new frontier models as they arrive without re-plumbing the system. Each task’s capability, latency, and cost requirements determine which model it uses, not system constraints. Intelligent prompt routing – A single serverless endpoint predicts response quality and routes requests between models in the same family. It sends simpler prompts to lower-cost models and complex reasoning to more capable ones. Prompt caching further cuts latency and cost. For more information, see Intelligent prompt routing in the Amazon Bedrock documentation. Custom model import – With Custom Model Import , the same governance and tooling extend to models that DXC or its clients bring themselves. Amazon Bedrock supports open-weight models alongside proprietary ones, so DXC pairs frontier reasoning with open-weight models a client can adapt and deploy under one set of guardrails. Every enterprise agent needs six capabilities. Some are substrate capabilities Amazon Bedrock provides directly. Others are things only the harness can provide because they depend on DXC’s operational context and accountability model. This boundary is also where agent safety is won or lost. Guardrails on model inputs and outputs are necessary, but only the harness can limit what an agent is allowed to do. The following table draws that line. To make the architecture concrete, the following use cases come from the DXC OASIS demo environment. The environment is built around AnyCompany Airlines, a fictional mid-sized airline running a hybrid on-premises and AWS estate.

title: Accelerating generative AI delivery with reusable assets
abstract: If you’re building generative AI solutions, reusable assets can help you stop rebuilding components that already exist: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines, document processors, agent scaffolding, and so on. This has a compounding cost: time not spent solving the customer’s actual problem. This post shows you how to access a curated catalog of 23 production-ready assets from the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center, now part of AWS Frontier AI Engineering & Services. These assets can reduce your development time from months to weeks, with evidence from companies like DoorDash , Lyft , and Ricoh . Since 2023, the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center has published open source reusable assets. These production-grade building blocks give you a validated foundation to start from instead of a blank file. These assets have powered customer solutions delivering measurable results: 50x increases in testing capacity, 90 percent reductions in engineering hours, and deployment timelines compressed from months to weeks. In this post, you will learn why teams keep rebuilding generative AI components, what makes an asset truly reusable, how companies like DoorDash and Ricoh achieved measurable results by using these assets, and how to access and deploy 23 open source assets from the catalog. For a complete list of all available assets, see the asset catalog at the end of this post. Three root causes drive redundant development across generative AI teams: The cost of rebuilding compounds. Each redundant build consumes engineering hours, delays customer delivery, and creates maintenance burden. Even AI-generated code requires production hardening, security reviews, testing at scale, and ongoing maintenance. These assets arrive already validated, security-reviewed, and production-grade, avoiding that verification burden. When teams finally reach production, they’ve spent weeks on undifferentiated heavy lifting, work that should have been reusable from day one. The AWS Frontier AI Engineering & Services resolves this challenge through reusable assets. A reusable asset isn’t a code snippet or a sample. It’s a production-grade, composable building block that implements a discrete generative AI capability. Reusable assets are validated for quality and security before publication. They include clear deployment guides for discoverability and are instrumented to track adoption across customer engagements. These assets are maintained across their lifecycle. Examples from the catalog include RAG pipeline components, document ingestion modules, agent scaffolding templates, evaluation frameworks, and prompt management patterns. The assets are tested in production environments, reviewed for security compliance, and refined based on real customer feedback. This is the difference between a one-off artifact and a building block you can trust. The value of reusable assets isn’t theoretical. Here’s what happens when teams build on proven foundations instead of starting from scratch. According to the AWS case study, DoorDash built a fully voice-operated self-service generative AI contact center solution using the Contact Center GenAI Agent asset. As reported, the solution handles over 100,000 calls per day with 2.5-second response latency, achieving a 50x increase in testing capacity. Using Amazon Bedrock reduced development time by 50 percent. The team reached live testing readiness in 2 months. Lyft used the same Contact Center GenAI Agent asset to bring agentic AI to life for riders and drivers, demonstrating the asset’s versatility across different customer engagement models. The Contact Center GenAI Agent provides automated question answering capabilities for both text and voice channels. It employs a RAG architecture to facilitate multi-turn conversations while maintaining context. The solution integrates with Amazon Connect and uses Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases , a fully managed RAG capability, for hybrid search and metadata filtering. Ricoh serves major health insurance payers, managed care organizations, and healthcare providers. These customers process hundreds of thousands of critical documents each month, including insurance claims, grievances, appeals, and clinical records. As Ricoh scaled to serve more healthcare customers, they needed a standardized, multi-tenant document processing approach. That approach had to onboard new implementations without requiring unique development and tuning for each one.
