Using the Accelerated Intelligent Document Processing on AWS asset as a foundation, Ricoh built a standardized, multi-tenant solution for automated document classification and extraction. This transformed their document processing from a custom-engineering bottleneck into a scalable, repeatable service. Results: As documented in the published case study, Ricoh achieved a 7-fold throughput increase, from 10,000–70,000 documents monthly. Engineering hours per deployment dropped by over 90 percent (80 hours to under 5). Onboarding time fell from 4–6 weeks to 2–3 days. The system now processes 1,000 documents in minutes during traffic spikes, delivering over 1,900 potential annual person-hours in savings. The GenAI IDP Accelerator, introduced in this 2025 blog post , is a scalable, serverless solution for automated document processing and information extraction using AWS services. This system combines optical character recognition (OCR) with generative AI to convert unstructured documents into structured data at scale. The AWS Frontier AI Engineering & Services continuously maintains the assets as well. Reusable assets become more valuable as teams shift focus from infrastructure to business logic. Two recently launched assets demonstrate how reusable building blocks can accelerate the development of next-generation agentic applications. The Fullstack AgentCore Solution Template (FAST) is a starter project repository. With FAST, you can quickly deploy a secured React frontend connected to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale with any framework or model. In this implementation, FAST uses a React-based frontend with the managed infrastructure of AgentCore to accelerate building full-stack agentic applications from weeks to days. FAST deploys in under 30 minutes using infrastructure as code (IaC), with built-in integrations for AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, along with Gateway, Code Interpreter, and Observability. Authentication uses Amazon Cognito, configured with enterprise security best practices, and the template is designed for AI-assisted development with extensive documentation and steering docs. With FAST, you can access a complete reference architecture that shows you how the pieces integrate, with a working full stack application that you can learn from and build upon. With the modular design, you can swap out major components (identity providers, frontend frameworks, hosting solutions, or agent frameworks) as your requirements evolve. The Agentic Chatbot Accelerator is a web application deployment solution that uses the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) for infrastructure as code so you can create agentic chatbots. Built on Strands Agents and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, this solution streamlines the development of agentic chatbot applications. The accelerator provides rapid deployment using AWS CDK, with scalable agent runtime management through Strands Agents and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. It is configurable and extensible for diverse chatbot use cases, with pre-configured patterns for authentication, hosting, and scaling, validated across customer deployments. Let’s walk through a concrete example of selecting and using the Contact Center GenAI Agent asset from the open source catalog.

title: Accelerating product development with AI-driven lifecycle management (AI-PDLC) in AWS Quick
abstract: This blog post focuses on how AI can improve and expedite the product development life cycle using agents built on AWS Quick, with human approval baked into the process. AI-driven software delivery is helping teams ship products faster than ever. As implementation accelerates, the upstream product development process becomes even more important. Coding agents can turn clear requirements into working software faster than before, but they can’t compensate for building the wrong product. With implementation becoming easier, your competitive advantage moves upstream to four critical activities: discovering the right customer problem, deciding which opportunity to pursue, designing the right experience, and validating it through a prototype. The signals that you need to make those decisions are scattered everywhere. Your customers leave feedback in Slack, your sales team logs insights in Salesforce, systems record incidents in ServiceNow, stakeholders document requirements in Microsoft SharePoint, engineers track work items in Jira, and teams make decisions in Outlook meetings and email threads. As your teams move between these tools, they disconnect context from the decisions it should inform, and lose more at every handoff. AWS Quick provides the connective layer for this fragmented knowledge. By grounding custom chat agents in connected enterprise data and storing their artifacts in shared Spaces , AWS Quick helps your team build with existing organizational knowledge instead of starting each initiative from a blank page. The AI-Driven Product Development Lifecycle (AI-PDLC) is a framework that applies these capabilities through a suite of six AWS Quick agents with specialized skills, producing a traceable set of artifacts at each phase. Agents gather and structure context, surface gaps, and draft artifacts. You and your team contribute judgment and approve every decision. The objective isn’t to produce documents faster. It’s to help your team think better, preserve why each decision was made, and give engineering and coding agents a specification grounded in customer evidence. We will show you how to configure the six-agent AI-PDLC suite in AWS Quick and use it to move from distributed customer signals to a validated prototype. Throughout, it preserves context from the first insight through the engineering handoff. The diagram shows the end-to-end flow of the AI-PDLC framework. Figure 1: End-to-end AI-PDLC flow, from scattered enterprise signals through AWS Quick agents to the coding-agent handoff It starts with the signals most teams lose track of, that is, the Slack threads, Jira tickets, docs, and call transcripts that hold the why behind a decision and what customers actually said. Enterprise connectors pull that context from Slack, Outlook, Jira, Salesforce, SharePoint, ServiceNow, and many more enterprise sources. Figure 2: AWS Quick builds a personal knowledge graph that links people, projects, and decisions across connected apps and folders AWS Quick can build a personal knowledge graph from your connected apps and folders, linking the people, projects, and decisions across your tools. Those signals feed the brain: the set of agents on AWS Quick, led by an Orchestrator that runs Discovery, Prioritize, Working Backwards, Spec Generator, and Designer. Everything they produce lands in one common language: a prototype_spec.md holding the acceptance criteria, personas, screens, data model. Every decision traces back to a source. AWS Quick can delegate development tasks to AI coding agents using the Agent Client Protocol (ACP) . ACP is an open JSON-RPC 2.0 standard with no vendor lock-in. Customers can use their preferred coding agent like Kiro or Claude Code to build against the specification generated by AI-PDLC. Underneath it all runs a human approval gate at every stage. You validate the pain points, approve priorities, sign off the spec, gate the build, and accept the review. Production data then flows back into Discovery, closing the loop. The agents do the work while you make the calls, and nobody has to leave their tool to do it. The AI-PDLC lifecycle spans eight phases: Discover, Decide, Design, Prototype, Engineer, Ship, Operate, and Learn. This post focuses on the first four, where the product team works. The last four are handled by coding agents such as Kiro, which build from the specifications the upstream phases produce. The upstream phases are implemented as six agents in AWS Quick. Figure 3: The upstream AI-PDLC phases implemented as six agents in AWS Quick Users interact only with an Orchestrator, which reads each specialist’s question framework at runtime, asks targeted questions for the current phase, and dispatches artifact generation to the right specialist. A single conversation drives the whole journey, and the pipeline advances only after human approval at each step in the workflow. Figure 4: A single Orchestrator conversation drives the pipeline, advancing only after human approval at each gate The Discovery agent guides structured pain point analysis across interactive Q&A, URL ingestion, and direct pulls from connected enterprise sources like Slack, Jira, support tickets, Salesforce, and research repositories. It scores every pain point for severity and frequency, producing a Pain Point Board that gives the team one evidence-grounded view of what customers struggle with. Figure 5: The Discovery agent produces a Pain Point Board scored by severity and frequency The Prioritize agent scores each use case against weighted criteria using two transparent 0–10 frameworks: one purpose-built for agentic use cases (large language model (LLM) capability match, tool availability, user acceptance) and one for traditional applications (feasibility, business impact, effort). The team can open the Scoring Matrix and trace exactly why one use case outranks another. Figure 6: The Prioritize agent Scoring Matrix shows why one use case outranks another Once the top use case is selected, the Working Backwards agent generates a full PR/FAQ using the Amazon Working Backwards method with customer FAQs and internal FAQs covering unit economics, failure modes, regulatory risk, and competitive landscape. If a concept can’t survive this scrutiny, the team learns that on paper before committing engineering resources. Figure 7: The Working Backwards agent generates a full PR/FAQ for the top use case The Spec Generator agent turns the validated use case and PR/FAQ into a build-ready specification, with separate templates for agentic versus application use cases plus a Design Handoff Brief for UX teams. Each spec contains acceptance criteria, user flow, constraints, and metadata that traces every requirement back to its source pain point, prioritization score, and the PR/FAQ that validated it. Those acceptance criteria serve a dual purpose: they’re the build contract the coding agent follows, and the review rubric the review agent audits against. What used to take multiple sprints of drafting and review becomes a focused session, detailed enough for engineering to build from design spec immediately, with few or no clarifying meetings required. Figure 8: The Spec Generator agent turns the validated use case into a build-ready specification The Designer agent generates journey maps , wireframes , and clickable HTML prototypes directly inside AWS Quick. It works from the Design Handoff Brief, personas from Discovery, user flow from the PR/FAQ, screens to design, brand context, and the emotional target drawn from the customer quote, so teams can validate concepts with stakeholders before committing to Figma or other design tooling. After the spec is approved, it’s dispatched to the engineering team for development. Figure 9: The Designer agent generates journey maps, wireframes, and clickable prototypes inside AWS Quick The entire loop is iterative, with humans reviewing and approving at every gate. Nothing ships without explicit signoff.

title: UAEF: A framework-agnostic system for closed-loop evaluation of AI agents
abstract: Teams building AI agents on AWS use a range of frameworks, including LangGraph, LangChain, Strands Agents, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Each framework records agent execution in its own way, so the structure of messages, tool calls, and handoffs between agents differs from one to the next. Evaluation tooling tends to follow the same boundaries: teams build metrics, scoring logic, and result storage against a single framework’s trace format, and they must rebuild them when they switch frameworks or run agents on more than one. This coupling makes a basic development question harder to answer: did a change to the prompt, model, or tools improve the agent? Answering it requires consistent metrics across versions of an agent and a shared record of past results to compare against. Agent quality also spans several dimensions that a single accuracy score does not capture: tool calling, response quality, responsible AI, performance, multi-turn conversation, multi-agent coordination, and reasoning. In this post, we introduce the Universal Agent Evaluation Framework (UAEF). Customers across 12 organizations in the telecom, healthcare, and financial services industries used UAEF to evaluate their AI agents with one consistent set of metrics and compare agent versions before release. UAEF is a framework-agnostic evaluation system: it uses adapters to convert traces from each framework into a common format, then scores those traces with 36 built-in metrics across 7 dimensions. It stores the results in Amazon DynamoDB and Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and generates reports and insights that inform the next iteration of the agent. This post describes how UAEF works, provides a playbook for choosing metrics and preparing datasets, and points to runnable notebooks for each supported framework. UAEF is a framework-agnostic evaluation system for AI agents. It takes the agent a team already has and scores it the same way across supported frameworks and runtimes. UAEF takes two inputs: the agent under test and a dataset to run it on. The dataset provides the inputs for each test case, and it can also include ground-truth answers, the expected output for each input. Ground truth is optional, and only metrics that compare the agent’s response against a reference use it. To evaluate tool calling, the ground truth must also include the expected tool calls for each test case: which tools the agent should call, in what order, and with what arguments. Everything after that happens inside the UAEF. Figure 1 shows the path a single evaluation takes, from the inputs to the reports and insights. First, an adapter reads the agent’s native execution, its messages, tool calls, and agent-to-agent handoffs, and normalizes it into one canonical trace, so that the steps that follow are identical no matter which framework produced the agent. Next, UAEF screens the trace for personally identifiable information (PII), such as email addresses, phone numbers, and credit card numbers, before data is stored. The evaluation engine then scores the trace on a selection from 36 built-in metrics across 7 quality dimensions. When you persist a run, UAEF records it as an experiment in Amazon DynamoDB and Amazon S3: Amazon DynamoDB holds the per-experiment metadata used for listing and comparison, and Amazon S3 holds the full results. With runs stored, a team can compare an agent version against a baseline to detect regressions and generate reports and insights that explain what changed and why. Those reports close the loop: the team evaluates the agent, learns what regressed or improved, changes the prompt, model, or tools, and evaluates again. Figure 1: UAEF closed-loop evaluation data flow The rest of this section follows that flow in order: the adapters that make UAEF framework-agnostic, the evaluation engine and its metrics, PII detection, experiment storage and comparison, and the reports that close the loop. Adapters are what make UAEF framework-agnostic. An adapter reads the record of an agent’s run, including its messages, tool calls, and agent-to-agent handoffs. It converts that record into one canonical representation called the AgentTrace , which is the only thing the rest of UAEF scores. Because of that conversion, UAEF works with the agent, whatever SDK it was built with (such as LangGraph, LangChain, or Strands Agents). It can run locally, behind an HTTP endpoint, or on a managed runtime such as Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with traces in Langfuse or not captured at all. UAEF provides an adapter for each of these, and they produce the same AgentTrace , so metrics, scores, and comparisons stay consistent across every one of them. A trace reaches UAEF two ways. If one already exists, from a past run, a log, or an observability store, it is handed to UAEF and the matching adapter normalizes it. If not, UAEF invokes the agent for you: given a runtime Amazon Resource Name (ARN) or an HTTP endpoint, it calls the agent on each dataset input, collects the response, and adapts it in one step. Either way, the output is the same AgentTrace . Because every metric, mode, and report operates on the AgentTrace rather than on a framework native format, the scoring that follows is identical no matter where the trace came from. That separation, normalization first and scoring second, is what lets a team compare an agent built on one framework against an agent built on another on a single scale. The evaluation engine scores a canonical trace across 7 quality dimensions, each capturing a distinct aspect of agent behavior that a single accuracy number would hide. Tool calling measures whether the agent selected the right tools, called them in a sensible order, and passed valid arguments. Response quality measures whether the final answer is relevant, complete, accurate, and grounded in the provided context rather than hallucinated. Responsible AI measures safety, bias, toxicity, and resistance to prompt injection. Performance measures operational cost in latency, token use, and throughput. Multi-turn measures how well the agent sustains a conversation, including context retention, coherence, and goal completion across turns. Multi-agent measures coordination in systems of cooperating agents, such as task delegation and the division of work. Reasoning measures the internal logic of the agent’s chain of thought, including consistency and freedom from fallacies. Each dimension is computed by one or more of 36 built-in metrics, and every metric returns a normalized score in the interval [0, 1], where 1 is best, so dimensions and the overall result share one scale. Metrics come in two families. Deterministic metrics compute a score directly from the trace and the ground truth and reproduce exactly on repeated runs. Large language model (LLM)-as-a-judge metrics score qualities that resist a closed-form definition, such as response relevance or safety, by prompting a judge model on Amazon Bedrock. You can also add your own custom metrics or draw on the RAGAS and DeepEval integrations. Because judge metrics feed an agent’s own output back into a prompt, that content is treated as untrusted input: an agent that can influence its judge can influence its own scores. The rubric is sent separately from the content, and the content is escaped so it cannot break out of its delimiter and be read as instructions. Each judge response is parsed strictly and must cite a verbatim span of the content it scored. A score whose evidence is not found is rejected rather than recorded. Judge scores are evaluation signal, not a safety decision, and should not gate a security control. For runtime enforcement on the agent itself, apply Amazon Bedrock Guardrails in its own invocation path. The full model is in SECURITY.md. UAEF records each evaluation as an experiment, so results from different agent versions can be compared later.

title: Introducing usage-based pricing for Amazon SageMaker AI bidirectional streaming
abstract: Usage-based metering for bidirectional streaming solves a software billing problem for real-time speech AI. Customers deploying streaming models on Amazon SageMaker AI bidirectional streaming pay for the endpoint infrastructure that hosts the model. Separately, model providers listing on AWS Marketplace need a way to charge for what customers consume during a live stream. Today, we’re announcing usage-based metering for Amazon SageMaker bidirectional (bidi) streaming inference, so model providers can report actual usage for the AWS Marketplace software charge. Amazon SageMaker AI endpoint infrastructure charges still apply. Deepgram , the real-time speech AI company, is the launch partner for this capability, bringing usage-based Speech-to-Text (STT) and Text-to-Speech (TTS) billing to AWS Marketplace. This post builds on a series of innovations between Deepgram and AWS. First, we introduced bidirectional streaming for real-time inference on Amazon SageMaker AI , which supports long-lived bidirectional streams between clients and model servers. Then, Deepgram enhanced Amazon SageMaker AI support with AWS Identity and Access Management (AWS IAM) temporary delegation , simplifying secure authentication for enterprise deployments, and expanded observability with enhanced metrics . Now, with usage-based metering, we further strengthen the foundation for production real-time AI, aligning billing with how customers consume streaming and real-time AI workloads. With AWS Marketplace software metering for SageMaker AI real-time request-response inference, model providers can report a unit count in an HTTP response header. AWS Marketplace uses that quantity for the software charge. This works for request-response APIs where the billable quantity is known when the response is sent. Bidirectional streaming is different. A client streams audio and receives transcriptions through the SageMaker AI API using an HTTP/2 event stream. SageMaker AI connects to the model server over WebSockets. A session can last 30 seconds or 30 minutes. Usage accumulates as the session runs, and the final total isn’t known until it ends. A response header alone can’t report periodic usage during that live session. Hourly software pricing can charge customers while a model is available, including quiet periods. With usage-based metering, providers can align the AWS Marketplace software charge with reported usage. SageMaker AI endpoint infrastructure charges remain separate and continue to apply while the endpoint is provisioned. The solution introduces a second WebSocket connection alongside the existing inference stream. When a bidirectional streaming session starts, SageMaker AI establishes two connections to the model server: Model servers opt in by returning one header on the WebSocket upgrade response: X-Amzn-SageMaker-Metadata-Stream-Supported: true SageMaker AI then opens a companion WebSocket to the model server at /invocations-bidirectional-stream-metadata . Both connections carry the same X-Amzn-SageMaker-Request-Id header, which the model server uses to correlate metering records with the active inference session. The model server sends metering data as JSON text frames on the metadata connection. Send records at a frequency that matches the billing model: incrementally as usage accrues (recommended), either as each unit is consumed or as periodic batches of units consumed since the previous record. Send any final record as soon as the session ends. Each frame contains exactly one metering record, rather than an array of records. The metadata stream has a rate quota of one message per second per connection, with a maximum message size of 512 bytes. We recommend sending metering records incrementally as usage accrues. This reduces the amount of usage left unreported if a session ends unexpectedly. Transport delivery alone does not establish that usage has been billed. Validate reported units against AWS Marketplace reports and buyer charges. Metering messages use the inference.count dimension, and ConsumedUnits supplies the quantity for that dimension. If the product charges per second of audio, a record reporting 12 minutes of metered audio carries 720 seconds as ConsumedUnits: 720 . The dimension name doesn’t mean one unit per request. The provider defines which audio counts as metered usage, and the AWS Marketplace offer maps the unit to its price. The listing shows one price per unit, labeled per request, with up to three decimal places. The ClientToken field supports idempotency. If a duplicate token arrives on the same connection, SageMaker AI drops the duplicate message silently. The metadata connection runs over TCP, which provides ordered, reliable delivery at the transport layer. If it fails to establish or drops mid-session, inference continues by default because X-Amzn-SageMaker-Metadata-Stream-Required defaults to false . Set this header to true when the provider must stop inference if the metadata stream becomes unavailable. This choice trades inference availability for metering continuity. It doesn’t guarantee that malformed or dropped records are billed. If you deploy real-time AI models for transcription, contact centers, voice agents, or captioning, the new metering model changes how the AWS Marketplace software charge is calculated. SageMaker AI endpoint infrastructure charges still apply. Transparent, per-unit billing through AWS Marketplace means usage flows directly into your AWS bill. You get consolidated AWS billing, negotiated rates through private offers, and no separate billing relationship with the model provider to manage. Pay for audio processed according to the product’s unit definition. If the product charges per second of audio, 12 minutes of metered audio equals 720 billable seconds and ConsumedUnits: 720 . An open connection lasting 12 minutes doesn’t, by itself, define the billable audio quantity. The provider’s counting rules determine the metered usage, whereas endpoint infrastructure charges remain separate. Model providers can offer negotiated per-unit rates or fixed-price contracts through AWS Marketplace private offers. We recommend discussing directly with your AWS account representative or partner representative. If you’re a model provider listing on AWS Marketplace, you can configure your model server to report usage during streaming inference sessions through companion metadata streaming. The SageMaker Marketplace Onboarding Agent Skill accelerates onboarding with an opt-in inference metering path. Its starter templates advertise metadata-stream support and build validated, incremental ConsumedUnits frames for the companion WebSocket. Review and production-harden the code before submission. Align billing with your pricing model by defining what one unit represents and reporting units as the session progresses. AWS Marketplace charges one per-unit price for real-time inference. The following three-step walkthrough describes how to integrate your model server to report metering data during bidirectional streaming inference sessions. When SageMaker AI opens the data WebSocket connection to your model server, include these headers in your WebSocket upgrade (101) response: After your model server returns X-Amzn-SageMaker-Metadata-Stream-Supported: true , SageMaker AI opens a second WebSocket connection to your model server at the default path /invocations-bidirectional-stream-metadata (or the custom path you specified by using X-Amzn-SageMaker-Metadata-Invocation-Path ). SageMaker AI includes the header X-Amzn-SageMaker-Request-Id on both the data and metadata WebSocket handshakes. Your model server must do the following: Send metering data as a JSON object in a WebSocket text frame on the metadata connection. Each frame must contain exactly one metering record.

title: Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro on Amazon Bedrock
abstract: Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed from Moonshot AI is now available on Amazon Bedrock . Part of Moonshot AI’s new K3.1 series, it’s a post-trained version of Kimi K3 with the same 3T-class open-weight architecture and 1-million-token context window, trained with substantially more post-training compute. According to Moonshot AI, that extra training targets long-horizon agentic work and fewer factual errors. It also improves professional tasks such as financial modeling and office documents, and coding for game engines, 3D scenes, and computer-aided design (CAD) scripts. Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed generates output tokens at a higher rate and Moonshot AI reports 2–3 times the speed of Kimi K3.1 Pro. Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed uses the same endpoint, APIs, and features as Kimi K3 on Amazon Bedrock. If you already build with Kimi K3, you can try it by changing the model ID in your existing code. Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed supports tool calling, structured output, configurable reasoning, image input, and streaming. You can adopt Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed without changing your security posture. Your data is processed within the AWS data boundary, isn’t shared with Moonshot AI, and isn’t used to train the model. Zero data retention is always enabled for inference requests, and with zero operator access, AWS operators can’t view your prompts and completions during inference. In this post, we show you how to get started with Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed on Amazon Bedrock. We also cover how to lower costs with the Flex tier, explicit prompt caching for repeated context, and how to use the model as a coding assistant in OpenCode. To try the model without writing code, open the Amazon Bedrock console , choose Test , then Playground , and select Kimi K3.1 . From code, Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed is available on the bedrock-runtime endpoint through the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions and Responses APIs, and through the Amazon Bedrock Converse and Invoke APIs. We recommend the Chat Completions API. You reach the model through cross-Region inference profiles: To follow the examples, you need: If your application already uses the OpenAI SDK, point it at the Amazon Bedrock endpoint and change the model name. The following example creates a short-term bearer token from your AWS credentials and sends one request: Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed always reasons before it answers. With reasoning_effort , you control how much: low , high , or max . If you don’t set it, the model uses max , so a lower value is the most direct way to reduce latency and output tokens on simpler tasks. The same client works with the Responses API, which uses reasoning.effort for the same setting: If you already use the Amazon Bedrock Converse API, the change is the model ID: The Flex tier serves Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed at half the Standard price, in exchange for potentially longer response times. It’s well suited to workloads where cost efficiency is a higher priority than response time, such as model evaluations, content summarization, and background tasks in agentic workflows. Because you choose the tier for each request, one application can mix tiers. For example, the same application could use Priority for latency-critical requests, Standard for everyday traffic, and Flex for cost-sensitive work. Your on-demand quota is shared across the Standard, Priority, and Flex tiers. To use Flex, set service_tier to flex . The following example reuses the Chat Completions client from earlier: On the Converse API, set serviceTier to {"type": "flex"} instead. To see how much of your traffic each tier served, use the ServiceTier and ResolvedServiceTier dimensions in Amazon CloudWatch . We recommend starting with a small share of your traffic on Flex and comparing latency and cost before you move more. Agents and coding assistants resend the same large prefix on every turn: system instructions, tool definitions, repository conventions, and reference documents. Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed caches repeated prefixes automatically, and with explicit prompt caching, you can mark where the stable prefix ends to improve your cache hit rate. Later requests reuse that prefix instead of processing it again, which lowers both latency and input cost for long, repeated context. The following example caches a long system prompt and adds a second breakpoint after the user content, so a follow-up question on the same document can reuse both layers: For more information, refer to Prompt caching for faster model inference . OpenCode is an open source, model-agnostic coding agent that runs in your terminal. You can connect it to Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed through the Amazon Bedrock Chat Completions API, using OpenCode’s OpenAI-compatible provider and an Amazon Bedrock API key . To create a key, open the Amazon Bedrock console in the AWS Region that you set in baseURL , then choose API keys . Short-term keys last up to 12 hours, work only in the Region where you generate them, and are recommended for production use. Long-term keys are intended for exploration. Add the following to ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json , replacing the Region in baseURL with your own: Start OpenCode in your project directory, enter /connect , choose Amazon Bedrock (Chat Completions) , and paste your API key as shown in Figure 1. OpenCode stores the key, so you connect once per key. To switch between Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed and other models during a session, enter /models . Figure 1: Connecting OpenCode to the Amazon Bedrock (Chat Completions) provider The capabilities entry in the configuration lists the reasoning effort levels that the model supports, so OpenCode offers low , high , and max as variants of the model, as shown in Figure 2: Figure 2: Reasoning effort variants for Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed in OpenCode Output speed matters most in agentic coding. To complete a single task, a coding agent makes many model calls in a row. It reads files, plans a change, edits code, runs tests, and fixes what fails. Each call has to finish before the next one starts, and much of that time is spent generating reasoning and code. A higher output-token rate shortens every step, so the whole edit-test-fix loop finishes sooner and you wait less between iterations. Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed is available on Amazon Bedrock through the global.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1 , us.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1 , and in.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1 cross-Region inference profiles. For supported Regions and model details, refer to the Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed model card and Regional availability . For pricing, refer to Amazon Bedrock pricing . To get started, try Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed on the Amazon Bedrock console . To discuss your use case with the Amazon Bedrock team, connect with us .

title: Build a daily dependency watcher with LangGraph and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore web search
abstract: AI agents increasingly handle work that depends on what changed today, such as security advisories, product releases, prices, and regulations. A model’s training data can’t answer those questions, so agents need web search. For production use, teams also need results they can cite, and control over which sources count. They want search queries to stay inside their cloud environment because those queries often reveal internal work. The Web Search API in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is now available. It gives agents and applications current web results through a single API call, signed with the AWS credentials they already use. AWS serves every query from a web index that Amazon operates, and doesn’t send it to a third-party search engine. Each result includes the page’s title, URL, publication date, and an extract relevant to the query. Requests can include or exclude domains, and limit results to a publication date range. On AWS Lambda , Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) , or Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime , your agent calls the API with its execution role. There’s no search API key to store or rotate. Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is also available through AgentCore Gateway , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. There, one administrator source policy covers every agent and Model Context Protocol (MCP) client. For LangChain developers, the AgentCore web search tool in LangChain’s AWS integration now calls the Web Search API. One function call gives an agent current, cited search results. The tool can also hold rules that the model can’t change, such as a date window, a source blocklist, and a search budget. It returns its results as data that your code can check. It works with LangChain agents, with LangGraph , the orchestration framework that runs them, and with Deep Agents , which adds subagents, a virtual filesystem, and context compression. In this post, you build a daily dependency watch for a security team as a LangGraph graph on the Web Search API. Every morning, the watch checks whether anything new affects the open source packages and container base images the team ships. It researches three package ecosystems in parallel, while your code keeps the date window, the blocklist, and the search budget out of the model’s control. It checks each finding against the sources it cites and remembers what it already reported. Then you run the watch on AgentCore runtime, and offer it across teams through AgentCore Gateway. In our test, the three branches finished in 36 seconds, against 99 seconds one after another. The model decides what to search for and writes the findings. Every rule that must hold, whatever the model does, stays in code: the date window, the blocklist, the search budget, and the checks on each finding. Figure 1 shows how these parts fit together when you run the watch from the notebook. Figure 1: A daily dependency watch with LangGraph and the Web Search API, run from a notebook Before you start, you need the following: Web Search and model calls are billed per use. For details, see Amazon Bedrock AgentCore pricing . One run of the watch makes at most 12 searches. The complete code is in this notebook . The notebook runs every cell, including setup. The following steps cover the parts that matter for search. First, give the identity you run as permission to search. The Web Search API needs one IAM action on one resource that AWS owns, so the statement is the same in every account. (For the full setup, see Grant permission to call the API .) This uses the same permission that a gateway’s service role uses for web search: Now build the search tool that each research branch uses. The watch can’t let the model choose the date window, the trusted sources, or the number of searches. The graph also needs the returned sources as data, to check findings against them later. The web search toolkit in the langchain-aws package covers all of that with its options: With no gateway argument, the tool calls the Web Search API. Every search carries the blocklist and the date floor, and a model’s own arguments could only narrow them. With model_filters=False , the model sees only a query argument. The tool stops after four searches, and it returns the results twice: as text for the model, and as an artifact for the graph. Each branch creates its own toolkit, so the branches search in parallel. You can give the same tools to a Deep Agents subagent. With the search tool in place, define what each branch returns. Each branch is a create_agent agent with a Pydantic schema as its response format, so it returns findings instead of prose. A finding has the package, a one-line title, and the CVE or advisory ID if the source gives one. It also has the severity that the source states, whether the source says it’s exploited, a recommended action, and the source URL. The notebook has the full schema and prompt. Now assemble the graph. fan_out sends one branch per ecosystem with the Send API in LangGraph, so the branches run in parallel. Before a branch returns, code runs four checks on every finding. The checks compare the finding with what that branch’s own searches returned: After all branches finish, keep_new compares the surviving findings with a LangGraph store, and report builds the table. These checks catch an unsupported URL, a source that doesn’t name the package, an invented ID, and an out-of-window source. They don’t confirm severity, exploitation status, affected versions, or the recommended action. They also don’t prove when an issue was first disclosed: a page that the index dates this week can describe an older incident. For a production security workflow, verify findings against authoritative vulnerability feeds. Have someone review a finding before anyone acts on it. You’re ready to run the watch with a 7-day window. In our run, the three branches made 12 searches and got 80 sources back. They finished in 36 seconds of wall time, against 99 seconds for the branches added together. The evidence check dropped two findings: one whose source didn’t name the package, and one whose CVE ID didn’t appear in its source. None of the sources came from the blocked domain. Four findings passed the checks, and keep_new reported two of them. Earlier test runs had already reported the other two, so the store held them back. Figure 2 shows the run in LangGraph Studio , the visual debugger for LangGraph. Every row of the report links to its source, which the Web Search acceptable use terms require for any output shown to users. Figure 2: A run of the dependency watch in LangGraph Studio. The three research entries on the right are the three ecosystem branches, which LangGraph ran in parallel. The report lists only findings that passed the evidence check and weren’t reported before, each linked to its source Finally, run the watch a second time to see the store at work. A scheduled watch runs every day, and the team shouldn’t see the same advisory twice. In our second run, the branches searched again and kept two findings, and the store had reported both before. So the report had nothing new, as Figure 3 shows. Figure 3: A second run with the same input. The branches search again, but keep_new finds every result already in the LangGraph store, so the report has nothing new For a scheduled job, swap InMemoryStore for a durable store with exact key lookups, such as DynamoDBStore from langgraph-checkpoint-aws . If you already have a LangChain agent, adding web search takes a few changes. Check these before you deploy: With Deep Agents, you define the agent with create_deep_agent : a model, tools, a system prompt, and subagents. Pass the toolkit’s tools in a subagent’s tools list. Set the rules as toolkit options, because the tool applies them on every search, whatever the model asks. To check findings against their sources, as in Step 4, run that check on the agent’s output or add it as middleware.

title: The agent evaluation playbook: Built-in, DeepEval, and AutoEval on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations
abstract: When you deploy an agent to production, one of the hardest questions is whether it’s actually working? The bar isn’t whether it runs. It’s whether it does what the business needs, at scale. Many teams will tell you they can’t really see this. They spot-check outputs, watch latency, and collect user feedback when they can get it. None of that tells you whether the agent finished the user’s task, stayed on topic across a long session, leaked personally identifiable information (PII), or quietly skipped half the steps it was supposed to follow. Figure 1: Teams usually watch surface signals, but business outcomes are decided by the agent behaviors below the waterline Agent evaluation solves this problem. What makes this challenging is that a good score on one metric can hide a failure on another. A support agent can resolve every ticket and still expose personal information in its replies. In this case, the agent is failing although it has a high completion rate. To get evaluation right, measure the behaviors that matter for each agent, at the right level of detail. This post shows how to do this on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. We use the AgentCore built-in evaluators together with the DeepEval and AutoEval evaluators directly from AgentCore Evaluations. The most common mistake is to start with the metric list and pick the names that sound right. “Helpfulness sounds good, so we use it.” The result runs and produces numbers, but it gives almost no useful insight. The metric fits its label, not what success means for the agent. Instead, start with three steps. Figure 2: Translating a business outcome into observable behaviors and then into specific evaluators at the trace or session level This three-step process is the mental model that makes evaluation useful. The rest of this post is about what AgentCore gives you to execute it. AgentCore has a broad catalog of evaluators from three sources: Figure 3: The three evaluator tiers trade AWS quality assurance for increasing control over the model and account that run inference After creation, a custom derived evaluator is used exactly like other ones. AgentCore ships with a broad catalog of evaluators, so you rarely start from a blank page. Before you write a custom judge, check whether one already measures the behavior you care about. The following figure shows the whole landscape. Figure 4: The full evaluator landscape on AgentCore across built-in, DeepEval, AutoEval, and custom sources Built-in AWS evaluators fall into five groups: Next to these are three ground-truth trajectory checks: TrajectoryExactOrderMatch , TrajectoryInOrderMatch , and TrajectoryAnyOrderMatch . They compare the agent’s actual tool path against the one you expected. Reach for them when how the agent got there matters as much as what it produced. DeepEval provides managed open-source metrics in four groups: These metrics are especially useful for multi-turn agents. ConversationCompleteness catches an agent that answers the latest message but quietly drops earlier requests. KnowledgeRetention catches an agent that forgets something the user said three turns ago. AutoEval offers more specialized signals: Custom evaluators . When no evaluator in the catalog fits, you can write a custom LLM-as-a-judge. Every evaluator’s exact definition, scoring scale, and input requirements are in the prompt template library in the AgentCore documentation . That includes the judge prompt it uses, the trace or session level it runs at, and whether it needs a reference answer or an expected trajectory. You can call the ListEvaluators API to get the full catalog and your own custom evaluators in one response. Each evaluator so far returns one score per trace or session. That works when you measure one behavior. But step 2 of the outcome mapping rarely gives one behavior per evaluator. A support reply must resolve the issue, follow refund and data policy, and stay professional. One judge that weighs all three returns one number, and you cannot tell which criterion drove it. A multi-dimension evaluator is a custom LLM-as-a-judge with a list of dimensions instead of one scale. Each dimension has its own name, instruction, and numeric or categorical scale. The judge reads the trace once and scores every dimension in the same call. AgentCore returns one result per dimension. Figure 5: A multi-dimension evaluator scores several dimensions from a single judge call and returns one result per dimension with no composite score Use a multi-dimension evaluator when your success criteria can fail independently, such as an answer that’s accurate but non-compliant, or resolved but rude. It also needs every criterion to be judgeable from the same evidence, so that one judge call replaces several near-identical evaluators re-reading the same trace. When you score the criteria separately, you can gate on each one. A release that improves tone but regresses policy compliance fails, and a single blended score would hide that. Keep criteria in separate evaluators when an established built-in or third-party metric already covers them, such as Builtin.Correctness or ThirdParty.DeepEval.PIILeakage . Also keep them separate when they need different levels or judge models, because the dimensions in one evaluator share a single level and model. Do the same when some criteria need ground truth such as {expected_response} or {assertions} . Keeping the reference-free criteria in their own evaluator means it can still run on live traffic. Each of the following stacks starts with two or three evaluators that best match the business outcome. Add the others when you find a failure mode the first set misses. Evaluators marked “needs ground truth” run in batch evaluation only, because live traffic has no reference answer or expected path. Builtin.GoalSuccessRate (anchor) ThirdParty.DeepEval.ConversationCompleteness ThirdParty.DeepEval.PIILeakage Builtin.TrajectoryAnyOrderMatch (needs ground truth) ThirdParty.DeepEval.GoalAccuracy ThirdParty.DeepEval.KnowledgeRetention Builtin.Correctness (needs ground truth) ThirdParty.DeepEval.PIILeakage ThirdParty.AutoEval.Security (sensitive account data) Builtin.SkillInstructionFollowing AgentCore supports three evaluation modes. On-demand evaluation is the fastest feedback loop. Pass a session directly to client.evaluate() during development or debugging. Every evaluator in the system, including third-party, works here. Online evaluation attaches to your live agent runtime and samples real traffic at a configured rate. This is your production health signal. Built-in and third-party evaluators mix freely in a single online evaluation config. Batch evaluation runs a defined evaluator stack against a fixed set of sessions: your golden dataset for regression testing before releases. Use this to confirm that a prompt change or model upgrade preserved quality across every dimension you care about. All three modes use the same evaluator IDs. Switching from on-demand development testing to production online evaluation is a configuration change, not a code rewrite. Increasingly, the hard part is choosing which evaluators to pick. Pick the two or three behaviors that best show whether you reached your business outcome, and measure those first. Add an evaluator when you find a failure your current set missed. To see the full catalog, call the ListEvaluators API. It returns the built-in, DeepEval, and AutoEval evaluators in one response along with any custom evaluators in your account. Before you pick any of them, answer two questions: “What does success look like for this agent?” and “What behavior in the trace shows that it happened?”

title: Autonomous treasury agents: How Trovata built an AI-native solution on Amazon Bedrock and AgentCore
abstract: Corporate treasury teams face a persistent challenge: fragmented banking data scattered across dozens of bank portals, manual reporting trapped in spreadsheets, and legacy Treasury Management Systems (TMS) that can’t scale for modern enterprise needs. For treasury teams these manual processes create delays, errors, and an inability to make real-time cash decisions when they matter most. Trovata is an AI-native cash and liquidity management platform with direct connections to over 10,000 banks, serving enterprises globally from a single cloud-based platform. In 2023, Trovata launched the first generative AI built specifically for treasury. Now, with Trovata’s latest AI-native updates, they’ve evolved from delivering insights to deploying autonomous agents that act on behalf of treasury teams. Trovata’s customers have seen measurable results: $1M+ in annualized cost savings, over 5 hours per day saved per accounting team, a 77 percent reduction in annual TMS costs, and treasury reporting reduced from hours or days to under a minute. In this post, we explore how Trovata built autonomous treasury agents on Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, the architecture secured with role-based access control (RBAC) that supports bank-branded AI deployment, and how agentic workflows are transforming corporate treasury from manual operations to real-time decision-making at enterprise scale. Trovata operates as an AI-native treasury operating system, providing direct connections to over 10,000 banks through a single system for cash reporting, forecasting, analysis, and money movement. Treasury teams today face a three-pressure problem: Trovata’s evolution from its first generative AI for treasury in 2023 to its AI-native capabilities with autonomous agents represents a fundamental shift. The solution moves from static insights to persistent agentic workflows that operate continuously on behalf of treasury teams. Critically, Trovata AI is built directly into the treasury operating system. It’s not a generic chatbot layered on top, but embedded intelligence tied to real treasury objects with a governed path to automation through agents. Trovata chose AWS for this transformation for three reasons. Its serverless, cloud-native infrastructure supports real-time execution, Amazon Bedrock provides large language model (LLM) inference for natural language queries and AI features, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore handles agent orchestration with RBAC security, rapid deployment, and global scale. The core AWS services powering Trovata’s AI-native solution include: The Trovata AI architecture centers on autonomous treasury agents operating within a bank-branded, RBAC-secured framework. The solution comprises several key components working together: Figure 1: Trovata AI architecture on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, from the bank-branded portal through to multi-bank connectivity Trovata built its AI-native solution on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, combining autonomous agents, natural language querying, and enterprise access controls. The following sections describe what the team built, the primary use cases, and the AgentCore capabilities behind it. Trovata AI delivers autonomous treasury management agents embedded directly within the Trovata treasury operating system. These AI agents turn repeatable operational work into persistent workflows that run continuously. This is the work that consumes hours of skilled professionals’ time. Agents operate on schedules, triggers, or rules to monitor activity, explain variance, detect anomalies, and deliver updates automatically. The entire system runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a secure, isolated environment purpose-built for enterprise AI. When a user asks a question, the AI retrieves data through Trovata’s own verified API layer, analyzes it, and presents the response within that secure infrastructure. Treasury teams have already started building AI agents in production. Trovata’s AI Agents Playbook provides a working library of ten agent patterns drawn from real customer deployments, covering the most common and high-value treasury workflows. Most treasury teams have 5–15 workflows that are ready for AI agents today. Trovata’s implementation takes advantage of several key Amazon Bedrock AgentCore capabilities: To explore a similar architecture, you will need: If you deployed any example resources while exploring this architecture, remember to delete them to avoid incurring future costs. Remove any Bedrock agents, AgentCore configurations, and associated infrastructure that were created for testing purposes. Trovata’s journey from manual treasury operations to autonomous AI-powered treasury management demonstrates the transformative potential of agentic AI in financial services. With over $1M in annualized cost savings, over 5 hours per day saved per accounting team, a 77 percent reduction in annual TMS costs, and reporting reduced from hours or days to under a minute, the impact is measurable. The bank-branded deployment model is especially effective. Banks and enterprises get production-ready AI without building it themselves. Trovata AI shows how, with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, independent software vendors (ISVs) can embed governed, autonomous AI agents directly into vertical software as a service (SaaS) applications, delivering AI with the security and compliance-awareness that financial services demands. Looking ahead, Trovata plans to expand its agent patterns, deepen enterprise resource planning (ERP) integrations, and extend global bank connectivity. The company continues to advance what autonomous treasury management can achieve.

title: How TCS built an agentic test orchestrator with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: This post was co-written with Varun Valsan from Tata Consultancy Services (TCS). Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) runs large-scale testing for Banking, Financial Services, and Insurance (BFSI) clients, where the slowest part of a release is rarely writing application code. The larger constraint is the chain of work that follows: interpreting requirements, designing scenarios, writing and maintaining automation, preparing execution environments, investigating failures, and assembling evidence for review. BFSI clients need to increase testing throughput while preserving the controls expected in financial services. The objective wasn’t to replace quality engineers. It was to remove repetitive translation and execution work so that engineers could spend more time on risk analysis, exploratory testing, and release decisions. These industry needs generated four specific requirements for TCS. First, every test must be grounded in project-specific context rather than generic prompts. Second, it had to cover both API and browser-based UI testing to match how BFSI applications are built. Third, security is paramount, so every tenant’s data and knowledge store must be isolated. Finally, it must provide a repeatable path from requirement ingestion to test evidence and reporting, so the gains hold across teams and releases. In this post, we show how TCS built an agentic test orchestrator that turns requirements into executable, governed tests, and what it changed for its BFSI testing teams. TCS already uses traditional test automation for its clients, and it does improve execution speed. But it leaves the slow work untouched: teams must still create the scenarios, convert them into scripts, maintain locators and dependencies, and diagnose failures. When a linked user story changes, scripts generated for an earlier story can quickly become stale. A single generative AI prompt also doesn’t provide the control needed for a multi-stage engineering workflow. TCS therefore designed the Agentic Test Orchestrator to decompose testing into specialized tasks. Each task has its own agent, tools, validation rules, and context. A deterministic supervisor routes work, while an execution workflow controls retries, error classification, persistence, and reporting. To run these agents, TCS chose Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , a service to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Three capabilities drove the decision. First, Amazon Bedrock offers a choice of models, so each agent uses the model that fits its task, such as scenario design or code generation, and TCS can adopt newer models as they become available. Second, AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, scales with demand, so testers across many tenants can run generation and execution sessions at the same time without TCS provisioning or tuning agent servers. Third, the runtime runs each session in its own isolated microVM, which gives TCS session-level separation for its multi-tenant platform without having to build that layer itself. Together, these capabilities let TCS focus its engineering effort on testing logic rather than agent infrastructure, which shortened the time to bring the platform to its BFSI clients. The following diagram shows the end-to-end flow of the platform across five stages, with a per-tenant security layer underneath. Inputs from Jira, business requirement documents (BRDs), and GitLab enter a tenant web application that runs on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) behind Amazon CloudFront , with sign-in through Amazon Cognito . TCS uses Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime to host the platform’s specialized agents, built with the Strands Agents SDK . These agents generate the tests, refine them with the tester, and manage their execution. Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) runs the generated tests. Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and Amazon DynamoDB store the results, and Amazon CloudWatch captures the logs. Throughout, AWS WAF , Amazon Cognito, AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) , and AWS Secrets Manager enforce per-tenant security and isolation. Figure 1: High-level solution architecture The TCS Agentic Test Orchestrator is a multi-tenant software as a service (SaaS) solution built on AWS. A tester provides requirements through Jira stories, business requirement documents (BRDs), Swagger specifications, uploaded documents, GitLab source folders, or captured UI flows. From those inputs the platform then generates test scenarios, Gherkin feature files, and executable Java or Python tests. It runs those tests on Amazon ECS, stores artifacts and results, and shows progress and reports in a per-tenant web application. The sections that follow describe how each part of the platform meets one of the four requirements TCS set. TCS required strict isolation of each tenant’s identity, data, and keys, so the platform uses pooled compute with siloed data and identity. A shared control plane provides the Amazon EKS cluster, container registry, administrative portal, tenant registry, onboarding automation, Amazon CloudFront distributions, and AWS WAF protection. Each tenant application plane receives its own Kubernetes namespace, Amazon Cognito user pool, AWS KMS key, Amazon S3 bucket, Amazon DynamoDB tables, and Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases . This separation gives each BFSI tenant the data and key boundaries that financial-services controls demand. Tenant onboarding is event driven. The administrative API writes a pending tenant record, emits an event through Amazon EventBridge , and starts an AWS CodeBuild project that deploys the tenant infrastructure with AWS Cloud Development Kit ( AWS CDK ). This pattern makes tenant provisioning repeatable while retaining tenant-specific identity and data boundaries that TCS needed. TCS’s first requirement was that generation reflect each project’s domain rather than a generic prompt, so grounding is built into the platform. The platform stores uploaded requirements and generated artifacts in Amazon S3 and session metadata in Amazon DynamoDB. Project documents and synchronized source files are indexed in Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases using vector embeddings. Before material reaches an agent, retrieval is filtered by tenant, project, and session context, so one client’s context doesn’t inform another’s tests. This context layer supports the many ways a BFSI team expresses requirements: Jira stories and linked story chains, BRDs, Swagger definitions, reference code, locator documents, setup modules, test data, and GitLab source folders. For UI automation, a separate capture service uses Puppeteer to convert a URL and a natural-language goal into a UI flow document and an XPath locator document. Because a single prompt can’t give a regulated workflow the control it needs, the platform divides the work among specialized agents that run as containerized services in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime using the Strands Agents SDK. A generation runtime routes requests to dedicated scenario, Gherkin, code-generation, and validation tools. Additional runtimes support conversational refinement, BRD-to-story conversion, incremental generation across linked Jira stories, and test execution. Each agent owns a stage of the lifecycle. Here’s a brief overview of each specialized agent: Generation agent: Creates structured scenarios, converts them to Gherkin, generates Java or Python automation, and validates generated code. Chat agent: Classifies a request as an information query or an update request, then answers or revises the active artifact. Dynamic task agent: Retrieves BRD context and produces a structured user story with requirements and acceptance criteria. Incremental agent: Extends scenarios, Gherkin, or code across a linked Jira story chain instead of starting from scratch.

title: Amazon Bedrock tokenomics data lake
abstract: If you need an observability data lake for your Amazon Bedrock workloads, you’re not alone. When you’re running thousands of model invocations a day across multiple accounts, after a request is sent you might be wondering, what happened? You can see the aggregate bill, but you can’t see what happened inside each call. You might start to ask questions: what prompt was sent, what the model returned, how many tokens it used, which model handled it, and whether the response was any good! If you’re a platform or machine learning (ML) engineer looking after a fleet of Amazon Bedrock workloads across teams, that’s a real problem. You can’t debug a spike, you can’t spot wasteful prompts, and you can’t tell one team’s usage from another’s. We built something to help: a centralized observability data lake for your Amazon Bedrock invocations. In this post, I cover what native data you have and how we designed the lake. I also show how to use it to see your prompts and derive the per-invocation cost. The AWS CloudFormation templates, AWS Lambda code, and SQL queries are all in the AWS Sample Bedrock Invocation Data Lake GitHub repository . This post walks through the architecture and deployment steps. The repo has everything you need to deploy it. Amazon Bedrock offers model invocation logging , and it’s genuinely powerful. You turn on invocation logs in the settings in each AWS account you are using Bedrock . It delivers a full record of requests and responses to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) or Amazon CloudWatch . The data exists, but it’s locked inside individual accounts. What you really want is a single, fast, queryable view of every invocation across your whole organization. That’s what the data lake gives you. A centralized Amazon Bedrock invocation log data lake pulls raw model invocation logs from your linked accounts into Amazon CloudWatch . Subscription log filters then forward those records to your central account. The central account processes the data through Amazon Data Firehose , and exposes them through Amazon Athena as one clean table you can query across your organization. Figure 1: Amazon Bedrock invocation observability data lake architecture across a central account and linked accounts Everything is deployed as Infrastructure as Code using two AWS CloudFormation templates, so you can roll it out repeatably across every account in your organization. This can be found in the AWS Sample Bedrock Invocation Data Lake GitHub repository . After we run this solution, you will have a combined set of data across the linked account you deploy to so you can query with Athena. What you get per invocation after the logs are flattened into the processed table: After every invocation is captured like this, you go from “We used X tokens on Amazon Bedrock” to “Here is exactly what each model calls contained, and how efficient it was.” That’s the visibility platform and ML teams have been missing. The data lake moves each invocation through five stages, from the moment Amazon Bedrock writes a log to the point you can query it in Athena. Every time an application calls an Amazon Bedrock model, Amazon Bedrock can record what happened: which model, which account, which IAM identity made the call, how many input and output tokens were used, and the prompt and response text. You turn this on once per account with a single API call, pointing Amazon Bedrock at a CloudWatch log group and giving it a role that can write there. Each source account gets a subscription filter on its Amazon Bedrock log group. Think of it as a permanent forwarding rule that says “send every new event to this address.” The address is an Amazon CloudWatch Logs destination living in your central account. Source accounts don’t get permissions on the central pipeline. They hand events to the destination, and the central account’s own role takes it from there. CloudWatch doesn’t hand over clean JSON. It bundles events into batches and wraps them compressed and encoded, so what arrives looks like gibberish until you unwrap it. A small Lambda function does three jobs: Amazon Data Firehose buffers the records and writes them to an Amazon S3 bucket, converting from JSON to Parquet on the way through. Firehose also files each object under a date path ( year=2026/month=08/day=27/ ). An AWS Glue table tells Athena how to read those files, so you can query the lake with ordinary SQL. You can see which users are using the most tokens, which models are commonly selected, and what people are prompting. If you want, you can also connect this to the AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR) to get the spend of user prompts by day. A few things need to be in place before you deploy: The order matters here. The central account stack has to exist before the linked account stacks can reference it. Deploy the central CloudFormation stack first, into the account that will own the pipeline. Note two values from the stack outputs before moving on: the CloudWatch Logs destination ARN (which every source account needs) and the AWS Quick Sight role ARN (needed later if you deploy the dashboard). Deploy the linked account CloudFormation. Repeat this for every account running Amazon Bedrock workloads. The source stack is small and takes a single input: the destination ARN from Stage 1. Deploying the stack doesn’t start the logging. Amazon Bedrock logging is an account-level setting, not a CloudFormation resource. Activate it once per source account, pointing Amazon Bedrock at the log group and the logging role from Stage 2. Turn on CloudWatch delivery only. Run a test invocation in a source account, wait for Amazon Data Firehose to flush its buffer ( roughly a minute, sometimes longer ), then confirm Parquet objects have appeared under the data lake’s data/ prefix. Finally, check your S3 bucket to see data. The central stack saves the view definition as a named Athena query but doesn’t run it. Execute that saved query once to create the flattened view. Run queries in the dedicated Athena workgroup, against either the raw table or the flattened view. The view is straightforward: token counts, cache tokens, stop reason, and prompt/response previews are already flat columns. When you want a dollar figure against all of this, join the processed table to your CUR 2.0 data. The join key is the IAM ARN. You can use the following example queries in the Bedrock Data Lake SQL file. That one join turns the observability lake into cost attribution too: which prompts cost the most, cost per team or account by day, and what your least efficient invocations are actually costing you. It’s a great addition, but the data lake earns its keep well before you get there. Tokenomics, the practice of managing the economics of artificial intelligence (AI) token consumption, was announced as a formal FinOps domain at the 2026 FinOps Foundation conference. It’s built on the same See, Save, Run, and Plan pillars as Cloud Financial Management, but applied to tokens instead of infrastructure. The challenge is that you can’t optimize what you can’t measure. Most organizations today lack the granular data needed to answer basic tokenomics questions: which teams are consuming the most tokens, and which prompts are wasteful. With per-invocation token and cost visibility, teams can match each workload to the model that fits it. That’s exactly what this data lake gives you. With per-invocation visibility into prompts, responses, token counts, models, and IAM identities, you have the foundation to start running a tokenomics practice rather than only tracking an Amazon Bedrock bill. If you want to visualize your token consumption, we have an AWS Quick Sight dashboard. This shows you the data from the table over time so you can share it with stakeholders in your organization. Using AWS Quick Sight, you can customize the dashboard and add organization metadata such as team information to make it your own. To deploy this, use the cid-cmd deploy CLI command.

title: 雙11直播間爆改AI秀場，羅永浩上手TRAE，秒變AI Coding的大眾嘴替
abstract: 雙11直播間爆改AI秀場，羅永浩上手TRAE，秒變AI Coding的大眾嘴替 聞樂 2026-11-11 14:41:26 來源： 量子位 價格、門檻全打穿 聞樂 發自 凹非寺 量子位 | 公眾號 QbitAI 真是活久見，今年雙十一最有技術含量的事兒，居然不是研究怎麼湊滿減了。 下了班刷直播準備買買買，沒想到越刷越熟悉，AI啥時候混跡各大賣場了？？ 前有直播一哥熱火朝天帶貨兩萬億Token，後腳刷到老羅直播間—— 好嘛，AI程式設計工具也直接掛上小黃車連結了。 全鏈路AI開發平臺 TRAE ，也就是羅永浩口中的“崔老三”，首月體驗直接甩出9塊9的真香價。 自稱“一行程式碼都不會寫”的五旬老漢，當場支起電腦投屏，在幾萬觀眾圍觀下直接秀起了操作： 幾分鐘生成一份帶資料圖表的短劇調研報告； 把5萬多字晦澀資料，爆改成兩套釋出會級PPT； 就憑一張手繪破草圖，硬生生搓出一款貨真價實、全域性可用的語音輸入法軟體。 絕了，平時只在技術論壇裡被程式設計師反覆測評、摳效能指標的 AI Coding ，一夜之間被推上了大眾狂歡的帶貨舞臺。 So？大主播們今年咋集體賣起了高深莫測的技術產品？ 雙十一大變天 往年的雙十一，咱搶的無非是按箱囤的衛生紙、算不明白折扣的護膚品、各種參數的數碼硬體… 今年畫風不一樣。 李佳琦直播間的兩萬億Token讓大家第一次見識到， 原來AI也是能“按斤囤”的 。 但熱鬧歸熱鬧，很多普通人跟風下單之後，腦門上瞬間冒出一排問號： 我買了一堆冷冰冰的Token，到底能在日常生活中幹啥？拿去跟大模型聊天玩成語接龍解悶？還是隨便搜搜素材水個文件？ 大眾對單純的技術參數和抽象數字脫敏得太快了，當吃瓜的獵奇心過去，大家真正關心的只有一件事： 這玩意兒能不能變成我手裡能用的東西？ 大眾這種心理轉變，恰好折射出了當下AI賽道正在發生的變化。 這兩場直播，其實正撞上了行業的一個切面。 權威機構Gartner的2026生成式AI成熟度曲線顯示： 市場已經走過早期的概念膨脹期，加速走向看重落地效果的務實階段。 單純聊天問答的大模型增長見頂，而程式碼生成、應用搭建這類緊貼業務場景的能力，正在受到更多關注。 業內直接把2026年叫 智慧體元年 ，連國家網信辦都專門給智慧體立了規矩。 AI程式設計，正是這輪換擋裡跑得最快的賽道。 Anthropic年初那份編碼趨勢報告裡也提到，軟體開發正經歷自圖形介面發明以來最大的一次範式轉移： 任何人都能成為開發者 不再是PPT上的口號，程式設計師的角色也在“從親手寫程式碼”慢慢往“指揮AI幹活”挪。 除了賣底層算力、賣對話視窗這類原材料生意，行業也開始輸出能直接交付可用工具的成品力。 所以你再品這兩場直播：李佳琦賣的是原料，是算力額度；老羅賣的是成品，是能直接上手用的工具。 兩場直播撞上的，正是這條從賣對話到賣結果的分水嶺。 作為承接算力、直接產出應用的Coding Agent，它補齊了從原料到成品的斷層。 軟體開發過去被視為天書，但在直播間的全網圍觀下，它被壓縮成了一場像打字聊天一樣自然的過程。 觀眾們也看懂了： 這次上架的不是隨時消耗掉的對話額度，而是一套能把腦洞隨時做成真實工具的數字化生產力。 大眾對技術的心防，也當場鬆動了。 羅永浩現場造物 以前是人學程式碼去迎合計算機，現在反過來，人負責描繪想法，AI工具負責把那些抽象的意圖變成一行行程式碼和能點選的介面。 TRAE就具備 多檔案感知能力、環境自動配置，以及底層的原生代碼排程能力 。 以往軟體工程裡最勸退外行的繁瑣環節—— 配環境、裝依賴包、搭專案框架、修配置檔案報錯……這一大堆讓人頭皮發麻的髒活累活，全被封裝在系統底層，靜默跑通。 咱再說直白點，它能直接讓你光靠想法就做軟體。 而老羅是啥人呢？ 全網皆知的愛挑刺人設，有他在臺上，整場帶貨都變成了一場高壓力測試。 結果這位較真的門外漢直接大方表明： 我一行程式碼都不會寫，以前做軟體得招齊設計師、產品經理和一堆工程師，溝通起來跟孫子似的；現在有了崔老三，改上一百遍它都不帶翻白眼的。 在直播間裡，老羅投屏展示了他在幾個小時裡搓出的三大戰果，個個直擊打工人的日常痛點。 面對短劇風口，老羅直接給TRAE下指令，要求分析今年1到10月的短劇市場。 AI花了不到4分鐘就吐出一版純文本報告。老羅當場化身挑剔領導開始挑刺： 光有字不行，直接匯入飛書，能上餅圖的上餅圖，能上柱狀圖的上柱狀圖，既要顯得認真糊弄老闆，又不能騙老闆，資料必須紮實靠譜！ 老羅的電腦中途還意外卡死了一次，重啟後他告訴AI“剛才宕機了，繼續完成任務”，TRAE不僅沒嘲諷老羅“理解萬歲”，反而穩穩續上進度，幾分鐘內就生成了一份圖文並茂的飛書文件。 更絕的是隨後的職場生存連招。 老羅讓它站在管理層視角做壓力測試，反向拉出一張應對清單，按“一句話核心答案＋詳實資料支撐＋追問應答”三層結構列齊預判。 這週一開例會不直接胸有成竹了嘛～ 面對行業前沿資料，老羅把一份長達5萬多字的深度文件直接投餵給TRAE通讀消化，要求它整理成PPT，要分“演講者版”和“自助閱讀版”兩套。 演講版每頁只留核心觀點、流程圖和案例，詳實推導全塞進底下的演講者註釋；閱讀版則圖文完整、自成邏輯，方便別人拿去默讀。 老羅還特意提了要求： 一會兒在後臺默默做，別搶佔前臺圖形介面耽誤我幹別的事，幅面按我們公司的寬屏改成21:9，用藍色主題。 TRAE老老實實全盤接單，不一會兒兩份排版講究的檔案就整齊交付。 當然了，最好玩的當屬老羅自己琢磨的一個工具，饅頭語音。 因為平時手裡的微軟滑鼠被戲稱為饅頭滑鼠，他就想利用那個閒置的滾輪中鍵： 在任何軟體里長按滾輪中鍵，游標處就彈出一個小懸浮窗開始語音轉文字；拖動鬆手到標點或傳送按鈕，就能一氣呵成完成輸入。 老羅先是手繪了一張極其潦草的線框草圖塞給TRAE，TRAE心領神會，不僅 還原了草圖裡的互動構想 ，還主動拆解了按鈕功能、失敗兜底方案和跨應用覆蓋範圍。 不僅是一次性跑出成品，TRAE還可以匯出專案包，隨時進行二次開發。 老羅發現自己剛開始選錯了模型，於是謊稱要換電腦（實則不然…），讓它把原始碼和專案說明打包出來，方便切換裝置。 好在TRAE把專案進度全保留了，保住了這位老產品經理的體面。。。 最終跑通的本地軟體在瀏覽器、聊天視窗甚至飛書裡都能用，按住滾輪說話，文字就能即時精準上屏；順手往右側按鈕一劃鬆手，逗號、問號就自動補齊，甚至可以直接觸發回車傳送。 不得不說，很優秀的產品理念，我們都是龍哥的技術粉（doge） 腦洞自由，創作自由 看完直播，很多人的第一反應肯定是看個新鮮，緊接著就是心裡直癢癢： 我不是程式設計師，我真的能用它乾點啥？ 能，而且門檻比你想的低得多。 以往做個小軟體，要麼自學幾年語法把自己熬成禿頭，要麼找技術團隊外包，起步成本動輒幾萬塊。 現在，底層程式碼編寫被TRAE深度託管，普通人驗證一個點子的成本一降再降，多則幾個小時的業餘時間，你就能把腦子裡的想法捏成一個可點選、可互動的原型。 截至今年6月， TRAE全球註冊使用者已超過1000萬，月活達160萬 ，甚至有相當一部分使用者每週有近5天都在開啟它工作。 所以普通人都拿它做什麼呢？ 兩個愛打羽毛球的高中生現身說法！ 因為長期請專業教練太貴，平時又看不清自己的動作細節，於是完全不懂程式設計的他們藉助TRAE，靠呼叫手機、手錶和耳機的感測器資料，做出了能分析揮拍動作並給出指導的App，甚至已經正式上架了應用商店； 還有個小夥子，糾結要不要給奶奶家裝監控。 裝了吧，老人跌倒的時候能及時知道，可一想到奶奶全天被鏡頭盯著，又實在於心不忍。 最後他用TRAE搭出了芳蓮守護助手，不靠攝像頭收音錄影，只依託藥盒和門磁感測器判斷情況，漏吃藥、異常出門才推送提醒，守住了老人晚年的體面和隱私。 全球開發者社群GitHub在年度報告《State of Octoverse》就提到： AI正在降低開發門檻，大量沒有傳統程式設計背景的公民開發者開始參與搭建應用；平臺上超40%的PR（拉取請求）由AI Agent發起，非專業人群的開源貢獻正在快速增加。 △源：《State of Octoverse》2026 麥肯錫的一項調研也指出，在輕量級業務指令碼與原型構建上，AI編碼輔助能將原本耗時數天的開發週期縮減一半。 雖然TRAE沒砸掉資深系統架構師的飯碗，也不會憑空讓你發財，但實打實給那些沒有技術合夥人的獨立創作者補齊了開發短板。 阻礙想法落地的，不再是看不懂的終端報錯，只要敏銳捕捉到身邊的真實痛點，並把它清晰地表達出來，就有機會無痛落地。 這簡直是超級個體時代最趁手的現實武器。 直播間就已經有人看明白了—— 會許願就行。 坐辦公室的行政和運營，日常被各種奇葩格式的表格折磨得痛不欲生，完全可以用它搓一個專屬的批次資料清洗指令碼； 獨立攝影師、插畫師，不用再買昂貴的建站模板，幾個自然語言互動就能搭出一個風格專屬的作品展示頁； 做電商的小賣家，可以隨手定製一套針對自己店鋪特有扣點規則的自動化算賬小外掛。 …… 一個人，憑藉一個清晰的業務構思，加上工具的無縫執行，就能撐起過去一個小團隊才能跑通的流程。 別說，我看直播還真看出需求了，立馬TRAE了一下！ 徒手造了個懸崖小屋，準備拉著“仇人”過來聊聊心結（doge）。 大家都想搓點啥呢？ 版權所有，未經授權不得以任何形式轉載及使用，違者必究。 TRAE 羅永浩 聞樂 騰訊混元躋身最強開源模型！一手實測Hy4：搭配WorkBuddy，多模態Agent交付力拉滿
