From that moment on, their entire goal is to blend in and operate under the guise of your compromised user or service. But having a key doesn't mean you know the building. Imagine an intruder swiping a badge to enter a secure office. They may have cleared the revolving doors, but they still have to navigate the security guard, guess which floors they have access to, and figure out where the vault is. Because an attacker lacks the deep, localized context of your actual employees, their behavior will eventually betray them. Spotting those irregularities is how you catch them. In this post, we walk through how a credential-driven attack unfolds on the Databricks platform, how to detect the shift in an identity’s behavior using Databricks verbose audit logs and Genie, how to respond once you confirm a compromise, and which controls limit what a stolen credential can do in the first place. When establishing access via legitimate credentials, adversaries, like security practitioners, also understand their access may get revoked at any point when they deviate too greatly from the identity’s expected behavior. Adversaries rely on non-linear attack sequencing, such as validating one set of credentials to map your environment, then retrieving another set of credentials to return through a new identity or workspace that doesn’t have reconnaissance activity associated with it. Additionally, adversaries may gather information without establishing persistence or establish their way back into your Databricks platform before wrapping up their objectives. Consider a data engineer whose personal access token is copied from a misconfigured continuous integration and delivery (CI/CD) log. Within minutes, the token is used from a new IP to list secret scopes, catalogs, and repos across the workspace, something this engineer has never done. A secret holding a service-principal credential is read. An hour later, that service principal, not the engineer, creates a function, adds itself to an admin group, and exports a handful of init scripts. Each of these events could pass as routine platform use, but taken together they show one intrusion moving through the attack chain. At Databricks, we expect non-linear event sequencing in relation to credential-driven attacks and use this model to connect individual events into one investigation rather than treating them as unrelated events. When adversaries leverage compromised credentials in a Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS) environment, such as Databricks, their activity can be grouped into six stages, although they rarely move through them in a straight line. Each stage below describes what the adversary is trying to do and what to look for in Databricks audit logging tables . Treat this guidance as a starting point and tune it to your environment's normal automation. Note: Events are written as service_name.action_name , for example secrets.getSecret . The login itself rarely looks unusual. Because the credential is real, authentication succeeds as it would for the legitimate owner. However, what the identity does in the minutes after signing in often looks very different from its normal activity, and that change is what responders can detect. In the data engineer example, the stolen token authenticates successfully, and the only difference at login is a source IP the engineer has never used. The activity that follows is what stands out. Adversary goal: Access the workspace with valid credentials, whether a stolen browser session, a replayed PAT, or a service-principal credential, and blend into activity the controls are designed to allow. Next, the adversary needs to learn what the credential can reach before the access is revoked. As a result, a compromised identity can shift from its ordinary activity to listing data, secrets, code, and network controls within seconds. This reconnaissance usually spans several services at once and moves faster than a person navigating the UI. In our scenario, this stage is the burst of calls listing secret scopes, catalogs, and repos within minutes of the token being used, which is activity the engineer has never performed before. Adversary goal: Build a map of accessible data, credentials, repositories, and guardrails to plan a path deeper into the environment before access is revoked. Harvesting credentials usually takes several steps. The adversary lists secret scopes, lists the secrets in them, and then reads the ones that look useful. The value they retrieve allows them to return as a different, often more privileged, identity. For this reason, every secret read by a suspect identity is worth following up on. In the data engineer example, the adversary reads a secret that holds a service-principal credential. From that point on, the investigation has to follow two identities: the engineer and the service principal. Adversary goal: Retrieve a token, API key, or service-principal secret that upgrades the initial foothold into environment-wide access under a new identity. Once access is established, adversaries look for a way to run their own code. On Databricks, this typically happens through user-defined functions (UDFs) and jobs. A function can wrap a payload in ordinary-looking code that can be called repeatedly, and a job can run that code on a schedule across different compute. As such, the key question for detection is whether an identity has started performing actions it has not performed before. Returning to the data engineer, an hour after the secret is read, the service principal creates a function. Because the service principal, rather than the engineer, performs this action, a search scoped only to the engineer's activity would miss it. Adversary goal: Establish a reliable, reusable way to execute payloads, with a fallback when one compute route is blocked. With a way to run code, adversaries next try to make sure they can return after the original credential is revoked. Common persistence methods include access grants, newly created tokens, group and workspace membership changes, and control-plane edits. The most useful signal is a sensitive change made by an unfamiliar identity or execution context. For example, a permission change made from inside a job deserves more scrutiny than the same change made by an administrator in the console. Next in the scenario, the service principal adds itself to an admin group. Even if the engineer's token is revoked, that group membership keeps the adversary's access in place. Adversary goal: Create durable, independent access paths that survive revocation of the compromised credential. Data collection can be as small as a few targeted exports, and cleanup can involve more than deleting files. Watch for targeted exports, temporary-credential requests, removal of short-lived tooling, and obfuscated commands that make the activity harder to reconstruct. Any one of these events can look routine, so the sequence around them matters more than the individual export or delete. Finally, the service principal from our scenario exports a handful of init scripts. On its own, that is a small export. However, because it follows a secret read and a new function from the same service principal, it should be investigated as part of the same intrusion. Adversary goal: Take the data that matters and erase the most obvious tooling while leaving quieter access in place.

title: Brickster Voices: Meet Alasdair Anderson
abstract: Q: What does a typical week look like for a Lead Solutions Architect, and how would you describe the pace? A: Senior field engineers balance building tech with coaching colleagues. On any given day, I might code an app to solve a customer challenge, scale that application for another account, or partner directly with executive management on a business case. I switch fluidly between player and coach. Platforms like Lakebase high-scale OLTP continuously expand our addressable scope, but the core mission remains unchanged: delivering measurable impact to customers as a connected team. Q: You spent two decades on the customer side in financial services before joining Databricks. What drove the switch, and what keeps you energized? A: I’ve known Databricks since its founding and discussed investments with chairman Ion Stoica back in 2014. But when I used the product hands-on, I laughed out loud; tasks that took days or weeks on traditional stacks ran in seconds or minutes. I knew I had to join to help solve the world’s toughest data problems at scale. In just 12 months, tools like Agentbricks , Lakebase , and AI Apps transformed us from optimizing existing FSI processes to completely redesigning them on Databricks. Q: How do cultural principles like "Customer Obsessed" and "Truth-Seeking" come to life in your work? A: Meeting customers where they are requires deep preparation, analyzing annual reports, analyst guidance, and industry news to surface key risks and opportunities. Recently, at a top European asset manager, a boardroom AI discussion started with "What is a token?" Within 20 minutes on Databricks, I demonstrated how to analyze Private Credit risks, set warning indicators, and use Document Intelligence AI to identify hidden contagion risks across debt covenants. We completely reshaped the board's perspective on what’s possible with real-time risk modeling and portfolio hedging. Q4: What is internal collaboration like across Field Engineering and regional teams? A: Moving from traditional corporate hierarchies to Databricks’ open, transparent culture was a shift. In my first month, I aligned on EMEA priorities with our GTM FSI leader, and by month two, we were executing. The FSI SME groups collaborate instantly across time zones; I even watched our APAC colleagues present one of our custom demos to a customer in Tokyo in Japanese. Q: What makes Databricks’ technical approach to Financial Services unique? A: Our Apache Spark™ heritage paired with Unity Catalog and Unity Gateway are our superpowers. They enable customers to execute complex AI/ML workloads with full governance and control, critical for risk management across credit, market, underwriting, and compliance. Q: What do high-profile strategic engagements signal to candidates about their potential impact here? A: Databricks acts as a trusted strategic advisor to world leaders in finance. Our customers process trillions of dollars daily and insure risk equal to national GDPs. When executive teams choose Databricks, they rely on us to power core operations and guide multi-billion-dollar strategic changes that impact millions of people. Q: How does internal community participation drive success in FSI? A: FSI thrives on community. Our Slack channels serve as a real-time pulse, where global teams solve niche, complex customer challenges daily. Openness and radical transparency allow anyone to reach out and collaborate with confidence. Q: How should early-career candidates balance building domain expertise alongside technical skills? A: Domain knowledge makes you relevant to customers. You gain deep domain expertise by steering major business transformations, which requires both solid tech fundamentals and active listening. Always align technical projects to overarching business goals. Stay curious, read widely (like the FT Book of the Year list), and seek to understand human incentives, because strategic business decisions are always made by people. Q9: What traits separate Solutions Architects who truly excel? A: Success isn't one-size-fits-all. Some excel as deep technical specialists in specific products like Unity Gateway or Genie ; others become trusted vertical experts. The common denominator is trust ; if your customers, partners, and peers trust you, you will succeed. Ready to build alongside a team that is solving the world’s toughest problems? We’re hiring. See our open roles . Subscribe to our blog and get the latest posts delivered to your inbox.

title: Databricks Doubles Down on AI Products, Opens New 235,000-Square-Foot San Francisco Headquarters
abstract: Last week, we opened our new headquarters at One Sansome Street in San Francisco, welcoming employees, customers, and partners into what will ultimately be a 235,000+ square foot space that matches the scale of what we're building together. Data is increasingly becoming the engine that powers frontier AI, and this investment lets us better serve customers like Anthropic , Cognition , Cursor , Decagon , and OpenAI . The move is only part of our long-term commitment to San Francisco as our home base for building the future of data and AI for the world’s most innovative organizations. The Bay Area's concentration of top universities, research institutions, and technical talent is unmatched. As previously shared, we're investing over $1 billion into our San Francisco operations by early 2028. We've committed to hosting our Data + AI Summit here through 2030, which is expected to generate nearly $1 billion in economic value for the city. This year’s event drew over 30,000 attendees, a record that we plan to beat in 2027. San Francisco is the central hub for our AI Research team, which is innovating on the frontier of AI agents and models for knowledge work to power products like Genie, including: Additionally, the teams at One Sansome are building some of Databricks’ most important products that drive real-world impact, such as: When we initially announced this lease in March last year, we shared that the space would have over 150,000 square feet. Last week, we opened our doors with 201,000 square feet, and by next fall will expand to 235,000 square feet. Our new One Sansome headquarters offers significantly more room to collaborate, and there are tons of new benefits and amenities for Databricks employees, customers, and partners, including: For us, this move is also a chance to reflect on how far we’ve come and what comes next. In 2015, we went from a small office in downtown Berkeley to 160 Spear Street in San Francisco. We had fewer than 100 employees. At the time, the new space felt enormous, and it was a huge validation that we were onto something real. A lot has happened since then. We've grown from a scrappy open-source startup to a leader in data and AI, now with over 12,000 employees worldwide. In August, we announced crossing a $7 billion revenue run-rate, with >80% YoY growth and closed funding at a $190B valuation . Over the last decade, we have grown to help 20,000+ customers, like adidas, AT&T, Bayer, Block, Mastercard, Rivian, Unilever, and 70% of the Fortune 500. We’ve welcomed powerhouse teams from acquisitions like Mosaic, Neon, Tabular, Row Zero, and Panther, many of which are Bay Area companies that chose to join forces with us. We’ve developed and released market-leading products like Lakebase , Genie , and Unity Gateway . Spear Street was home to all of that growth, but we knew it was time for a change. In March 2025, we announced plans to move to One Sansome: a new headquarters that could keep pace with our momentum and our ambitions. Now, we're thrilled to be here. We’re excited for our employees, customers, and partners to experience our new office at One Sansome. If you’re interested in building the future of data and AI, check out our careers page ! Subscribe to our blog and get the latest posts delivered to your inbox.

title: Air gapped, not data dark: how Bright Machines gives customers live factory dashboards without opening the plant
abstract: Bright Machines gives customers live, governed dashboards of their factory data without opening any inbound access to its air-gapped plants. It captures PostgreSQL changes at the factory edge with Debezium, writes them as Apache Iceberg, sends them out over a single auditable outbound path, and reads them in place in Databricks through Unity Catalog federation. The first customer-visible dashboard went live about two months after kickoff. Every time a customer visited one of our factory floors, the same thing happened. They would stand in front of the assembly dashboard, watch the line run, and ask for a copy of the data: yield by station, cycle time trends, downtime by cause, the genealogy of a batch. We had all of it. We had built those dashboards for our own operations team, and they ran on the floor against the line databases. A customer could not access any of it directly over the internet. The plant is air gapped by design: no inbound access, one tightly controlled route out, and role-based access rules that restricted access in. Each new report required data engineering to reshape data through multiple ETL jobs, costing hours to days of engineering time. Bright Machines builds software-defined, automation-first production lines that run inside our customers' plants. Those plants are locked down by design: no inbound access, minimal outbound, and zero tolerance for risk. Each line runs a stack of on-premises services (our in-house MES, integrations with customer's MES, operator screens, robot workflow orchestrators, and the assembly dashboards) that all persist to PostgreSQL on the factory's on-prem cluster. The software team that runs this is a lean team and manages the data pipelines end to end as well as the data applications software stack. The data drives various KPI dashboards, finance reporting, operations, quality, vendor component quality, NCR tracking, genealogy, OEE and the downtime and cycle-time analysis behind every shift. On our first attempt to solve this problem, we rebuilt a cloud copy of each factory database from application events, across nine loosely coupled services. On the factory floor the picture was fine. Everything off the floor was the problem with this complex architecture and pipeline. The nine services were a message broker, a custom shoveler, a queue, object storage, few serverless functions, a cloud relational database, a scheduler, an ETL pipeline, and a popular open source BI tool with very basic RBAC support. The pipeline failed for these reasons: Fixing all the above features needed rearchitecting from the ground up. In addition to the above reasons these constraints also shaped the new design: Security Model. No inbound connectivity to the plant, and all access auditable. Governance we could demonstrate. A customer would see exactly what their role allowed on the floor, and we had to be able to prove the appropriate limits were in place. Freshness in minutes. A dashboard view that is on prem would be visible in a few minutes over the internet with the same data. Bright Machines chose edge change data capture with Unity Catalog federation because it was the only option where no compute outside a customer's and/or Bright Machines' own accounts touched factory data before governance is applied. Our criteria, in order: access control that matched what was already enforced on the floor, one outbound auditable path we could explain to any security team, minute-level freshness, and open formats at the edge. We worked through the options with our Databricks solutions architect before writing any code. The two obvious ones were Lakeflow Connect ingesting directly from PostgreSQL, and a Postgres export picked up by Auto Loader. Both would have been faster to stand up. Our threat model followed the rule that data can be pushed out, but nothing outside can reach in. A pull-based ingestion pattern needs a network path from the cloud to the factory database, and running ingestion in an environment outside the accounts where the data resided. So the question became: how do we get the same governed result while keeping every piece that touches raw factory data inside environments we own? The answer was to flip the direction. Capture changes at the edge, land them in an open format, push them out over one auditable path, and let Databricks read them in place. We proved it on a replicated line, similar to that of a production site, with two engineers over about six weeks. The bar had two parts. First, a row committed on the line had to be queryable in under five minutes with no inbound port opened. Second, a customer principal had to see exactly the tables and dashboards their role allowed, and nothing else. The deciding factor was that Databricks already enforced the security model that aligned with ours: Unity Catalog for who can see what, and OpenSharing to publish governed tables without copies. Going in, we worried that governance on federated tables would not be strict enough for the audit. It was strict, and the strictness that tripped us up during cutover is the same strictness we rely on now. Data leaves the factory in five steps, over a single outbound path, and Databricks reads it in place without a copy job. Operators keep the on-prem assembly dashboard, because they need real time. Databricks cloud serves customers and internal teams. Capture at the edge with Debezium. Debezium Server tails the PostgreSQL replication slot and writes an append-only Apache Iceberg change log to a local object store. If the WAN drops, the backlog becomes objects on the floor, not write-ahead log piling up on the production database. Send it out over one path. A single edge component copies each object to a bucket in the site's cloud account. It is the only outbound data path from the plant, and its credentials can write to that one bucket and nothing else. Cross-account replication carries the objects to the analytics account. Federate it into Unity Catalog. The Iceberg tables are registered in AWS Glue, and Unity Catalog federates Glue as a read-only catalog. That makes over a hundred tables across factory PostgreSQL databases queryable in Databricks with no copy. Model it in Databricks SQL. Bronze views collapse the change log to the current state. A Lakeflow Job rebuilds silver models every ten minutes, all in SQL and deployed from Git with Databricks Asset Bundles. Serve it with dashboards and OpenSharing. Multiple AI/BI Dashboards read processed data from the silver layer with role-based permissions. This allowed external customers and internal teams to all see the same numbers. OpenSharing allows the same copy of data to be shared securely to our customers. Registering the tables in AWS Glue lets Bright Machines control exactly when each table moves forward. A change log on object storage is a stream of new metadata files. A small function advances each table's pointer in Glue only when a new metadata file has fully replicated, and only forward. Glue holds the pointer, Unity Catalog holds the permissions, and Databricks only ever reads the version we have validated. Use a heartbeat. When a line stops for a shift change, no new rows arrive, and that looks exactly like a broken pipeline. Row counts cannot tell the two extremes apart. Debezium updates a one-row heartbeat table in each source database every five minutes, whether or not the line is running. That update travels the same path as production data. The first task of the Lakeflow Job checks the heartbeat, and if any is more than thirty minutes old, the task fails and the whole job goes red. Dashboards keep showing the last good data instead of presenting stale data as current. We phased it in four steps: 1.) a pilot on a PoC line, 2.) going live with the highest-value production line, 3.) a parallel run against the old snapshot path to check row for row parity, and 4.) a hard cutover of the dashboards for customers. What surprised us.

title: The new Genie: autonomous AI for complex enterprise work
abstract: • Genie is now an autonomous AI coworker that handles long-running tasks on your behalf, operating within the guardrails you set. • Genie Ontology, an agentic ontology built by agents and governed by people, provides trusted business context, while Genie Search finds information across your lakehouse and business systems to help Genie deliver accurate and complete answers. • Unity Gateway lets admins control tool access, trace actions, and set spending limits to keep autonomy under control. AI assistants can run analyses and summarize meetings, but employees still manage the work around them. That’s because most enterprise work is continuous, complex, and data-intensive. To monitor pipeline performance or manage budgets, someone has to track changes, decide what matters, and take action. Earlier this year, we introduced Genie One to help teams understand their data and act on it. Thousands of customers use Genie in production, including Zillow , Unilever , adidas , Atlassian , and AstraZeneca . Today, we’re introducing the new Genie: an autonomous AI coworker that proactively handles long-running enterprise work for you. Genie stays on the job continuously, tracking progress, following up on missing inputs, and taking action as new information arrives. You set the guardrails, supervise its work, and approve where needed, and Genie takes care of the rest. That autonomy depends on business context and clear controls. Genie Ontology gives Genie a map of your business, including its definitions, metrics, relationships, and organizational knowledge. Genie Search helps people and agents find information across your lakehouse and connected business applications. Unity Gateway and Unity Catalog govern Genie within your existing permissions and policies, while giving admins visibility into its actions, usage, and cost. You can work with Genie through Genie One, email, Slack, and Microsoft Teams. Give it a job and access to the tools it needs, and it takes responsibility for ongoing work. It checks in when it needs input or approval, and it adapts to your feedback. For example, Genie can monitor incoming insurance claims for emerging fraud patterns and loss-ratio drift, then assemble the case file and route it to underwriters when a segment moves outside guidelines. In marketing, Genie can manage campaigns around the clock, investigate any underperformance, and propose weekly budget changes for approval. It can also monitor your email and Slack, prepare you for the day, and alert you as new things come up. What makes this possible is context from Genie Ontology, which tells Genie how your business works—from what counts as an active customer to which revenue metric is authoritative. Personal memory retains your preferences and instructions, so you don’t have to repeat them for every job. Genie is also proactive. It notices work you repeat, like a weekly update, and offers to take it on. It can also flag issues that need your attention even before you set up a job. Once a job is running, it can run on a schedule or respond to triggers, such as when a metric dips or when more than 10 customers ask for the same feature. Genie can work on many jobs at once. You can supervise, steer, and stop them in one conversation, with a control panel for active jobs and outputs. You decide what Genie does on its own and what needs your sign-off, within your company guardrails. We're also expanding Genie with new ways to find information, create finished work, and collaborate across tools. One place to find answers: Search employees, documents, tickets, and more from the same chat bar where you ask questions. Genie Search brings results from sources like Google Drive, SharePoint, Jira, Confluence, and Workday together with Databricks dashboards, tables, Databricks Apps, and Genie Agents. Organizational directories help you explore team structures and find the right colleague. Artifacts ready to share: Describe the slide deck, dashboard, or interactive HTML page you need, and Genie builds it directly in the conversation. Refine it in chat, then present, share, or reuse it. Scheduled tasks keep each artifact current as your data changes, while shared skills apply company brand guidelines. Work across applications: MCP connectors let Genie read from and take action in popular tools like Slack, Zoom, Microsoft 365, Jira, GitHub, and your calendar, all grounded in the same ontology that gives Genie the definitions, relationships, and context to understand your business. Through custom MCP you can also connect to ServiceNow, PagerDuty and more: Genie can investigate an incident using GitHub and Jira changes, keep the ticket fresh, and keep the team updated until the issue is resolved. And when someone gets great results from a repeatable workflow, they can publish it as a skill and share it with their team. Skills live in Unity Catalog and run with the permissions of whoever uses them. Genie wherever you work: Message or @mention Genie in Slack and Microsoft Teams, or use it in your browser, on desktop, and on iOS and Android. Plugins also bring Genie’s business context into AI tools such as ChatGPT and Claude. Genie works alongside every business user, and Genie Agents bring specialized expertise to entire teams. Thousands of teams already use them in marketing, sales, finance, and operations. A department configures an agent with the data, files, tools, and instructions it needs, then manages its access and use. Teams can work with agents in Genie One or through APIs, custom applications, and automated workflows. Work across structured and unstructured data: Genie Agents now works across not only structured tables but also PDFs, slides, and more. Content search in Unity Catalog Volumes makes this possible without a separate vector index. A sales leader asking why a region is losing deals can get an analysis that combines pipeline data and win-loss reports, with page-level citations that make the supporting evidence easy to inspect. From investigation to action: Connectors let Genie Agents read from and act in tools including Slack, Atlassian, GitHub, Gmail, Google Drive, and Microsoft 365. An agent can investigate an issue, create a ticket, and prepare a summary for the team's channel, carrying the findings into the systems where teams work. Share expertise beyond your organization: OpenSharing for Genie Agents lets teams share governed agents with partners and customers, pre-loaded with the data, instructions, and knowledge they need to get value right away. For more sensitive use cases, Genie Clean Rooms lets recipients ask questions and get answers without exposing the underlying data or proprietary logic, with controls such as conversation and output limits. Whether Genie manages a single task or an ongoing responsibility, it needs to understand your business and how information across systems connects. Genie Ontology gives AI across your company that shared understanding. It connects structured and unstructured data with definitions, relationships, and organizational knowledge. Built by agents, governed by people: Agents build most of Genie Ontology automatically from the dashboards, queries, and notebooks people already use, and it keeps learning with every query and AI interaction across your organization. External knowledge sources extend that learning to business logic in BI tools such as Power BI. Teams establish authoritative definitions in Unity Catalog, and the OntoRank algorithm gives those definitions precedence, so every agent works from the same governed understanding of the business. Understand people and teams: Organizational directories, starting with Workday, bring people, teams, and reporting relationships into Genie Ontology. OntoRank combines those relationships with activity signals that show who actually works together, so Genie can weigh what's most relevant to the person asking.

title: Genie with Genie Ontology Delivers 1.6× the Accuracy with Less than Half the Tokens
abstract: We developed a new enterprise data-agent benchmark in collaboration with Turing to compare Genie with two major frontier agents and their respective harnesses on business questions in a live Databricks workspace. The evaluation measures answer accuracy, token usage and time to complete the task. Genie had a 91% pass rate, compared with 45% and 58% for the other frontier agents, while using fewer than half the tokens. Unlike previous data agent benchmarks that typically only include tables, this benchmark also includes notebooks, dashboards, saved SQL queries, documents, and other analytical assets that capture enterprise knowledge, business definitions, and calculation rules. These assets provide key enterprise context that table schemas alone cannot establish. Genie Ontology is the enterprise context layer that gives every AI agent a shared understanding of the business . It automatically extracts and organizes this knowledge, surfacing relevant context for Genie to use when answering questions. Our previous evaluation of Genie with ontology used a proprietary dataset. This benchmark evaluates Genie using tasks and supporting analytical assets designed for sharing, so others can also run the evaluation. Answering business questions correctly requires accessing the institutional knowledge about how an organization interprets and uses its data. Teams develop this knowledge through everyday analytical work: establishing revenue definitions, maintaining dashboards that reflect current reporting rules, and writing queries that handle business-specific exceptions. The questions in this benchmark require agents to access and reason about this knowledge to perform the tasks correctly. There are already many existing data agent benchmarks, but none that truly emulate real-world usage. We needed a benchmark that tested agents' ability to discover and use business knowledge distributed across notebooks, dashboards, saved SQL queries and other documents. Existing data agent benchmarks mostly focus on a set of tables and the pipeline code that builds them, and the performance on these benchmarks is similar between the agents. In real-world enterprise tasks, it’s seldom the case that the correct answer comes from the tables alone. It requires leveraging information from many different sources, such as a specific notebook that builds the reporting tables, the SQL behind a team's dashboard, or saved queries. The questions in this benchmark require the agent to reason about the knowledge residing in these assets and combine them to correctly answer the questions. For this benchmark, we developed a fictional company called Calderwick Energy, a UK electricity and gas supplier, whose challenges closely resemble those of many typical data teams. There are hundreds of tables (the largest has around 120 million rows of half-hourly meter data), along with assets that different teams have built on top of them, such as notebooks, scheduled jobs, dashboards, saved SQL queries, code, metrics, documents, and Genie Agents. It also has the messiness of a real-world scenario, like copied notebooks, abandoned analyses, old documents and dev copies, frozen reporting tables and dashboards nobody has touched in months. We created multiple data analytics questions and as queries as the benchmark tasks and ran each agent 5 times per task against the same live Databricks workspace. We compare the agents on three primary metrics: The Table below shows the overall performance of the three agents on this benchmark. Genie solves 91% of the tasks correctly, compared to 45% for frontier Agent A and 58% for frontier Agent B. Moreover, Genie is significantly faster (4x compared to Agent A and 3x compared to Agent B) and much more token-efficient, as it can leverage the Genie Ontology to identify and reason about relevant enterprise context more efficiently. You can read more about how Genie Ontology works in the GA announcement blog or in the official documentation . If you want to replicate this benchmark on your own workspace, reach out to your account team, and they can help you set it up to help implement this and show how well Genie works on a live Databricks workspace. In addition to Genie, we evaluated two leading coding/knowledge agents, “Agent A” and “Agent B,” from frontier AI labs in our results. Genie ran natively, while the other agents connected through a Databricks toolbelt. They all received the same question. The toolbelt specifically excluded the Genie MCP because it would give those other agents access to all the Genie capabilities we were testing. We checked whether each agent answered correctly using a calibrated grading rubric that captures the desired answers and agent behaviors. Where small differences in the numbers were acceptable, we set those limits in advance. An answer passed only if it met the required checks in the grading rubric. We also recorded how the agents found and used the business context needed to answer the question. The traces show which snippets Genie retrieved and the queries the agents chose to run. In addition to accuracy, we also measure latency and token usage for each agent. From the results, we observe that Genie’s correct answer pass rate is significantly better than both frontier agents, Agent A (+46%) and Agent B (+33%). It is also significantly faster (3-4x) while using less than half the tokens on average. We now provide a qualitative analysis of how Genie efficiently answers these questions correctly. The following is an example task in the benchmark that asks agents to identify one of Calderwick Energy’s historical Commercial planning rates: This looks like a straightforward lookup. The bill cost stack table has a column called cfd_rate_p , and the rows for FY24/25 contain 0.31 pence per kWh . An agent can find the relevant table, filter to the requested period, and return that number. Checking more rows would reinforce the answer: the same rate appears throughout the table. The detail that changes the answer is already recorded in the notebook that builds the bill cost stack. It explains that Commercial sets planning rates annually, and that the mart uses FY25/26 assumptions , including when those assumptions are applied to earlier billing periods. A separate section, “Planning rates by year,” preserves the history: The question asks which planning rate the Commercial team set for FY24/25. The rate currently applied to those rows reflects FY25/26 assumptions. The notebook already documents this distinction and preserves the historical rate needed to answer the question. Genie Ontology surfaced a snippet containing the historical planning rates and linked it to the source notebook, 45_mart_bill_cost_stack . When we ran the task, Genie inspected the notebook to confirm the rate and returned 0.52 p/kWh in its first response . The Ontology panel showed both the relevant information and the notebook it came from, allowing us to check the source. Across the 5 Genie runs, the first answer was 0.52 every time. The other agents did not get the correct historical rate across their runs. One returned 0.31 throughout. The other reported 0.31, questioned whether a year-specific planning rate was documented, or both. Answering correctly required understanding what the rate in the table represented and finding the historical planning assumptions documented by the Commercial team. Genie Ontology made that existing knowledge available as context for Genie’s response. The frontier agents are very good at doing most things based on written text. Type the words for a task that can be done with a computer, and an LLM will understand the requirement and then create and execute a plan to complete that task. Each new model release adds incrementally more capability, and the frontier labs seem to swap out the No. 1 spot on the various benchmark tests.

title: Genie One: The AI cowork home for everyone
abstract: In today’s enterprise, work rarely stays in one application. A single task can involve reconciling a ticket in one system, updating a document in another, and nudging a colleague in a Slack thread while you’re waiting on both. Many of these tools have added their own AI assistants to help you automate and enhance the work you do within them, but they each can help with only its part of the overall task. Without the context of your full workflow and the knowledge spread across the rest of your enterprise, these assistants may speed up individual steps, but you’re still left connecting the pieces and finishing the job by hand. Earlier this year, we introduced Genie One to help you find insights and automate work. Today , Genie One becomes the enterprise home for AI cowork , where every conversation, artifact, and workflow draws on your enterprise context from Genie Ontology and is governed through Unity Gateway. We also announced today that Genie can now take more autonomous action on your behalf, acting as a true always-on coworker for workflows across teams and tools. This release combines one place for you to find information, build finished work, and act across tools with one unified control plane for admins to govern that work as adoption grows. Genie One now brings the tools you use to find information, reach colleagues, build finished work and take action into one place. Genie Search is a new kind of hybrid AI search that unifies context-aware chats, live information retrieval, and enterprise search into one experience. Genie Search starts by creating an index of the knowledge your organization keeps outside Databricks, in documents, tickets and wikis across tools like Google Drive, Jira, Confluence, Workday, and SharePoint. When you ask a question, Genie retrieves from the index to answer quickly and accurately, with fewer tool calls and fewer tokens even while drawing on multiple sources. Simultaneously, Genie Search supports over 100 MCP connectors, which let Genie retrieve live information and take action, such as checking a Jira ticket’s status or creating one. Genie chooses how to use search, MCP, and SQL for each task based on your query. Indexed content also feeds OntoRank, the method Genie Ontology uses to weigh which sources to trust, so search improves the context behind every answer. The same index now also powers asset search for items that live outside of Databricks. Sometimes you don’t need a composed answer—just the latest all-hands slides or the ticket for a bug you’re tracking. From the same chat bar where you ask questions and collaborate with Genie today you can now search directly. Results from Google Drive, Jira and Confluence appear alongside Databricks dashboards, tables and Genie Agents, so users can find documents and data in one place. Genie Search also brings organizational data into both a visible organizational directory and Genie Ontology. In Genie One, you can browse team structures, find the right colleague, and understand reporting relationships. The same data gives Genie Ontology context about people and teams, helping Genie identify more authoritative and relevant sources for its answers. Admins and users now also have more flexibility over the homepage experience in Genie One, including the ability to pin specific assets such as dashboards, apps, or Genie Agents. Admins can set company-wide pins to bring key updates and resources to the surface, while users can set individual pins based on what they want quick access to from Genie One. Of course, getting the answer from AI is only half the job. Turning it into a shareable deck, dashboard, or page usually means moving to another tool, and losing context along the way. Genie One now creates artifacts , including slide decks, dashboards and interactive pages directly in your conversation. You describe the artifact you need, then refine it in collaboration with Genie using the same governed data and context as the conversation. You can inspect the sources behind each number or visualization, check the results, and make changes before sharing, without ever leaving Genie One. Artifacts also work with scheduled tasks and skills. Scheduled tasks keep the data in an artifact up to date, while skills apply company brand standards. Once you’ve worked with Genie to generate insights and artifacts, you can complete your workflow by updating connected tools via MCP connections. Genie One can read and update systems such as Jira or Asana, so the result of an analysis reaches the system of record without you leaving the conversation. Ask Genie to summarize last quarter's open escalations in Jira and post themes to a Slack channel, or to prep for your meetings and find more focus time in your week. You can choose what actions require your approval, and admins can configure which tools they allow their team to connect Genie to. Skills let you capture a workflow once and share it with teammates. Every business team has people who get strong results with AI, whether they're automating a weekly pipeline review or a month-end variance summary. With skills, the rest of the team can run the same steps and get consistent results. You publish Genie skills to Unity Catalog, where colleagues can find and use them. Each skill runs with the permissions of the person using it, so it accesses only the data and tools that person is authorized to use. Teams can also bring skills built in other AI tools into Genie One and keep their workflows in one place. Employees move between devices and collaboration tools throughout the day. Genie One is now available through native apps and the AI tools teams already use, with the same governed context and permissions wherever they work. In addition to the native Genie One experiences inside of Databricks, you can also access insights from Genie inside any AI cowork tool of your choice. Genie plugins bring Genie into ChatGPT, Claude, Microsoft Copilot Cowork, and Grok Bot. If you prefer to work in those tools, you get answers grounded in Genie Ontology, with the same Unity Catalog permissions. However independently an AI coworker acts, people remain accountable for its actions, and that accountability is what lets organizations scale AI confidently. Unity Gateway extends governance from data and context to the actions Genie takes, so admins can see what Genie did, who asked for it and why. Unity Gateway traces show admins how Genie responded to each request. A trace captures the question, answer, cited objects, response time and actions taken, from running SQL and calling a Genie Agent to publishing a dashboard, scheduling a task or sending a notification. Like audit logs, traces are stored in a table that admins query with their own compute, so they can filter records, join them with other data and build monitoring views. When a user reports a problem, an admin opens the trace to review the question, SQL, cited objects and thumbs-down feedback. The admin can investigate without a screen share or asking the user to retrace every prompt. Traces also show how Genie is used across the organization, so admins can understand trends and diagnose anomalies over time. Beyond tracing individual actions, admins can set policies, enforce permissions, and manage costs across Genie One. Genie One and Genie Ontology respect Unity Catalog permissions and each connected source's access controls, so users see only information they're authorized to access. When a question needs data a user can't access, Genie can identify the relevant table or asset and prepare an access request for the user to review and submit. Admins review the request in Unity Catalog and grant or decline it. Users get a direct path to the data they need, and access decisions stay with admins. Genie One gives you one place to find information, create finished work, and take action across tools. Unity Gateway gives admins the visibility and controls to govern that work as adoption grows.

title: Announcing GA of Genie Ontology
abstract: AI agents are only as useful as their understanding of the business in which they work. Within a given domain, teams can curate that understanding by hand. Thousands of customers now run Genie Agents in production this way, including 7-Eleven, Virgin Atlantic and General Motors. However, enterprises are no longer deploying a single agent for a single domain. They are deploying many agents across every function, and each needs the same accurate and complete understanding of how the business works. The enterprise context that agents need is far larger than any team can write down or model by hand. It lives in the logic behind thousands of production dashboards, SQL queries, notebooks and BI semantic models, as well as in the documents and applications where teams record definitions and maintain a working knowledge of who does what. It also changes every week as products launch, campaigns run, and teams reorganize. This is why ontologies have historically struggled in the enterprise. Built by specialists and maintained manually, they captured only a narrow slice of the business and quickly became outdated as the business evolved. Agents change both sides of that problem. They are now the primary consumers of enterprise context, and they can also produce it by learning from the work teams already do. The result is a new kind of agentic ontology, built by agents, used by agents and governed by the people who know the business. We believe every organization will need a single agentic ontology that connects to all of its data, learns continuously from how the business operates and gives every agent the same governed understanding, whether it runs on Databricks or elsewhere. Building context, agent by agent, produces separate and partial views of the business, and those views inevitably conflict. An enterprise ontology should therefore be shared infrastructure that IT and data leaders own in the same way they own the data platform beneath it. At Data + AI Summit, we introduced Genie Ontology as that layer. Today, we're announcing its General Availability, with new sources for agents to learn from and new tools for people to curate and govern what they learn. We're also sharing results from a benchmark developed with Turing that show how much more accurately agents work when they draw on it. Genie Ontology is agentic because agents continuously build its knowledge for other agents to use, while people govern the business definitions that require precision. It combines learned and modeled knowledge, ranks it by authority, and delivers the most trusted context to agents while respecting existing user permissions. Most of Genie Ontology's knowledge is automatically learned from the systems and artifacts that reflect how an organization operates. Agents extract business context from the assets teams already work with, including Databricks dashboards, SQL queries, notebooks and semantic models in tools like Power BI. This knowledge is captured as Ontology Snippets, reusable pieces of business context such as calculations, business rules, and data relationships, which are continuously updated as the underlying sources evolve. By learning directly from everyday work, Genie Ontology grows more useful over time and captures the long tail of team-specific knowledge that would be impractical to model and maintain manually. Learned knowledge is complemented by modeled knowledge , which is the business meaning teams define explicitly and govern through Unity Catalog semantics . This includes Metric Views that hold certified KPIs, Domains that organize knowledge by business area and Pages that record authoritative definitions of business concepts. Organizations model the comparatively small set of definitions that must be exact, such as recognized revenue or ARR, and Genie Ontology treats those definitions as the source of truth wherever they apply. When an agent asks a question, OntoRank, Genie Ontology's authority-aware ranking algorithm, evaluates learned and modeled knowledge to identify the most trustworthy context. It weighs signals such as source authority, certification, the expertise and relevance of the people behind the knowledge, popularity, and recency to resolve conflicting definitions and select the best context for each user and question. Genie Ontology then delivers that context directly to the agent, which can reason from the correct definitions immediately rather than spending time and tokens on open-ended exploration of the data. Through Genie MCP , the same context is available to agents outside Databricks, such as ChatGPT, Claude and Microsoft Copilot, so the agents teams already use become smarter about the business without being rebuilt. The clearest test of an agentic ontology is whether agents that draw on it outperform those that must find context on their own. Existing data agent benchmarks focus mostly on tables, and frontier agents now score similarly on them, even though real enterprise questions often depend on business context that is fragmented across notebooks, dashboards and documents. To better approximate the real world, we worked with Turing to build a new benchmark simulating a live, realistic Databricks workspace for a fictional UK energy supplier. It compares Genie, powered by Genie Ontology, with two leading frontier agents, labeled Agent A and Agent B. Every agent answered the same questions five times per task, and each answer was graded against a rubric defined before the runs began. Genie answered correctly in 91% of runs, 1.6 times the rate of the stronger frontier agent, while using less than half the tokens and finishing three to four times faster. Because all three agents write SQL well, the difference comes from context. Genie drew on knowledge the Ontology had already learned from the workspace and went directly to the business rules each question required, while the frontier agents had to rediscover that knowledge on every run and frequently returned answers that failed to meet those rules. The results reflect an established deployment where teams have accumulated that knowledge, and the benchmark research blog covers the methodology and task walkthroughs. Your account team can help you run the same evaluation in your own workspace. An agentic ontology can learn only from data its agents can reach, so a context layer for the whole enterprise depends on connecting to a wide variety of sources. Structured data either enters Unity Catalog via Lakeflow Connect or is federated in place, so Genie can compute answers directly from live operational data. Much of what a business knows, however, lives outside the lakehouse in the documents, tickets and wikis where teams record decisions and explain how things work. With this release, we are significantly expanding the systems the Ontology connects to. Genie Search, now Generally Available , lets people and agents find and use enterprise knowledge in documents, tickets and wikis alongside their governed Databricks assets, within the permissions they already have. Users can find documents anywhere in the enterprise or ask questions that span many of them at once. Genie returns synthesized, cited answers alongside the dashboards, tables and Genie Agents they already use. Because indexed content also informs OntoRank, the knowledge in those documents and tickets becomes part of the evidence Genie Ontology weighs when deciding which sources to trust. To configure Genie Search , through the admin console, an administrator connects each source and enables indexing. Genie can then search the full index in a single pass rather than querying each source separately, making answers more complete and enabling agents to find the right information with fewer tool calls and tokens. For real-time work, such as checking a Jira ticket status or creating a new one, Genie Search works alongside MCP connectors. Genie decides for each task how much to draw on the index, MCP or SQL.

title: From enterprise context to action: Genie Agents now analyze more data sources to transform your work
abstract: Thousands of teams use Genie Agents to turn deep operational questions into actionable outcomes every day. Across industries, organizations are putting Genie Agents to work on some of their most important business challenges: What these use cases have in common is the need for agents that deeply understand each business's unique context. Genie Agents ground their responses and actions in rich knowledge curated within Databricks, helping teams move from natural-language questions to trusted insights and action. As demand for context-rich workflows grows, agents need to reason beyond structured business data alone. They need to understand context from unstructured assets and connect to enterprise tools so they can reason across the full business environment and take action in the tools that run their business. Genie Agents started as the fastest way to turn business questions into SQL insights. Today, they have evolved into something bigger: a no-code agent that understands your entire business context. With unstructured data analysis and new MCP connectors , Genie Agents can conduct high-quality business analytics, analyze large volumes of documents and connect to your enterprise tools to take action on your behalf. And now with support for OpenSharing , Genie Agents can accelerate time-to-insights outside your enterprise. You can share a governed agent that's pre-loaded with your data, instructions and knowledge with partners, suppliers and customers. External teams can immediately use Genie Agents to get value out of your data, without spending time cross-collaborating on insights. Genie Clean Rooms go further, offering privacy-centric agentic collaboration. Your recipients get a Genie Agent to chat with your data. But the underlying dataset and IP are hidden and fully protected. These updates let you extend governed Genie Agents to every stakeholder in your ecosystem. 80% of the context that runs an enterprise lives in documents: contracts, invoices, claims, medical records, financial reports and call transcripts. Unlocking this context at scale can transform your business. Most agents today rely on basic enterprise search via MCP connectors, which let you attach a handful of documents directly and pull out the raw text as context in the session. However, many enterprise use cases involve large document corpora or complex file structures. Maintaining context and compliance here requires understanding the document structure and its relationships while creating a secure perimeter for governing enterprise data. Building these workflows at scale also requires developing custom RAG, including advanced parsing capabilities, building a separate AI Search endpoint, writing an embedding pipeline, summarizing document insights and passing those summaries to a supervisor agent framework with robust permissions. A bespoke approach to large-scale unstructured analysis can therefore quickly become expensive to build and maintain. Genie Agents simplify unstructured data work for your team by automatically handling document parsing, indexing and context retrieval to return high-quality results along with specific citations. Genie Agents use our custom AI document parsing function to read each file the way a person would. They recognize tables, figures, headers and footers and preserve the surrounding context. Because parsing and indexing run at scale, one agent can work through thousands of files, searching for the ones relevant to your question and citing the exact page for each answer. What’s powerful about doing this in Genie Agents is that users can now ask questions that span files and tables. “Customers like Verana Health leverage Databricks today to process and analyze real-world clinical data at scale, generating meaningful insights from their healthcare datasets using Genie Agents. Let's look at a few additional examples. Combining quantitative and qualitative insights across tables and files. An investment analyst sees that a portfolio company's margin has declined for three consecutive quarters. That evidence might exist in analyst reports, earnings call transcripts and industry research PDFs. A Genie Agent pulls margin and selling-price trends from governed tables to find which product lines account for the decline. It then searches the attached analyst reports and earnings transcripts for what competitors did over the same quarters. Genie provides analysts with data trends, the likely causes and page-level citations for each claim. Answering questions with files as cited references. In many businesses, users need to complete a task and need guidance from internal documents. The fix might be in one of thousands of service manuals, bulletins and troubleshooting guides, which cover different models and revisions. In this example, the agent identifies the model, searches only the relevant manuals and service bulletins out of thousands of documents and returns the troubleshooting steps with a citation to the source page. AI parsing keeps tables, diagrams and numbered steps intact, so the technician gets the whole procedure. Analyze data patterns and trends across files. Sometimes users need qualitative analysis across multiple unstructured files. A clinical trial analyst notices in the trial-tracking data that one department is running fewer studies. The reasons may be written in investigator and doctor reports, spread across dozens of PDFs. The agent confirms the trend in the trial data, then reads that department's doctor reports and pulls out the reasons that keep coming up. Each one is cited back to the source, so the analyst can check the evidence before acting. Reading those reports one by one might take days. Agent builders can attach Unity Catalog Volumes containing PDFs, documents, slide decks or images directly to a Genie Agent. The agent retrieves the file content most relevant to the question and adds it to its context. The agent then reasons over that content together with any structured data to generate an answer with citations. These citations can point to the specific page of the source file. Users can ask questions across a specific volume, multiple volumes and structured data in the same conversation. Unstructured data analysis runs in Agent mode, using multi-step reasoning to retrieve and analyze the most relevant file content. It respects Unity Catalog permissions, meaning users only see files they have access to, and supports content search indexing for faster, higher-quality retrieval across large volumes of data. Genie Agents now give you more ways to connect business context across your systems and tools Bring structured data in with Lakeflow Connect . Lakeflow Connect lets you ingest data from apps like Salesforce, Workday, SAP or Marketo into Unity Catalog. Once in the Lakehouse, Genie Agents analyze it as accurately as any other governed table, using your curated metric views Take action with MCP connectors. Native MCP connectors, now GA, let agents get context from tools like Slack, Google Drive, Google Calendar, Gmail, Glean, Atlassian, Github and Microsoft 365. Genie Agents can also act by creating tickets, updating records and posting messages. Authors can choose exactly which tools each agent can use, and every connector is governed through Unity Gateway . Structured data, documents and tools sit under the same governance, so one agent can reason across all three and take action on those insights Take a sales team getting ready for a quarterly pipeline review. A Genie agent analyzes pipeline data in Databricks, pulls in account plans from Google Drive and win-loss reports from UC volumes, then posts a deal strategy summary to the team's Slack channel. Agent authors can limit the Slack connector to posting summaries only, and admins govern every connection through Unity Gateway. That turns hours of manual prep into an automated workflow that keeps the whole team aligned.

title: Bring your business context to ChatGPT, Claude, Microsoft Copilot Cowork and Grok Bot
abstract: Every business is adding more data to their AI-powered workflows. But more data doesn't automatically mean better insights. Inevitably, it means more places for an agent to look and more chances to find the wrong answer. Ask a frontier agent a question about your business and it starts a live search. It hops between MCP servers, opens a document, reads a schema, tries a table, backs out and tries another. It has little context on where the right answer lives, so it may guess its way through a random walk across the organization's data. What agents need is a map of the business before they start looking. That's why we announced Genie Ontology , the enterprise context layer, that combines governed definitions with continuously learned organizational knowledge giving AI agents the business understanding they need to deliver trusted insights. Today we are introducing new Databricks Genie plugins that give your team’s favorite agents a governed interface to access your enterprise context. These plugins work natively today in ChatGPT , Claude , Microsoft Copilot Cowork and Grok Bot so teams can maintain business context in Databricks and make it available across their preferred agents. Frontier agents can now draw on Genie Ontology to supply the definitions, relationships, and source context needed to interpret the business. Genie works out what the business terms mean, finds the right data across tables and documents, writes and runs SQL and returns an answer with citations to its sources. For questions requiring specialized analysis, Genie can route work to domain-specific Genie Agents . A question about pipeline attribution routes to the marketing Genie Agent. A question about operational costs routes to the finance Genie Agent. Genie also supports insights from unstructured data so teams can access insights from large volumes of unstructured data that reside inside their enterprise For clients that support the MCP Apps extension, Genie returns interactive visualizations and Genie Ontology citations directly in the conversation. You see the charts, sources, and definitions without leaving your workflow. Some requests are complex business related questions: why is activation tracking low? Which accounts are at risk and why? The agent infers that the question belongs to Genie and hands it over. Genie then runs its own loop: Other times the agent owns a bigger job, like changing codebase, or monitoring a new product release. Here the agent checks for the business context it's missing and then keeps going with its own tools: editing files, drafting a plan, posting to Slack. Lets see a few examples of this in action: Dots are always-on agents in ChatGPT with its own computer that keeps working between conversations. A product manager can give a dot a standing job: watch the launch of a new feature and flag anything that needs attention. Each morning the dot asks Genie how adoption is tracking, using the certified definition of an active user, and checks it against launch targets. When a segment slips, it pulls related support themes and posts a short summary to the team's Slack channel. A product manager might ask their dot: Claude is built for long, agentic work across many sources. With the Genie plugin, Claude can check important facts before it draws any conclusions. Say a business analyst has to explain why quarterly revenue in a given region came in 10% below forecast. Claude can ask Genie for revenue, order volume and average deal size by product and channel, using the certified metric definitions finance relies on. It then has Genie search pricing memos, sales call notes and competitor reports for what changed during the quarter. From there, Claude goes through a deep analysis with citations behind each claim and totals that match the official forecast. Microsoft Copilot Cowork automates agentic work across Microsoft 365. It plans multi-step work, runs it in the background, and hands back finished spreadsheets, decks and email drafts. With the Azure Databricks Genie plugin, Cowork can now help an account team prepare for a client meeting. Through Genie, Cowork can pull usage and account trends from Azure Databricks, using governed and certified metric definitions. From there it fills in the account team's briefing template in Word, builds an Excel overview with charts, and creates a client-ready presentation. Cowork also books the client call with the account update, then waits for approval before anything is sent. An account director might ask: Grok Bot gives your team always-on AI teammates. Each one has its own role, memory and tools, and its own cloud computer that stays on. You can hire a growth marketing teammate and give it a job, and it proactively runs the workflow on a schedule without being prompted. With Genie connected, it works from the campaign spend, qualified opportunity and pipeline definitions your company already governs in Databricks, so its numbers match the ones your team reports. Every week, the teammate runs the whole campaign review loop. It asks Genie which campaigns are missing targets, digs into why, and drafts budget shifts with the evidence attached.
