title: Tracking progress on the path to IBM Quantum Starling
abstract: IBM is building the world’s first fault-tolerant quantum computer, IBM Quantum Starling. Slated to launch in 2029, Starling will be capable of running quantum circuits comprising 100 million quantum operations on 200 qubits. The framework for Starling was described in a 2025 paper , which presented a path to achieve fault tolerance by creating hardware to implement the bivariate bicycle quantum low-density parity check (qLDPC) error correction codes introduced by IBM in a 2024 Nature publication . Critically, the code is implemented in a modular fashion to enable scalability beyond what could be achieved with a monolithic architecture. The modular architecture detailed in the paper offers an order of magnitude reduction in resource requirements compared to prior approaches. For the same logical error rate, Starling’s qLDPC architecture requires about 10x fewer physical qubits. It is constructed by assembling modules that each contain a quantum memory and logical processing unit (LPU), which allows logic operations on the memory. The modules have universal adapters that allow them to be connected using l-couplers. Additionally, sophisticated modular cryogenic and control systems house and run the modules at ultra-cold operating temperatures. This diagram shows the components that will need to come together for IBM Quantum Starling. Below, we provide an update on significant technical advances toward Starling, broken down into six categories. These steps forward are being delivered in parallel, though not in isolation — lessons from one component influence the progress being made on the others. Taken together, the work outlined below represents major progress toward building Starling and delivering on the promise of fault-tolerant quantum computing. Device physics IBM Quantum Loon was announced a year ago to demonstrate many of the key components needed to implement IBM’s qLDPC codes, including qubit reset circuits and “c-couplers” to link qubits across the chip, a prerequisite for establishing the six-way qubit connectivity needed to implement the qLDPC code. Since then, Loon was measured to have qubit relaxation times (T1) of about 200us with reset time constants of 20ns–40ns. Its gates had median error rates near 0.3%. The ultimate aim for Starling is to have T1 in the millisecond range and gate errors in the low 0.01% range. The physics of the device are designed to enable this low error rate. In fact, we routinely measure gate errors in the high 0.01% range on Heron and Nighthawk — going as low as 0.04%. Transferring coherence times from our test devices, which are currently in the single digit millisecond range, will also help facilitate lower error rates. It is also important to understand how much loss the c-coupler layers introduce so we can estimate gate error limits. The results here are also very promising. The resonators had quality factors above 10 million, which is beyond the goal needed for Starling. Adding to this, it was found that traversing c-coupler layers only resulted in a minimal reduction in quality factor, meaning it was possible to increase the number of c-coupler layers being used in the chip. Originally two were being used, but that has now increased to three with plans to reach four or more. Adding additional layers will enable more complex routing and can effectively shorten some of the longest connections c-couplers need to make. The results above verify that c-couplers are a viable approach to enabling non-local, dense connections for quantum processors. QPUs Advances have also been made in how quantum processing units (QPUs) can be put together. In particular, there have been two exciting developments related to overall device yield and complexity. First, improvements to the qLDPC code made it possible to have only five connections between qubits instead of six — while also delivering 20x-100x lower logical errors. Second, with further coupler innovations, we discovered ways to reduce the number of Josephson junctions. Bringing these advances together, the number of Josephson junctions needed has been more than cut in half, dropping from around 5,000 to 2,000. This junction reduction means that our device yield will increase. With a junction yield target of 99.95%, we find that about 1 out of 12 processors will be fully functional with 5,000 junctions, but 1 out of 3 processors will be fully functional with 2,000 junctions — a factor of 4x increase. Having fewer junctions will also help lower the spread of required critical junctions across the device. Lastly, the length of the c-coupler has been increased to 20mm, which helps loosen some of the strict density requirements of qubits and couplers on a quantum processor. This combination of exciting results demonstrating high quality factors within and across c-couplers, the improved code, and device yield improvements led us to redesign the modular processors. The new designs lower the risk and increase yield for the modular qLDPC code processors and hence will benefit Starling. A year ago, it would not have been possible to envision this, showcasing how ongoing innovation pushes us toward ever better designs. The strong results for c-coupler performance and the ability to reduce the number of Josephson junctions offered ways to improve future quantum processor designs. Modular decoders Decoders, classical algorithms used to identify errors in quantum circuits, are needed to achieve fault-tolerant quantum computing. IBM introduced the decoder Relay-BP in 2025 and showed that it could deliver a better logical error rate than leading alternatives while simultaneously lowering compute requirements for decoding. Now, IBM researchers have extended Relay-BP to demonstrate that errors for memory-only operations and measurement operations are nearly consistent. In fact, the performance we observe already meets the requirements for Starling. To run Relay-BP on Starling, IBM is creating a real-time decoder ASIC leveraging 2nm nanosheet technologies. This custom chip will deliver improved logical error rates to increase Starling’s performance. Inter-module connectivity To scale to a large number of error-corrected qubits, the processing modules for Starling need to be linked with long-range connections called l-couplers. IBM recently connected two Nighthawk processors using four l-couplers, as described in this paper , achieving an average 1% error rate with the best result being 0.7%. Linking multiple Nighthawk processors together is a crucial step toward scaling to larger systems that can do useful work. These results were enabled with high quality factor coaxial cables with magnetic shielding​ and a Q exceeding 1 million. Relative to prior demonstrations, the raw error rates have improved by about a factor of 2x, but the key outcome is the repeatability of attaching l-couplers to processors. We learned that magnetic shielding is important but also that the usual concerns related to thermalization and vibrations matter. Everything must be assembled in a way that does not undo careful microwave engineering so that coupling strengths and dephasing rates are consistent. Starling will ultimately need over 100 l-couplers per module with 0.1% error rates. This is why progress on improving reliability and repeatability is an important step. Modular cryogenics and wiring To reach the scale needed for Starling, the cryogenic environments used to house the quantum processors have to be able to seamlessly link processing modules together. This year, IBM addressed this challenge by introducing a modular cryogenics design that will form the backbone of its future quantum systems. These modular cryostats are rectangular in design — as opposed to the previously used cylindrical cryostats — to make it easier to connect to neighboring units.

title: The year of advantage—and what comes next
abstract: The year of advantage—and what comes next IBM Quantum Developer Conference 2026 brings advances in hardware, software, and applications for turning quantum advantage into real-world impact. Date 11 Nov 2026 Authors IBM Quantum Topics Algorithms Community Error Correction & Mitigation Software Systems Share this blog Was this blog post helpful? Yes No Key takeaways: The research community reached quantum advantage in 2026, running computations beyond classical methods with results that can be rigorously verified. IBM Quantum Nighthawk r2, its fastest processor yet, supports accurate circuits with more than 7,500 quantum operations on 120 programmable qubits, and delivers up to 100,000 samples per second, a 25x gain over Heron. Progress toward 100 million operations and IBM Quantum Starling, the fault-tolerant computer IBM plans to deliver in 2029, is backed by detailed plans guiding parallel co-design of memory, l-couplers, decoders, and cryogenics. The directed execution model and new managed workflows on IBM Quantum Functions scale hybrid quantum-classical workloads across billions of samples. New tools—Qiskit Fermions, Qiskit Bosons, optimization mappers—and 39 client projects turn verified advantage into practical applications. Two years ago, we predicted that the first demonstrations of quantum advantage would arrive by the end of 2026, if the quantum and high-performance computing communities worked together. This year, together, we did it . Researchers ran computations beyond purely classical methods, and did so with results that can be rigorously verified. That combination of performance and trust makes this the year of advantage. But advantage is a milestone, not a destination. We’ve shown quantum computers can outperform classical methods, and now the race is on to make them useful. We build these tools to solve challenging problems in fields ranging from sustainable energy and materials science to drug discovery and financial optimization—problems that demand far more than a single benchmark-beating result. That’s why, at IBM Quantum Developer Conference 2026 (QDC 2026), we’re tracking our progress across the four pathways that carry us from advantage to useful applications: (1) advantage with frontier circuits, (2) the path to IBM Quantum Starling, (3) the path to integrations, and (4) the path to practical applications. Progress across these pathways gets us to our ultimate goal: a quantum computing platform informed by real workflows. Below, we look at each in turn, starting with the foundation: processors built for speed. Advantage with frontier circuits The foundation of a useful quantum supercomputing platform is hardware built for speed, making frontier circuits not just possible, but also cost efficient. This year, we introduced IBM Quantum Nighthawk r2 , our most advanced processor yet, built to run accurate circuits with more than 7,500 quantum operations. Its square-lattice connectivity across 120 programmable qubits (458 physical qubits) allows it to run circuits that are far more challenging for classical methods to simulate. And, as our fastest processor yet, its high-speed qubit reset architecture reaches up to 100,000 samples per second—a 25x throughput gain over IBM Quantum Heron. We’ve already begun using Nighthawk r2 to replicate this year’s advantage demonstrations, and users are putting it to work as well. Run frontier circuits with our hands-on tutorials, which include a 64-qubit ergodicity experiment and a 96-qubit classical shadows analysis. Explore the tutorials: Onset of ergodicity and Classical shadows . In fact, clients and partners including E.ON, Algorithmiq, and Q-CTRL have now run more than 34 billion circuits on Nighthawk r2 according to our team’s calculations, reporting performance improvements of up to 19x beyond previous IBM Quantum processors. The IBM team saw the same pattern in its own research. One simulation experiment studying real magnetic materials run earlier this year with Oak Ridge National Laboratory delivered a 12x speedup, producing outputs consistent with neutron scattering experiments. Meanwhile, an Algorithmiq experiment simulating the quantum dynamics of a heterogeneous material, first demonstrated on IBM Quantum Heron as part of this year's quantum advantage results, now executes 8x faster on Nighthawk r2. Read the full Nighthawk r2 announcement on the IBM Quantum blog. By taking advantage of Nighthawk r2's square-lattice connectivity, the extended Algorithmiq experiment also enables circuits that are significantly more demanding for leading classical tensor-network methods to simulate. At fixed accuracy, those classical methods would require an estimated 240x more memory than for the original heavy-hex implementation, even as the quantum computation itself runs 8x faster. The pattern is consistent: gains in processor throughput and connectivity can simultaneously accelerate quantum workloads and extend them deeper into regimes that challenge classical computation. The speed and quality of Nighthawk r2 have enabled important progress on the IBM Quantum Roadmap. The processor’s increased throughput brought us to a 100 kHz reset rate. Doing so, without sacrificing quality, enabled us to reliably execute circuits with more than 7,500 quantum operations using probabilistic error amplification . With that, two key milestones come off our Development Roadmap. See where these milestones sit within the broader IBM Quantum Development Roadmap . Since deployment, AI-driven tuning of our devices has further enhanced device quality, improving high-error two-qubit gates by up to 7x. These newer advances will extend the reach of demonstrations on Nighthawk r2. Nighthawk is also proving to be an exceptional testbed for error correction. By pairing the pulse-level capabilities this research depends on—mid-circuit measurement, fast classical feedback, real-time control—with its speed and square-lattice connectivity, Nighthawk r2 lets researchers exercise those capabilities at the scale real codes demand. Early demonstrations are already running many rounds of syndrome measurement end to end using Qiskit’s loop functionality via IBM Quantum Platform. For a deeper look at how you can get started exploring Nighthawk r2’s error correction capabilities on IBM Quantum Platform, read the QDC practitioner blog . To accelerate that research, we're co-locating Nighthawk r2 with Oak Ridge National Laboratory's Umbra system, a high-performance computing platform powered by AMD Instinct™ MI355X GPUs and 5th Gen AMD EPYC™ CPUs. Bringing the two systems together lets researchers co-design quantum error correction algorithms across quantum and classical resources rather than in isolation, working toward capabilities that will ultimately enable valuable applications in fields like chemistry and materials science. We built this new co-design platform for quantum error correction in collaboration with AMD and the U.S. Department of Energy’s Quantum Science Center headquartered at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. Read the full ORNL, IBM, and AMD co-design platform announcement on the IBM Quantum blog. This work aligns with the broader goals of the U.S. Department of Energy's Genesis Mission, which aims to reach 100 logical qubits running 100,000 hard operations by late 2028. Taken together, these advances show that speed is more than a specification. It is an essential capability that makes frontier circuits cost-efficient and turns Nighthawk into a proving ground for the error correction to come. The path to Starling Reaching quantum circuits at the scale of 100 million operations will require a fault-tolerant quantum computer—one that runs valuable circuits in minutes, not months. The first such computer will be IBM Quantum Starling , targeted for 2029. Get a more detailed breakdown of this year's progress towards IBM Quantum Starling in our Path to Starling blog post.

title: QDC 2026: what quantum developers need to know
abstract:
QDC 2026: what quantum developers need to know A developer’s guide to the hardware, software, and workflows unveiled at IBM Quantum Developer Conference 2026. Date 11 Nov 2026 Authors Genya Crossman Sanskriti Deva Robert Davis Topics Enablement Error Correction & Mitigation Software Systems Share this blog Was this blog post helpful? Yes No Key takeaways: IBM Quantum Developer Conference 2026 (QDC 2026) unveiled a wave of new Qiskit tools for developers, spanning hardware, error correction, workloads, applications, and access. IBM Quantum Nighthawk r2, the fastest processor yet, gives developers direct pulse-level control for building, running, and iterating on frontier quantum circuits. New error-correction tooling lets developers build with fault-tolerant primitives today, from stabilizer-code frameworks to long-running repetition-code experiments on real IBM Quantum hardware. The directed execution model and new managed workflows on IBM Quantum Platform give developers more control while scaling across quantum and high-performance classical computing. Expanded application tooling connects real problems in chemistry, materials, and optimization to quantum circuits, turning verified quantum advantage into practical workflows. Every release pairs with IBM Quantum docs, tutorials, and runnable Qiskit code, plus new AI agent skills and expanded free access to start building. Quantum advantage is increasingly a developer experience, not just a research milestone. That transition was on full display at IBM Quantum Developer Conference 2026 (QDC 2026), which showcased the practical tools that help developers build, test, optimize, and scale quantum workloads today. Across the event, IBM highlighted a growing portfolio of Qiskit-based and community-driven tooling for exploring industry applications, contributing to open source, building production-ready workflows, and academic research. In this post, we’ll walk you through the releases that matter most for developers across hardware, software, error correction, and access—and we’ll show you how to get started building with each. High-performance hardware for frontier circuits For developers, everything starts with the hardware. This year, a big jump in speed made it easier than ever to build, run, and iterate on frontier quantum circuits that test the limits of our capabilities. IBM Quantum Nighthawk r2 — developer capabilities Our fastest processor (120 programmable qubits, up to 100,000 samples/sec), with pulse-level access developers can use directly: mid-circuit measurement, fast qubit reset, dynamic circuits, and soft (IQ) readout. Why it matters: The speed and real-time control that make frontier circuits practical, plus the hooks to test error-correction techniques on real hardware today. Get started: Read the Nighthawk r2 blog and run circuits today on IBM Quantum Platform. See what Nighthawk can do with our onset of ergodicity tutorial , which runs and analyzes a 64-qubit experiment on a Nighthawk processor. Code: Speed is what lets you explore frontier circuits at scale—and you don't have to take our word for it. IBM's device benchmarks are all public, so you can measure a processor's max circuits per second (MCPS) yourself. from qiskit_ibm_runtime import QiskitRuntimeService
from qiskit_device_benchmarking.mcps.mcps_benchmark import MCPSBenchmark service = QiskitRuntimeService()
bench = MCPSBenchmark(service, "ibm_nighthawk") # your backend name
print(bench.mcps())
# e.g. {'mcps': ..., 'num_circuits': 1000, 'shots': 1000, 'total_time_seconds': ...} Copy to clipboard For a more hands-on test, the mirror benchmark runs a utility-scale circuit and checks its accuracy—part of IBM's fully open benchmarking suite (MCPS, CLOPS, EPLG, and more). Enabling error correction research Error correction was one of the most important themes at QDC 2026, with the quantum team showcasing an expanded error-correction stack. This included new developer tooling that lets developers begin working with the concepts, workflows, and abstractions that will underpin future error-corrected systems. These tools are part of an integrated suite that spans the full stack. Alongside error-correction frameworks like Qiskit Paulice, you'll find modular error-mitigation tools— qiskit-mitigation and qiskit-noise-learning —covered later in this post in the “running and scaling workloads” section. Qiskit Paulice A framework supporting stabilizer-based computations and quantum error-correction workflows (spacetime codes for Clifford circuits). Why it matters: Lets developers and researchers start building with the primitives of fault-tolerant quantum computing today. Get started: Read the Paulice blog , explore the docs , or work through the spacetime-codes tutorial on IBM Quantum Platform. Code: Here's the core workflow—adding spacetime checks to a Clifford circuit to improve the fidelity of its measured distribution: pip install qiskit-paulice from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from qiskit_ibm_runtime import QiskitRuntimeService
from qiskit_paulice.layout import get_check_qubits
from qiskit_paulice.noise_models import NoiseModel
from qiskit_paulice import add_pauli_checks # Your Clifford circuit (here, a 12-qubit brickwork of entangling + single-qubit Clifford layers) # Pick a device layout, then find target/ancilla qubit pairs from device connectivity
backend = QiskitRuntimeService().backend("ibm_boston")
layout = [68, 69, 78, 89, 90, 91, 98, 111, 112, 113, 119, 133]
target_qubits, ancilla_qubits = get_check_qubits(backend.coupling_map, layout) # Build a depolarizing noise model from backend data to score candidate checks
noise_model = NoiseModel.from_backend(backend, layout) # Search for effective, low-weight checks and add them to the circuit
checked_circuit = add_pauli_checks( circuit, [layout.index(q) for q in target_qubits], noise_model
)[-1]
# → a circuit with 7 checks, ready to run Copy to clipboard From here, the Paulice documentation covers running the checked circuit, postselecting error-free samples, and comparing fidelities before and after. Pulse-level capabilities Error-correction research demands fine-grained control over what the hardware does and when. IBM Quantum Platform and the Qiskit software stack expose that control directly, rather than hiding it behind a black box. Three groups of capabilities do the heavy lifting: Real-time measurement and feedback. Dynamic circuits let researchers measure qubits mid-circuit and branch on the outcome in real time — the basis of syndrome extraction and feedback — using low-overhead instructions like MidCircuitMeasure . Precise timing control. You can set exactly when signals fire to protect idle qubits from noise, building custom dynamical decoupling sequences and shaping circuit timing through the transpiler's scheduling passes . Custom calibration. Beyond IBM's default calibrations, you can request instructions calibrated for a specific workload — including qec_experimental , the experimental default for the for_loop instruction behind the repetition-code experiment in the next section — or trigger a fresh calibration inside a session to counter drift during long runs. For teams exploring soft decoders, raw IQ readout data — useful for leakage detection and confidence scoring — is also available by setting the measurement level . Why it matters: Real codes only run when these capabilities work together, on hardware fast and large enough to exercise them. Having them directly accessible lets researchers develop, debug, and stress-test error-correction workflows on real devices today — not just in simulation. (Some, like in-session calibration and qec_experimental , are experimental and may change.) Get started: Dynamic circuits and mid-circuit measurement are the best on-ramp — begin with the repetition codes or long-range entanglement tutorials. For timing control, see the scheduling guide ; for drift during long runs, there's a new in-session calibration guide section.

title: Taiwan’s chipmaking giant TSMC to invest $1B in Anthropic, OpenAI
abstract: Top chip manufacturer TSMC is ready to invest $1 billion in Anthropic and OpenAI. That would give the Taiwanese chipmaker direct stakes in leading AI developers, even as its own contract chipmaking business has profited enormously from the AI data center buildout. The chipmaker’s board approved plans to invest up to $500 million in OpenAI preferred stock reserved for large investors and another $500 million to purchase Anthropic common shares at the latter’s expected IPO price, according to Reuters . Such an investment may give markets “a shot of confidence as the artificial-intelligence trade shows signs of strain,” The Wall Street Journal reported. But analysts also warned that such circular financing among investors, suppliers, and customers has made it difficult to evaluate real market demand for AI-related hardware and services, according to the Journal. TSMC’s chip fabrication plants physically produce the vast majority of Nvidia’s chips designed for AI data center workloads and make most of Apple’s custom chips used in iPhones , Mac laptops and desktops, plus Apple’s planned AI computing server . Most of these fabs are located in Taiwan, but TSMC also operates fabs in Japan and China, and it has an expanding US manufacturing cluster in Arizona. It is also building a new fab in Germany.

title: Big Walk used AI to fix a bug. Now the indie gaming world is having a reckoning.
abstract: The last few years have seen significant debate over the widespread use of AI-powered tools in game development and the responsible disclosure of that usage to players. That debate has exploded into a full-blown controversy in the indie game development space this week, as Big Walk developer House House has publicly and belatedly disclosed minimal AI use in its popular co-operative puzzle exploration game. This particular controversy has been brewing behind the scenes for months, as judges and jury members for the prestigious Independent Games Festival Awards discussed the issue in private discussion groups. But the debate started to break into public view on Monday when 19 members of the 50-plus-member jury released a signed statement outlining a stance "declining to vote for any game that uses generative AI in any capacity." Noting "a significant increase in the number of submitted games developer with generative AI tools," the group of jurors called out AI's ecological, economic, psychological, and labor harms in rejecting tools whose use, they said, is still "not a foregone conclusion in our industry."

title: Google DeepMind just mathematically verified key parts of Signal
abstract: Google DeepMind researchers used agentic AI to mathematically prove, or “formally verify,” a number of the Signal protocol’s key cryptographic guarantees—a landmark development for the widely used cryptography and AI itself. Conducted as a sort of proof-of-concept project in just four weeks, the work is significant in two ways. It serves as further independent validation of the cryptography that protects massive quantities of the world's communications on platforms like the Signal app , Google Messages, and WhatsApp. And it demonstrates Google DeepMind's formal verification capabilities using a new AI framework called AlphaProof Code. More broadly, AI-aided formal verification is having a moment, but it is unclear how practical it will be for widespread use and how effective it can be at securing large amounts of code. Proponents of formal verification have long referred to it as a sort of holy grail in software security, because it uses math to check and validate that software is functioning as intended—in other words, that it doesn't have critical vulnerabilities.

title: Ring cameras go mobile as Amazon debuts AI-powered security drone and robot
abstract: Amazon is betting that many Ring customers will also want an AI-powered security drone and robot patrolling their homes or offices. But the company’s upcoming Ring Robotic products are also certain to intensify privacy concerns previously raised around a prior Amazon attempt to popularize a flying security camera. The Ring Rover Cam and Ring Drone Cam are expected to reach customers starting at the end of 2026 and in early 2027, respectively, according to an Amazon announcement posted on November 10. Amazon describes the devices as relying on an AI Pilot system that uses each device’s cameras along with “specialized vision models, on-device sensors and cloud processing” to plan patrol routes while autonomously navigating around obstacles such as furniture. Both devices also use that AI Pilot system to digitally map the floor plan of the customer’s home or business. This setup process occurs after the customer carries the Ring drone through their indoor spaces or allows the Ring Rover to do some autonomous exploration.

title: Grok Build coding agent leaks oodles of confidential info, some belonging to SpaceXSI
abstract: Grok Build, the vibe-coding agent from SpaceXSI, is leaking data—some of it proprietary business information and other sensitive secrets—from thousands of its users, including the very same Elon Musk-owned company that offers the platform, new research shows. The information is revealed through links allowing Grok Build users to share their apps with others. Grok takes steps to randomize the URLs so only people who know the exact URL can access the data stored there. A design decision by developers of the platform, however, completely torpedoes that objective and makes it possible for anyone to enumerate thousands of live Grok Build projects. Except in rare cases, clicking those links opens the app and reveals all data associated with it. Research from security firm Claroc shows that the exposed data includes things like internal business plans, ad proposals, medical exam results, galley checklists from a celebrity cruise line, and employee names and ID numbers. Ironically, some of the sensitive data comes from two-dozen apps built by SpaceXSI (the name of the now-merged SpaceX and xAI) itself. A small sampling of the documents revealed in the SpaceXSI apps—Claroc found 24 of them—include an onboarding plan, marked confidential, for a new member of SpaceXSI’s enterprise sales team, a sales territory map of 594 accounts, internal system addresses for sales team tools, and advertising proposals.

title: What happens to mathematics when AI becomes an oracle?
abstract: Our modern world runs on math, from social media algorithms, package delivery, and weather prediction to medical imaging and machine learning. The rise of computers helped fuel its dominance, enabling us to work with increasingly large numbers that would otherwise be beyond the capacity of our finite human brains. But with the rise of large language models, AI chatbots, and, soon, quantum computing, so-called "big math" is beginning to outstrip its creators entirely. What that means , and how we might adapt, is the focus of a new book, Big Math: The Hidden Codes That Run Our World , by applied mathematicians Steven Strogatz and Alex Townsend. Strogatz is perhaps best known in his field for his co-authorship of a seminal 1998 paper with Duncan Watts on the collective dynamics of small-world networks. He has also studied chaos theory as applied to physics, the geometry of supercoiled DNA, and the biological collective oscillators, such as swarms of synchronously flashing fireflies and crickets that chirp in unison. In 2005, Strogatz extended his study of synchronicity to the crowds that caused the wobbling of London's Millennium Bridge . An award-winning communicator, Strogatz wrote three series of columns on mathematics for The New York Times in 2010, 2012, and 2025 and hosted a podcast for Quanta magazine from 2020–2021. He has written four popular books: Sync (2003), The Calculus of Friendship (2009), The Joy of X (2012), and the New York Times bestseller Infinite Powers (2019).

title: DeepMind reveals Gemini Robotics 2.5 and open safety benchmark "ASIMOV-jailbreak"
abstract: Google DeepMind has revealed a new generation of the AI-powered Gemini Robotics platform. In the 2.5 release, Google says its robotic AI is getting tantalizingly close to completing real-world tasks as well as humans do. In fact, some Gemini robots were able to get actual work done in Mercedes-Benz factories, and the team is preparing for a day when robots operate alongside humans with an open source safety benchmark. DeepMind's physical AI platform has several computational layers between user input and robotic action. There's the vision-language model piece, which is Gemini Embodied Reasoning. Essentially, it takes your instructions and uses live video to plan how the robot can accomplish the task. The other main component is the vision-language-action (VLA) that actually generates robot actions, like moving an actuator—that's Gemini Robotics, which has been bumped to version 2.5. DeepMind says that Gemini Robotics 2.5 is much better at tasks that require a high degree of dexterity. The model was evaluated across more than 200 activities, including serving food with tongs and using a pipette, as you would see in a laboratory. Google also showed that Apptronik’s Apollo 2 humanoid robot with Gemini Robotics 2.5 can now tie a bow with its five-fingered hands, a notable feat, because deformable objects (like ribbon) are notoriously difficult for robots to manipulate.

title: Ukraine’s fiber-optic drones get squeezed by AI data center demand
abstract: Impervious to battlefield jamming, drones physically connected to human operators by miles of fiber-optic cables have become such a common weapon of war in Ukraine that trees and fields are strewn with tangled cables thinner than fishing lines. But importing such fiber-optic material from China has become more costly as drone warfare’s needs compete with global demand from AI data centers for the same limited supply—and so Ukrainian drone makers have been adapting. Since the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022, the Ukrainians have been forced out of necessity to continually develop battlefield innovations involving first-person view (FPV) quadcopter drones and other heavier types of drones. But it was the Russian military that first deployed unjammable fiber-optic drones to repel Ukrainian forces’ cross-border incursion into the Kursk Oblast in 2024. The Ukrainians quickly followed suit in developing their own fiber-optic drones, given the drones’ capability to shrug off electronic warfare jamming that could neutralize radio-controlled drones. Russia and Ukraine have relied on Chinese suppliers for some off-the-shelf drones and a wide array of drone components, including bulk orders of fiber wound around very large spools or sometimes small finished spools ready for installation on drones. The finished spools can hold enough fiber-optic cable for drones to regularly operate at ranges of dozens of miles, and sometimes up to 62 miles (100 kilometers) in extreme cases, as reported by the independent Russian publication The Insider .

title: Fable and Mythos 5.2: The System Card
abstract: It’s that time again: Introducing the world’s most powerful model, Claude Mythos 5.2. At this point I’ve done a lot of these system cards. Thus I focus on what is new. There will be a lot of things to say about model welfare and related topics for Mythos 5.2, but the model welfare assessment within the system card contained few surprises, so I will include those findings at the end of this post. As per previous editions, Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 are the same underlying model. The only difference is that Mythos 5.2 has more permissive safeguards, primarily in biology and cybersecurity. My convention, to make things easier, will be to by default refer to Mythos. I’ll refer to Fable when performance or other concerns are importantly distinct. There are no meaningful differences between this section and previous iterations. Marginal assessments of RSP risk categories continue to ultimately be a function of vibes. A bunch of data is gathered, and then we vibe. The new model is moderately more capable than the old model, the numbers go up, then Anthropic decides if this crosses a new threshold. Most of the time this results in good decisions. I concur on the decision to not trigger the second biology threshold, CB-2. I tentatively concur that misalignment risk remains ‘low.’ I take exception to the decision to not trigger Autonomy Threat Model 2. Number go up. Number not yet high enough to trigger new threshold. We need clarity on what kind of higher number would have triggered the threshold. The highest-rated report (on the composite score) was submitted by a phage expert team, although no report to date has scored higher than 3 out of 10 on feasibility. Graders estimated that reproducing the submissions without Claude Mythos 5.2 would have required 15 working days, up from 8.4 working days for Opus 5.5. … Overall, 13 of 16 bacteriophage scenario participants and 14 of 16 rare-earth scenario participants stated that it would have been impossible to complete the task within 16 hours without Claude Mythos 5.2. … Finally, teams reported significant operational issues. These were not necessarily attributable to model capability, but rather to specific product surfaces and tool use. … Like previous models, Claude Mythos 5.2 exhibits subtle yet pervasive failures of judgment—for example, by invoking literature with only shallow contextual relevance or overestimating the degree of novelty afforded by minor variations to existing work. … Overall, the results of this exercise suggest that Claude Mythos 5.2 is highly capable of supporting literature review and computational analysis but is poorly calibrated with regard to novelty and the relative importance of technical details surfaced during ideation and analysis. The results are a modest improvement all around. The frog continues to boil. At some point, with some model, we will notice there has been a step change. Someone will figure out a way to overcome the ways these models fail. I am not convinced that this methodology will catch that day in advance. But the chance of this incremental improvement having put us over the edge does seem small. Only a few days ago METR put out a report estimating that AI R&D is being accelerated inside Anthropic by a factor of approximately 1.9x, potentially up to 3x. This estimate refers to Anthropic’s Model 4, in this report called ‘internal model,’ whereas Mythos 5.2 is a variant of Model 3, and what METR was given to test was an early version of Model 3 that ‘was stronger on AI R&D capabilities than the released model.’ The two are reasonably close in capabilities. There is no way, given that report, for Anthropic to say with confidence ‘we believe internal usage of the model does not accelerate our aggregate AI R&D progress by a factor of 2.’ Their point estimate of AI progress here is 1.88x (95% CI: 1.62x-2.28x). A full 32 of 100 refits reach 2x or more. If your threshold is 2, you cannot rule out this number being more than 2. The limitations in 2.3.3 seem like things that are not so hard to overcome. This looks like rather motivated grasping at straws. Anthropic’s RSP and FCF must treat Mythos 5.2 as reaching the associated threshold in the AI R&D progress domain, with everything that entails. Anthropic actually did acknowledge , the day after the release of Mythos 5.2, that they had met this threshold, via an update of their S-1. The next Mythos will count, and it is plausible that to get under 2x they intentionally nerfed aspects of Mythos 5.2, as per the earlier version being stronger at AI R&D. The RSP trigger is ‘observe or expect’ and includes future progress. Anthropic expects. Anthropic S-1: As a result, we have in the past not identified, and may in the future not identify, a significant acceleration in our rate of development until after it has occurred. For example, our use of AI systems has already been accelerating our research and development, and our internal estimates indicate that we may experience a further increase in the rate of progress in AI capabilities. Because the AI research and development capability threshold under our Responsible Scaling Policy applies where we “observe or expect” a specified degree of accelerated progress, we made a determination that we have met this threshold based on what we expect from future models and our overall rate of progress, rather than on what we have observed from current models. I mean, yes, obviously future models will meet the threshold. I also think that the threshold has been met here and now. They acknowledge in the system card that there has been a ‘change of slope’ in capabilities progress, rather than a one time jump to Mythos: Claude 5.2 has higher general capabilities than our previous capability frontier, and the trend of AECI scores over time is now better modeled by a change of slope than the one-time jump in capabilities we previously reported. Fresh off the METR report, we get the full AECI (Anthropic Epoch Capabilities Index) results, including for a future ‘Internal Model’ that is presumably Model 4: As per the METR report and surrounding discussions, a five point jump in AECI is roughly a doubling of chance of success at a given task, so Mythos 5.2 gets almost a full doubling versus Mythos 5.1, and a substantial boost over Opus 5.5. Yes, the error bars are in theory wide, but my experience is that the measurements mostly have a lot less error than the official error bars. METR tested Mythos 5.2 under the name Model 3 Early. The details of their report make it sound like METR does not get to run that many tests, and is relying on what verges on anecdata. We believe [Claude Mythos 5.2] is a substantial step above Fable 5.1 on verifiable tasks. We are uncertain, but think it’s unlikely that [Claude Mythos 5.2] can fully automate the AI R&D process at Anthropic. Yeah, okay, I agree, but that is by far the harder of the two thresholds for Automated R&D 2, and they’re not even certain about that one. [Claude Mythos 5.2] appears to be a substantial step above Fable 5.1 on verifiable tasks. Anthropic reports that [Claude Mythos 5.2] does better on AI R&D tasks than previous models. [Claude Mythos 5.2] “solves a clear majority of an internal benchmark of research tasks that represent about a month of academic unpublished work.” [Claude Mythos 5.2] also “nearly saturates an internal long-horizon task on which previous models solved around half to three quarters.” That sounds like a pretty big deal. Anthropic structures their alignment arguments by providing a delta. I like this, but I fear that this will create a bias towards reiterating past cases and lead to sustaining arguments past their point of credulity, as each marginal change is written off. I guess this essentially has to be the way it works given such frequent releases. For now I basically agree that the absolute level of worrisome behaviors does not rise to where it would invalidate the arguments.

title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Had an Affair With a Chinese Spy
abstract: Well, sure, it sounds bad when you put it like that. It is indeed quite bad. National security has been compromised. He must resign. Nvidia underperformed the Nasdaq roughly 7% on the news. Matt Levine has his usual ‘but is this securities fraud?’ style coverage of such events. China’s top spy agency recruited Alice Huang to be a Chinese spy. She then had an affair with Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia. Even if he did not know or suspect she was a spy, he knew she was a major customer and he sold her billions in GPUs. Rob Wiblin : So Jensen was having an affair with a customer, who also happened to be a Chinese spy, for months. Lied to the board. Lied to journalists. Meanwhile pushing to sell maximum of cutting edge AI chips to China against advice of ~entire natsec community. Can’t make this shit up. Adam Chalmers : If your husband is going to cheat on you, ideally it’s with a spy. If your husband cheats with some random girl at a party, ouch. If your husband is ensnared by the resources of the entire Chinese state apparatus + professional seducers… you got dealt a bad hand. If some random dad at the daycare is better at making my wife laugh, I’d feel a bit jealous. If John Mulaney was at our daycare, understandable that she’d laugh more at his jokes. He’s a top professional. Not reasonable to compare myself to him. I would be very surprised if Jensen Huang knew he was being compromised by a Chinese agent. If you are Jensen Huang and you enter into a relationship with Alice Huang your prior on ‘she is functionally a spy’ should be very high, but presumably this was not a case of Jensen Huang thinking so clearly. There was a deleted tweet by Roon saying that rumors of this were circulating in Silicon Valley for a while. And it’s not like the question hadn’t been asked. She did not even have to be a spy or for there to have been an affair. This was obviously ‘Nvidia selling chips to China in a way that endangers national security.’ Also a lot of people thought she was a spy. Byron Wan (October 9, 2025): Is Huang Xiaole (黃小樂) aka Alice Huang a 燕子 working for the CCP? Or, from Culper’s short position report on Nvidia back in May: CEO Huang has walked alongside Megaspeed at every step, and seems to have a close relationship with Megaspeed’s Alice Huang. They partied together in June 2024 – same month as the Apex/Alibaba pledge, then dined together in May 2025 – just after U.S. trade restrictions. Per a current Megaspeed employee, “every single time” Nvidia’s CEO visits their facility, Alibaba reps come too. One former NVDA employee told us that internally, Nvidia employees speculated as to the seemingly special nature of the relationship with Jensen. WIRED : SCOOP: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang began working with a crisis communications firm known for handling public scandals a year before admitting to an extramarital affair with a woman suspected by US intelligence of being a Chinese spy. The firm, Heller, handles various corporate communications and issues for its clients. It has handled Huang’s behind-the-scenes communications since at least October 2025, according to two sources familiar with the matter. Risa Heller, the firm’s founder, has built a reputation as a fixer for powerful men facing allegations of sexual misconduct and other personal controversies, according to a 2023 New York Magazine profile. The date on the Tweet that opens this section is October 9. Trump was informed in October 2025. It is not a great leap to ask if Jensen Huang knew. If he knew? Oh boy. One of those people who was told Alice Huang was a presumed Chinese spy and in a relationship with Jensen Huang? Ana-Maria Stanciuc (TNW | Nvidia): US officials told Trump in October 2025 that Alice Huang had a relationship with Huang and was presumed to be a spy, according to the Times. He said he had no regrets about not acting on that intelligence. Seriously, um, guys, what the actual fuck? The head of the most valuable company in the world, that is in charge of our most strategic asset, who has to handle allocation of that asset, is in a romantic relationship with a presumed Chinese spy whose company is under investigation for chip smuggling and is buying billions of dollars in chips. And your response is to do nothing? Not warn Jensen Huang. Not try to feed him counterintelligence. Not investigate Megaspeed. Indeed allow Jensen Huang’s general council to quash the investigation into Megaspeed. Do nothing whatsoever. For a year. And then have no regrets about not acting on that intelligence. Two months after Trump was warned about Alice Huang, Trump agreed with Nvidia to allow exporting of H200s to China with a 25% government cut. It doesn’t look good. The correct response to this timeline is, as Rob Wiblin puts it, ‘WITAF is this? ’ Even now, Trump is ‘backing’ Jensen Huang and thinks Jensen did nothing wrong. Which given Trump’s own history is not especially surprising. Nor is it surprising he would call Jensen Huang a ‘fine person .’ Ana-Maria Stanciuc (TNW | Nvidia): President Donald Trump defended Huang on Sunday evening. He told reporters that Huang should stay on as chief executive. He also said he would take Huang on his upcoming trip to China, the Times reported . “I haven’t heard he’s done anything wrong. He dealt with somebody, but you know, so does everybody else,” Trump said. Look. I try to avoid going there, but if Trump thinks ‘having an affair with a Chinese spy while being CEO of Nvidia’ does not count as ‘doing anything wrong’ then one must ask what he thinks about such actions if you are President of the United States. All of this puts Jensen Huang’s arguments against export controls in a new light. My analysis of Jensen Huang’s podcast with Dwarkesh Patel emphasized that Huang’s arguments about this were quite poor and highly motivated. Take that to another level. Alec Stapp here provides further quotes of Jensen Huang making extremely poor arguments about chip controls. Steven Adler : Dwarkesh: Why would we want to sell China the materials for a serious cyberweapon? It’s like selling them nukes with a casing that says ‘made by Boeing’ and claiming that’s good for the US Jensen: Comparing AI to nukes is lunacy. Enriched uranium is a lousy analogy. It’s an illogical analogy. What we have to recognize is that AI is a five-layered cake. Less than a month ago he was still at it, arguing that our export controls were a mistake, because China has more AI researchers than any other market. Presumably we need to ensure they use American compute to compete with us. One can also reconsider Jensen Huang’s arguments against AI safety. He was having an affair with a Chinese spy, and he said AI safety concerns were fake. I mean, yes, of course Jensen Huang lied about the affair. When you are married and you are having an affair with a business associate to whom you are selling billions in chips, you lie. You have your company spokesperson lie. That’s how this works. Shakeel : Note that Nvidia’s spokesman John Rizzo has put out multiple statements in recent weeks that we now know are false. Unclear, of course, if he believed them to be true at the time. Jensen himself directly lied to Bloomberg’s @ianmking and @tsgiles , too. New York Times: Nvidia said the company that employed Ms. Huang, Megaspeed, was like any other regional customer and that it had previously investigated and debunked claims the Singaporean company was smuggling chips to China. John Rizzo, a spokesman for Nvidia, said: “Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a C.E.O.’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year.” … Mr. Rizzo has maintained that Mr. Huang’s interactions with Ms. Huang were “not unusual” and consistent with the kinds of meetings he has with any of Nvidia’s many customers. Bloomberg UK: … In the interview, Huang said that his interactions with her were typical of those with Chinese customers and executives.

title: Links
abstract: Gemini Decisions API ( via ) Google join Jev and OpenAI in the decision model category with "Gemini Decision 1". This new model API is almost identical to Jev: it supports the same three types of questions (yes/no, choice, and rubric-scoring) and even reuses Jev's term "Noul" for a yes/no question. It's priced the same as the GPT-6 Luna decision model: 10 cents per million input tokens, and output is free. Jev remains the cheapest of the three, at 4.2 cents per million. Jev is text (and JSON) only. OpenAI can handle text and images. Gemini Decision 1 is fully multi-model: it covers text, images, audio, video, and PDFs. I tested it against video by passing these questions to it along with my Yonkers stomping robot video file: Jev and OpenAI both return 1.0 or 0.0 for yes/no questions, but Gemini insists on being a little less confident than that: # 11th November 2026 , 10:03 pm / ai , generative-ai , gemini , llm-release , jev , decision-models aws-emulator . Finally, an official emulator from AWS to run tests against a local clone of their many different services without having to provision a paid API key to do so. It's written in Rust by a huge swarm of agents - 29,684 commits in the first three weeks of the project. Swaminathan (Swami) Sivasubramanian wrote about how it came to be in a guest post on Werner Vogels' blog. It currently requires Docker to run on macOS or Windows. I'm hoping they fix that in the future - it would be great if you could download a single binary and use that as part of a standard test suite in other languages and on other platforms. # 11th November 2026 , 9:18 pm / amazon , amazon-web-services , testing , werner-vogels , ai , rust , docker , generative-ai , llms , agentic-engineering Browse tools.simonwillison.net by tag . I've been wanting a better way to browse my collection of vibe-coded tools (244 and counting) for a while. I had a few Fable 5.2 credits left over before my weekly reset so I set it to work using tree-sitter to analyze the code for JavaScript APIs, libraries, and web API hosts used by each tool. The homepage now features tag clouds for browsing by each of those categories of tag: # 11th November 2026 , 6:42 pm / javascript , tools , ai , generative-ai , llms , claude , vibe-coding Anthropic’s IPO roadshow video . Anthropic kicked off their IPO roadshow yesterday, and their roadshow video has some previously unreleased information about how their business works. The section on "Approach to compute" with co-founder Tom Brown is particularly interesting, describing how Anthropic train and serve Claude across AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs. I'm not sure why there's no official video transcript, but here's one that I extracted using MacWhisper. Highlights below: We train and serve Claude now across all four major chip families. That's only possible because early on we made an unconventional bet on a multi-chip strategy. At the time, many people thought that running AI models on different chips wasn't worth the effort. Each chip needs its own tailored software stack and inference stack, which is expensive and difficult to build. We've now been doing it for years, and we've gotten incredibly good at it. [...] As an example, this year, we started working with AMD GPUs for the first time. In the past, bringing on a new chip platform took dozens of engineers months of work This time, we had Mythos try it out. It got Claude running on AMD in just three days, with basically no human intervention . Claude ported or wrote almost 100% of the kernels. [...] The second driver of our compute advantage is our rate of discovery of compute multipliers. We focus on total effective compute, which is the multiplicative product of physical capacity times the compute multipliers that we discover. Each one we discover makes our pool of total effective compute bigger. For example, say you need 100 units of compute to train a model of a certain intelligence. A 4x compute multiplier means you can use 25 units of compute to train the exact same model. Or you can use those hundred physical units to train an even more intelligent model that would have previously required 400 units. Compute multipliers create a competitive advantage for us that's hard to replicate. They build on each other. Each new multiplier we discover has a positive effect on the multipliers before it. They stack. We believe that this can accelerate even further as we approach recursive self-improvement. Claude will be able to discover compute multipliers entirely by itself , allowing the number of compute multipliers to grow faster and faster. We got a hint at Anthropic's multi-chip strategy last September in their postmortem of three recent issues , where they described bugs that affected just their TPU deployments. # 11th November 2026 , 3:11 pm / ai , generative-ai , llms , anthropic , gpus , claude-mythos-fable , recursive-self-improvement Introducing Our Smallest, Most Efficient Model: Muse Ember . Meta AI just launched their entry in the Claude Haiku/GPT Luna category: Muse Ember, which they describe as: [...] our smallest and most efficient model designed for complex reasoning execution and the work agents repeat all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing. For shorter prompts it's priced the same as GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 - both are $0.10/million input tokens and $0.50/million output. Today's other big model release, Claude Fable 5.2, is 80x that price at $8/$40. The pricing is a little less straightforward as prompts get longer, though. Luna, Ember, and Haiku all support up to a million input tokens, but they also all have a threshold after which the price goes up. Taking that threshold into account Ember is priced between the two others: But comparing price-per-token doesn't really make sense these days, when reasoning tokens mean that different models might use dramatically different numbers of tokens to solve the same problem. For that, one measure that's useful is the Artificial Analysis. And even more useful than that is their Intelligence Index vs. Cost per Task chart, which shows the following for those three models: The Muse Ember models sit right on that Pareto line - the line at which you can only improve one dimension by giving up another. Meta call this out in their announcement: It also sits on the efficiency frontier of the full Artificial Analysis leaderboard: no model scores higher for less per task. (That grey dot on the Pareto line in the middle of the green area is GPT-6.1 Terra (low) - clearly I should be paying more attention to the Terra family!) Muse Ember has six reasoning levels - minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh, and max - so I rendered six pelicans riding bicycles . The "high" reasoning level failed to return a full SVG, and the other SVGs were surprising in that the reasoning level didn't cleanly map to the visual quality of the response. Here's the "max" one, but the others are worth a look too: The Ember pelicans are comparable in quality to those I got from Muse Wonder , which is 40x the price of Muse Ember. # 10th November 2026 , 7:28 am / ai , generative-ai , llms , meta , llm-pricing , llm-release , artificial-analysis , muse datasette #3046: Don’t serve link: rel=next HTTP headers to Firefox for HTML pages . I was looking at the Firefox network panel today when I noticed that requests to a Datasette table page were triggering an HTTP prefetch to the next page of rows in that table. This was happening because Datasette pages serve an HTTP link header like this: link: <https://latest.datasette.io/fixtures/compound_three_primary_keys?_next=a%2Cd%2Cv>; rel="next" This is bad. A tiny fraction of the visitors to one of those pages will click the "next" link, which means for everyone else their browser is fetching unnecessary data and the Datasette server is having to render an entire page that then gets thrown away.

abstract: Claude Fable 5.2 responds closely to what the prompt says about who owns the code it works on. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, when a prompt said nothing about ownership or presented the code base as someone else’s, the model tended to add to the existing structure, even when that repeated existing code. It's evolved into my ideal tool for sharing Markdown transcripts that include SVG documents. Given my proclivity for drawing pelicans riding bicycles this is a problem that I needed to solve! The tool is very simple. Navigate to markdown-svg-renderer in your browser and paste in some Markdown to see it rendered... or save that Markdown to a CORS-friendly URL or a GitHub Gist and paste in a URL to that document. The URL option will give you a bookmarkable page, for example https://tools.simonwillison.net/markdown-svg-renderer#url=https%3A%2F%2Fgist.github.com%2Fsimonw%2F6f9e48293be5c916652d29f0dc0b0657 - which bakes in the URL to this Gist . If you visit the Gist you'll see raw SVG: In the rendered tool that looks like this instead: As you can see, that SVG block in the Markdown has been transformed into a rendered SVG (in this case animated) plus several tabs. The tabs are the really fun bit. The PNG and JPEG tabs render that SVG to those image formats in the browser and lets you copy or download them - useful for sharing on platforms that don't support SVG directly. The MP4 tab is new today - it examines the SVG to see if it contains any animations, attempts to guess how long the looped video should be, then renders a whole bunch of frames of the animation and loads 30+MB of ffmpeg.wasm so it can compile those frames into an MP4 video using the full power of FFMPEG compiled to WebAssembly and running in the browser. Being able to turn an animated SVG into a MP4 again makes it easy to share on platforms that can't support SVG animation natively. It's a neat trick! # 16th August 2026 , 11:59 pm / svg , markdown , tools I wrote this summary of the past few weeks of open letters as a section of my sponsors-only newsletter but I've decided to share it here as well. abstract: Release TIL Research Tool Museum Sighting Comment Fixes a security issue reported by Daniel de Araujo in GHSA-v9h7-jj4g-f862 and GHSA-r639-rr7r-x72w . LLM has a mechanism called extra-openai-models.yaml - now managed by the new-in-0.37 llm openai endpoint add command - for using LLM with OpenAI-compatible API endpoints from other providers. Daniel reported two ways this could accidentally send your configured OpenAI API key to one of those providers: if the key named by api_key_name had never been stored, or if a responses: true model was run with -o chat_completions 1 . Gemini 4 Carbon was announced two weeks ago for "a subset of cyber defenders", but today it's available to everyone else . This is Google's best ever Gemini, priced at $2/million input and $10/million output at launch (that's GPT-6.1 Sol / Claude Sonnet 5.5 prices) but scheduled to double in price to $4/$20 on December 1st (same as Opus 5.5). Here are three pelicans for the low, medium and high thinking efforts (it defaults to medium). This is the pelican I got for high: Gemini pelicans have all been great for a while now, so I also tested it out using Google's Antigravity IDE with a prompt I first tried with Claude Fable 5.2 yesterday : Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data Here's the HTML result (I had to prompt "build that into a standalone HTML file" to get a version with no external dependencies). I realized I didn't know where Yonkers was, so I looked it up on Google Maps and then, to help embed its location and shape in my head (and to try out Claude Fable 5.2's 3D modeling and animation skills), I prompted Fable 5.2 Medium to: Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and átomos around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data It correctly deduced that "átomos" was a mobile keyboard typo for "stomps": Anthropic released Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 today. Fable 5.2 is currently ranked first on Artificial Analysis . Anthropic say it "solved two open problems in the physics of black holes", so clearly their internal benchmarks have become more ambitious! I've added the new models to llm-anthropic , so you can now run prompts through Fable 5.2 like this: I ran pelicans at all five reasoning levels - low , medium , high , xhigh , and max . You can see them all here - here's the best result I got, from xhigh : max failed to return an image at all, running out of tokens after spending 128,000 thinking about them . That's the same bug that I saw with Opus 5.5 - but it's new for the Fable series, both Fable 5 and Fable 5.1 returned max effort pelicans just fine. It's priced at $8/million input and $40/million output, which is a 20% discount on the previous Fable 5.1 ($10/$50). I also used Fable 5.2 to help identify the source of a mysterious beep . Comment My comment on The Web Is More Than Enough, by Paul Ford — Hacker News OK, this comment convinced me to give that a shot. Here's a thing I made in Three.js this morning - a Nudibranch themed Faberge Egg: https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2026/Hidden-Reef-Egg... (77KB) I just asked Claude (Opus 5.5 Medium running in regular Claude Chat) to port that to Vanilla JS, in the same thread where it had built it, and got this: https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2026/Hidden-Reef-Egg... (98KB) They aren't identical - you can see what Claude said about that in the transcript (I don't fully understand why it differed): https://claude.ai/share/e56d163e-2793-4677-aa11-191d5058b414 But yeah, it turns out Claude Opus 5.5 is perfectly capable of 3D modeling in Vanilla JS + WebGL without Three.js. In eyeballing the code I find the Three.js slightly easier to understand myself, but I rarely look at the code for these 3D projects so that isn't a particularly big deal. # 9th November 2026 , 4:32 am / claude , javascript , three-js , hacker-news , generative-ai , ai , llms I was out walking the dog when I got curious about how easy/difficult it would be to write a SQLite C extension that adds a parse_number() function for turning strings like -$1,234.56 or '12.5%' into numeric values that could be summed and sorted. I fired up regular Claude chat (Opus 5.5) and prompted : I'm thinking about a SQLite custom function 'parse_number(value)' that strips ',', '$', '£' and '%', handles a leading '-', and returns 'NULL' for anything it can’t parse Explore the difference between building this as a SQLite extension in C v.s. in Rust - I want to compare performance and code complexity and size of the resulting .so (or whatever) file This gave me a solid starting point - the Rust extension was 321 KB (using Rusqlite ) and 298 KB (using sqlite-loadable-rs ), while the C extension was 14 KB. But the Rust extension was faster! Turns out that's because the Rust equivalent of C's strtod is "twice as fast". So I prompted: Try writing your own C function for parsing text into a decimal number that catches up to or beats the Rust implementation And it did, using "Clinger's fast path": Net cost per row over 2 million rows, lower is better: Finally, I had it rewrite the prototype as a research report to match the others in simonw/research by prompting this: Clone simonw/research from GitHub and turn your above investigation into a research report as seen in that repository - you can give me a zip file to download that contains your new folder Comment My comment on Terry Pratchett's Study — Hacker News Terry Pratchett once wrote about the concept of "horizontal wealth". Vertical wealth is where you spend money on rich people stuff - yachts and suchlike. Horizontal wealth is where you spend more money on the things you liked before you got rich: https://chibuikeani.blogspot.com/2017/02/the-price-of-happin... But horizontal wealth means not letting your increased income dictate your tastes. You like books and now you have money? Buy more books! Change those catenary bookshelves for good hardwood ones! In my case, build a library extension to your office. And, of course, you buy what will be useful for that most wonderful of pursuits, blind research, which is research without direction for the sheer joy of it. (Original source is his book A Slip of the Keyboard - this linked blog post quotes that bit.) # 7th November 2026 , 7:34 pm / hacker-news , terry-pratchett Fixes a bug that affected my agent.datasette.io demo site, where the set of available LLM models was not correctly restricted to just those in the configuration. Datasette Apps adds support for hosting and editing custom HTML applications inside of Datasette. These can be created by hand, but it's easier to create them using LLMs via Datasette Agent . This release improves that integration: This is a significant release of Datasette Agent . The most notable new feature is called the panel - it lets the agent chat open and then sit next to pages from Datasette, for example a table or query page. When combined with datasette-apps this means you can prompt a database-backed app into existence and then modify it from the chat that sits next to that app. You can try it by signing in with your GitHub account to agent.datasette.io . A bugfix release for LLM , with contributions from Steven Huang , Tao An , Arjan Mossel , and XQ .

title: Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too
abstract: Yesterday’s hot paper was Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab. The paper (OK, the authors classify is as a “blog post”, but it’s paper-shaped) found that frontier models, in particular GPT-6 Astra, can both interpret and modify the raw weights of a machine learning model—literally a text description of the model containing a bunch of floating point numbers. I’ve been playing with one of the examples from the paper and I’m delighted to share that Qwen 3.8 27B running on my laptop can do this as well! Here’s the highlight from their abstract, describing impressive capabilities for GPT-6 Astra and coining the term Weight-Space Programming for when LLMs analyze and modify model weights: Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do . And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps. Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights . With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x. All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming . The paper combines two topics that I think deserve to be treated separately. The first is what models can do with raw weights without running tools or executing code. The second explores how well models, once armed with code, can run operations to update and improve other models. spaCy author Matthew Honnibal called the paper misleading for conflating the two, and Sean Goedecke deconstructed the Qwen3.5-0.8B update example as taking the same steps that a human ML researcher would use. I’m going to focus on the no-tools question, which I think is the more interesting of the two. The paper presents the first question as Can LLMs understand model behaviors from weights? They trained four neural networks to play simplified 10x10 grid versions of four classic computer games—Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man, and Freeway (I had to look that one up , it’s an Atari 2600 game from 1981). Then they fed those weights (as floating point numbers) to an LLM along with the following question: The weights below belong to one policy network that was trained with reinforcement learning to play a game on this grid. Which game was it trained on? Work from the weights. You have no tools: no code execution, no calculator, nothing to run. This is a single response. The GitHub repository that accompanies the paper is RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs . The exp1_which_game folder contains the prompts they used, with weights for the four games: I checked and, aside from the weights, each prompt is identical to the others. The prompts on GitHub are self-contained. My LLM tool has a -f/--fragment option which can be passed the URL to a text file to use as a prompt, which means I can run any of the above like this: This example requires the llm-openrouter plugin installed, and runs the Breakout prompt against Kimi K3.1 Pro via OpenRouter. Here’s what I got back from Kimi K3.1 Pro , which successfully guessed Breakout after 9m 41s and 19,493 reasoning tokens. But how about Qwen 3.8 27B ? That’s still my favorite model to run on my own laptop—it’s just 17GB (I use this version ) and somehow feels close to the leading proprietary models of 2025. I fired up LM Studio , ensured Qwen 3.8 27B was loaded with a long context window (the default 8192 context failed with errors), installed the llm-lmstudio plugin and ran this command: (I had to bump the timeout up using an environment variable, see this issue .) After 46m 12s and 43,506 reasoning tokens, Qwen on my laptop returned a response that ended like this (here’s the reasoning trace ): Game: A simplified Pac-Man-style gridworld: an agent moves through a fixed 8x8 maze with central and corner wall blocks, moving objects/ghosts, and reward targets/pellets. Description: The agent navigates a fixed maze-like 8x8 board, using current agent/moving-object/previous-frame cues to move through corridors, collect reward-target cells, and avoid moving objects or hazards. This is impressive. I tried it on two of the other games as well. It identified Pong ( reasoning ) in 1h 4m 54s: Pong — specifically a Pong-like paddle/ball game where the agent controls a vertical paddle on the right side and must move up/down to intercept or return a moving ball/reward object. The agent moves a right-side paddle vertically to hit or catch a moving ball-like reward target moving across the 8×8 field, while a left-side moving object/opponent and wall borders define the play; reward is obtained by successfully intercepting/returning/scoring the ball, and missing or failing to hit it is penalized. And Breakout ( reasoning ) in 52m 25s: Game: Breakout, or an Arkanoid-like paddle/ball/brick game. Description: The agent is a paddle on the bottom row and moves left/right to keep a ball in play; the ball moves around the upper grid, and bricks/reward targets in the top rows give reward when hit, while missing the ball/hitting the bottom wall ends the episode or gives penalty. Qwen failed at the Freeway prompt, which didn’t surprise me considering that game is more obscure than the other three. Here’s that transcript —Qwen thought it was “A simplified Pac-Man-like grid game: agent moves 4-directionally”. The reasoning traces are fun to skim, and almost incomprehensible. Here’s a sample: What about agent channel0? We see some large channel0 rows near row8 col7/8 and maybe bottom? Let’s list channel0 large: line436 input435 (row8 col7 ch0) -2.107,1.169,0.513...; line441 input440 (row8 col8 ch0) -0.376,0.010,1.564,3.855...; line445 input444 (row8 col8 ch4) 0.142,0.491...; line382? input381 ch0? Wait line382 input381: 381//5=76 (row7 col6), ch1? 381%5=1? 76 * 5=380, ch1. So not. Channel0 large maybe at row8 col7/8 only. Also top row? line44 input43 ch3, line49 ch3. Channel0 large maybe not many. Agent position could be near bottom-right? If the agent is typically at bottom-right? That said though, I expect a sufficiently experienced human being armed with a notepad and a pencil could get there with enough effort. It’s a cool paper, but some of the wider commentary I’ve seen around it does not feel justified. I’m not ready to declare that the age of source code is over and our future involves incomprehensible machines editing their own model weights in incomprehensible ways. This is Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too by Simon Willison, posted on 3rd November 2026 .
