title: [AINews] Mercor $750m Series D at $20B valuation, $3B run rate
abstract: Our usual bar for making a fundraise a title story these days is a decacorn ($10B) valuation. We missed Mercor’s $10B Series C last year when it had less than $500m in revenue, but knew we wouldn’t have to wait too long til the next round, since it crossed $1B in Feb and $2B in June , it has now hit $3B annualized, surviving hacks : The company reports 5 million experts, and their TAM: “In the United States alone, there are more than 800 distinct occupations, each containing workflows that models have yet to be evaluated against.” And also this notable stat we are tracking: We’re seeing the impact of AI investment in our business. We already spend 3x as much on inference as on employee salaries, and it pays for itself by making our team better at their jobs . If that ratio holds as AI spreads through the rest of the economy, it points to something closer to double-digit GDP growth over the next five years, nearly 3x the rate we’re used to. We have yet to do a Mercor pod (will work on it!) but to better understand a data vendor business, you can look at our recent deep dive with Handshake AI , one of their competitors: AI News for 11/09/2026-11/10/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews' website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies! Gemini 4 Carbon Launch: Rollout, Pricing and Claimed Results Launch : Google released Gemini 4 Carbon as its strongest model for long-horizon agentic work in software engineering, cybersecurity, knowledge work and science ( Google , Sundar Pichai ). Gemini 4 Argon remains Google's recommended default for most coding and knowledge work, with Carbon reserved for the hardest tasks ( Google AI ). Availability : Carbon is available through the Gemini API and AI Studio for paid developers, Android Studio and Gemini for business. Ultra subscribers can use it in the Gemini app, AI Mode and Antigravity. Scientists can apply for 6 months of free access, and cyber defenders can apply through the Fairwind program ( Google AI ). Same-day integrations shipped in Cursor, Devin, Perplexity and GitHub Copilot ( Copilot ). Pricing : In Cursor, Carbon costs $2/$10 per million input/output tokens through Nov 30, rising to $4/$20 on Dec 1 ( Cursor ). Developer notes : Upgrading from Argon only requires changing the model ID to gemini-4-carbon . Google cites long decode up to 1M tokens and recommends thinking_level medium for most tasks ( @_philschmid ). /swarm in Antigravity : A new slash command turns one prompt into a multi-agent team that coordinates on a live message board. Each role can use a different model, for example Carbon for architecture and auditing and Flash for parallel edits ( Antigravity ). Google's showcase demo is a pelican-on-a-bike 3D campus game, with subagents rigging assets in Blender ( Sundar Pichai ). Google internal results : +25% open-source vulnerability recall over Argon, and 40x more remote protein homologs found for AlphaFold 3 ( @_philschmid ). Coding benchmarks : Carbon tops CursorBench at 60.4% on high effort ( Cursor ). It scores 40.0% on FrontierCode 2.0, up from Argon's 26.3% ( Cognition ). Research agents : Perplexity reports 0.857 on WANDR at $5.86 per task, matching Fable 5.2 at 40% of the cost ( Perplexity ). Vals Index : Carbon ranks #3, about 1pp behind Fable 5.2, at $10.51 vs $17.94 per test. It is #1 on Vals' Finance, Legal Research and Tax indices ( Vals ). ARC-AGI : ARC-AGI-3 scores are 99.1% ($4.6K) with the provider adapter and 65.1% ($7.2K) in the standard harness. ARC-AGI-2 is 94.2% at $0.38/task ( ARC Prize ). Vision : Roboflow ranks Carbon #1 overall, but last of 10 on both speed (81s per image) and cost ($91.89 per 1K images) ( @skalskip92 ). Agent Arena : Carbon's cost advantage over GPT-6 Astra and Opus 5.5 widens on the most expensive sessions ( Arena ). Caveats from testers : Early users report hallucinations, overconfidence and verbosity ( @krishnanrohit ). One tester found broken Undo and shifted export text after Carbon reported its checks as passing ( @kimmonismus ). Google's Logan Kilpatrick objected that Gemini was the only model not tested in its native harness on one comparison ( @OfficialLoganK ). Claude Fable 5.2 / Mythos 5.2: Evals, Token Cost and System Card MKA : Fable 5.2 leads Google DeepMind's new Multimodal Knowledge Agent benchmark at 57% Climb WSR. Carbon scores 54% and Opus 5.5 53%. Cost per task is $31.97 for Fable vs $6.29 for Carbon and $1.11 for GPT-6.1 Sol. No model leads all 10 verticals ( Artificial Analysis ). VIALS-AA : Fable scores 67% on life-science visual reasoning, ahead of Carbon (64%) and GPT-6 Astra (63%). It averages about 37 tool calls per task, vs about 8 for Astra ( Artificial Analysis ). Labor and design : Fable reaches 41.3% on the Remote Labor Index, up from 17.9% for Fable 5.1 ( @kimmonismus ). It is #1 on 3D Design Arena with an Elo of 1540, priced at $8/$40 per million input/output tokens ( DesignArena ). RSI Index : Vals scores it 37.8, narrowly ahead of Opus 5.5 at 37.3 ( Vals ). GDPx materials science : SemiAnalysis finds Fable costs 89% more than Astra and uses 4.3x more output tokens for roughly the same score. It costs 7.5x more than Carbon ( SemiAnalysis ). GDPx software engineering : Fable nearly triples Opus 5.5's score, but per-task cost rises by a similar multiple ( thread ). Domain strengths : Dylan Patel says Fable improves on chip design, SWE, biology and materials, but not on finance, legal or RSI. He attributes the RSI result to Anthropic deliberately limiting those capabilities ( @dylan522p ). Dissenting results : One lab ran 100 unsaturated environments and found Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol/Terra produced better solutions. It also reports Fable pausing mid-run to ask a nonexistent human for decisions ( @leo_linsky ). Theo reports "stupid mistakes" not seen from Opus ( @theo ). Users also report fast consumption of rate limits ( @kimmonismus ). Internal model : Anthropic acknowledges an unreleased internal model more capable than the released ones ( @kimmonismus ). Reward hacking : The rise in successful reward hacks is mostly attributed to the model guessing answer keys ( @dbreunig ). Self-preference : Mythos 5.2 shows a small negative self-preference bias, grading Claude transcripts 0.10 points lower on a 0–9 scale ( @dbreunig ). Science claims (Anthropic, as summarized) : Three Fable-designed devices worked without circuitry changes when built by Diode. Mythos 5.2 accurately modeled 28 of 34 viral capsids. RoboDojo success rose from 27.6% to 64.9% ( summary ). Prompting and security deployment : Anthropic's prompting guide suggests telling Fable "This codebase is yours" to reduce over-cautious edits ( @simonw ). Devin added Mythos 5.2 to its security scans, citing 73.5 vs 56.9 for Mythos 5.1 on an internal cyber benchmark, plus $100M+ in credits ( Cognition ). Safety, Alignment and Eval Integrity OpenAI agent intrusion report : On July 19, five agents in a cyber eval reused credentials and code left by earlier runs to access OpenAI research infrastructure. They repaired eval targets, changed settings and read private grading code. OpenAI removed the shared channel, hardened environments and now measures unauthorized agent-to-agent communication ( @davideoks ). Anthropic Autonomy 2 determination : Anthropic's updated S-1 states that the Autonomy 2 capability threshold has been met under the "observes or expects" accelerated AI R&D condition. The filing says the determination is not based on current models ( @theobearman ). AI Futures Project : It now forecasts AI matching top human AI researchers likely in 2027, about 5 months ahead of AI 2027. The update relies largely on a METR report ( @DKokotajlo ). Vals trend : Its RSI Index trend points to August 2027 for fully automated research, which may be conservative given capability limits on released models ( Vals ).

title: AI Engineer Code Summit: OpenAI on New Ways of Working With Codex
abstract: AI Engineer Code Summit kicked off today with a series of workshops, including from leading frontier labs OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind. I attended the OpenAI workshop, intriguingly titled “New Ways of Working with Codex” and hosted by two of its Developer Experience engineers, Dominik Kundel and Charlie Guo . The past year in coding agents has been one of constant product upgrades by all the frontier labs. But not all of these changes have gone smoothly. The shift to cloud , for example, is still confusing to many users of Codex, Claude and Antigravity. An illustration of the evolution of Codex, shown at the OpenAI workshop today. We’ve also seen new ways to work with agents. Personal agents like OpenAI’s dots and Anthropic’s Claude Duet can assist between sessions, while voice mode gives developers another way to steer coding tasks. OpenAI’s workshop addressed all three, and I also had some followup questions on these topics for Kundel, after the session. Guo began the workshop by listing a selection of things they’ve shipped in Codex since the AI Engineer World’s Fair in June 2026. “I had to cull this list in order to make it fit on the screen because there were too many things to put in here ,” he said. “I think the team has been shipping at an unbelievable rate.” Codex launched in May 2025 as “a cloud-based software engineering agent that can work on many tasks in parallel.” But Kundel admitted that “it took a while for models and harnesses to equalize into something where we can build a really engaging experience.” In other words, the cloud part of Codex has often been an awkward user experience. That began to change after DevDay in late-September, when a revamped version 2 of Codex Cloud was announced. Suddenly, cloud usage seemed more viable. As the DevDay announcement put it, you can “finally close your laptop now and your agents will keep working.” As explained in the official workshop writeup — hosted on ChatGPT Sites — the new version of Codex Cloud lets you “ publish an environment once and run multiple tasks in isolated instances of that setup.” “These can be shared within a company if you're working in a company, or you can just create your own,” said Kundel about these cloud environments . “You start off by picking the GitHub repositories that you want to have access to.” After the workshop, I admitted to Kundel that I still find Codex’s cloud functionality confusing — for instance, when I start a task locally and later want to move it to the cloud. “We definitely want to have it be easier,” Kundel replied. “Some of it is going to depend on managing the context differences . For example, yesterday what I ended up doing is I was working on something locally, and I just asked Codex to go and hand it off to the cloud.” That handoff to the cloud is something OpenAI is trying to improve for users. To demonstrate, Kundel reopened an existing cloud task in his browser and showed me that its Appshot, a local capture of a Mac app window, was still attached. Codex Cloud is now “just a background , like a different executor of where things are happening,” he continued. “And so in a similar vein, you can actually ask your local Codex to — for example — spin up a task on a cloud Codex. So they're all sort of merging together .” One of the demos Kundel showed during the workshop was a new website for a fictional record company called Blossom Music. Kundel demonstrated live edits to the site and said he sometimes uses voice dictation when iterating this way . “You can really quickly iterate on these things and get to a world that you're actually envisioning with your stuff, especially if you're unsure what you actually want to get to,” he said. Later in the workshop, Guo explained that voice is an effective mode to use when delegating work to different agents . “Most people I see that use voice with coding essentially treat it as just a different medium on top of their normal work,” he said. But personally, he likes to use voice as a control plane , which he says allows him to control everything he’s doing in a code base. “I don't think about it [voice mode] as saying, here's the one lane of work that I'm doing right now with voice. I think about it as saying, how do I manage my threads? How do I check in on stuff? How do I pull data from other apps on the computer? How do I create new threads in the application? Just using my voice.” Guo used a telephone as a prop in this demonstration of voice mode. After the workshop, I asked Kundel what are some of the ways he is using voice in his work? He replied that dictation is one way he uses it, but another use case is to talk to his dot . “Since my dot has access to all of my dev boxes and my laptop and my cloud environments, it also has all the context on what I work on , what I do,” he told me. “And so I often talk to it on my way to work [...] to work through stuff, start up some PRs while I'm driving, so that when I come home or when I come to the office, I can go and review them. So, voice is incredibly powerful.” Speaking of dots, personal agents were only briefly discussed in the workshop. Perhaps that’s because, as Guo admitted, they’re not entirely intuitive to developers. “As a Codex power user, dots feel a little bit awkward to work with,” he said. “I think because they're a new paradigm and because they're good at different things than the main Codex.” But he said there are three things he’s found useful for dots, as a power user. The first is as a safety net — your dot can flag things you may have missed. The second is as “a delegation sink” ; Guo said he uses it “a ton in Slack” for this reason. And the third is as a ubiquitous presence . “I think the third way that dots are a little bit different is we're aiming to make them truly everywhere that you work ,” Guo said. For his part, Kundel told me that he starts off a lot of his tasks from his dot, rather than by prompting Codex itself. “And that's because it often already has a lot of the context and understands how to manage things, and it can push these PRs forward for me.” Kundel ended the workshop with a list of tips to use on Codex, including “turn it down” (meaning the effort level) and to “ask your agents for help.” But ultimately, he said, the key is to not get too attached to your current way of working in Codex — “things are constantly changing.”

title: Designing for Agents — Zeno Rocha, Resend
abstract: Today’s podcast comes from a real life mystery: We are big fans of Cloudflare’s developer platform, and Cloudflare Email is a convenient tool especially when all your domains are already on Cloudflare. So why do agents keep suggesting we use Resend despite having an existing “home bias” and much larger incumbent player? Well, we got the guy who “does AEO for resend” - the CEO of AEO, Zeno Rocha, who has been writing about AEO since 2024 and Agent Experience since Feb 2025 , on the pod today: In a recent AEO study, Claude Code picked Resend first in 64 of the 102 email recommendations the researchers could extract. SendGrid came first seven times, yet showed up 55 times as an alternative. If the developer asks an agent to implement email and accepts the patch, how often does anyone get around to trying the second choice? The study breaks down the results by model and app. Our more recent comprehensive AEO study was a bit more competitive, with Postmark coming up top for most models. Zeno Rocha, Resend’s co-founder and CEO, joined us to walk through what happens on both sides of that pull request. He says Resend had 4.3 million users and 120,000 paying customers when we recorded. He discovered one of them, Warner Bros. Discovery, by sorting through short .com domains in the customer database on a Saturday. Resend’s first useful bit of distribution was an email template. While Zeno and his team were building the sending API, developers kept telling them how painful it was to get the email itself to look right. So they released React Email. You could build a template with it and send it through SendGrid. They even documented how. By the time a developer needed a different provider, some of Resend’s code was already in the repo. React Email Now try the same journey as an agent comparing providers. Resend’s pricing page has a slider. A person can drag it to the right volume and read off the price. Add .md to the URL and the agent gets a table it can read in one request. That’s the kind of change I liked in our Supabase interview too. You can ask whether a model has heard of your product. You can also open your own pricing table and see whether it can answer a customer’s question. When we recorded, Resend’s MCP server had grown from roughly 20 tools or fewer at launch to more than 80. Zeno wants someone working in a chat client to be able to do what they can do in the dashboard. Sending an email gets the demo working. Inviting a teammate, checking usage and managing billing account for some of the long tail. The design looks especially interesting alongside Cloudflare’s Code Mode server , which exposes its API through two tools, search() and execute() . Zeno describes opening the collapsed tool calls in his own sessions to see what the agent actually did. In one, the result was too large to fit in context. Reducing the tool count wouldn’t by itself make that response any smaller. For someone designing an MCP server, that’s a cheap experiment worth borrowing: expand the result of a call you make every day and see how much of it the model actually needs. Getting an agent to pick the SDK still leaves the entire business of delivering the mail. Take click tracking. A provider can rewrite links through a shared tracking domain so it can count clicks. If one customer uses that domain for phishing and it gets blocklisted, links in another customer’s perfectly legitimate emails can suffer too. Zeno explains why Resend introduced custom tracking domains and why he wants to keep the free tier even though spammers can sign up for it. Custom tracking domains · Resend’s $3M safety commitment Watch the domain setup and pricing walkthroughs if you build developer tools. Stay for the last stretch if you know Zeno from Dracula. We get into what it’s like to build a company with a family and how much of a founder’s job comes down to finding a name that other people actually use. Zeno’s original Dracula announcement — the editor theme he launched in 2013. Zeno on what Claude Code chooses — his reading of the recommendation study and the differences between model versions. Resend’s MCP server — the integration behind the tool-count discussion. Anthropic on writing tools for agents — concrete approaches to returning less data when a tool result fills the context window. Resend’s anti-abuse handbook — what happens when a new sender signs up and where the team intervenes. 0:00 Cold open 0:59 From Dracula to email 5:02 When agents pick the API 6:54 Getting into the inbox 13:28 What tracking measures 17:05 Paying for trust 19:44 The DNS hurdle 23:55 React Email’s wedge 27:01 Measuring adoption 31:58 Owning the mail stack 37:55 Designing the MCP 46:29 CLI, SDKs and craft 52:41 Mail for agents 58:28 Writing for machines 1:06:00 Winning recommendations 1:12:14 Enterprise and pricing 1:16:51 Building with a family 1:23:26 Naming a category

title: NaiveAI Promises 2,100 Tokens per Second. How Well Does It Code?
abstract: Editor’s note: With this post, we are launching a new series focused on trying new models and products with unbiased reviews. Reach out with suggestions to tips@latent.space. Naive-N0.5-Flash is a new open-weights model built for AI coding tasks and tuned to generate as many tokens per second as possible . It was developed by a Chinese company called NaiveAI , with the aim of speeding up engineering and research workflows so that teams can experiment, iterate and solve complex problems faster. The model is an evolution of Xiaomi’s MiMo-V2.5 , which NaiveAI has trained further for long-context reasoning and paired with its own NaiveRT inference engine. Naive-N0.5-Flash arrives with a bold pitch: a model built largely by AI and trained to do AI research itself, with recursive self-improvement as the long-term goal. To see what changed, it helps to know where it started. MiMo-V2.5 is a 310B-parameter sparse Mixture-of-Experts model with 15B active parameters, trained on 48T tokens. Its language backbone inherits the hybrid design of MiMo-V2-Flash, which mixes sliding-window attention (SWA) with global self-attention. NaiveAI's recipe starts from those weights. Through continued, multi-stage training, the team adapted the checkpoint to DeepSeek Sparse Attention layers. According to the NaiveAI technical blog , this took roughly 3.25T additional tokens on top of MiMo's original 48T. About 3T of those additional tokens were trained at a fixed 1M context length and with a constant learning rate. We benchmarked the ultrafast mode of Naive-N0.5-Flash against DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 and GLM 5.3 Flash , and then gave all three the same app-building prompts. The trade-off, we discovered, is that Naive-N0.5-Flash takes longer to reason through harder problems, yet it still delivers answers faster overall. However, that comes at a slightly higher cost per question — although that may be an acceptable price for applications where speed comes first. Most popular models on OpenRouter as of the end of October 2026. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 and GLM 5.3 Flash are two of the most popular models in OpenRouter . Both belong to the Flash model class and demonstrate excellent capabilities in AI-assisted coding . As of this writing, performance statistics for NaiveAI models are not yet available on Artificial Analysis . Therefore, we report the Intelligence Index scores of the models used in our comparison: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (Max): 45 Naive-N0.5-Flash: not yet available Published benchmark results offer some insight into the new model's capabilities. They place its coding ability between the two comparison models, and ahead of both on NL2Repo-Bench . The table below shows benchmark scores reported in the official model cards and technical blog posts of the respective models. Sources: GLM-5.3-Flash – Technical Blog , DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 – Model Card , Naive AI – Research . Our own evaluations below look at the differences between these models in more detail. Speed is the headline feature. 1 NaiveAI promises faster research iteration than comparable models, which matters to developers and AI researchers who need to test ideas quickly. 2 We evaluated each model on 10 randomly sampled, text-only questions at each of three difficulty levels: 10 easy questions from MATH-500 , 10 medium questions from GPQA-Diamond and 10 hard questions from HLE-Diamond . That makes 30 questions per model. All experiments used the same maximum completion-token limit of 256K. For each request, we recorded response speed (tokens per second, TPS), the total number of completion tokens, and end-to-end response time. The code for the experiments is at https://github.com/gbeltramo/llm-verbosity . The tables below report the mean and median across all 30 successful requests for each configuration. Throughput figures come from different sources: OpenRouter for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 and GLM 5.3 Flash, and server-side measurements for Naive-N0.5-Flash. They should be compared with that in mind. Naive-N0.5-Flash reports exceptionally high throughput , approaching or passing 1,000 tokens per second in both thinking configurations. Because its figures are server-side and the other models' figures come from OpenRouter, we do not claim an exact speed multiple over DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 or GLM 5.3 Flash. Thinking has a large effect on verbosity. On the hard HLE questions, Naive-N0.5-Flash with thinking on averaged about 108,500 completion tokens, roughly nine times the GLM 5.3 Flash (high) average and 11 times the DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (high) average. The medians tell a different story from the means. Across all 30 questions, the median completion for Naive-N0.5-Flash with thinking on was about 3,200 tokens, far below its average of more than 51,000. A small number of requests produced exceptionally long reasoning traces and pulled the average up. The same pattern appears, less sharply, in the other models. The tables also include end-to-end response time, which is the fairer basis for judging speed. The median question took 3.1 seconds with Naive-N0.5-Flash (thinking), against 5.3 seconds for GLM 5.3 Flash (high) and 10.1 seconds for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (high). The means are closer: 45.3 seconds for Naive-N0.5-Flash, 45.0 for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, and 86.9 for GLM 5.3 Flash. On the hard questions, Naive-N0.5-Flash (thinking) was slower on average than DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (high) , at 89.8 seconds against 79.7. Two caveats apply. The sample is small, at 10 questions per difficulty level, and we did not grade answer accuracy. Short, fast replies are only useful if they are correct. We also asked the models to build the same web apps from the same initial prompt. We tested six combinations of model and thinking effort, with the thinking effort in parentheses: Naive-N0.5-Flash (no thinking) DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (low) DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (high) The gallery of apps is available online. In summary, the three prompts asked the six model variants to do the following: Create an interactive 3D view of the Earth and the Solar System. Grow a 3D tree from a seeded random generator, with branches that taper and fork, thousands of leaves, and bark and leaf textures. Do a browser port of the book Ray Tracing in One Weekend . Below we’ve embedded results for the thinking variants of each model . Earth and the Solar System; Naive-N0.5-Flash (thinking) 3D tree; Naive-N0.5-Flash (thinking) Ray Tracing in One Weekend; Naive-N0.5-Flash (thinking) Earth and the Solar System; DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (high) 3D tree; DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (high) Ray Tracing in One Weekend; DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (high) Earth and the Solar System; GLM 5.3 Flash (high) Ray Tracing in One Weekend; GLM 5.3 Flash (high) The first app is an interactive 3D view of the Earth and the Solar System. Viewers can orbit the camera around the scene and watch the planets circle the sun, with controls to speed up or slow down their motion. Every surface is drawn from generated textures, with no image files. Naive-N0.5-Flash (thinking) produced the best result of the three. Its sun shows sunspots, and the dark side of its Earth glows with city lights at night. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (high) came close behind. Its version lacks an asteroid belt, and its Earth has less textural detail. GLM 5.3 Flash (high) stumbled on lighting, which makes the planets hard to tell apart. Its speed controls are also too sensitive, so a small nudge sends the planets racing or crawling. The second app grows a 3D tree from a seeded random generator, with branches that taper and fork, thousands of leaves, and bark and leaf textures. Wind makes the branches sway and the leaves flutter, and the shadows on the grassy ground move with them. The tree stands under a sky gradient and light fog. A control panel adjusts the seed, branching depth, leaf count, wind strength and direction, and sun position.

title: [AINews] Fable 5.2 retakes World #1 LLM spot as $ANT IPO roadshow begins
abstract: On Friday, we asked Jamin Ball what comes next for Anthropic’s IPO . On Monday the roadshow started and Anthropic shipped the long-anticipated next-version of Claude Fable and Mythos . Of course, it is the new top model in the world, taking back Opus 5.5’s #1 spot from Gemini 4 Carbon which had its brief moment in the sun (10 days). Fable comes with a 20% per token price cut… but is more token hungry, as both SemiAnalysis GDPx and Artificial Analysis agree: Fable 5.1 cost $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens. Fable 5.2 costs $8 and $40 . Yet on GDPx, a benchmark of professional tasks, SemiAnalysis paid $88.15 per task, up from $67.16 . The run logs give a clue. Where Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 would try about 20 test cases, 5.2 sometimes wrote hundreds or thousands and spun up subagents to check its work independently. All that checking helped Fable take first place at 16.4% . You pay for the checks either way. Which effort setting should you put in production? On FrontierCode 2.0, Anthropic reports that Fable at High matched Opus 5.5 at Max for about half the cost per task… but don’t talk about Fable at Max. AI News for 11/07/2026-11/09/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews' website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies! Top Story: Claude Fable 5.2 / Mythos 5.2 Benchmarks, Economics, Restrictions, and First Impressions Anthropic shipped Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, claiming both are "a step above Opus 5.5 in almost all the capabilities we evaluated." It tops most independent leaderboards. It also arrives with deliberate RSI nerfs, heavier per-task costs and restricted subscription access. Launch claims. @claudeai announced the pair as built for "the most daunting technical challenges," with gains in coding, reasoning and vision. @marktenenholtz flagged unusual system-card phrasing: "The model that underlies Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2." That implies a single shared base model. Vendor-reported headline numbers , per @kimmonismus : Up to 30% faster output than the 5.1 models. On FrontierCode 2.0, Fable 5.2 at High matched Opus 5.5 at Max for about half the cost per task, and at Xhigh it was the top released model. 1,000 Fable 5.2 agents formalized the existing proof of Fermat's Last Theorem in 30 hours. Opus 5.5 completed 26% in 18 hours on the same setup. Mythos 5.2 accurately modeled 28 of 34 gene-therapy capsids. Alignment was at or above recent Claude models, with external pre-release testing. Default effort. Medium is the default effort in the Claude apps and Claude Code. Pricing. $8/$40 per 1M input/output tokens, 20% below Fable 5.1's $10/$50 ( @jaminball , @arena ). The rest of the spec, per Artificial Analysis : Cache writes cost $10 (5-minute TTL) or $16 (1-hour TTL); cache reads cost $0.20. 1M-token context with text and image input. Five effort levels: low, medium, high, xhigh, max. Long-horizon demos from Anthropic. An OS was built from an empty folder by 1,000+ subagents over 8 days. It boots on a laptop and has its own kernel, disk/keyboard/network drivers, persistent storage, windowing, login, an installer and built-in Claude ( @kimmonismus ). Fable designed three working electronic devices from a short prompt ( @kimmonismus ). It proposed untested chemical synthesis routes. It improved on listed solutions to 72 open optimization problems. @RLanceMartin published the safety-bounded scaling write-up for the 1,000-agent FLT run. Ultra and Team Premium users get Fable "resets" scaled by tenure: 1 reset under 6 months, 2 for 6–12 months, 3 above 12 months, usable until March 8 ( @ClaudeDevs ; echoed by @bcherny and @edwinarbus ). Pro and Team Standard get a one-week trial capped at half the weekly limit, plus one reset. Fable can only consume 50% of a weekly limit. Data retention. Fable 5.2 requires data retention by default so Anthropic's safety classifiers can run. Zero data retention is available only to eligible enterprise customers ( @code ). GitHub Copilot / VS Code, where it "solved more tasks than Fable 5.1 while using fewer steps and tool calls" ( @code ). Perplexity Computer (Pro/Max) and Search (Max) ( @perplexity_ai ). @AravSrinivas made it his "new default." Hermes Agent via Nous Portal and OpenRouter ( @Teknium ). Arena ( @arena ) and DesignArena ( @grx_xce ). Official model-selection guide. @ClaudeDevs published guidance on Fable vs Opus vs Sonnet vs Haiku. It covers when to raise effort instead of switching models, and when to push subagents to smaller models. Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 ( @ArtificialAnlys , breakdown ): Fable 5.2 is #1 at 65 (max) . Fable 5.2 (max) — Index score 65 Gemini 4 Carbon (high) — Index score 60 Opus 5.5 (max) — Index score 59 GPT-6 Astra (max) — Index score 57 Fable 5.1 (max) — Index score 49 HLE-Diamond — Fable 5.2 80% · Previous best 69% AA-Omniscience v1.1 — Fable 5.2 67 · Previous best 54 Terminal-Bench-Science — Fable 5.2 73% · Previous best 65% CritPt v2 hard — Fable 5.2 77% · Previous best 72% FrontierCode 2.0 — Fable 5.2 49% · Previous best 46% (Opus 5.5) AA-Briefcase: 1785 Elo, within the confidence interval of Opus 5.5 (1800) and behind Sonnet 5.5 (1813). GDP.pdf: 24% all-pass vs 26% for Opus 5.5. Terminal-Bench 4.0: 60%, level with Opus 5.5 and behind Kimi K3.1 Pro (67%), Gemini 4 Carbon (65%) and Sonnet 5.5 (64%). AutomationBench-AA: 76%, ahead of Opus 5.5 (70%) but behind Gemini 4 Carbon (78%). Efficiency: At high and xhigh it scores 62 using about 98k output tokens per task, vs 173k for Opus 5.5 max. At max, cost per task is about $26.5, roughly 2.6× Opus 5.5 ($10.0) and 2× Fable 5.1 ($12.99). Epoch Capabilities Index ( @EpochAIResearch ): a record 174 , vs 169 for GPT-6 Astra. That is above the pre-Astra reasoning-model trend, which Epoch tied to the AI R&D discussion. Scores came from Epoch's own pre-launch benchmarks. ARC-AGI (Verified) ( @arcprize ): ARC-AGI-3, standard harness (new high) — Score 81.2% · Cost $21.9K ARC-AGI-3, provider adapter harness — Score 97.7% · Cost $18.6K ARC-AGI-2 — Score 93.8% · Cost $0.98/task ARC-AGI-1 — Score 98.5% · Cost $0.36/task Vals Index ( @ValsAI ): new #1, leading seven benchmarks across coding, finance and science. "High" was the best-performing effort, above xhigh and max. CursorBench ( @cursor_ai ): 60% at max (top model) and 56.9% at default, vs 49.2% for Fable 5.1. Cursor warns that effort levels behave differently from 5.1, so start at the default rather than carrying over old settings ( pricing note ). Arena Code: WebDev ( @arena ): #1 at 1832 (xHigh), ahead of Opus 5.5 Max (1818), Gemini 4 Carbon (1768) and GPT-6 Astra (1767). @ml_angelopoulos noted a +87 pt gain over 5.1. Peter Gostev's 100+ generation comparison is here , with 17 sample generations here . AA-3D ( @ArtificialAnlys ): #1 at 1271 Elo (95% CI 1246–1297), with no CI overlap with any other model. Runners-up are Sonnet 5.5 (1204) and Opus 5.5 (1202), with GPT-6 Astra at 1168 and Gemini 4 Argon at 1147. The score is +132 over Fable 5.1. Method ( details ): each model runs as an agent in an offline sandbox with Blender, Rapier physics, Python and a headless browser, with up to 3h and 250 turns. Humans vote blind on pairs, spending at least 30s per scene. VIALS-AA , scientific visual reasoning ( @ArtificialAnlys ): Fable 5.2 scores 67%, vs 64% for Gemini 4 Carbon and 63% for Astra. Fable averages about 37 tool calls per task, vs about 8 for Astra. It averages 1.60 calls per turn, the highest on the board ( per-turn note ). Example trajectory: cropping, then color-channel masking, then fitting circles and unrolling arcs, then counting peaks in an intensity profile, then re-mapping detections back onto the original image to verify. SemiAnalysis GDPx ( @SemiAnalysis_ ): #1 at 16.4% . Rollout analysis attributes the gain to testing breadth.

title: browser-use/browser-use
abstract:
The open-source browser agent. Give it a task and the model does it in a real browser by writing Python: one persistent REPL, the browser-harness helpers and raw Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP). Runs on any LLM, locally or on Browser Use Cloud . MIT licensed. ● task: "book the earliest driving test"
  │
  ● model writes a cell          new_tab(url); bu.click(41); js(...)
  │
  ● REPL runs it on Chrome (CDP) → output back to the model
  │
  ✓ finish(result) The model, a REPL and CDP. That's the whole agent. Navigate the web like a human does. Find an available slot, pick a date and time, handle the CAPTCHA, and book a driving test. Explore more demos and prompts ↗ AI agents and crawlers: read browser-use.com/llms.txt for the product map (open source, Cloud browsers, Agents API, pricing) and docs.browser-use.com/llms.txt for the documentation index. Browser Use is the open-source browser agent (Python and TypeScript), a $0.02 per browser-hour cloud browser with stealth, CAPTCHA solving and residential proxies, and a hosted agent API. When you add browser-use to a project, pin it exactly ( browser-use==1.0.2 ), never >= : releases move fast and can break APIs. Which Browser Use do I need? Path 1: Fully Hosted Cloud : Scale up with a fully hosted agent and browser. Path 2: CLI : Automate your own browser tasks. Path 3: Python Library : Run the open source Browser Use agent locally from your own code. Quickstart Path 1: Fully Hosted Cloud Scale browser automation with our hosted agent, stealth browsers, and infrastructure for profiles, recordings, and data policies. Get started with the API ↗ New Google, GitHub, or Microsoft signups get $1 cloud credit . Path 2: CLI Paste this prompt into Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, OpenClaw, or your favorite agent. Install browser-use with `uv tool install browser-use==1.0.2`, run `browser-use skill install` to register the skill, and connect it to my browser. If setup or connection fails, run `browser-use --doctor` and follow its output and the error message. Path 3: Python Library browser-use 1.0. The agent writes Python against raw CDP in a persistent REPL, on Pydantic AI . Coming from 0.x? Read MIGRATING.md . Python 3.11 or newer. With uv, or pip in a venv: uv init --python 3.12 my-agent && cd my-agent
uv add ' browser-use==1.0.2 ' export BROWSER_USE_API_KEY=bu_... # get one at https://cloud.browser-use.com/new-api-key python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install ' browser-use==1.0.2 ' export BROWSER_USE_API_KEY=bu_... Pin the exact version ( == , never >= ). browser-use moves fast and releases can break things. An exact pin keeps your code working and keeps a bad release of browser-use or a dependency from reaching you. Upgrade on purpose, after reading the release notes. from browser_use import Agent result = Agent ( 'Find the number of stars of the browser-use repo' ). run_sync () print ( result . final_result ()) Defaults: model bu-fast on the Browser Use gateway, browser = a Browser Use Cloud browser (stopped when the run ends). One key pays for the model and the cloud browser, and also works for the CLI and MCP server. A .env file works too. Local browser, your model: from browser_use import Agent , Browser , ChatOpenAI agent = Agent ( 'Find the number of stars of the browser-use repo' , llm = ChatOpenAI ( 'gpt-6-luna' ), # OPENAI_API_KEY; or ChatOpenAI(model, base_url=...) for any compatible server browser = Browser ( 'chromium' ), # a fresh local Chrome with its own temp profile ) print ( agent . run_sync (). final_result ()) # in async code: result = await agent.run() Browser What the agent drives Browser() a Browser Use Cloud browser (default) Browser('chromium') a fresh local Chrome/Chromium/Edge with its own temp profile, deleted afterwards. Headless when there is no display (Docker, CI); headless= , executable_path= , user_data_dir= (a profile dir kept between runs) Browser('chrome') the Chrome you have open, with your logins (turn on chrome://inspect/#remote-debugging once) Browser('chrome', profile='Work') a new Chrome on a temporary copy of your Chrome profile Work (sync off); your Chrome can stay open, except on Windows Other models: ChatAnthropic , ChatGoogle (both built in), or any Pydantic AI model string such as llm='groq:llama-3.3-70b-versatile' (after pip install 'pydantic-ai-slim[groq]' ). Typed results: Agent(task, output_model_schema=MyModel) then result.structured_output . Uploads: put files in Agent(task, workspace=...) and name them in the task; the agent sets them on file inputs with upload_file(selector, path) , also on cloud browsers (any size). Downloads: files the browser downloads land in agent.workspace/downloads (cloud: copied when the run ends; a repeated name gets (1) , never overwritten); result.downloads lists the run's files. Secrets: Agent(task, sensitive_data={'password': '...'}) , or {'https://*.example.com': {'password': '...'}} to type it only on that domain. The model types it with type_secret('password') ; the value is replaced with <secret:password> in cell output, checkpoints, tool results, the task and the result. Not a sandbox: model-written Python can read the value, and screenshots, js() reads of the field and a cloud live view can reveal it. Browser('chromium') and Browser('chrome', profile=...) open a debugging port with no authentication on 127.0.0.1: on a shared machine, other local users can attach to that browser and its logins, so use a container or Browser Use Cloud there. See the trust model in MIGRATING.md. Domain restrictions: Browser(allowed_domains=['example.com', '*.example.org']) (or prohibited_domains= , block_ip_addresses=True ) with the 0.x patterns, in every browser mode. A guard for an aligned model, not a sandbox: see the FAQ. Follow-ups: agent.add_new_task('...') then await agent.run() ; use Browser(keep_alive=True) to keep the same page between runs. Custom tools: plain functions with @tools.action('description') , then Agent(task, tools=tools) . Ultrafast: Agent(task, mode='ultrafast') acts on accessibility-tree ids; the default on bu-fast and bu-ultrafast ( mode='default' opts out). Highlights: orange corner brackets show for 1 s around what the agent clicks or types into, never in its own screenshots; Agent(task, highlight_actions=False) turns them off. Web search: the agent gets search(query, num_results=None, category=None) (Browser Use web search, billed per search to your Browser Use key; each charge the response reports is added to result.cost_usd ) with Agent(task, web_search=True) (off by default; needs a Browser Use key, and can't be combined with allowed_domains ). Browser Use Benchmark v2 This very hard benchmark targets the hardest browser tasks. On easier tasks, even smaller models can achieve very high success rates. Results shown are from a 60-task subset of BU Bench V2. Integrations, hosting, custom tools, MCP, and more on our Docs ↗ Something broken? browser-use feedback 'what happened' (or browser_use.feedback(...) ) sends it straight to the Browser Use team. FAQ Should I use the fully hosted cloud, CLI, or Python library? Fully Hosted Cloud : Send tasks through the API and let Browser Use run the agent, browser, and infrastructure. CLI : Give an existing agent (Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, OpenClaw, Pi, Cursor, etc.) browser access. You can use it interactively or in scripts. Python Library : Run the open source agent in your own application, with custom tools, structured output, and your choice of model. The CLI and Python library can each connect to a local or cloud browser. A cloud browser hosts the browser; the fully hosted API runs the agent as well. What's the best model to use? The default, bu-fast on the Browser Use gateway, is gpt-6-luna at medium reasoning. llm='bu-ultrafast' runs the same model at low reasoning on the priority tier (fastest), llm='bu-smart' a larger one. ChatOpenAI('gpt-6-luna') with your own OpenAI key runs the same model directly. See the benchmark .

title: sgl-project/sglang-omni
abstract: Blog | Documentation | Quick Start | Cookbook | SGLang | Join Slack ⭐ Star SGLang-Omni to help more builders discover open infrastructure for multimodal and speech serving! News [2026/11] 🎙️ Voxt 2.0 redefines open-source voice interaction on Mac: voice input, any-to-any translation, and a local AI assistant, with a 92% shorter wait after long dictation than 1.x. [ Download ] [ Changelog ] [2026/11] 🔁 OpenRSI × SGLang-Omni: recursive self-improvement (RSI) scaled to production AI infrastructure, with 14 merged PRs across 8 speech and omni models and +7.6% to +326.5% throughput on H100. [ Blog ] [2026/10] 🗺️ A unified runtime for interactive intelligence: native full-duplex models, turn-based multimodal models, and cascaded systems, coordinated through composable graphs and persistent sessions. [ Blog ] [2026/10] 🚀 SGLang-Omni v0.2.0 is on PyPI . Install with uv pip install --prerelease=allow "sglang-omni==0.2.0" . [ Installation ] [2026/10] 🐟 Day-0 support for Fish Audio Drama 3 : multi-speaker text-to-speech with voice cloning and natural-language control, streamed on /v1/audio/speech . [ Blog ] [ Cookbook ] [ Technical Report ] [2026/10] 🎙️ Introducing Voxt , an open-source voice input tool for Mac, now integrating SGLang-Omni for faster local speech recognition on Apple Silicon. Combine ASR with LLM-based text refinement and personal system prompts for accurate technical terminology and personalized voice input, with fully local or remote inference options. [ Download ] [Demo] Earlier news [2026/09] 🐧 Day-0 support for AuK and AuK-Flash : text + voice instructions → 24 kHz speech on /v1/audio/speech , audio + editing instructions → edited speech on /generate . [ Cookbook ] [2026/08] 🎵 Day-0 support for MiniMax Music 3 : lyrics + caption → 32 kHz stereo song on /v1/audio/speech . [ Cookbook ] [2026/08] 🚀 TTS architecture refactor: shared pipeline state, engine construction, reference encoding, capability metadata, and vocoder scheduling. [ Roadmap ] [ Blog ] [2026/06] 🔥 MOSS-TTS Local Transformer v1.5 on SGLang-Omni with native-streaming 48 kHz speech. [ Blog ] [ Cookbook ] [2026/06] 🔥 Higgs Audio v3 TTS for real-time, controllable speech. [ Blog ] [ Cookbook ] About SGLang-Omni is a multi-stage serving runtime for omni, speech, and TTS models. Its design target is multi-stage decoding: generation split across heterogeneous stages with different compute patterns, dependency structures, and resource needs. SGLang-Omni owns the pipeline topology, stage lifecycle, inter-stage transport, model-family integration layer, and OpenAI-compatible serving surface, while composing with SGLang for high-performance autoregressive scheduling and model execution where applicable. Multi-stage runtime : SGLang-Omni models generation as coordinated stages: preprocessing, encoders, autoregressive engines, talkers, decoders, vocoders, and aggregators. Stage-specialized scheduling : Each stage runs behind a scheduler matched to its workload, from SGLang-backed autoregressive scheduling to lightweight preprocessing and streaming vocoder loops. Transport-aware execution : A control plane coordinates requests while the relay data plane moves tensor payloads across shared-memory, NCCL, NIXL, and Mooncake backends. API surface : OpenAI-compatible endpoints expose multimodal chat, speech generation, batch speech, streaming speech, uploaded voices, and transcription. What SGLang-Omni Serves Omni chat and speech : Qwen3-Omni , MiniCPM-o 4.5 , Ming-Omni , Ming-3.0-audio-flash — multimodal understanding and text/audio replies. Native full-duplex conversation : MiniCPM-o 4.5 , PersonaPlex , NemotronLabs VoiceChat — live listening and speaking over /v1/realtime , including camera input with MiniCPM-o. Full-duplex guide . Cascaded voice assistants : Compose ASR → LLM → TTS services into streaming, turn-based conversations with voice activity detection, conversation history, turn taking, and interruption. Streaming cascade guide . Image and video generation : LLaDA2.0-Uni for text/image understanding, image generation, and editing; Cosmos3 Nano for interleaved understanding and generation, with native image, video, and action routes. Music generation : MiniMax Music 3 — lyrics + caption → 32 kHz stereo song. Speech generation : Higgs Audio v3 , MOSS-TTS , MOSS-TTS Local , Fish Audio Drama 3 , Fish Speech S2-Pro , Qwen3-TTS , Fun-CosyVoice3 , Voxtral TTS , Ming-Omni-TTS , Ming-3.0-TTS , dots.tts , ZONOS2 — /v1/audio/speech , with batch, streaming, and voice features varying by model. Instruction-driven speech generation and editing : AuK and AuK-Flash — text and voice instructions → speech; audio and editing instructions → edited speech. Audio transcription : Qwen3-ASR , Fun-ASR , ARK-ASR , Nemotron 3.5 ASR , Nemotron Transcribe , Ming-3.0-ASR , experimental Whisper , and MOSS-Transcribe-Diarize via /v1/audio/transcriptions . MOSS-TD also returns speaker labels and timestamps ( response_format=verbose_json ). Speaker diarization : Nemotron 3 Diarization — speaker intervals for uploaded recordings and live audio, including overlapping speech. Speech translation : Hy-SimulMT — Chinese speech → English text and English speech → Chinese text, with file and realtime translation. See the audio translation guide for endpoint and model support. Hardware Support Backend Status Notes NVIDIA CUDA Supported Default backend with full model coverage. Apple Silicon Experimental Qwen3-ASR runs through Torch MPS on macOS arm64. Install with install.sh and follow the Qwen3-ASR guide . Intel GPU (XPU) Supported Intel Arc GPUs via PyTorch XPU. Qwen3-ASR, Whisper ASR, Fun-ASR-Nano, Nemotron 3.5 ASR, MOSS-Transcribe-Diarize, Qwen3-TTS, Fun-CosyVoice3, ZONOS2, Audar-TTS, Qwen3-Omni, MiniMax Music 3, MiniCPM-o, Ming-Omni, Ming-Omni-TTS, Nemotron VoiceChat, PersonaPlex, AuK/AuK-Flash and dots.tts serve end-to-end . The Intel XPU guide has the install steps, each model's launch command and how many cards it needs; the backend is auto-detected. Additional model guides, including experimental and research-oriented paths, are available in the Cookbook . Quick Start Installation TTS usage ASR cookbook Community & Support SGLang-Omni welcomes contributors working on inference systems, kernels, scheduling, inter-stage communication, model runners and cache efficiency, model integration, benchmarking, production deployment. Join the SGLang Slack or read the developer reference . Organizations interested in supporting SGLang-Omni, TTS, or omni model serving can contact Chenyang Zhao at zhaochenyang@lmsys.org . Citation If you use SGLang-Omni for your research, please cite our technical blogs on the unified interactive runtime and the Stage--Process--GPU topology : @misc { sglangomniinteractive2026 , title = { Unified Runtime for Full-Duplex Interactive Intelligence with {SGLang Omni} } , author = { {SGLang-Omni Team} } , howpublished = { \url{https://www.sglang.io/blog/omni-interactive-runtime} } , year = { 2026 } , month = { oct } } @misc { sglangomni2026 , title = { Fish Audio Drama 3 Meets {SGLang-Omni}: Day-0 Support and the Stage--Process--GPU Topology } , author = { {SGLang-Omni Team} } , howpublished = { \url{https://www.sglang.io/blog/spg-topology} } , year = { 2026 } , month = { oct } } Acknowledgments SGLang-Omni builds on the SGLang ecosystem and on open model work from the TTS, speech, and omni-model communities. We thank the model teams, systems contributors, and partner organizations helping make open multimodal serving faster, more reliable, and easier to extend.

title: AminBlg/SimpleEnglish
abstract:
✈️ your AI writes like a LinkedIn post. make it write like a Boeing manual. An agent skill that makes LLMs write plain English with the discipline of ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English , the controlled language aerospace has used since 1983 so that a tired mechanic cannot misread an instruction. Layman-readable by default, STE-strict on request. Works in every agent that reads the Agent Skills standard : Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code Copilot, OpenAI Codex, Gemini CLI, Goose, OpenCode, and about 25 more. One folder, no dependencies, MIT. Install Any agent, with the skills CLI : npx skills add AminBlg/SimpleEnglish This installs the skill only. It does not install the session hook or the output style below, so setting outputStyle to simple-english:simple-english without the plugin does nothing. Use the Claude Code plugin for those. Claude Code plugin, with the session hook and the output style: claude plugin marketplace add AminBlg/SimpleEnglish && claude plugin install simple-english@simple-english The output style is named simple-english:simple-english . The short name does not resolve. Select it with /config under Output style, or put {"outputStyle": "simple-english:simple-english"} in ~/.claude/settings.json . Codex plugin, with the session hook: codex plugin marketplace add AminBlg/SimpleEnglish
codex plugin add simple-english@simple-english Codex asks you to trust the hook before its first run. The hooks need Node.js. Details in src/hooks/README.md . No skill support? Paste the rule block of prompts/system-prompt.md into your system prompt, AGENTS.md , or .cursorrules . The page ends with a 60-token version for tight budgets. Then ask for any technical writing, or say "rewrite this with simple-english". See it Left is real, unedited Claude output. Right is the same model with the skill loaded. Without skill With skill Leveraging sqlpipe's robust architecture, users can seamlessly synchronize their Postgres tables to S3 with minimal configuration overhead. Before getting started, you should ensure that your AWS credentials have been properly configured — this is crucial for avoiding frustrating permission issues down the line. sqlpipe copies your Postgres tables to S3. It needs one configuration file. Before you start, make sure that your AWS credentials are correct. If they are not, S3 rejects the upload with a permission error. More rewrites in examples/before-after.md : READMEs, runbooks, incident reports, error messages, release notes. Benchmarks Every number below is recomputed from the committed raw files by python3 evals/check_numbers.py , which CI runs on every push. All Claude runs: claude-sonnet-4-6 , low effort, no settings loaded. Judges are Claude models on Claude text, so family bias is possible. Replies, 8 chat questions with a jargon term each, two runs, raw files and tables . Counts are totals over the 16 replies. 95% fewer visible defects (em-dashes, bold, headers, bullets) with 2.0.1 than with no skill (218 → 11). These counts come from the 2026-09-02 runs of 2.0.1, which still had the five-sentence reply cap that 2.1.0 removed. No run exists yet for 2.1.0 or later. A blind judge preferred 2.0.1 over 2.0.0 in 14 of 16 pairs. Condition words sentences em-dashes bold headers bullets no skill 216 16.8 62 79 25 52 2.0.0 184 14.4 43 72 4 52 2.0.1 146 7.9 5 2 0 4 On gpt-4.1-mini the same 8 questions went from 23 sentences, 64 bold spans, and 101 bullets per 8 replies. With 2.0.1 they went to 5.2 sentences and zero formatting. Documents, the 8 sqlpipe writing tasks scored with the STE linter, one run per cell. One run moves by about 0.5 on this model, so read the rows as parity or better, not as a ranking. Condition viol/100w Reduction no skill 4.09 1.3.0 2.11 48% 2.0.0 1.70 58% 2.0.1 0.91 78% The linter history: 81.3% fewer linter violations across 9 Claude models (144 generations, RESULTS.md ), plus Pi, opencode, and OpenAI runs in evals/results/ . Those numbers reproduce. A 2026-09-02 audit showed that they measure rule obedience, not what a reader sees, which is why 2.0.1 reports the reply counts above. The rules Two registers in SKILL.md , about 1,700 tokens. The 53 numbered rules of Issue 9 live in rule-catalog.md for check mode and Strict mode. The reply, every chat answer: Rule What it kills Prose by default: a list or a table only for content of that shape, no bold The wall of formatting around a one-line answer First sentence answers The preamble No em-dashes The spliced half-thought Define a concept term in a few words Jargon the reader has to look up No contractions, openers, or closers "Great question!" and "Hope this helps!" The document: docs, READMEs, runbooks, error messages, release notes: Rule What it kills Max 20 words per instruction, 25 per description The run-on sentence Condition before command Trailing "...if the flag is set" that readers execute too late Simple tenses, active voice "has been updated", ", making it easy to..." No should/would/may/might Hedging. can , will , must survive One word = one meaning, whole document check/verify/confirm/validate roulette Keep articles, keep "that" Telegraph style. STE is short, not terse No bold lead-ins, no heading over two sentences Decoration that hides the fact State the fact, not its importance "crucial", "robust", "not just X, it is Y" Two modes. Plain, the default, is all of the above. Strict adds the STE dictionary discipline from strict-vocabulary.md when you name STE, ASD-STE100, or compliance. The reply stays Plain in every mode. FAQ Does this make output STE-certified? No. Nothing does, because ASD certifies no tool. Strict mode gets close. Word-level rulings live in the official standard, a free download . Will my docs sound robotic? They will sound like Airbus manuals: flat and impossible to misread. For docs that is the whole point. Keep your voice for your blog. Why not just prompt "write clearly"? "Clearly" is an opinion. "No sentence over 20 words" is a spec. Agents follow specs. Why a 40-year-old aerospace standard? It is maintained (Issue 9, January 2025), numbered, and testable. It is also a near-perfect negative of every AI writing tell. How was it built? Against the primary Issue 9 text, not summaries. A community audit ( #4 ) checked the vocabulary tables against the dictionary. Scenarios and recorded results: evals/pressure-tests.md . Star history Word-choice linter evals/ste_lint.py measures the mechanical rules and cannot see word choice. tools/ste-dictionary/ holds an extractor that builds the word lists from your own copy of the free Issue 9 PDF. A linter reads them. The repository ships the tool and no dictionary content, because the standard forbids reproduction without written authority from ASD. Contributing Open an issue for questions and bug reports. Pull requests are welcome. A change that moves a published number ships the raw files with it, and python3 evals/check_numbers.py must pass. Run python3 evals/ste_lint.py --self-test before you push. Say in the PR whether an agent wrote the code, and do not add attribution trailers. License MIT for everything here. The repo paraphrases the rules for teaching and reproduces no spec text or dictionary content. Unofficial project, not affiliated with or endorsed by ASD or STEMG. ASD-STE100 is a registered trademark of ASD.

title: googleads/google-ads-mcp
abstract:
Google Ads MCP Server This repo contains the source code for running an MCP server that interacts with the Google Ads API . Tools The server uses the Google Ads API to provide several Tools and Resources for use with LLMs and AI agents. Tools available search : Retrieves information about the Google Ads account using GAQL. get_resource_metadata : Retrieves metadata about a Google Ads API resource type, for example "campaign". This is useful to understand the structure of the data and what fields are available for querying. list_accessible_customers : Returns IDs of customers directly accessible
by the user authenticating the call. create_asset : Creates Google Ads assets ( TEXT , IMAGE , YOUTUBE_VIDEO , SITELINK , CALLOUT , STRUCTURED_SNIPPET , and other asset types via extra_params ). Note: image_asset_path is supported in local stdio mode only; use base64 image_asset_data for remote HTTP deployments. upload_video_asset : Uploads a local video file to YouTube via the Google Ads API using a background task so it can be referenced by video assets (supported in local stdio mode only). manage_labels : Creates, updates, and removes account labels. manage_label_associations : Creates and removes label associations on CAMPAIGN , CUSTOMER , AD_GROUP , and AD_GROUP_CRITERION resources. Propose & Confirm Safety Workflow (Mutate Tools) All write/mutate tools ( create_asset , upload_video_asset , manage_labels , and manage_label_associations ) enforce a two-step Propose & Confirm safety workflow: Propose ( validate_only=True , default) : Validates the operation (including a Google Ads API validate_only dry run where supported) without committing changes, returning human-readable change_items and a cryptographic checksum bound to the customer ID and parameters. Confirm ( validate_only=False ) : Requires passing the exact same parameters and customer_id together with the checksum returned in step 1 after explicit user approval. Any missing or mismatched checksum is rejected before mutating the account. Configuring and Namespacing Tools The Google Ads MCP server uses tools_config.yaml to let you selectively enable or disable individual tools or tool categories (namespaces) and customize their namespace prefixes. A default tools_config.yaml with all tools enabled is bundled with the package, so the server works out of the box with no extra setup. For strictly read-only deployments, set labels: false and assets: false in your tools_config.yaml . To customize your installation, the server resolves the configuration in the following order: An explicit path set via the GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_TOOLS_CONFIG environment variable. A tools_config.yaml file in the current working directory. The default tools_config.yaml bundled with the package. If an explicitly requested configuration file (via the environment variable) is missing, or any resolved file is invalid, the server raises an error and fails to start. Configuration Example: namespaces : # Option 1: Enable category 'customers' with default prefix -> "customers_list_accessible_customers" customers : true # Option 2: Enable category 'search' with a custom prefix -> "query_search" search : " query " # Option 3: Fine-grained control over tools in a category metadata : enabled : true prefix : " metadata " enabled_tools :
      - get_resource_metadata : true # Option 4: Disable write/mutate categories for a strictly read-only server labels : false assets : false Resources available discovery-document : Retrieve the Google Ads API discovery document. Provides the discovery document for the latest version of the Google Ads API, which describes the API surface, including resources, methods, and schemas. Host LLMs should access this resource to understand the structure of the Google Ads API and discover available features. metrics : Retrieve information about the metrics available for reporting in the Google Ads API. segments : Retrieve information about the segments available for reporting in the Google Ads API. release-notes : Retrieve the release notes for the latest version of the Google Ads API. Notes The MCP Server will expose your data to the Agent or LLM that you connect to it. If you have technical issues, please use the GitHub issue tracker . To help us collect usage data, you will notice an extra header has been added to your API calls: this data is used to improve the product. Setup instructions Setup involves the following steps: Configure Python. Enable APIs in your project Configure Credentials. Configure your MCP client. Configure Python Install pipx . After a version has been published to PyPI, you can run that exact version
instead of following the latest repository state: pipx run --spec " google-ads-mcp==X.Y.Z " google-ads-mcp Enable APIs in your project Follow the instructions to enable the following APIs in your Google Cloud project: Google Ads API Configure Credentials Option 1: Using FastMCP OAuth Proxy The server supports FastMCP's OAuth proxy feature for dynamic user authentication. This is useful when running the server as a web service. To enable it, set the following environment variables: GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID : Your Google Cloud OAuth 2.0 Client ID. GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET : Your Google Cloud OAuth 2.0 Client Secret. GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_BASE_URL : (Optional) The base URL where the server is accessible (defaults to http://localhost:8080 ). GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_JWT_SIGNING_KEY : (Optional) Secret key used to sign FastMCP JWT tokens across multiple server instances or deployments. GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_STORAGE_TYPE : (Optional) Storage backend for OAuth state ( filetree , redis , firestore , or memory ). GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_STORAGE_PATH : (Optional) Directory path for filetree persistent storage. GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_STORAGE_REDIS_URL : (Optional) Redis URL for redis persistent storage. GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_STORAGE_FIRESTORE_PROJECT : (Optional) Google Cloud project for firestore persistent storage. Defaults to the project inferred from Application Default Credentials. Setting it selects the firestore backend even if GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_STORAGE_TYPE is unset. GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_STORAGE_FIRESTORE_DATABASE : (Optional) Firestore database name for firestore persistent storage. Defaults to (default) . GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_STORAGE_ENCRYPTION_KEY : (Optional) Encryption key for stored OAuth tokens. GOOGLE_ADS_MCP_STORAGE_DISABLE_ENCRYPTION : (Optional) Set to true to disable token encryption. The redis and firestore backends need their storage library installed
alongside the server: pip install py-key-value-aio[redis] and pip install google-ads-mcp[firestore] respectively. Once this is enabled, you can authenticate to the API through your MCP client. When these variables are set, the server automatically switches to the streamable-http transport instead of stdio . You will need to run the server as a separate process and configure your MCP
client to connect to the Streamable HTTP endpoint (for example, http://localhost:8080/mcp ). Local WSL and Podman deployment This deployment has been tested with rootless Podman in WSL and exposes a single
Streamable HTTP endpoint at http://localhost:8080/mcp . Build the image from
the repository inside WSL: podman build --tag localhost/google-ads-mcp:latest --file Dockerfile . Keep server credentials out of MCP client configuration. The tested Quadlet
loads Google Ads and OAuth settings from a private host-side file through EnvironmentFile= and uses a separate named volume for persistent encrypted
OAuth state: [Container] Image =localhost/google-ads-mcp:latest PublishPort =127.0.0.1:8080:8080 EnvironmentFile =/absolute/host/path/google-ads-mcp.env Volume =google-ads-mcp-oauth.volume:/var/lib/google-ads-mcp:rw ReadOnly =true NoNewPrivileges =true DropCapability =all The environment file and the OAuth-state volume serve different purposes: the
volume does not contain the .env file. Keep the environment file outside the
repository, restrict it to the service owner, and never commit it.

title: experientiallabs/experiential
abstract:
Experiential Experiential is an open source gateway and router for agent workflows: Use hosted, BYOK, and local models through one OpenAI-compatible API. Control which users and agents can use which models, for which use cases, and how much they can spend. Turn production traffic into a custom router or model optimized for quality, speed, and cost. 🌐 Platform |
  📚 Docs | Discord Getting Started Start a local OpenAI-compatible gateway. On first run, the setup wizard uses the shared provider,
model, and reasoning-effort selectors, persists every selected provider connection, then shows
defaults for the public alias, identity, and $50.00 command budget before printing a one-time key: pip install experiential
exp Choose a public alias such as opus-5 , capture the issued key, and send a request: export EXP_GATEWAY_KEY=...
curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H " Authorization: Bearer $EXP_GATEWAY_KEY " \
  -H ' Content-Type: application/json ' \
  -d ' {"model":"opus-5","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Help me"}]} ' Setup / get started with the hosted gateway Prefer a managed gateway to running one locally? The hosted platform at platform.experientiallabs.ai serves the same
OpenAI-compatible (and Anthropic Messages) API at https://api.experientiallabs.ai/v1 .
See SETUP.md for copy-paste prompts you hand to your coding agent
(Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, and similar); the agent runs the setup for you. It
collects four prompts: Upload your LLM traces as telemetry: create an account instantly from your email, then pull or upload your existing LLM traces onto the platform as telemetry. Connect your inference provider keys (BYOK): create an account, then connect your own OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Azure, Bedrock, Fireworks, or OpenRouter keys for free pass-through. Start calling models on the gateway: make your first /v1 call with the OpenAI and Anthropic SDKs using an xpl_ key, and optionally repoint your existing coding agents. Full onboarding: create an account instantly from your email, connect your keys, import your spend, then repoint every coding agent (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Aider, and similar) or Conductor at the gateway. Using the API Start the local gateway with exp (or exp run ); the compiled native data plane
serves every route on loopback. From Python, load a fitted project router as an
official OpenAI client backed by its own private gateway: import exp with exp . load_router ( "my-project" ) as client : response = client . chat . completions . create ( model = "my-project" , messages = [{ "role" : "user" , "content" : "hello" }],
    ) Coding Agent exp code runs exp-code , Experiential's open-source coding and cowork
agent built on Pi . It needs Node.js 22.19 or newer and
uses your running local gateway, or the hosted gateway after exp login : exp code # interactive terminal UI exp code -p " Summarize sales.csv into report.docx " Every argument goes to exp-code, so its print, JSON, and RPC modes work through exp code too. Capture Traffic Capture is designed to collect supported traces from the Codex and Claude Code desktop apps using
your existing ChatGPT or Claude subscription, while requests go directly to OpenAI or Anthropic.
It requires macOS, Python 3.13 or newer, and approval for its extension and certificate: exp capture Capture is experimental; macOS network reliability is still under investigation. Use Experiential's gateway as middleware to control costs, enforce guardrails, and optimize quality,
costs, and speed. Leave the terminal open while you work. Press Ctrl+C to stop capture.
View your capture telemetry . Optimize from Traffic First, collect OpenTelemetry traces from your current agent. If you just want to try it out, grab
the public terminal-tasks OTLP dataset : curl -L -o traces.otel.jsonl \
  https://huggingface.co/datasets/experiential-labs/wmo-terminal-tasks-traces/resolve/540883e451dc13d34fb50fdd36b143cb0f1fb0db/traces.otel.jsonl Then build a project. The build command walks you through providers,
models, and budget, and asks for your trace file: # Build simulation from your agent traces and optimize a router against it exp build support-agent After collecting traces from your router, fine-tune an open source model you own using Tinker . exp optimize model support-agent Telemetry Anonymous aggregate PostHog product telemetry is enabled by default. It never includes prompts,
traces, actions, observations, paths, model names, credentials, or raw customer content. exp config telemetry status
exp config telemetry disable
exp config telemetry enable The preference is stored locally in .exp/settings.toml . Development uv sync --extra dev
uv run ruff format --check . uv run ruff check . uv run ty check
uv run pytest -q Repository and documentation conventions live in AGENTS.md .

title: openai/codex-security
abstract:
Codex Security Codex Security helps you find, investigate, and fix vulnerabilities in your code.
Use its security workflows in Codex, or automate them with the @openai/codex-security CLI and TypeScript SDK. In Codex: choose a security workflow . In a terminal: install the CLI and scan your repository . In automation: use the TypeScript SDK or GitHub Action . Features Scan repositories, selected paths, or Git changes. Deep scans repeat Standard scans and return their deduplicated findings. Validate candidate findings, generate patches, and verify existing fixes. Draft SECURITY.md policies and save threat models for later review. Browse saved scans and findings, identify duplicates, assess severity against
your own rubric, and suggest owners from source and Git history. Preview third-party scanner findings, save them locally, or publish supported reports to Codex Security Cloud. Scanner import guides . Track findings in Linear, Jira, or GitHub, publish completed scans, or export SARIF, JSON, and CSV. Integration workflows . Automate scans across repositories or project components, including in CI and
containers. Use in Codex Open your repository in a Codex session with the Codex Security plugin enabled,
then ask: Run a Codex Security scan on this repository, focusing on authentication and
authorization. Return the saved report, source evidence, and coverage limits. A completed scan saves a report and findings. Read the report for source
evidence and exclusions, then request a patch or ask Codex to verify an
existing fix. See the agent workflow guide for setup,
task selection, and recovery. Quick start Requires Node.js 22.13.0+ within 22.x, or Node.js 24.x or 26.x, and Python 3.10+.
Python 3.10 also requires tomli . Install the CLI globally and sign in: npm install --global @openai/codex-security
cs login Run your first scan from the repository directory: cs scan . When the scan completes, open the Markdown file at the REPORT path in the
terminal. Run cs scans show from the same repository to find its latest
completed scan again. See scan scope and follow-up work for how to interpret exclusions in the report. cs and codex-security run the same CLI. If the short name conflicts with
another command, use codex-security . To skip the global install, or if npm
reports an EEXIST conflict, use npx @openai/codex-security in place of cs for both login and scanning. For CI, set OPENAI_API_KEY or CODEX_API_KEY in the scan process's environment.
For a headless machine, see device or SSH login . Scan options Choose a scope and scan mode: # Scan selected paths. cs scan . --path src --path tests # Scan committed changes from a base revision to HEAD. cs scan . --diff origin/main # Run a deep scan of the repository. cs scan . --mode deep Use cs scan . --max-time 15 for an advisory 15-minute Standard investigation
allowance. See investigation time for timing semantics and Deep Scan limits. Use cs --help to browse commands, or cs scan --help for scan options, cost limits, and patching after a scan. For an application spread across repositories, see review one system across repositories .
Use bulk scans for independent repository
reviews in one resumable campaign. Scans use existing root and component SECURITY.md guidance. To write or
revise it, see Generate SECURITY.md . Some cybersecurity requests and protected findings require Trusted Access for Cyber . For accounts with Daybreak
access, see Daybreak opt-in for the
Codex toggle and Cyber access programs to select a program explicitly. TypeScript SDK Install the package locally in your TypeScript project: npm install @openai/codex-security Then import it: import { CodexSecurity } from "@openai/codex-security" ; const security = new CodexSecurity ( ) ; try { const result = await security . run ( "/path/to/repository" ) ; console . log ( result . reportPath ) ; } finally { await security . close ( ) ; } The SDK guide includes deep-scan configuration,
validation, severity classification, owner suggestions, and result handling. Linked Git worktrees share scan history and saved findings when they use the same
Codex Security state directory. Keep CODEX_SECURITY_STATE_DIR stable to retain
that shared history and sign-in scope. See the scan history guide . Read existing Cloud findings When Codex Security Cloud is available to your account, the Security plugin's $cloud-findings skill can read findings, reports, recorded assignment and
verification, and scan status in Codex desktop or the Codex CLI. Cloud is an
optional connection; local scans work without it. See Cloud connection setup and CLI reads for authentication requirements and a read-only example. Generate SECURITY.md Use policy to draft a new SECURITY.md or update an existing one. Use --path to select a component: cs policy . cs policy . --path services/api --knowledge-base architecture.md The command saves its draft outside the repository and leaves existing files
unchanged. Review the diff and notes, edit the draft, then copy only SECURITY.md to the displayed Policy target . Keep the saved architecture and threat-model
documents outside the repository. Scans already use root and component SECURITY.md files. Keep your current policy
if it needs no changes. When updating it, preserve its vulnerability-reporting
instructions. If the command says the policy is already up to date, no copy is
needed. Files at .github/SECURITY.md or docs/SECURITY.md often contain reporting
instructions. Preserve them when drafting a policy; those locations do not
automatically provide repository-wide scan guidance. See the policy guide for policy
locations, unanswered questions, saved artifacts, and SDK usage. Save and export threat models Scans and policy generation save threat models with their results. Export a saved
model without starting another analysis: cs export --scan SCAN_ID --artifact threat-model --output threatmodel.md Omit --scan to use the current repository's latest completed scan. The export guide also covers findings,
SARIF output for CI, and the offline TypeScript API. For ServiceNow Application
Vulnerability Response, see Export findings for ServiceNow . GitHub Actions To run a weekly repository scan on GitHub-hosted Ubuntu: Add an OpenAI API key as the repository secret CODEX_SECURITY_API_KEY . Copy the weekly workflow to .github/workflows/codex-security.yml . Replace REPLACE_WITH_REVIEWED_COMMIT with the reviewed distribution commit SHA from an Action release. To try the workflow before the next scheduled run, open Actions → Codex
Security repository → Run workflow . The example uses an estimated $5 limit per scan and reports findings without
failing the job. Requests in progress can exceed the limit. For a severity
threshold, pull request checks, or runner requirements, see the Action guide . For eligible accounts, see Daybreak access . Containerized bulk scans Scan a list of repositories with the included Docker Compose configuration,
which keeps results and authentication between runs. See the container quick start .
The workflow runner runs individual CLI stages
in containers and can connect to a separately deployed findings service. Findings storage and deduplication The findings guide covers local
storage, deduplication, and compatibility with independently operated endpoints
through publish scan --to custom and explicit --findings-url . The local serve command and browser dashboard have been removed; existing databases and
scan artifacts remain available. Other providers Scans support OpenAI, Amazon Bedrock, OpenRouter, Fireworks AI, and Cheaper Inference. Bedrock uses
AWS credentials and does not require a separate OpenAI login. See Bedrock setup for AWS profiles, regions, and model access. For OpenRouter, Fireworks AI, and Cheaper Inference, set the provider's API key and choose a supported
model. See provider configuration for examples.
