story isn't limited to fixed node types. Bring your own agent: Claude Code, Codex, or OpenCode can run the
conversation, or you can bring OhMyGame to them. Plugins: build in Godot, Unity, Unreal Engine, or Cocos Creator; make
assets in Blender, Aseprite, or Tiled; ship to WeChat Mini Games, Douyin
Mini Games, or TapTap, and earn from your game . What it is Making a game takes design docs, 2D art, 3D models, video, code, and somewhere
to put it when it's done. Today those live in five or six different tools.
OhMyGame puts them in one app: describe your game, and the agent designs it,
makes the assets, builds it, plays it to check it works, and publishes it to a
link you can share. Two core design ideas shape it: Everything lives on a canvas. Design docs, concept art, 3D models, and
video sit side by side on one board. One character sketch can grow into more
art, a video, or a rigged 3D model, and everything is ready to use in your
game. The agent does the work. It drives the canvas the way you would:
drafting the design doc, turning a character sketch into a rigged 3D model,
writing the code, and playtesting the result. It's open source and works with 40+ model providers through Pi, from Anthropic
and OpenAI to DeepSeek and Qwen. Your keys stay on your machine, there are no
per-run credits, and what you make is yours. Features 🤖 Agent: drives the canvas, builds and plays the game The agent works the canvas the way you would: it drafts the design doc, lays
out boards, and generates assets on them. It reads the design doc, writes the
code, and runs the game in a live preview. Then it opens the game in a window
you can watch and plays it, including real-time canvas and WebGL games. When it
finds a problem, it tries a fix and plays again. Along the way it can generate
images, video, 3D models, and audio, search the web, and use MCP servers and
plugins. ▶ The agent playtesting a new item feature on desktop and mobile, then reporting
what it found (sped up 4×). playtest-demo-v3.mp4 🎨 Canvas: design docs, art, video, 3D, and audio on one board Every game project has a design space: a main design doc plus boards where
the doc, images, video, 3D models, and audio sit side by side. Nodes can use
each other as references, so one character design can lead to more images, a
video, a voice line, or a rigged and animated 3D model. Results go into a shared Asset Library that
your games can use. canvas-demo-2x.mp4 🔗 Publish and earn: one link, or the platforms where players pay Sign in and publish: OhMyGame builds your game and gives it a link anyone can
play in the browser. Republishing updates the same link. Published games are
listed in the in-app Community, where you can play what others have made,
sort by latest, most viewed, or most liked, visit creators' profiles, and like
the games you enjoy. A one-person studio should pay for itself. Beyond the Community, plugins take
your game to the platforms where players pay. Ship to Earn from How WeChat Mini Games, Douyin Mini Games Ads, in-app purchases Platform plugins TapTap Downloads, in-app purchases TapTap Maker plugin Steam and other stores Sales Export from Godot or Unity with their plugins itch.io, Poki, CrazyGames Sales, ad revenue share Upload your Web Game build Your game, your revenue. OhMyGame takes no cut of what your game earns. 🧑‍💻 Bring your own agent Already use Claude Code, Codex, or OpenCode? Choose it in the model picker and
it runs the conversation with its own sign-in. It gets the whole studio: the
canvas, media generation, playtesting, plugins, and Undo, with your history
kept in OhMyGame. See coding agents . 🔌 Use OhMyGame from Claude Code, Codex, and other agents Already working in another coding agent? Turn on Settings → MCP Server and
add OhMyGame to Claude Code or Codex with the command shown there.
They get OhMyGame's media generation with your providers, the canvas, and
playtesting, plus a Skill that explains the workflow. DeepSeek Harness and
other MCP clients can add the ohmygame-studio command shown there. See External agents . 🧩 Plugins: connect with more game dev tools Plugins let the agent work in the engines and tools you already know: Engines: Godot, Unity, Unreal Engine, and Cocos Creator. Platforms: TapTap Maker, WeChat Mini Games, and Douyin Mini Games. Assets: Blender, Aseprite, and Tiled. Turn them on in Plugins , or build your own with Plugin Builder. Engine
plugins use each engine's own editor and tools, so install those first. See Plugins . What you can make Three games our team made with OhMyGame: Interactive film Island builder Deckbuilding roguelike 🎮 Web games The best place to start. 2D and 3D games for the browser, built with
Three.js, React Three Fiber, or Phaser. The agent follows a complete web game
workflow: a design doc, key-screen mockups, production art, a playable core
loop, and playtesting in the live preview. Games fit any window size, support
touch, and publish to a shareable link. The project is a normal web project you
can open in any editor. 🎬 Interactive stories Interactive films, visual novels, and story games. Each screen is a free web
page with its own images, video, and code: a main menu, a case archive, a
dialogue, a puzzle. You connect them on a graph, and the runtime handles state,
saves, music, and navigation. The story plays as its own web page, and the
runtime is part of the project, so the agent can change anything about how it
plays. The architecture and authoring model are documented in Playable Nodes . 🎲 General games: any engine or stack General Game doesn't assume an engine or stack. Start from an idea, bring a
project in any engine, or make tools and content for your game. The Game Studio
plugin coordinates design, production art, implementation, and verification
across engines, and the engine plugins work in the engine you use. For Godot, start a Godot project from the
sidebar. When the output is a web page, preview, playtesting, and publishing work as
they do for Web games; native games use their engine's own tools. See General Game details . Making a browser
game? Choose Web Game : it is tuned for the browser. How it's built The idea that holds this together: one agent drives every part of the studio. 1 · A full Pi agent with a GUI. OhMyGame runs Pi with its
full toolset and persistent sessions, in a GUI built for watching results
rather than reading diffs. Close the app, come back, and the project,
conversation, and context are still there. You describe, review, and steer;
editing by hand is always possible, but it is not the main path. 2 · Every workspace is files. A web game is a normal web project. A design
doc is Markdown, and boards and the Asset Canvas share one JSON node model. An
interactive story is a node graph on disk. Each comes with an AGENTS.md and
JSON schemas, so the agent edits them the same way it edits code, and the
visual editors read and write the same files. 3 · Games are tool calls. Playing the game ( game_use ), generating media,
and checking story nodes are ordinary Pi tools, next to its coding tools. That
is why the agent can chain them: draft a design, make the art, write the code,
and play the result in one conversation. Any model, your keys OhMyGame does not lock you into one model or charge per run. Coding models from 40+ providers through Pi, including Anthropic,
OpenAI, Google, DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi, GLM, MiniMax, xAI, Mistral, Groq,
OpenRouter, Amazon Bedrock, and Vercel AI Gateway.

title: google-labs-code/stitch-skills
abstract:
Stitch Design Skills A collection of agent skills and plugins for Google Stitch , following the Agent Skills open standard. Compatible with coding agents such as Codex, Antigravity, Gemini CLI, Claude Code, Cursor, and OpenCode (manual install). Quick Start 1. Install Plugins (Recommended) The fastest way to set up the full Stitch plugin suite globally. Codex Add the Stitch Skills marketplace, then install the plugins you need. Via CLI (recommended) codex plugin marketplace add google-labs-code/stitch-skills --ref main \
  --sparse .agents/plugins \
  --sparse plugins/stitch-design \
  --sparse plugins/stitch-build \
  --sparse plugins/stitch-utilities [!TIP]
The --sparse flags are optional — they limit the checkout to only the
listed paths for a faster clone. Omit them to pull the entire repository. Via the Codex UI Navigate to Settings → Plugin Marketplaces → Add and fill in: Field Value Source https://github.com/google-labs-code/stitch-skills Git ref main Sparse paths (optional) .agents/plugins , plugins/stitch-design , plugins/stitch-build , plugins/stitch-utilities Once the marketplace is registered, install any combination of: stitch-design — design-focused skills stitch-build — build and component skills stitch-utilities — utility and helper skills Claude Code & Cursor # Claude Code — installs into the current project npx plugins add google-labs-code/stitch-skills --scope project --target claude-code # Cursor — installs into the current workspace npx plugins add google-labs-code/stitch-skills --scope workspace --target cursor OpenCode OpenCode does not use npx plugins / npx skills or the Codex/Claude marketplace layout.
Install skills and the Stitch MCP server manually: 1. Skills — copy the skill folders you need into a discoverable path: # Project-local (recommended) mkdir -p .opencode/skills
cp -R plugins/stitch-design/skills/generate-design .opencode/skills/generate-design # repeat for other skills under plugins/*/skills/ OpenCode also discovers .claude/skills/ and .agents/skills/ (see OpenCode skills docs ). Naming: OpenCode requires skill name frontmatter to be lowercase kebab-case and match the directory name. Skills that use stitch::… names (or other non-kebab forms) need the name field and folder renamed before OpenCode will load them. Extra frontmatter such as allowed-tools is ignored. 2. Stitch MCP — add a remote MCP entry in project opencode.json or ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json after completing the Stitch MCP setup : { "$schema" : " https://opencode.ai/config.json " , "mcp" : { "stitch" : { "type" : " remote " , "url" : " YOUR_STITCH_MCP_URL " , "enabled" : true }
  }
} Replace YOUR_STITCH_MCP_URL with the endpoint from the Stitch MCP setup flow (credentials/env vars from that guide still apply). Tool names inside skill instructions may differ from OpenCode builtins ( webfetch / bash instead of web_fetch / run_command ). Prefer the OpenCode tool names when adapting a skill for OpenCode. 2. Install Skills Selectively Choose only the specific skills you need. Important Stitch Design Skills often have inter-dependencies. If you choose to install skills selectively, ensure you include all required dependencies. npx skills add google-labs-code/stitch-skills You can run the following commands to see the help documentation for plugins and skills: npx plugins --help

npx skills --help Prerequisites These skills require the Stitch MCP server to be configured and running in your agent's environment. Make sure you have followed the Stitch MCP Setup Instructions to register the server and set up appropriate environment variables and credentials. Docs navigation: If a link on stitch.withgoogle.com/docs redirects incorrectly, open the target path under the same host (e.g. https://stitch.withgoogle.com/docs/learn/device-types/ ). Available Plugins Design ( stitch-design ) Core design workflows for creating, managing, and optimizing designs within Stitch. Skill Description Prompt Example stitch::code-to-design Convert frontend code (React, Vue, etc.) to a Stitch Design via HTML extraction + design system + upload "Upload the frontend code at /path/to/dashboard into a Stitch project named 'Dashboard-Migration-2026'." stitch::generate-design Generate new screens from text or images, edit existing screens, and create design variants · "Make a browse tab for a mobile app for romance and date night ideas." · "Edit the login screen to add a 'Remember Me' checkbox and change the button color to blue." · "Generate 3 design variants of the home screen with dark mode and high-density layouts." stitch::manage-design-system Manage design systems in Stitch — upload DESIGN.md and apply themes to screens "Upload our design system from .stitch/DESIGN.md and apply it to all screens." stitch::extract-design-md Extract a comprehensive DESIGN.md directly from frontend source code "Scan /src and extract the design system into .stitch/DESIGN.md ." stitch::extract-static-html Extract self-contained static HTML from running web apps, inlining CSS and images "Extract a static HTML snapshot of http://localhost:3000/profile ." stitch::upload-to-stitch Upload local assets (images, mockups, HTML) to a Stitch project "Upload .stitch/landing_page.html to Stitch project projects/987654321 ." Build ( stitch-build ) Code generation, framework integration, and asset compilation from Stitch designs. Skill Description Prompt Example stitch::react-components Convert Stitch screens to React component systems with automated validation and design token consistency · "Convert all screens in Stitch project projects/123 to React components." · "Sync the app to the last updates of the Stitch project 13039335308618232534 ." stitch::react-native Convert Stitch HTML designs to production-ready React Native components with StyleSheet and platform-specific code · "Convert the Stitch design to React Native components with proper theme and navigation." · "Sync the app to the last updates of the Stitch project 13039335308618232534 ." remotion Generate walkthrough videos from Stitch projects using Remotion with smooth transitions and zooming "Generate a walkthrough video of the Stitch project projects/456 ." shadcn-ui Expert guidance for integrating and building applications with shadcn/ui components "Set up shadcn/ui and build a data table with sorting and filtering." react-vite-dashboard Convert Stitch screens to React + Vite dashboards with TanStack Query, DESIGN.md tokens, and Web3 read patterns "Build a DeFi portfolio dashboard from this Stitch screen using our DESIGN.md." Utilities ( stitch-utilities ) Supporting tools for enhancing prompts, generating design specs, and enforcing design standards. Skill Description Prompt Example design-md Analyze Stitch projects and generate comprehensive DESIGN.md files in semantic language "Analyze Stitch project projects/123 and generate a DESIGN.md." enhance-prompt Transform vague UI ideas into polished, Stitch-optimized prompts with UI/UX keywords "Enhance this prompt: 'make a settings page'." stitch-loop Generate complete multi-page websites from a single prompt with automated validation "Build a 5-page portfolio website with Stitch." taste-design Generate DESIGN.md files enforcing premium, anti-generic UI standards "Generate a premium DESIGN.md with strict typography and calibrated colors." Repository Structure plugins/
├── stitch-design/          — Core design workflow plugin
│   ├── plugin.json
│   └── skills/
│       ├── code-to-design/
│       ├── generate-design/
│       ├── manage-design-system/
│       ├── extract-design-md/
│       ├── extract-static-html/
│       └── upload-to-stitch/
├── stitch-build/           — Code generation & build plugin
│   ├── plugin.json
│   └── skills/
│       ├── react-components/    — stitch::react-components
│       ├── react-native/
│       ├── react-vite-dashboard/
│       ├── remotion/
│       └── shadcn-ui/
└── stitch-utilities/       — Design utilities & assistants plugin
    ├── plugin.

title: dream-num/univer
abstract: Build your own AI office with Univer Office SDK. Start with open-source Sheets and Docs, then connect your own application or agent. 🚀 Quick start · 📚 Documentation · ⚖️ Feature comparison · 🌐 Website · 🎮 Showcase · 🔧 API Reference · 📝 Blog English · Français · Deutsch · Español · 簡體中文 · 繁體中文 · 日本語 · 한국어 Table of contents 💡 What is Univer? Open-source capabilities 🚀 Build on the open-source foundation Quick start: an open-source spreadsheet editor Connect your application to editable content 🏗️ Explore the open-source architecture Give custom features clear boundaries Compose cross-feature edits and undo/redo Connect applications and agents through Facade APIs and events 🧩 Extend your application with Univer Office SDK Scope and licensing 🌐 Application patterns and ecosystem Univer Workspace: an Office SDK reference application CLI, agent integrations, and developer skills 📚 Documentation and contributing Runtime compatibility 💬 Community 🔒 Security ❤️ Sponsors 📄 License 💡 What is Univer? Univer is an Office SDK for building Office applications inside your own product. It provides Office editing, calculation, collaboration, and file processing for people and existing agents, using your data and permissions. The product family covers spreadsheets, documents, presentations, relational tables, canvases, and PDFs. Univer Office SDK has three parts: Web SDK is the foundation: content models, editing, rendering, formula calculation, and Facade APIs (application-facing APIs). Compose its plugins into an embedded editor or your own Office application, and reuse the content models, commands, and calculation for Headless processing without an interactive editor. Server SDK adds backend services for real-time collaboration, edit history, and Office file import and export. AI SDK connects Office capabilities to existing agents and workflows, with content tools, execution, and review integrations. This repository provides the Web SDK's core architecture and engine implementations under Apache-2.0 : content models and snapshot formats, plugin and dependency management, the command system, formula and rendering engines, Facade APIs, UI foundation, and Sheets and Docs editing capabilities. Commercial Web SDK plugins, Server SDK, and commercial AI SDK extensions are distributed and licensed separately. Agents can use the same open-source APIs; your application supplies the model and tool orchestration. The quotation example demonstrates editing, calculation, and saving without an AI SDK dependency. Open-source capabilities Area Selected capabilities Sheets · Editing and layout Cell styles, merged cells, in-cell rich text, freeze panes, floating images, and undo/redo. Sheets · Data and calculation Formulas, defined names, filtering, sorting, data validation, conditional formatting, hyperlinks, comments, and find and replace. Docs Rich-text editing, paragraph formatting, lists, hyperlinks, comments, and drawing integration. Features are composed through plugins and presets; the quick start uses only the Sheets Core preset . Images use the corresponding drawing plugins. See the feature comparison for detailed open-source and commercial coverage. The demos below showcase the wider Univer Office SDK , including commercial capabilities. They show more than the default open-source setup; see open source and commercial extensions for scope. 🚀 Build on the open-source foundation Your goal Use the open-source foundation Start here Embed Sheets or Docs Add an editable Office surface to your application or agent product, and connect your data through Facade APIs. Quick start Process content without an editor Reuse content plugins, models, commands, and calculation in Node.js for editing, snapshots, and automated tasks. Headless guide Develop custom features or editors Reuse the engines, UI components, plugin boundaries, dependency injection, and command/undo systems. Follow existing features to extend Sheets and Docs or develop your own editors. Open-source architecture Coordinate edits and undo/redo across features. Inserting a row inside a filter range changes both the base content and the filter range; undo needs to restore both. Each feature supplies its own changes and undo data, and the command composes their execution and history. The architecture walkthrough explains how to extend these editing workflows. Quick start: an open-source spreadsheet editor In a browser application using a bundler such as Vite: pnpm add @univerjs/presets @univerjs/preset-sheets-core Create the container before initializing Univer: < div id =" app " style =" height: 100vh " > </ div > import { UniverSheetsCorePreset } from '@univerjs/preset-sheets-core' import UniverPresetSheetsCoreEnUS from '@univerjs/preset-sheets-core/locales/en-US' import { createUniver , LocaleType , mergeLocales } from '@univerjs/presets' import '@univerjs/preset-sheets-core/lib/index.css' const { univerAPI } = createUniver ( { locale : LocaleType . EN_US , locales : { [ LocaleType . EN_US ] : mergeLocales ( UniverPresetSheetsCoreEnUS ) , } , presets : [ UniverSheetsCorePreset ( { container : 'app' , } ) , ] , } ) univerAPI . createWorkbook ( { } ) Your page now contains a spreadsheet editor. Use the returned univerAPI to work with its content. This example uses open-source packages and needs no commercial Univer license or Server SDK. For component frameworks, retain the univer instance returned by createUniver and call univer.dispose() when the component unmounts. See the lifecycle guide . Presets compose plugins and register their Facade APIs. For manual control, see the Plugin Mode example below. The installation guide covers both modes, peer dependencies, and framework integrations. Keep coordinated @univerjs/* packages on the same version. Commercial packages must use the matching release line; independently released packages such as icons follow their declared compatibility. See the API Stability Policy . Connect your application to editable content Facade APIs are the application-facing interface to workbooks, worksheets, and ranges. Continue from the quick start to populate a quotation, update a quantity from application code, and read the recalculated total: // Wait for formula controllers before editing a newly created workbook. await new Promise < void > ( ( resolve ) => { if ( univerAPI . getCurrentLifecycleStage ( ) >= univerAPI . Enum . LifecycleStages . Steady ) { resolve ( ) return } const listener = univerAPI . addEvent ( univerAPI . Event . LifeCycleChanged , ( { stage } ) => { if ( stage === univerAPI . Enum . LifecycleStages . Steady ) { listener . dispose ( ) resolve ( ) } } ) } ) const workbook = univerAPI . getActiveWorkbook ( ) ! const sheet = workbook . getActiveSheet ( ) sheet . getRange ( 'A1:D4' ) . setValues ( [ [ 'Item' , 'Quantity' , 'Unit price' , 'Amount' ] , [ 'Seats' , 2 , 25 , '=B2*C2' ] , [ 'Support' , 1 , 100 , '=B3*C3' ] , [ 'Total' , '' , '' , '=SUM(D2:D3)' ] , ] ) // An application control or agent can make the same edit. sheet . getRange ( 'B2' ) . setValue ( 4 ) univerAPI . getFormula ( ) . onCalculationResultApplied ( ) . then ( ( ) => { console . log ( sheet . getRange ( 'D4' ) . getValue ( ) ) // 200 localStorage . setItem ( 'quotation' , JSON . stringify ( workbook . save ( ) ) ) } ) . catch ( console . error ) The editor and your application operate on the same workbook; formula changes are recalculated automatically. workbook.save() returns a JSON snapshot containing the workbook and its registered plugin data. Your application owns persistence; this example uses browser storage. On a later page load, after initialization, restore the snapshot instead of creating a blank workbook : const saved = localStorage . getItem ( 'quotation' ) if ( saved ) { univerAPI . createWorkbook ( JSON . parse ( saved ) ) } This workflow uses only open-source packages.

title: My AI agents found an unmapped Maya site
abstract:
My AI Agents (Re)discovered a Maya Site in 72 Hours 5 min read (Last edit: 11 Nov) Update (11 November): it turns out the site had already been mapped in Estrada-Belli et al. 2025 . The agents missed it while going through the literature, so they rediscovered it rather than discovered it (it just wasn't in the register of Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History, INAH, yet). Still work to do then! The rest of the story still holds. By analyzing NASA lidar data, my AI agents found a Maya site in Mexico that wasn't in the official register. (It turned out archaeologists had mapped it already, more on that at the end.) It took less than 72 hours to go from a random thought while traveling to an official reply from the Mexican government. This is by far the best time ever to be alive. Lidar: bare ground, 2013 Satellite image today Drag the slider. The same hilltop today from a satellite (just trees) and in lidar (no trees). Colours show height. Satellite © Esri, Maxar, Earthstar Geographics. Disclaimer: I'm not an archaeologist. I'm going to tell this story as a diary, because the timeline is probably the best part. 18 October I was traveling in Peru, Gemini-ing about the history of the place, when I learned about Hiram Bingham , the American explorer who "discovered" Machu Picchu in 1911. "What luck!" I thought. He was actually looking for a different city, Vilcabamba , the last refuge of the Incas, when a local farmer in the valley below guided him to the ruins. "Imagine if Bingham had our tools," I thought. "What would he do?" Left: Bingham at his tent, 1912. Right: Machu Picchu, photographed by Bingham the same year. Public domain, Wikimedia Commons ( left , right ). I brainstormed a bit with a few agents (Gemini, ChatGPT, Claude and Grok), and they all said lidar . From above, a ruin in the jungle is just a bunch of trees (like Machu Picchu before it was cleared), so satellite photos don't help much. Lidar, instead, fires laser pulses through the gaps in the canopy and maps the ground underneath. [1] So the agents went looking for lidar data. Peru isn't well covered, and hiring a company to do a survey meant permits, costs and bureaucracy, so I gave up on that. Then I thought: why not the Maya ? Their region is much better covered by public lidar. That night, I asked the agents to analyze it and went to bed. 19 October I woke up and checked the agents' reports. 'DAMN!' They had found lots of villages and other regular shapes that looked like structures or houses. A few of the sites the agents flagged overnight. Keep an eye on the bottom-left one. So how did they do it? They turned the lidar strips (about 1,200 km² of jungle) into images, and 48 agents went through them one by one like very patient archaeologists, looking for pyramids, platforms, and plazas while filtering out natural hills, sinkholes, and roads. There was no special model or classifier involved: the agents literally looked at the pictures, following a precise guide. Me: That's awesome! Please check which of these villages haven't been discovered yet. Search both the literature and the archives. …a few hours later… Agent: One major village doesn't seem to have been registered. This is the hilltop from the top of this post. It sits on the edge of a cliff, under the jungle, and it has straight edges and sharp corners. Nature doesn't really do straight lines. Zooming in, there's a levelled plaza, an oval pyramid at least 8–12 m tall, a raised courtyard attached to it and a flat-bottomed hollow that might have been a water reservoir. The hilltop with the trees removed (top), and a zoom into its civic centre (bottom). And this is what it looks like in 3D. The site in 3D, from the lidar. Heights exaggerated ~1.5×. Me: OK, what should I do? Agent: You should contact INAH (Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History), write a report on your discovery, and check whether the site is in their register. Sometimes they have unpublished results. Me: OK, how do I contact INAH? How does the reporting process work? Agent: …instructions for the report… + email addresses Me: OK, please do the report. And I went to bed. 20 October I iterated on the report a bit, since a few things were off, and translated it into Spanish to improve the chances of getting a reply (at least, that's what Claude suggested). I don't speak Spanish, so I had to trust the agents on that one. The agents also checked the raw point cloud, to make sure the shapes were really on the ground and not created by the trees. Green dots are leaves, brown dots are the ground. Two slices through the raw lidar points. Under 10–17 m of forest, the ground (brown) traces the plaza, the pyramid and the courtyard. Then I sent the report to INAH. The top of my letter to INAH. The exact coordinates went in a confidential annex, not shown here. 21 October INAH replied: they checked their records and found no registered archaeological site at that location . INAH's reply. The highlighted part: "…no registered archaeological site was identified at the location given in your report." At that point I thought nobody had put it on a map before. I was wrong (see below). So what was it? This part is speculation, from a long chat with the agents. It looks like a small Maya civic centre from the Classic period (roughly AD 250–900), basically the "downtown" of a local elite. The plaza is where people gathered, for ceremonies and maybe even a market. The pyramid was probably a temple, and the raised courtyard next to it might have been where the local ruler lived. The hollow could have been an aguada , a rainwater reservoir: Maya towns needed them to get through the dry season. Or it's just a hole. The three platforms around were probably houses. I asked Gemini to imagine how it looked back then: How it might have looked around AD 700. Generated with Gemini from the lidar layout For similar studies, have a look at how NASA's G-LiHT instrument works ( Cook et al. 2013 ) and how lidar collected for environmental research can be reused for archaeology ( Golden et al. 2016 ). In 2024, archaeologists found a whole Maya city in Mexico this way ( Auld-Thomas et al. 2024 ), others mapped settlements across the Maya lowlands, including this very site ( Estrada-Belli et al. 2025 ), and another study found what may have been ancient Maya marketplaces ( Šprajc 2026 ). What's next The site is now in the hands of the people who should have it: Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH) and the archaeologists who mapped it first. If anything comes out of it, I'll post an update. What I've learned You can just do things. I'm not an archaeologist, so I didn't know this was supposed to be hard. I just picked an old problem, tried the most obvious thing and threw some compute at it. Being a naive outsider might be a superpower now. And it turned out professional archaeologists had already mapped the same site. I guess that's a good sign: an outsider with agents ended up in a similar place to the experts. And I don't think this is really about archaeology. So far, most agentic AI stories have been about coding, math and physics, but it's much more general than that, and I hope this small example makes it a bit more obvious. We are on the brink of a revolution in all the sciences, and the only bottlenecks left will be curiosity and imagination (and compute). At this point, we should probably lidar the whole planet and let the agents discover the rest. If you don't know how lidar works, copy and paste this prompt into your favorite AI tool: "Build an HTML page that explains how lidar works, with beautiful visualizations." ↩

(903 points, 332 comments on Hacker News)

title: Apple has new Mac app coming to make running local AI models easy
abstract:
Leaker Aaron Perris has discovered evidence of a new Mac app in the works at Apple called Harbor, which makes it easy to run local AI models across one or more Macs. New ‘Harbor’ app revealed at Apple: ‘turns your Mac into a private AI inference server’ The Mac has been getting a lot more popular this year, both because of budget-friendly options like MacBook Neo but also as a tool for running AI models locally on Mac Studio, Mac mini, and more. It seems Apple plans to lean harder into the latter use case, as leaker Aaron Perris has discovered a new Mac app called Harbor that’s been designed to turn your Mac into a private AI inference server. Here’s Perris’s post on X with the details: Apple is working on a new app called Harbor Harbor turns your Mac into a private AI inference server. Run open-weight models locally on Apple silicon—your data never leaves your hardware, and nothing reaches the cloud. Connect multiple Mac computers over Thunderbolt 5 to pool… pic.twitter.com/UYJBQeX4Nf — Aaron (@aaronp613) November 10, 2026 As the post notes, here’s what the app does: Harbor turns your Mac into a private AI inference server. Run open-weight models locally on Apple silicon—your data never leaves your hardware, and nothing reaches the cloud. Connect multiple Mac computers over Thunderbolt 5 to pool unified memory, enabling large models and higher concurrency that a single computer can handle alone. And here are the feature highlights: Setup in minutes, not hours : “Harbor automatically detects your devices over Thunderbolt 5 to form a cluster. Plug in, start, and you’re running—no manual configuration, no command line, no infrastructure expertise required.” Download and run models directly : “Browse, download, and load open-weight models from within the app. Harbor handles model management so you can focus on the work, not the setup.” Cluster for scale : “Connect two or more Thunderbolt 5-capable Mac computers and Harbor pools their unified memory into a single inference resource. Run models that exceed any single computer’s capacity, or serve more concurrent requests across your cluster.” Harbor is currently in a private preview under Apple’s Claris brand, but it seems likely that we’ll see it launch to the public in the weeks and months ahead. title: AI is becoming an information gateway. Audiences still don’t want it making news
abstract:
All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites. Nearly there — check your email. We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder. An average of 24% of respondents across nine countries said they’d seen a label noting that content was made with AI in the last week, and 20% had seen a bullet-point AI news summary. In my Nieman Lab prediction this time last year, I wrote that “in 2026, the use of AI as an information gateway will only rise further.” As it turns out, I was right. In new research that I published with my colleagues Rasmus Kleis Nielsen and Richard Fletcher, one of our many findings is that generative AI systems are becoming ever more significant information intermediaries, both when intentionally used and when incidentally encountered. For our new report, “Generative AI and News Report 2026: From Standalone Tools to Information Infrastructure,” we surveyed audiences across nine countries, including the United States, on their use of AI in their everyday lives, what they think its impact will be on different sectors of society, and what they think about its use in news and journalism specifically. I obviously think you should read the whole report, but here are some of the major takeaways. The use of standalone conversational AI systems such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini continues to grow rapidly, with 51% of respondents across the six countries where we have past data saying they now use AI weekly (49% in the U.S.). That’s a faster spread, at least in the U.S., than smartphones or the internet saw. Many people also encounter AI through “incidental” AI exposure in the AI-infused services and platforms they’re already using. Search engines such as Google and Bing are key drivers: 57% of respondents across countries said they saw or engaged with AI-generated answers or summaries in the last week. News media, too, drives AI exposure. An average of 24% of respondents across nine countries said they’d seen a label noting that content was made with AI in the last week, and 20% had seen a bullet-point AI news summary. Despite all the talk about AI agents, we find that, so far, they haven’t broken into the mainstream. The vast majority of respondents across all nine countries (67%) said they had not used an AI agent in the last week. Fourteen percent used one for a real task and 13% tried one just to experiment. Our data provides solid evidence that a broader transformation of the information environment is afoot. Conversational AI systems have arrived as information intermediaries. Trust is not the main reason people use them. Instead, people see conversational AI systems as friction-reducing machines that get them information more quickly. “Getting information” continues to be the most common use case. Thirty-eight percent of respondents across countries (35% in the U.S.) said they had used generative AI for getting information in the last week, up from 24% in 2025 and 11% in 2024. We looked more closely at what people do when they say they use AI for getting information. Across the six countries we’ve surveyed since 2024, we primarily see a mixture of search-equivalent behaviors like “researching a topic” (24%) or “answering factual questions” (18%). People are also increasingly turning to AI for advice (20%). Using AI directly for news, meanwhile, remains a niche activity, as we demonstrated in the Digital News Report earlier this year . But that use is increasing: 9% of respondents across our six core countries say they use AI for news, up from 6% in 2025 and 3% in 2024. Many people don’t hold clear or strong views about whether AI output is trustworthy. But people who do rely on it for information trust it. Across the nine countries, 75% of those who used AI to answer factual questions trusted the answers, as did 76% of those who used it for advice and 72% of those who used it for news. Only small minorities expressed distrust. At the same time, trust and trustworthiness do not, at this stage, seem to be central to why people rely on AI systems. Instead, people tend to see these systems as friction-reducing machines. The convenience of getting a faster and easier answer was chosen by 64% as the main reason they use AI, followed by the interactivity afforded by natural language interfaces (56%). Only a minority (21%) said they use AI because they get more reliable information from it than from other sources. As AI systems become widely used, their growing popularity is likely to affect the use of legacy content offerings and digital platforms and services. As my coauthor Rasmus Kleis Nielsen put it on LinkedIn, rapid growth in AI use isn’t just eating into what news sites have to offer. It’s eating into search, too — with people who use AI for information saying they use not just news, but search engines less, too, and by a wider margin. Challenging times may be ahead not just for news publishers, but also for the incumbent digital giants previously seen as unassailable. As in previous years, we wanted to know what people think of AI’s use in journalism and news. We find that people’s attitudes here are remarkably entrenched and negative — though they also haven’t worsened significantly. People across countries remain uncomfortable with the use of AI in the newsroom, especially with the idea of news being made entirely or primarily with AI. On average across nine countries, just 12% of respondents say they are very or somewhat comfortable with news made entirely by AI. That figure rises to 19% if there is some human oversight. This has hardly changed since 2024, and the gap between human- and AI-made news appears in every country we surveyed. This also remains true regardless of whether it is breaking news or reporting. People are even more uncomfortable with AI being used for commentary or opinion — formats where the expectation that a human should share their view is strongest. Our findings raise several important questions for journalists and publishers navigating the rise of generative AI. First, generative AI is becoming an increasingly significant information intermediaries, with a number of possible knock-on effects on news. People are using AI to reduce friction by getting “good enough” outputs for some information needs — and skipping legacy platforms, established publishers, and the time and effort it takes to find the best available information. Discovery, brand attribution, data collection, and monetization all grow more challenging for publishers in this context. Second, even though use continues to grow, the public remains skeptical of AI in news. This isn’t just a challenge for newsrooms’ internal adoption. It also shows that publishers using AI need to communicate to audiences what’s in it for them. Third, beyond news, our findings speak to wider debates about AI’s societal impact. As in other studies on this topic, we find that uptake of AI is uneven. Weekly use is more common among people in professional occupations than those in entry-level or service occupations. Most people rely on free — usually less advanced — AI models. The differences in how — not just whether — people use AI may become a new dividing line. As AI researcher and OpenAI cofounder Andrej Karpathy recently argued , there is a widening “gap in shared understanding of LLM capability,” with most people not seeing what has left those inside AI firms both excited and worried. Expectations of what AI will do differ far more between daily users and people who have never used it than between any other groups in our survey. When two groups form very different views of the same technology because they have such different starting points, there will likely be consequences.

(57 points, 77 comments on Hacker News)

title: LLMs Play Zachtronics' TIS-100
abstract:
Twelve nodes. Two registers per node. Fifteen lines of code. In TIS-100 , even multiplying two numbers is a small engineering project, and players have spent a decade optimizing these programs on a public community leaderboard . We gave 16 LLMs the game and its manual, withheld the leaderboard, and told them to keep improving. 133 new frontier points 18 / 55 puzzles with new frontier points 3 outright cycle records Within days, players picked up the models’ programs and improved on most of them. Watch the launch video. Each node is a tiny processor, and neighboring nodes have to wait for one another to exchange values. The game scores a working solution on cycles, nodes, and instructions , and you start wondering whether one more instruction could disappear. Lower is better, but improving one score can make another worse, so each puzzle has a frontier of tradeoffs instead of one best answer. Leaderboard We ran 16 LLMs, covering leading frontier and open-weight models. Every model attempted all 47 puzzles in the game, plus eight community tournament puzzles , in one scored attempt each (pass@1), with 10 to 45 minutes per puzzle, depending on difficulty, to find a working program and keep improving it. Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra lead, and the data doesn’t separate them. Both solved all 55 puzzles and both found new frontier points on 11 . Opus 5.5 found more points, 72 to 32 , while GPT-6 Astra has the higher record proximity, 78.0 to 77.2 . Record proximity measures closeness to the community records, where 100 means matching them. The proximity gap’s 95% bootstrap interval includes zero, from −0.7 to +2.4 points. GPT-6 Astra also leads in all six tested hypervolume settings, which measure the space covered by each model’s tradeoffs. Solving and optimizing are also different skills. Gemini 3.8 Flash solved 53 puzzles and found new points on 1; Fable 5.1 solved fewer, 52, and found new points on 5. Full rankings Expand the table TIS-100 benchmark model rankings. Select column headings to sort. Model ↕ Solved (pass@1) ↕ Puzzles with new points ↓ Record proximity ↕ 01 Opus 5.5 55 / 55 11 77.2 02 GPT-6 Astra 55 / 55 11 78.0 03 Gemini 4 Argon 54 / 55 8 76.2 04 Sonnet 5.5 53 / 55 7 69.9 05 GPT-6.1 Sol 54 / 55 6 75.6 06 Fable 5.1 52 / 55 5 70.2 07 Kimi K3.1 Pro 52 / 55 2 64.6 08 Gemini 3.8 Flash 53 / 55 1 66.0 09 Muse Wonder 1.0 49 / 55 1 58.8 10 Haiku 5.5 45 / 55 1 53.7 11 GLM-5.3 30 / 55 1 35.5 12 Grok 4.7 44 / 55 0 50.1 13 DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 40 / 55 0 46.8 14 Muse Spark 1.3 39 / 55 0 45.1 15 GPT-6 Luna 39 / 55 0 42.8 16 MiMo-V2.6-Pro 10 / 55 0 12.8 Counts are out of 55 puzzles. Methods RL environments & traces are available upon request for research teams. Get in touch ↗ How it works: harness design Every result here is a program we can run and test on fresh inputs, which makes a programming game a useful benchmark. Models get what a player can inspect, through text tools instead of a mouse and screenshots: the manual, visible test inputs, registers, and game feedback. They don’t get community code or exact records, only the game’s coarse score histograms. Read, edit, run Models read the puzzle and language reference, edit programs, and run them in the real game. Diagnostics Wrong outputs and deadlocks return mismatches, registers, and blocked ports, so the next edit can respond to evidence. Saved progress Every passing program joins the model’s own frontier and can be recovered with get_best , so a risky edit can’t lose an earlier result. Reminders If a model ends its turn early, a reminder asks it to keep testing, so quitting early doesn’t decide the score. Reminders contain no solution hints. A visible clock Models see time used against a 10-, 30-, or 45-minute limit. Setup doesn’t count; thinking and game calls do. Models can’t end an episode early. Run limits Game execution stops after roughly 1 second without state changes, 5 seconds without output, or 60 seconds overall, and returns diagnostics. Why test 100,000 inputs? The game checks a small set of cases per run. Our headline count requires a fresh-game replay and 100,000 passing tests on the independent TIS-100-CXX simulator , providing stronger evidence that a program generalizes to new inputs. One record up close Undecimal Twin Rounder SPEC44149538 , one of the eight tournament puzzles, rounds an input to the nearest multiple of N on one output and of 11−N on the other. When we froze the leaderboard, the best community program took 2,694 cycles . Opus 5.5 passed its first program after 6.5 minutes, at 5,669 cycles. It went under the record 16 minutes in and finished at 1,918 , which is 29% faster . That speed cost one more node and 28 more instructions than the old record. The core of the program is a two-speed search. Instead of subtracting N one step at a time, nodes 5 and 6 subtract 4N until they overshoot, then add N back until the value turns positive. Each drives a small coprocessor, node 2 or node 7, by sending it jump offsets through a port, so the coprocessor works as a lookup table for 4N and N. title: Show HN: Yogurt – Free, private, open-source alternative to Granola
abstract: Hey HN, I’m Eric and I want to share an OSS project that I’ve been building in my free time. Yogurt is a free, MIT licensed desktop app that uses on-device AI models to transcribe, summarize, and chat with your meetings. Here's a quick demo video:  https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BFfbXAwRq98  Similar to Granola, Yogurt runs in the background and does not join your calls. But unlike Granola, Yogurt is open-source, free to use, and private. Your meeting transcripts, call recordings, and summaries never leave your computer. As small OSS models have gotten faster and more powerful, Yogurt seemed like a pretty obvious win for privacy and cost conscious folks. You do not need a frontier model to summarize meeting notes or answer questions about them. And if you want to make your notes available to a frontier model, you can just share it with Anthropic, OpenAI, etc. directly via Yogurt’s local MCP server. There’s no need to use a paid cloud service as a middleman. I tried some of the most popular OSS note taking tools, and most were missing features like calendar integration, MCP server, etc. or required you to connect or create an account. And more than that, they didn’t feel polished enough for it to be something I actually wanted to use daily, and so I built Yogurt to scratch that itch. I spent a lot of time fine-tuning every UI interaction/animation and optimizing the model calls to get the most out of your hardware + make it snappy. To support Windows/Mac/Linux, I decided to go with Electron. I use whisper.cpp for transcription and Apple’s on-device SpeechAnalyzer if your system supports it. For call summaries and questions, I use a local open weight LLM that automatically gets downloaded and set up based on what your hardware can handle without your cooling fans firing off like crazy (this part uses llama.cpp). I’ve spent a lot of time working on details like echo detection/reduction, global/folder/local level search respectively, and auto-end recordings. Hope this is useful for any of you who have held out on using AI note tools for privacy or cost reasons, or for folks using cloud tools who want to switch to something free and open source that still feels great to use. Would love to hear what you think about the onboarding and note taking experience :)

title: Show HN: Black Ops II statically recompiled to native ARM64 macOS
abstract: I grew up with Black Ops 2 and wanted to see if I could make it work on my 2020 MacBook Pro. So I used Claude Opus 5.5 to create a tool that converts your copy of the game (from Steam) to a native ARM64 Mac app, with almost 60fps in all areas. The whole game is statically recompilated ahead-of-time (AOT) and does not use any emulator whatsoever, be it Wine, Crossover or Rosetta. The best thing is the performance, although some heat issues are still to fix. You get to play the whole Campaign, local Multiplayer (with bots) and local Zombies (all DLCs maps; you need to have them in your Steam library obviously) at about 60fps. Split-screen was not in the PC version, but I've been working on it lately; it's coming soon! LAN mode is on the roadmap for later too :)

title: Show HN: Get your coding agent off ~2019 JavaScript, onto modern web primitives
abstract:
Browsers natively handle a lot of what used to take 50 lines of JS (or a dependency): `CSS.highlights` for text range highlighting without <span>s everywhere, `<dialog>` and showModal() give you backdrops and ideal focus management, `field-sizing` to auto-grow textareas as the user types.. (Something yesterday's ftrain post touched on [0]) Models know about some of these by name, but consistently won't default to using the platform-native solution and instead prefer the incumbent <div>+JS based pattern.  We started an effort in Chrome to supplement coding agents with this key domain knowledge and we're shipping our 1.0 today, in collaboration with Firefox, MDN, and Edge. 200+ guides (~1.7MB) of curated, hand-crafted implementation best-practices from web experts, updated as the web evolves.  (Open source, obv, so.. we'll welcome your bikeshedding ;) Readable versions here: [1] I've spent the last 9 months obsessing over how to ship this as an agent skill + (Agentic RAG) CLI without blowing up your context window. (Or cedeing activation mechanics to MCP dynamic tool search). The skill description is minmaxed for activating on relevant frontend tasks. The RAG work I'm pretty proud of… originally a 500mb native stack down to a ~7MB pure-JS package, ~10ms search on your CPU. We just introduced a deterministic 'legacy-scan' (trained on 30k github repos) to identify old 'n dusted patterns that your agent can modernize. (92% avg precision on held-out repos.) People make a lot of claims about what coding agents are good/bad at. We wanted receipts, so we invested heavily in eval infra [2] to help us hill-climb, but also to identify when knowledge is common enough we can prune our guides. (Ofc, some of the things we thought AI didn't know turned out to be wrong :)  We run codex/claude/agy against 200 tasks without the skill and then with.. In total ~1,700 playwright/AST-based assertions. Agents go from 55% pass unguided to 92% guided. Try it out:       DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 npx modern-web-guidance@latest install
    DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 npx modern-web-guidance@latest search "animate dialog modal"
    DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 npx modern-web-guidance@latest legacy-scan ./src
  
If you spot something wrong or weird, give us a holler! Longer write-up on the 1.0:   https://developer.chrome.com/blog/modern-web-guidance-v1  --- 0:  https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50416456  1:  https://developer.chrome.com/docs/modern-web-guidance/guides  2:  https://googlechrome.github.io/modern-web-guidance-src/

title: Protecting SSH Keys with macOS Secure Enclave
abstract:
Update, November 11, 2026: I’ve since switched to Secretive , which keeps keys in the Secure Enclave with a much better prompt. Part 2 is coming. I’ve also corrected one error, marked below. I’ve been paranoid about my SSH keys for a while now. They just sit there in ~/.ssh/ , protected by nothing but file permissions. Any malicious script that gets access to my filesystem could just copy them and get into all my servers.
Also, there have been many stories out there online about fake interview assignments that asked to clone a repo and run it on your local machine.
This is one of the reasons I switched completely to using devcontainers, but even that was not really enough for me (and it shouldn’t be enough for you or anybody else really). So I finally decided to do something about it. TL;DR I have decided to NOT go with the native macOS Secure Enclave approach (using only out-of-the-box tools) because it ended up plain ugly and I can’t live with that. However, it is a fully functional, working solution that I would definitely use otherwise. The Options After some research, I found several ways to protect SSH keys: Native macOS Secure Enclave — no third-party apps, built into the OS Secretive — third-party app that stores keys in Secure Enclave YubiKey — hardware security key with FIDO2 support 1Password / Bitwarden — store keys in an encrypted vault, use their SSH agent I already use 1Password, but I might switch to something else in the future. Bitwarden recently added SSH key support (even on the free tier!), but it’s still a software solution — the keys are encrypted at rest but decrypted in memory when used. What I really wanted was hardware-backed security. The private key should literally be impossible to extract, even if my Mac is fully compromised. That left me with YubiKey or Secure Enclave. I have a YubiKey 5C, but I wanted to try the native approach first — no extra hardware to carry around, no third-party apps to maintain. What is Secure Enclave SSH? Since macOS Sequoia (and Tahoe), macOS supports SSH keys backed by the Secure Enclave, a security subsystem on the Mac’s chip that is isolated from the main processor. The private key is created inside it and never leaves. When you SSH somewhere, your Mac asks the Secure Enclave to sign the authentication challenge. If you enable Touch ID, you have to approve each signing operation. The actual private key never exists in memory or on disk. The workflow is surprisingly similar to regular SSH keys: Aspect Regular SSH Key Secure Enclave Key Where private key lives ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 (a file) Secure Enclave What’s on disk Actual private key Just a reference (useless without this Mac) Setup on remote server Copy public key to authorized_keys Same Connecting Just works Touch ID prompt, then works Setting It Up Step 1: Create the Secure Enclave Key macOS provides the sc_auth command (Smart Card Authentication) to manage CryptoTokenKit identities. Despite the name, it works with Secure Enclave too. sc_auth create-ctk-identity -l "ssh-MacBook" -k p-256-ne -t bio Breaking this down: -l "ssh-MacBook" — a label for your reference (only visible locally) -k p-256-ne — NIST P-256 curve, n on- e xportable (the key can never leave Secure Enclave) -t bio — require bio metric (Touch ID) for every use You’ll be prompted for Touch ID to create the key. Problem 1: Touch ID Error When I first ran this command, I got a scary error: Error: Error Domain=NSOSStatusErrorDomain Code=-25293 "Failed to generate keypair"
(errKCAuthFailed / errSecAuthFailed: / Authorization/Authentication failed.)
UserInfo={..., NSUnderlyingError=... "Failed to get bio catacomb UUID for user 502." ...} Turns out my Touch ID enrollment got reset somehow. After re-enrolling my fingerprint in System Settings → Touch ID & Password , the command worked fine. You can verify the key was created: sc_auth list-ctk-identities Output: Key Type Public Key Hash Prot Label Common Name Valid To Valid
p-256-ne A71277F0BC5825A7B3576D014F31282A866EF3BC bio ssh-MacBook ssh-MacBook 2027-01-26, 10:18 YES Step 2: Export the Key Handle Now we need to create a “key handle” file that SSH can use. This is NOT the private key — it’s just a reference that tells SSH “go ask the Secure Enclave to sign this.” ssh-keygen -w /usr/lib/ssh-keychain.dylib -K -N "" When prompted for PIN, just press Enter (it’s not used for biometric keys). Touch ID will pop up. This creates id_ecdsa_sk_rk and id_ecdsa_sk_rk.pub in your current directory. Move them to your SSH directory: mv id_ecdsa_sk_rk* ~/.ssh/ Step 3: Configure SSH to Use the Secure Enclave Provider Add this to your ~/.zshrc (or ~/.bashrc ): export SSH_SK_PROVIDER = /usr/lib/ssh-keychain.dylib Reload your shell: source ~/.zshrc Problem 2: Outdated Commands Everywhere If you search for “macOS Secure Enclave SSH” online, you’ll find a lot of guides telling you to run ssh-add -K . Don’t. It’s deprecated: WARNING: The -K and -A flags are deprecated and have been replaced by the --apple-use-keychain and --apple-load-keychain flags, respectively. And even the new flags don’t work for Secure Enclave keys — they’re for the traditional macOS Keychain, not CryptoTokenKit. The SSH_SK_PROVIDER environment variable is the correct approach. Step 4: Get Your Public Key cat ~/.ssh/id_ecdsa_sk_rk.pub Output: sk-ecdsa-sha2-nistp256@openssh.com AAAAInNrLWVjZHNhLXNoYTIt... ssh: That ssh: at the end is the comment. The key’s FIDO2 application ID is stored inside the key itself (the last field of the base64 part). ssh-keygen -K copies it into the comment, so the line shows it twice. You can replace the comment with anything when copying to authorized_keys ; the key stays the same: sk-ecdsa-sha2-nistp256@openssh.com AAAAInNrLWVjZHNhLXNoYTIt... macbook-secure-enclave Correction, November 11, 2026: An earlier version said the trailing ssh: was the FIDO2 application ID. It’s the comment; the application ID is stored inside the key. Thanks to computerfriend on Hacker News for pointing it out. Step 5: Copy to Your Server ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ecdsa_sk_rk.pub user@your-server Or manually paste the public key (with your comment) into ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the server. Step 6: Configure ~/.ssh/config Problem 3: SSH Doesn’t Find the Key After setting everything up, I tried to SSH… and it asked for my password. The verbose output ( ssh -vvv ) showed SSH was only trying my old RSA key: debug1: Offering public key: /Users/sergii/.ssh/id_rsa RSA SHA256:... The problem: SSH doesn’t automatically look for files named id_ecdsa_sk_rk . It only auto-discovers standard names like id_rsa , id_ed25519 , id_ecdsa . The fix is to explicitly add it to your ~/.ssh/config : Host * IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ecdsa_sk_rk IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_rsa IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 SSH tries identity files in order, so put the Secure Enclave key first if you want it to be the default. ⚠️ Note: If you’re using 1Password’s SSH agent ( IdentityAgent ), it might conflict with this setup. I had to comment it out while testing. Step 7: Test It ssh user@your-server You should get a Touch ID prompt, then connect. The Ugly Touch ID Prompt Touch ID prompt One thing I’m not thrilled about: the Touch ID dialog says “ctccardtoken needs to authenticate to continue” instead of something friendly like “SSH wants to use your key.” This is because the prompt comes from CryptoTokenKit — a low-level framework that Apple hasn’t polished for end-user SSH. If this bothers you, Secretive provides a much nicer UI while still using Secure Enclave under the hood. Why Touch ID for Everything? I initially thought about creating two keys — one with Touch ID for “important” servers, one without for convenience (like Git operations). But then I realized: without -t bio , malware could use my key silently. With -t bio , I always know when something is using my SSH key. A few extra taps per day is a small price for that visibility.

title: Greg Kurtzer's Ginux is now a userspace kernel
abstract:
Ginux Ginux is a configurable userspace kernel for isolated Linux compatibility
instances. It runs as an ordinary Linux process and places an explicit,
versioned contract between managed workloads and the host kernel. Important Ginux began as an independent Rust kernel that booted directly through UEFI
and ran a Rocky Linux 10 userspace. That research phase is complete. Its
final source is permanently preserved on the bootable-kernel branch and at the bootable-kernel-final tag. Active development now continues here as a userspace kernel. Why the project changed direction The standalone-kernel experiment proved that an AI coding agent, directed by
an experienced human through architecture, gates, and executable tests, could
construct a new kernel capable of running meaningful Linux userspace. It also
made the limits of that result obvious. Linux is much more than source code. It is a stable interface, a development
process, a global community, vendor and hardware alignment, and decades of
compatibility and operational experience. Reimplementing kernel mechanisms
does not reproduce that ecosystem, and competing with Linux was never the
goal. The more useful result is the boundary the experiment exposed. Linux must
preserve a broad userspace ABI; as Linus Torvalds put it, “And we simply do
not break user space.” The kernel regression documentation records that rule. Ginux can sit above Linux and deliberately offer a smaller
contract to each managed instance. Before a managed syscall has a host effect,
Ginux decides whether to emulate it, perform a validated mediated operation,
or deny it. Put bluntly: Linux must not break userspace; Ginux is designed to break the
full Linux ABI guarantee deliberately and selectively. A instance receives
only the capabilities and interface behavior its approved workload requires.
Every departure is intended to be explicit, versioned, reviewable, and tested,
rather than accidental incompatibility. This pivot is also a result of the development method. AI made it practical to
build disposable but executable prototype code, test an architectural idea,
learn from the running system, and carry the valuable parts into a better
design. The prototype was evidence, not an obligation to turn every experiment
into a product. What Ginux is now Host Linux kernel `- host systemd (real PID 1) `- ginux (ordinary trusted host process) `- instance contract |- virtual processes and identities |- virtual descriptors and kernel views |- assigned devices and resources `- managed Rocky Linux userspace `- instance systemd (virtual PID 1) Ginux supervises native x86-64 programs and intercepts managed syscalls before
their host effect. Its central dispatcher resolves the instance contract and
chooses one of three outcomes: Emulate: answer entirely from Ginux-owned state. Mediate: validate and translate the request, then perform a narrow
Ginux-owned host operation. Deny: return a configured Linux-compatible error or terminate the task. The current implementation includes: a security-focused x86-64 interpreter and a balanced native ptrace backend; strict, versioned instance configuration and lifecycle; a digest-pinned OCI root, immutable filesystem index, and bounded overlay; Ginux-owned process, credential, signal, synchronization, timer, and event
models; virtual devices with explicit assignment, ownership, and revocation; and bounded virtual /proc , /sys , cgroup v2, mount, namespace, machine, and
boot-identity views; a host-shared network backend that remains syscall-mediated; and a pinned Rocky Linux 10 systemd baseline that reaches multi-user.target ,
authenticates a managed console login, updates through Rocky's enabled
repositories, and shuts the instance down cleanly. This is a named compatibility baseline, not a claim of complete Linux or
systemd compatibility. Its exact image, readiness marker, tests, evidence, and
limitations are recorded in hdae/gates-done/9-systemd-baseline.md . Agent containment research Ginux is also being tested as a containment boundary for AI agents and other
automated software that can execute commands, modify files, open network
connections, and start additional processes. Instead of giving an agent the
host's complete Linux ABI, an operator can place its process tree inside a
instance whose kernel contract exposes only the operations and virtual resources
required for the task. The research goal is a reviewable boundary spanning syscalls, ioctls,
filesystems, devices, networking, process authority, and virtual /proc and /sys state. For example, a contract may allow an agent to read time, inspect
its own processes, and modify one assigned workspace while denying clock
changes, host filesystem access, unapproved network listeners, and unrelated
devices. Ginux can then audit the contract decisions made while the agent and
its child processes run. This is an active verification target, not a claim that Ginux is currently a
production-grade agent sandbox. The contract inventory, configurable policy,
adversarial tests, performance costs, and escape boundaries are tracked through
the HDAE gates and must be demonstrated before stronger containment claims are
made. Relationship to other systems The userspace-kernel idea is established research and engineering territory.
Ginux explores a particular point in that design space: Approach Primary boundary Difference in emphasis Linux seccomp Filters host syscalls Restricts the existing ABI rather than defining a complete virtual contract User-Mode Linux Runs Linux as a host process Reuses a complete Linux kernel over virtual hardware gVisor Implements an application kernel in userspace Closely related model with different compatibility and performance goals Gramine Packages applications with a library OS Uses manifests and a library-OS boundary Proxos Routes calls between private and commodity OSes Makes trust placement configurable across the syscall interface Ginux Gives each instance a versioned kernel contract Treats the declared contract, virtual state, devices, resources, and lifecycle as one reviewable boundary Ginux does not promise the complete Linux ABI. Compatibility claims apply
only to named contracts, workloads, and executable evidence. Development and testing The reference development environment is macOS arm64. QEMU TCG boots a pinned
Rocky Linux 10 x86-64 host where Ginux runs as an ordinary unprivileged
process. The host systemd remains real PID 1. Check prerequisites: make doctor Prepare the pinned assets with explicit network operations: make host-image-fetch
make image-helper-fetch
make instance-image-fetch
make systemd-image-fetch Build and run the deterministic suite offline after the caches are populated: make build
make check
make test Inspect the latest completed capability directly: make test-systemd # cached image, external networking disabled make test-multi-instance # two concurrent Rocky systemd instances and isolation make bench-prepare # one-time networked setup for the pinned benchmark image make bench # matched native/Ginux matrix plus mandatory budget checks make bench-modes-prepare # one-time setup for the three-way dispatch comparison make bench-modes # native/selective/paranoid tables and graphs make demo-gate-15 # bounded reproducible three-way comparison make demo-gate-17 # operator-readable concurrent-instance isolation check make test-systemd-live # shared network plus real upstream dnf -y update make host-run # general interactive Rocky host with Ginux installed make host-reset # discard that host's cache, instances, and writable state make demo-gate-9 # Gate 9 checkpoint through the same host workflow Instance recipes select syscall control under [contract.syscalls] : [ contract .

title: Physically Controllable Relighting of Photographs
abstract:
Physically Controllable Relighting of Photographs Chris Careaga Yağız Aksoy Proc. SIGGRAPH, 2025 Patent pending We present a photograph relighting method that enables explicit control over light sources akin to CG pipelines. Users can insert different types of light sources, such as spot lights, point lights, or environmental illumination into the scene. We achieve this in a pipeline involving mid-level computer vision, physically-based rendering, and neural rendering. We introduce a self-supervised training methodology using differentiable rendering to train our neural renderer with real-world photograph collections for in-the-wild generalization. Abstract We present a self-supervised approach to in-the-wild image relighting that enables fully controllable, physically based illumination editing.
We achieve this by combining the physical accuracy of traditional rendering with the photorealistic appearance made possible by neural rendering.
Our pipeline works by inferring a colored mesh representation of a given scene using monocular estimates of geometry and intrinsic components.
This representation allows users to define their desired illumination configuration in 3D. The scene under the new lighting can then be rendered using a path-tracing engine.
We send this approximate rendering of the scene through a feed-forward neural renderer to predict the final photorealistic relighting result.
We develop a differentiable rendering process to reconstruct in-the-wild scene illumination, enabling self-supervised training of our neural renderer on raw image collections.
Our method represents a significant step in bringing the explicit physical control over lights available in typical 3D computer graphics tools, such as Blender, to in-the-wild relighting. Poster BibTeX @INPROCEEDINGS{careagaRelighting, author={Chris Careaga and Ya\u{g}{\i}z Aksoy}, title={Physically Controllable Relighting of Photographs}, booktitle={Proc. SIGGRAPH}, year={2025}, } License The methodology presented in this work is safeguarded under intellectual property protection. For inquiries regarding licensing opportunities, kindly reach out to SFU Technology Licensing Office <tlo_dir ατ sfu δøτ ca> and Dr. Yağız Aksoy <yagiz ατ sfu δøτ ca>. Related Publications Colorful Diffuse Intrinsic Image Decomposition in the Wild Chris Careaga and Yağız Aksoy ACM Transactions on Graphics (Proc. SIGGRAPH Asia), 2024 Best Paper Award Honorable Mention Abstract Intrinsic image decomposition aims to separate the surface reflectance and the effects from the illumination given a single photograph. Due to the complexity of the problem, most prior works assume a single-color illumination and a Lambertian world, which limits their use in illumination-aware image editing applications. In this work, we separate an input image into its diffuse albedo, colorful diffuse shading, and specular residual components. We arrive at our result by gradually removing first the single-color illumination and then the Lambertian-world assumptions. We show that by dividing the problem into easier sub-problems, in-the-wild colorful diffuse shading estimation can be achieved despite the limited ground-truth datasets. Our extended intrinsic model enables illumination-aware analysis of photographs and can be used for image editing applications such as specularity removal and per-pixel white balancing. Manuscript & more BibTeX @ARTICLE{careagaColorful, author={Chris Careaga and Ya\u{g}{\i}z Aksoy}, title={Colorful Diffuse Intrinsic Image Decomposition in the Wild}, journal={ACM Trans. Graph.}, year={2024}, volume = {43}, number = {6}, articleno = {178}, numpages = {12}, } Intrinsic Image Decomposition via Ordinal Shading Chris Careaga and Yağız Aksoy ACM Transactions on Graphics, 2023 Abstract Intrinsic decomposition is a fundamental mid-level vision problem that plays a crucial role in various inverse rendering and computational photography pipelines. Generating highly accurate intrinsic decompositions is an inherently under-constrained task that requires precisely estimating continuous-valued shading and albedo. In this work, we achieve high-resolution intrinsic decomposition by breaking the problem into two parts. First, we present a dense ordinal shading formulation using a shift- and scale-invariant loss in order to estimate ordinal shading cues without restricting the predictions to obey the intrinsic model. We then combine low- and high-resolution ordinal estimations using a second network to generate a shading estimate with both global coherency and local details. We encourage the model to learn an accurate decomposition by computing losses on the estimated shading as well as the albedo implied by the intrinsic model. We develop a straightforward method for generating dense pseudo ground truth using our models predictions and multi-illumination data, enabling generalization to in-the-wild imagery. We present exhaustive qualitative and quantitative analysis of our predicted intrinsic components against state-of-the-art methods. Finally, we demonstrate the real-world applicability of our estimations by performing otherwise difficult editing tasks such as recoloring and relighting. Manuscript & more BibTeX @ARTICLE{careagaIntrinsic, author={Chris Careaga and Ya\u{g}{\i}z Aksoy}, title={Intrinsic Image Decomposition via Ordinal Shading}, journal={ACM Trans. Graph.}, year={2023}, volume = {43}, number = {1}, articleno = {12}, numpages = {24}, } Intrinsic Harmonization for Illumination-Aware Compositing Chris Careaga , S. Mahdi H. Miangoleh , and Yağız Aksoy SIGGRAPH Asia, 2023 Abstract Despite significant advancements in network-based image harmonization techniques, there still exists a domain disparity between typical training pairs and real-world composites encountered during inference. Most existing methods are trained to reverse global edits made on segmented image regions, which fail to accurately capture the lighting inconsistencies between the foreground and background found in composited images. In this work, we introduce a self-supervised illumination harmonization approach formulated in the intrinsic image domain. First, we estimate a simple global lighting model from mid-level vision representations to generate a rough shading for the foreground region. A network then refines this inferred shading to generate a harmonious re-shading that aligns with the background scene. In order to match the color appearance of the foreground and background, we utilize ideas from prior harmonization approaches to perform parameterized image edits in the albedo domain. To validate the effectiveness of our approach, we present results from challenging real-world composites and conduct a user study to objectively measure the enhanced realism achieved compared to state-of-the-art harmonization methods. title: $30M Raised to Redo the CPU
abstract:
$30M Raised to Redo the CPU As of today, Tendrils has completed a $30M round led by Benchmark to rebuild general-purpose computing. Contemporary CPUs are made under the constraint of backwards compatibility with sequential, single-core chips. Accumulated layers of historical designs are locking engineers into decisions dating back to the 1970s. As a result, all existing CPUs are bottlenecked by complex cache coherency protocols and elaborate reorder buffers. CPU scaling is sabotaged from the start. At Tendrils, we believe that the future of general-purpose computing lies beyond legacy architectures for legacy software. Tendrils is answering the question: what if we redo the CPU? Instead of starting from a sequential design, we’re building our processor to have thousands of cores operating in parallel. This requires moving beyond the notion of shared mutable memory and linear instruction sequences. To make this possible, we’re working in tandem on the open-source language Vine , which has been designed from the beginning to target a new wave of parallel-first architectures. We’re delighted to announce that Tendrils has raised $30 million to support this vision. This round is led by Benchmark, with significant participation from Visionaries Club, the UK Sovereign AI Fund, FR8, Antimatter, Cloudberry VC, Conviction, Embassy Ventures, and SV Angels. We are grateful for additional support provided by all of our angel investors. Additionally, we wish to extend a warm welcome to our newest board member, Jack Altman. With thanks to all who have supported us, The Tendrils Team At Tendrils, we insist that the chips of the future will be a result of close collaboration between hardware and software engineers. If this strikes you, consider joining us .

title: An Open Field Guide to Inference Engineering
abstract:
