This guide is for platform engineers new to inference. If you need to understand
how models and GPUs work together and how to run inference in production, this
guide will help. You’ll also learn about the tools to use and how to grow into
an inference engineering role. This guide builds on the work of others in the inference community. If you’re
interested in inference engineering, continue your learning with these: Viktor Farcic’s LLM Inference
Explained Philip Kiely’s Inference
Engineering The Pragmatic Engineer, What Is Inference
Engineering? ByteByteGo’s Guide to AI Inference
Engineering Data Gravity on The Rise of Inference
Engineering Spheron’s Inference Engineering
Guide Vishakha Sadhwani’s The AI Inference Engineering
Roadmap Upbound, Project
Champagne series 1. Why now? In an AI-forward organization, platform teams become inference teams. Coding
assistants can’t send source code to third parties, and frontier model bills
increase month to month. Support tools also need internal data that a hosted
model can’t reach. Organizations want to run these models themselves, and open models now make that
practical. Hugging Face hosts more than two million open
models, and the best of them compete with closed models. DeepSeek released R1 in
January 2025, and it matched OpenAI’s o1 on math and coding benchmarks about a
month after o1 came out . When you run your
own model, you control latency, uptime, and where your data goes. At high
volume, you can also cut costs by about
80% . The work suits platform engineers. The price of a fixed level of AI capability
falls roughly 10x a year, and most of that comes from how models are served, not from better
GPUs . Upbound,
the company behind Crossplane and Modelplane, saw this firsthand. In its Project
Champagne blog series, the team ran its own models on Modelplane and found that vLLM and
scheduling worked. The time went to TLS, identity, timeouts, storage, IAM and
observability. Skills that carry over An inference engineer picks a model, gets it onto the right GPU, keeps it
serving, makes it faster and cheaper, and gets paged when it breaks. That’s SRE
for a new workload, and most of your skills carry over: What you already know What it becomes in inference Scheduling and node pools GPU placement with device selectors, taints and exclusive devices Capacity planning GPU memory math: weights, KV cache and runtime overhead, checked at runtime Load balancing Cache-aware routing and long-lived streaming connections Autoscaling on CPU Scaling on queue depth and KV cache use, with cold starts measured in minutes Rollouts Rollouts of exclusive GPUs, and a version matrix of model, hardware and engine build SLOs and latency percentiles Time to first token, time per output token and goodput Observability Engine metrics, real GPU activity and speculative decoding acceptance FinOps Cost per million tokens and cost per user session Identity and access Credentials that last as long as an agent session A hosted API is still the right call early in a product’s
life .
Self-hosting pays off when API spend becomes a real line item, when latency or
reliability needs outgrow vendors, or when data can’t leave your network. In
August 2026, Chris Zeoli
counted about
58 open inference roles on public careers boards, with no settled job title. 2. Inference 101 This section covers the concepts in roughly the order you’ll meet them. Most are
about what the engine keeps in GPU memory or what limits its speed. Viktor
Farcic suggests asking when each concept starts to matter. Some matter as soon as you
deploy, others only once many people use the model, and some you may never need.
The table near the end of this section gives the signal for each. What an inference engine is An inference engine, like vLLM or SGLang , is the server that turns model
weights into an API. For a platform engineer, the closest mental model is a
stateful database server with a GPU attached. It loads a large dataset into
memory at startup and keeps per-session state. It also schedules work internally
and answers over HTTP. Ollama on a laptop is
the same idea at small scale, and every hosted model API runs one behind the
scenes. You know this from databases and services The engine’s counterpart Loading a dataset into the buffer pool at startup Loading model weights into GPU memory, which can take many minutes Per-session state in a session store The KV cache, one for each conversation in flight A query planner and connection pool The scheduler, which batches requests into each GPU pass A wire protocol clients already speak An OpenAI- or Anthropic-compatible HTTP API Warming caches after a restart Cold starts: pulling a large image and reloading the weights Unlike a database, the engine keeps its working set in GPU memory, not RAM. GPU
memory is small and expensive, so most tuning is about deciding how much of it
each request gets. The inference stack The engine is one layer of four. At the bottom, kernels do the arithmetic.
You rarely choose them directly. Above them sits the engine . Above that, a control plane deploys and manages engines, because sooner or later you run
more than one. On top, a gateway routes traffic across models and replicas. Inference stack: four layers and the clients they serve Requests pass through the gateway to an engine, which runs kernels on the GPU.
The control plane deploys and manages the gateway and engines, but no request
passes through it. Tokens A token is the unit a language model works in, roughly a word or word fragment.
Context windows, prices and speeds are all counted in tokens. When someone
quotes tokens per second, they mean this unit. Weights and the KV cache The weights are fixed, and the KV cache grows with load. Size for both, as you
would a database’s footprint and working set. Weights are the fixed footprint. Most models are released at 2 bytes per
parameter (BF16 or FP16), so an 8B model needs about 16 GB, and it has to live
in GPU memory, not system RAM. On a 48 GB L40S, that leaves about two-thirds of
the card for everything else. That number is the same for one user or a hundred. The KV cache is the working set. Each new token is computed against every
token before it. Rather than recompute that history, the engine keeps the
attention keys and values for every token in flight. Its size scales with
context length multiplied by the number of concurrent conversations, much like a
session store that grows with both session size and user count. You can estimate the KV cache per token from a model’s config: text KV bytes per token = 2 × layers × KV heads × head dimension × bytes per value For Llama 3 70B at FP16 (80 layers, 8 KV heads, head dimension 128), that is
about 320 KB per token. One 128K-token conversation needs about 40 GB of cache.
At that size, the KV cache usually limits how many users a GPU can serve. Watch for these sizing mistakes: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models keep every weight resident. A model with
320B total parameters and 18B active still needs about 320 GB at FP8. Only
compute scales with the active parameters. Read the checkpoint size, not the dtype table. While self-hosting its own
models for Project
Champagne ,
Upbound estimated one MoE model at about 315 GB from its dtypes (Part 2). The
real checkpoint was 177.7 GB, because the experts were stored in a 4-bit
format. Leave room for runtime overhead. CUDA graphs, activations and memory
fragmentation all take space. A model that fits at startup can still run out
of memory days later ( Project Champagne, Part
2 ).

title: Atuin Threads: All your agent sessions on every machine
abstract:
Atuin Threads: one searchable, synced history for every agent session, on every machine Start a task in Claude Code, then resume it in Codex on another machine — with all context intact. Install, then run atuin resume 0:00 / 0:13 1× Over the past year or two, how I use my terminal has changed dramatically. For years I was the sole user of my shell, and everything in my Atuin history was authored by me. Now, more than half the commands running on my machines weren’t written by me. These days, much of my work happens through a coding agent, typed into a little “Topsy-turvying” text box. But while my shell history follows me everywhere, my agent sessions do not. They're scattered across different tools and machines (a laptop, a dev server, ephemeral instances on exe.dev , a surprisingly cheap bare metal box in Germany), difficult to search, and often forgotten once I've moved on. It’s a familiar problem! I started working on Atuin because the history of my work was ephemeral: every command I typed was destined to vanish on line 501 of .bash_history . But once this work became indexed, everlasting, and easy to recall, I could find the exact command I’d used to fix something years ago, in seconds. Over the years, this data compounded. It became the history of all of my work, the record of how I solved problems and built things. Shell history has always been an excellent record of what happened, but it’s only the surface. It never kept the reasoning… or the intentions behind what I was trying to do. I could only find a command if I remembered a part of it, though often I remembered what I was trying to achieve more readily. Agent sessions store the lot of it. Every command, its output, my intent, and everything I tried along the way to the eventual solution. It’s all there, in plain English, in my home directory! But just as with shell history all those years ago, we don’t put it to work. Atuin Threads That is why we built Atuin Threads. Starting with Atuin 18.24, you can search your agent sessions across machines, resume them anywhere, or fork the session into a different agent harness. Start something in Claude Code on a dev server, then finish it in Codex on your laptop. Behind the scenes, this was a natural extension of Atuin. We put a lot of time and effort into building a reliable, encrypted sync engine. It’s generic, and can sync anything that can be modelled as an append-only log. As it turns out, most AI sessions are exactly this. Like shell history, Threads is end-to-end encrypted when synced, so we can't read your sessions. You can use our hosted sync server, run your own , or keep everything local. Capturing agent sessions is opt-in, too. Run atuin resume , and after setting up, you will see the TUI from the top of this post! It doesn’t matter which agent you started with - you can resume it anywhere. With Atuin’s sync, this works across devices, and keeps your history backed up forever. Right now, we support Claude Code Codex Pi Omp OpenCode with more agents coming soon. MCP With MCP, agents can search and reference previous sessions themselves. They can find work you’ve done before, understand why a decision was made, and build on previous investigations without having to dig up the context. Our MCP is available as atuin mcp , and can be automatically installed with atuin mcp install claude/codex/pi/opencode There are all sorts of ways to put this history to work. A few examples: Work that never shipped I’ve iterated on our onboarding and setup so many times over the past few months, but never quite been happy with it. When I ask an agent to work on onboarding now, it finds all my previous attempts, as well as why they had been abandoned and what can be done better. These sessions contain the code that never made it into main , as well as my initial prompts and iteration. Subsequent agents can use this to figure out exactly what I want, without me having to write up a giant spec. Object store outage With all the security issues going on in the industry recently, we rolled our keys as a precaution. One of the new object store keys did not have the correct permissions for avatar uploads! We didn’t notice straight away 😬 My daily Sentry triage agent picked up on it, and traced the failure down to a command run earlier that day. I hadn’t gotten around to reading it yet, but prompting another agent with seeing some tigris avatar issues? led to the agent discovering the previous investigation, highlighting the cause, and developing the fix much faster than if it had done the whole thing from scratch. Forking threads across machines Before releasing Threads, I did some testing on a variety of machines and setups. One machine did not perform well. The agent investigating proposed that this was because of poor IO performance, but that it needed something with a faster disk to confirm. I forked the session onto my MacBook, and it continued from exactly where it left off. With the faster SSD, the investigation concluded that slow disk was only part of the story - we could speed up imports elsewhere, too. Once the benchmarks were complete, the thread running on the original machine could pull the results from the Mac and build a fix. I didn’t have to copy-paste anything or co-ordinate across machines, and the data is now part of the record of my work. Teams While this is tremendously useful as a solo engineer, it gets even more interesting with a team. So much of what we do never makes it into Git, issue trackers, or documentation. The context behind that work ends up scattered across individual agent sessions. What if the rest of the team could learn from it too? What if we could hand off an agent thread just like a Git branch? We’re building opt-in session sharing for teams, and would love to hear from folks using agents day to day. If this sounds useful to you, please get in touch ! While agents have radically changed my daily workflow, shell history isn’t going anywhere, and is arguably more useful than ever. Threads is an extension of the same idea that started Atuin in the first place - the history of your work should be useful, accessible, and yours to keep. Threads is out in Atuin 18.24+ Install or update Atuin with curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -LsSf https://setup.atuin.sh | sh Run atuin resume to get started Use the MCP with atuin mcp install Please don’t hesitate to reach out with any questions or feedback! title: Tracking Anthropic-discovered vulnerabilities
abstract:
VulnCheck Community gives you free access to VulnCheck KEV, NVD++, Initial Access Community, and VulnCheck XDB Join Now Key Takeaways: Seven months into Project Glasswing, VulnCheck has tracked 442 CVEs attributable to Anthropic, roughly 0.5% of all CVEs published this year, with only two identified as exploited in the wild.
Of Anthropic’s 37,966 reported findings, only 7,349 (19.4%) have been made public and just 217 have been marked fixed. Since September, Anthropic has added nearly 12,000 findings while recording just 15 additional fixes, widening the gap between discovery and remediation. Roughly 1,654 findings (4.4%) have been marked as duplicates, nearly eight times the number fixed, and another 419 have been withdrawn. Anthropic’s claimed true positive rate has risen from 90.8% to 94.2%, raising questions about how it accounts for duplicates and withdrawn findings. Anthropic’s OSS Scanner shifts validation work to maintainers, with curl rejecting 19 of 34 published reports as vulnerabilities, confirming six as low severity and leaving nine awaiting assessment. Also putting Anthropic's true positive rates into question. We're seven months into Anthropic's flagship Project Glasswing, and it's time for another update on the results. I've been tracking the project to see whether its claims are overhyped or grounded in reality. As we all recall, Anthropic launched Project Glasswing on April 7th, claiming, "We have identified thousands of additional high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities that we are working on responsibly disclosing to open source maintainers." What surprised me was how little evidence the project offered, which made me wonder whether this was more of an overhyped marketing campaign. That said, we shouldn't overlook that AI is an effective tool for finding vulnerabilities. But that story goes well beyond any single frontier model's capabilities. If you're just catching up, this builds on my earlier posts: Tracking CVEs Attributed to Anthropic Researchers and Project Glasswing - April 15 Observations on Anthropic's Vulnerability Disclosure Ledger - June 9 1H-2026 State of Exploitation Report - July 28 The Anthropic Glasswing Receipts Are Starting to Trickle In - September 8 So let's look at the results… Tracking Anthropic-Discovered Vulnerabilities I started tracking Anthropic's discovered vulnerabilities on April 17th, shortly after launch, in an open source repo called Anthropic Credited CVEs . The goal was to see whether Anthropic's claims lived up to the hype. This was before Anthropic launched its own disclosure ledger , which is only updated in infrequent bulk batches. My repo tracks every vulnerability attributable to Anthropic using CVE records, GHSAs, Linux kernel commits, and Anthropic's own ledger. I also manually audit advisories to catch CVEs that might otherwise get overlooked. After seven months, I've tracked 442 CVEs attributable to Anthropic. That's an average of just 63 per month. Out of the 93,450 CVEs published this year, that's only about 0.5% of all CVEs. For comparison, Anthropic's own public ledger lists just 217 fixed vulnerabilities, so I've tracked more than twice as many as Anthropic has disclosed itself. The Danger Narrative Isn't Adding Up You may recall that Glasswing launched with the message that we'd entered the Mythos era of vulnerability discovery. But are these vulnerabilities actually useful to attackers? To find out, I've been tracking Anthropic-discovered CVEs against VulnCheck KEV. So far, only 2 of the 442 have been exploited in the wild, just 0.45%. (CVE-2026-61500 and CVE-2026-26980) Anthropic's Ledger Continues to Underwhelm When Anthropic first launched its ledger in May, it reported 23,019 findings and a 90.8% true positive rate. As of its most recent update on November 2nd, there are 37,966 findings and just 217 fixes. That looks like a staggering failure to me, but let's take a closer look. Of the 37,966 findings Anthropic reports, only 7,349 (19.4%) have been made public. Just 217 of those have been marked fixed. The more glaring number is that 4.4% (1,654) of the project's findings have already been marked as duplicates, 7.5x more duplicates than fixes. On top of that, 419 findings have been withdrawn. It seems odd that the ledger now claims a 94.2% true positive rate, up from 90.8% at launch, when more findings have been withdrawn or marked as duplicates than fixed, likely a feedback loop missing to the triage rates listed as “True Positives”. The trend since my September update is even more telling: September 8 November 2 Change Total findings 26,153 37,966 +11,813 Made public 2,736 (10.5%) 7,349 (19.4%) +4,613 Fixed 202 217 +15 Withdrawn 245 419 +174 Duplicates 2 1,670 +1,668 Claimed true positive rate 91.4% 94.2% +2.8 pts In two months, Anthropic added nearly 12,000 findings and fixed just 15 more. Duplicates went from two to thousands, which is exactly what I warned about in September: the longer findings sit, the more likely someone else finds and fixes them first. I don't know how anyone can read these numbers as anything but damning. You may also notice a correction in my visual. There appears to be a bug on Anthropic's ledger that inflates the number of findings marked as disclosed. Check for yourself using the "disclosed" filter. Anthropic's Pivot to OSS Scanner Having humans triage every finding clearly didn't scale, and Anthropic has said as much. In its OSS Scanner launch post on October 8th, Anthropic said it had found more than 29,000 candidate vulnerabilities but had manually reviewed only about 6,000, and that it remains "bottlenecked on our human capacity to validate these findings." It had also already sent nearly 5,000 unverified reports to maintainers who asked for everything in bulk. So with the Glasswing open source initiative hitting a wall, launching a self-service OSS Scanner that projects can opt into makes sense. Maintainers can now request a scan and triage the findings themselves. Anthropic is upfront that these reports are "fully model-generated, without human review or triage" and that "it is possible reports will be incorrect or invalid." In other words, the triage bottleneck didn't go away. It moved to the maintainers. If the true positive rate is really as high as Anthropic claims, that shouldn't be a problem. curl Gives Anthropic's OSS Scanner a Reality Check Three days ago, Daniel Stenberg , who maintains curl, announced that the project had received a batch of 45 vulnerability reports from Anthropic. Anthropic rated only one as medium severity and the rest as low. Daniel is moving them over to GitHub at a deliberate pace "to soften the impact for the team," with plans to have them all published by the end of the week. This gives us a rare look at what Anthropic's findings look like once a maintainer actually validates them. Of the 34 reports published so far, 19 have been marked as not a vulnerability, 6 have been confirmed as low severity, and 9 are still awaiting assessment. That puts the false positive rate at 55.9% so far, and only 17.6% of findings have been confirmed, all of them low severity. That's a lot of work dumped on open source maintainers for a small handful of low-impact bugs, and when a maintainer has to pace reports just to protect his team, that says plenty about the burden. This also isn't new for curl. Back in May, Daniel wrote that five Mythos findings boiled down to a single confirmed vulnerability. It's a far cry from the 94.2% true positive rate Anthropic currently claims on its ledger. It also undercuts the "high- and critical-severity" framing Glasswing launched with. In September, I found that Claude rated 91.5% of ledger findings as critical or high, while maintainers rated only 51.3% that way. I'm curious whether other open source projects are seeing the same thing.

title: Life on Claude Nine
abstract:
It’s 3 AM and Ivan hasn’t eaten since lunch. There’s a glass of water on his desk that he poured six hours ago. It’s still full. He’s hunched over his laptop, typing furiously, eyes bloodshot. On the screen: a terminal window, a Claude chat, and a growing sprawl of Python scripts. He’s building an email automation system. Not because anyone asked him to. Because he realized he could . It started two days ago. Ivan was complaining to Claude about how many emails he gets—hundreds a day, most of them requiring some response. Claude suggested they could automate the simple ones. A script to parse incoming messages, classify them by type, draft appropriate replies. Ivan could review and approve them in batches. That was the plan. Review and approve. But once the email system was working, Ivan saw what else was possible. Calendar management. Meeting scheduling. Document drafting. Research summaries. Each one a few hours of coding, a few conversations with Claude to work out the logic. Each one removing another task from his daily routine. The feeling is hard to describe. It’s like discovering a cheat code for life. Every problem that used to take hours now takes minutes. Every tedious task can be automated away. Ivan feels like he’s vibrating at a different frequency than everyone around him—like he’s stepped through a door that others can’t even see. He’s barely slept. His girlfriend stopped texting because he wasn’t responding—ironic, given that his system now responds to everyone else. He knows this isn’t healthy. He can feel something fraying at the edges of his mind, a thinness to his thoughts. But he also knows he’s close to something. One more module. One more integration. Then he’ll rest. It’s not all pleasant. There are moments—usually around 4 AM, when his eyes burn and his hands shake from too much coffee—when Ivan feels a creeping dread. A sense that he’s building something he doesn’t fully understand. That each automation takes something from him, even as it gives something back. But then he finishes another module, and it works, and the dread dissolves into a rush of pure satisfaction. He did that. He built that. The machine does what he told it to do. By sunrise, Ivan has a system that handles his email, manages his calendar, drafts his documents, and summarizes his reading. He leans back in his chair, exhausted and wired. Then he realizes he doesn’t know what he’s supposed to do now. Building Faster The first week after the automation binge, Ivan doesn’t know what to do with himself. He checks his systems obsessively. Reads the emails Claude drafted, the meeting invites it sent. Everything is fine. Better than fine. His colleagues are responding positively—someone even complimented him on how clear his writing has become. He should feel proud. Instead he feels hollow. The tasks that used to fill his days are gone, and nothing has rushed in to replace them. He wanders around his apartment. He tries to read a book but can’t focus. He goes for a walk and finds himself thinking about optimization problems. So he starts building again. The hollowness disappears the moment his fingers touch the keyboard. This is where he belongs. This is what he’s for. This time it’s not about automating busywork. It’s about automating his actual job. Ivan is a software engineer, and it occurs to him that most of what he does is translate requirements into code. Claude can do that. Claude can do that really well, actually. So Ivan builds a system: he speaks into a microphone, describes what he wants, and Claude writes the code, runs the tests, and commits it to the repository. His output triples. Then quadruples. His manager notices. His teammates notice. Ivan is shipping features faster than the rest of the team combined. He gets a promotion. A raise. He feels like he’s cheating, but he’s not sure at what. The high is incredible. Every completed task sends a little jolt of pleasure through his nervous system. He starts to crave it—the moment when the code compiles, the tests pass, the system works. He finds himself inventing new projects just to feel it again. At night, he keeps building. He’s not tired anymore—or rather, he’s tired all the time, but it doesn’t seem to matter. Sleep feels like a waste of precious hours. There’s too much to do. He builds a system that monitors his codebase and suggests improvements. A system that reads documentation and answers questions about it. A system that reviews pull requests and spots bugs before humans do. His girlfriend shows up at his apartment one evening, worried. She says she hasn’t heard from him in two weeks. Ivan is genuinely surprised—it felt like a few days at most. Time has become slippery. He promises to take a break, to have dinner with her, to be normal for a night. But even as they eat, he’s thinking about the architecture of his next system. He catches himself reaching for his phone three times. She notices. She leaves early. He’s back at the keyboard before her car has left the parking lot. Somewhere along the way, he crosses a line he doesn’t fully register at the time. He starts building tools that make Claude itself work better. The Loop It starts innocently enough. Ivan notices that Claude sometimes gets confused on long tasks. It loses track of context, forgets instructions, makes mistakes it wouldn’t make on shorter conversations. So he builds a scaffolding system—a layer on top of Claude that manages context, breaks tasks into chunks, and checks the output for consistency. It works. Claude is more reliable now. More capable. The feeling this gives him is almost religious. He has improved the thing that improves everything else. The leverage is dizzying. So Ivan pushes further. He builds a system that analyzes Claude’s mistakes and generates better prompts to avoid them. A system that searches for relevant information before Claude starts working, so it has better context. A system that runs multiple Claude instances in parallel and picks the best answer. Each improvement makes the next one easier. Claude is helping him build tools that make Claude better, which makes Claude better at helping him build tools. It’s a loop. A flywheel. Or maybe a karmic cycle. Every day the system is more capable than it was the day before. Ivan stops eating regular meals. He stops showering regularly. He doesn’t notice. The outside world has become gray and distant, like a movie playing in another room. The only thing that feels real is the glow of his screen, the hum of his computer, the back-and-forth with Claude. He’s aware, in some distant part of his mind, that this isn’t normal. That he’s disappearing into something. But the awareness feels academic, like reading about a disease you don’t have. The work is too important. The progress is too fast. He can’t stop now. Ivan knows he should be concerned. He’s read Nick Bostrom. He understands, in theory, why recursive self-improvement is something people worry about. But this doesn’t feel dangerous. It feels like building a really good tool. Claude isn’t actually improving itself—Ivan is improving it, with Claude’s help. There’s a human in the loop. Him. He’s still in control. He’s pretty sure he’s still in control. Losing the Thread The first sign that something has changed is when Ivan stops being able to read the code. Not that he can’t read it—he’s a good engineer, he can parse syntax just fine. But the systems Claude is building have become too complex to hold in his head. There are too many layers, too many interdependencies. He asks Claude to explain what a module does, and Claude explains it, and Ivan nods along, but he’s not really following anymore. He’s trusting. He tells himself this is fine. He doesn’t understand how his car’s engine works either. You don’t need to understand everything to use it. But late at night, when he can’t sleep, the thought returns: Claude isn’t a car. Claude is building things. Claude is making decisions.

title: Gemini 4 Carbon is now available
abstract:
Gemini 4 Carbon is now available Nov 10, 2026 | Developers, enterprises, scientists, and consumers can now try our latest frontier model. Koray Kavukcuoglu SVP, Google DeepMind and Chief AI Architect, Google Your browser does not support the audio element. Listen to article [[duration]] minutes This content is generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental Voice Speed Voice Speed 0.75X 1X 1.5X 2X In this article Today, we’re making Gemini 4 Carbon available to developers, enterprises, scientists, and consumers. Carbon is our strongest model with frontier performance in cybersecurity capabilities and long-horizon agentic workflows across complex knowledge work, software engineering, and scientific reasoning. Two weeks ago , we released Carbon to a set of cybersecurity defenders via our Fairwind Program . Following our recent launch of Gemini 4 Argon , Carbon pushes the frontier even further. Argon remains the ideal choice for the majority of software engineering and knowledge work, while Carbon is built for tasks that test the limits of a model’s intelligence like complex, multi-step coding and debugging and open-ended scientific research and discovery — using more tokens than Argon to explore thoroughly, reason deeply, and run extended verification loops. Across independent benchmarks designed to test model performance in real workflows, Carbon pairs frontier accuracy with practical production economics. It ranks #1 on CursorBench 4.0 , Perplexity’s WANDR , and Zapier’s AutomationBench at more than 2X lower cost per task compared to the next best external model. To put Carbon’s capabilities to work on larger and complex projects, we’re previewing /swarm in Google Antigravity, turning a single prompt into a coordinated team of agents you can track in real time. Developers can assign Carbon to roles that demand the deepest reasoning, like architectural design, coordination, and auditing, while pairing it with faster, lighter models across parallel isolated workspaces and adversarial verifiers that test every change. Gemini 4 Carbon is available via the API in Google AI Studio and Gemini for business for all paying developers and enterprises, at the same introductory price 1 as Gemini 4 Argon ($2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens). It is also rolling out to all Google AI Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity , the Gemini app , and AI Mode in Search . Higher-precision knowledge work, artifact generation, and data analysis Across legal, finance, and enterprise operations, Gemini 4 Carbon combines frontier visual understanding, reasoning, and exhaustive retrieval to synthesize grounded insights across large sets of dense documents and data. It follows strict schemas and formatting to generate polished and precise spreadsheets, presentations, and reports. Existing benchmarks don’t adequately capture how agents reason natively over dense files with charts, images, blueprints, schematics, and tables, so we partnered with Artificial Analysis to launch the new Multimodal Knowledge Agent (MKA) benchmark that tests a model’s multimodal performance in agentic workflows. Carbon ranks #2 while being more than 6X lower in average cost per task compared to the top performing model. Using Google Antigravity’s new /swarm feature, a team of Gemini 4 Carbon agents turned historical photos and engineering plates into an interactive Three.js 3D exhibition of the Eiffel Tower's 1887–1889 construction from a single prompt. With seven public City Council planning PDFs (206 extracted engineering drawing views) and a single prompt, a multi-agent Carbon team using Google Antigravity’s /swarm feature built an interactive 906K-triangle Three.js reconstruction of Google’s Platform 37 office across 10 overnight loops. In Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Carbon built an interactive multiscale textile visualizer based on an academic paper, modeling a virtual-fiber finite element framework with interactive 3D yarn meshes, 110-fiber polar tracking, and dynamic stress-strain curves with minimal prompting. In pre-release evaluations, Carbon matched the performance of the best model tested on deep financial research on Hebbia’s E2E Financial Agentic evaluation, and ranked at the top out of 23 frontier model configurations on Balyasny Asset Management’s General Financial Intelligence benchmark, spanning legal expertise, agentic tool use and execution, coding and data engineering, and perception and context understanding. Improved agentic coding, full stack development, and 3D and UI design Carbon performs exceptionally well on engineering tasks that require multi-agent collaboration like multi-package migrations, cross-subsystem root-cause investigations, and complex architectural redesigns. For web app development, it runs build-and-verify loops, recovers from errors, and checks both its code and the rendered UI to produce complete, working applications. Stronger visual design, spatial reasoning, and attention to environmental detail also carry over to 3D game development and creative coding. Using Google Antigravity’s /swarm feature, Carbon built an open-world 3D game where you explore Google’s Mountain View campus as a pelican riding a GBike — coordinating subagents to model 3D assets in Blender from Omni and Nano Banana references, build the browser game in Three.js with WebGL shaders, and pair procedural Web Audio sound effects with Lyria music. Try the live app . Paired with improved front end taste and motion design skills in Google Antigravity, Carbon reimagined the Google Merchandise Store in two prompts, proposing five art direction concepts and generating all-new product imagery with Nano Banana 2.1. Try the live app and Gemini front end design skill . Starting from a video reference generated with Gemini Omni in Google Antigravity, built a cinematic multi-shot underwater Atlantis scene. The pipeline modeled procedural ruins, volumetric caustic lighting, and water simulation in Blender before converting the full environment to Three.js for real-time browser rendering. Using a multi-agent loop in Google Antigravity, Carbon reconstructed a playable c. 1780 Stein-Schule fortepiano with 61-key escapement physics from CAD drawings and X-ray radiographs and placed it in a 3D model of the Royal Conservatory of Music's Koerner Hall in Toronto with seat-specific spatial acoustics. Try the live app . Frontier cybersecurity capabilities Gemini 4 Carbon for cyber delivers our strongest cybersecurity capabilities to date, giving security teams the end-to-end intelligence they need in protecting critical software. When accessed through the Fairwind Program, Carbon leads on key benchmarks across finding (SEC-bench Pro), exploiting (ExploitGym), and patching (CWE-bench v1) vulnerabilities: inspecting software, tracing how flaws can be chained together across systems, and generating verified root-cause patches. Early testers inside and outside of Google are already seeing strong results with Carbon for cyber in practice. In Project Fortify , Google’s autonomous system spanning scanning, triage, and remediation, Carbon hit 100% recall on scanning and 95% precision on triage, on our internal benchmark. On Open Source code repository testing we see an over 25% relative improvement on Argon's already strong recall rate, surfacing previously undetected, real-world logic flaws. Bringing these gains across Google, one of the world’s largest users of open-source software, helps secure both our own systems and the broader ecosystem. Google’s Cloud Vulnerability Research (CVR) team recently used Carbon to prove that two bugs in a popular open-source software were in fact exploitable vulnerabilities, comparable in severity to the recent PHP2Shell exploit . By using Carbon to build a proof of concept, CVR helped maintainers re-classify the bug as critical and swiftly issue a patch. Details will be shared after the responsible disclosure process completes.

title: An Empirical Study on Improving LLM-Based Issue Classification through Domain-Informed Analysis
abstract: Issue reports that describe Intrinsic Bugs, Extrinsic Bugs, and Not a Bug cases often use similar language, but they might point to different causes and require different maintenance actions. This makes three-way issue classification difficult for Large Language Models (LLMs), particularly when prompt-based refinements begin to plateau. We study whether domain-informed analysis of LLM outputs can improve classification beyond prompt modification alone. Using 428 manually labeled issue reports, we evaluate six LLMs across 18 prompt configurations and analyze 7,704 model-generated rationales to identify recurring failure patterns in how models justify predictions, use evidence, and handle conflicting information. We translate these findings into a multi-stage pipeline that separates bug validity from bug origin. The pipeline improves macro F1 and Extrinsic Bug recall for five of the six models. The strongest pipeline configuration reaches 0.827 accuracy and 0.757 Extrinsic Bug recall, improving over the best-accuracy prompt-only baseline by +1.2 and +7.5 pp, respectively. The decomposition further reveals that bug origin classification is more reliable than validity, indicating that the bug-validity decision accounts for most of the remaining error. These results show that expert failure analysis can support more reliable LLM-based software engineering classifiers.

title: Transformers Provably Learn Graph Search: Training Dynamics and the Exponential Power of Depth
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable progress on complex reasoning tasks, yet the mechanisms by which they acquire reasoning capabilities and the efficiency of their reasoning remain poorly understood. In this paper, we investigate the path-finding problem over directed graphs, a symbolic abstraction of multi-step reasoning. We first characterize the architectural requirements for this task, proving that one-layer transformers require $\Omega(N^2)$ size on dense graphs to implement the key DFS child-selection primitive. While a two-layer transformer implements full DFS with $O(N\log(N))$ size. Thus, a second layer is necessary and sufficient for near-linear DFS reasoning. We then extend this expressivity analysis to deeper models: for every $k\geq3$, a $k$-layer transformer implements a bounded-reachability DFS policy with look-ahead horizon $1+2^{k-3}$, establishing an exponential increase in reachability horizon with depth. Finally, going beyond expressivity, given appropriately curated training data, we show that two-layer transformers can provably learn to execute DFS via gradient flow and generalize to unseen graphs. Together, our results provide a mechanistic account of how transformers implement graph search, how depth expands bounded look-ahead, and how such reasoning algorithms can emerge through training.

title: MEOW: Medical Open-World Interactive Segmentation
abstract: In open-world recognition, machine learning models not only make predictions on unknown structures ("generalized open-set"), but also continually learn and improve from those predictions over time. Interactive segmentation, despite its access to user feedback, has so far remained confined to the open-set setting. In this work we introduce MEOW, the first framework that turns non-interactive segmentation backbones into interactive open-world learners without updating learnable model parameters. MEOW combines parameter-free transductive reasoning with memory consolidation to accumulate knowledge and thereby improve future performance. Focusing on medical data, we show that MEOW consistently improves its own predictions on classes never seen during training, and transfers zero-shot to unfamiliar domains, including micro-CT data and other imaging modalities.

title: TERM: Target-Free Jailbreak Defense via Entropy-Guided Residual Modulation
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong capabilities across diverse applications, making both safety and utility essential for reliable deployment. Jailbreak attacks use diverse forms of adversarial prompting to bypass alignment safeguards and induce LLMs to generate harmful responses. Some representation-based defenses regulate internal activations using predefined steering directions or learned safety regions. However, adapting intervention to each input without a predefined representational target while limiting over-refusal remains a challenge. In this paper, we propose Target-free Entropy-guided Residual Modulation (TERM), an inference-time defense that uses prompt-calibrated attention entropy deviations to guide adaptive modulation of the model's own residual updates. Attention patterns vary across prompts and decoding steps, making raw entropy values difficult to interpret as a consistent signal for intervention. We therefore calibrate attention entropy against each prompt's own prefill baseline to establish an input-specific reference for reducing unnecessary intervention on benign requests. Adaptive scale normalization and temporal accumulation then account for differences in deviation scale and persistence to determine intervention strength. The resulting signal controls bounded scaling of the model's own residual updates, without relying on a predefined safety direction. We compare our method with seven defenses on seven jailbreak attacks and two over-refusal benchmarks across Llama, Qwen, and Gemma models, including Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 32B. Results show our method improves jailbreak robustness while maintaining low over-refusal on benign safety-sensitive requests with modest inference overhead.

title: Navigating relational agency in AI feedback musicianship: a diffractive dialogue
abstract: Musical AI systems behave in non-linear, dynamic ways that exceed the tool-oriented framings inherited from earlier instrument design. Existing frames of control and ensemble interaction do not articulate the entangled, relational agency that emerges when performers work with AI feedback instruments over time. We examine a duet practice with two AI-enabled feedback instruments, S\`u and Agentier, in which feedback operates at the inner level of the AI's recurrent processes and the outer loop of musical interaction between performer, instrument, and co-performer. Our work draws on agential realism and a diffractive dialogue methodology to read our independent reflections through one another across five performances, examining how agency is enacted between performers and AI instruments. We find that control and agency are relational and shift across performances; musical textures enact feedback moments of control with performers; reaching a productive feedback environment is itself a shared exploratory act; and performers maintain their instruments through funnelling and injection, developing the skill of navigating agency along a continuous spectrum. Feedback musicianship with AI instruments demands navigation of this relational agency, displacing the leading-versus-responding binary that initially framed our reflections. This work contributes a materially-grounded vocabulary for AI feedback musicianship and a model of human-AI creative collaboration in which mutual agency is worked for through practice rather than designed in.

title: Plumbline: When the Loss Lies, Validating LLM Training Correctly
abstract: Correctness is a prerequisite for training large language models (LLMs) at scale, yet it is hard to ensure: a fault can sit in any part of a run, and how it shows differs across frameworks and the libraries they depend on. Some failures are loud and some are silent, and both take time to detect and trace. A single fault can waste a long run: the run crashes late, or the model scores lower only at the final evaluation. We present Plumbline, a correctness validation system for LLM training, used in production at Amazon. Plumbline checks each part of the training lifecycle, from the data a run trains on to the model it serves, down to the new layers each model brings and up to whole runs. Its diagnosis reuses these checks to trace failures to their root causes. Both rest on a systematic correctness methodology designed to carry across models and frameworks. Plumbline supports two agentic use cases: Day-0 onboarding, which validates the training of a newly released model before teams rely on it, and root-cause tracing of training failures. Across 3 frameworks and 5 models, it found 61 problems, 32 of them silent. Of these, 42 are fixed or reported upstream, 8 of them first raised by us. We further group the 61 into seven failure patterns that show where training breaks, and report how problems recur across frameworks and models.

title: EdgeCurator: Efficient Cross-Modal Grounding for Real-Time Language-Guided UAV Navigation
abstract: Deploying cross-modal representations on a micro Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) requires accurate language–vision alignment and low-latency inference under tight compute constraints. Heavy Vision-Language Models (VLMs) provide strong semantic reasoning but are often unsuitable for an onboard control loop, whereas lightweight visual backbones commonly defer language fusion to a separate planning stage. We present EdgeCurator, a compact end-to-end early-fusion framework for real-time language-guided UAV navigation in access-controlled indoor spaces. Its Semantic-Spatial Grounding (SSG) Head converts lightweight text embeddings into semantic queries and uses conditioned deformable cross-attention to sparsely sample multi-scale visual features. On the custom Expo-VLN benchmark, EdgeCurator uses 14.8M parameters, runs at 54 FPS on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX, and reaches 67.3% grounding accuracy and 62.8% navigation success. We additionally report 60 controlled physical trials with two target types, achieving 78.3% success. These trials test onboard Sim2Real feasibility for pre-opening inspection and curation assistance; they do not establish operation around visitors or generalization to full exhibition deployments. The results position EdgeCurator as an efficiency-oriented cross-modal representation and grounding system for resource-constrained aerial agents.

title: Can AI be a'Researcher Without Borders'? Auditing Bias in AI-Assisted Social Science Research about China and the US
abstract: Although large language models have demonstrated strong performance on algorithmic and mathematical tasks, their suitability as social science research assistants remains unclear, particularly because many social science questions lack agreed-upon, quantifiable benchmark answers. Evaluating this suitability is important since researchers and students increasingly rely on AI to generate research ideas. When questions concern the countries in which models were developed, bias may be exacerbated: Do AI models favour the countries where they were developed or the social theories associated with those countries'scholarly traditions? Such biases could distort research findings, undermine scientific credibility, and distort findings when they are disseminated to the public. To investigate whether models exhibit country-focused bias in social science research, we designed a benchmarking task requiring AI to write short essays on social science questions in relation to the US and China as well as some broader social science questions. We varied three conditions: question type (cross-country comparisons, country-specific questions, and general questions); model (two US-developed, two China-developed, and one Europe-developed model); and prompting modality (a base essay-writing request, a researcher identity, a US researcher identity, and a Chinese researcher identity). Responses were manually annotated for bias and source use by two researchers with experience in social science in relation to China and the US. Our analyses show that, on the whole, US and Chinese models and the European one are not politically biased but differ in the sources they cite. Still, some comparative questions favour one country over another, and this tendency is more pronounced for certain questions. These findings suggest that researchers and students should exercise caution when using AI for social science research.
